title: Edgewright
pitch: A redirect console a human and an agent drive together, over WebMCP. Test, audit and fix routing across 11 hosts, then prove a migration never breaks a link.
about_excerpt: A redirect console a human and an agent drive together, over WebMCP. Test, audit and fix routing across 11 hosts, then prove a migration never breaks a link. Like Comment Story Updates Edgewright turns your redirect and rewrite rules into a live console a human and an AI agent work together, over WebMCP. Test any URL, catch the rule that shadows another, translate a config to another host, then prove nothing breaks, all in the browser. The problem: redirect rules are ordered and first-match-wins. A broad rule above a specific one makes the specific one dead code, so a link works locally then 404s in production. Edgewright makes that visible and fixable, by a person or by an agent on the same page. How the tools are used: the console registers fifteen tools with document.modelContext.registerTool. In the demo the agent runs test_url to find the 404, audit_rules to name the shadowed rule, reorder_rule to fix the order, then test_url again. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint so the agent runs them without a prompt. The tools that change rules omit it, so the agent asks first. The UI and the tools mutate one shared store, so a human clicking a button and an agent calling a tool run the exact same code. The product is three apps on one engine: the Console, Preflight (a pre-deploy gate), and Studio (migrate a config between hosts and prove every URL still resolves). Live: https://edgewright.vercel.app Source: https://github.com/zkasuran/edgewright Video: https://youtu.be/8Hry7ozQTe8 Built for the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge. The engine, @edgewright/core, covers eleven hosting platforms grounded in their own docs, with 148 passing tests, no build and no dependencies. For platforms whose routing is code, like Fastly and CloudFront, the engine resolves the trivial static patterns and labels the rest as not-simulated rather than guessing. Everything shown in the demo is the deployed product on the live URL or a real source file. The narration is synthesised speech. The design, the code, the review and the verification are the author's. title: The Intent Horizon
pitch: An Asimov-inspired WebMCP RTS strategy game about why agentic instruction matters: bits take years to reach Alpha Centauri and Earth’s view is already old, so Daneel needs intent, not clicks.
about_excerpt: An Asimov-inspired WebMCP RTS strategy game about why agentic instruction matters: bits take years to reach Alpha Centauri and Earth’s view is already old, so Daneel needs intent, not clicks. Like Comment Story Updates Cover art Mission and Setup with webmcp Mission debrief Earth command sends build intent First mission Game home screen Inspiration WebMCP has a story problem, demos are mostly for storefronts, operating tools, reduce computer use context burn, but they don't demonstrate what its useful for beyond the base ideas as of now. With this game I thought, I would help make a demo for WebMCP as a game, to show what agentic things can achieve and help overcome even such long intent horizons and constraints such as even the speed of light. I read Foundation when I was young. I have been binge-watching the show recently, and it brought back the part of those stories that always stuck with me: people making decisions for futures they will never live to see. That feeling led to The Intent Horizon. I wanted to build a city builder where distance makes ordinary control break down. You are on Earth, managing a colony at Alpha Centauri. Every image of the colony is 4.37 years old by the time you see it. If you respond with a mouse command, that command takes another 4.37 years to arrive. A normal instruction can be perfectly reasonable and still fail. By the time it reaches the colony, the tile may be flooded, the workers may be elsewhere, or the problem may have changed completely. So Earth sends Daneel something more useful: a goal, constraints, and a little room to act. Earth sends intent: goals, constraints, and preferences. Daneel uses WebMCP tools to interpret that intent against the colony’s current reality. Keep food reserves above 24 months. Keep power above 20%. Protect the wetlands. Prefer expanding the existing agricultural district. Daneel receives that message beside the colony as it actually is, then has to decide what to do with it. The game is not a Foundation adaptation. Its influence is more personal than that. I wanted to make a small game about long horizons, delegated power, and the uneasy question underneath both: if you cannot control the future directly, what should you ask for? What it does The Intent Horizon is a city builder where Earth and a local AI steward play different roles. Earth sees an old reconstruction of the colony and decides what it values. Daneel sees the current colony and uses WebMCP tools to inspect it, build infrastructure, assign robots, manage resources, send reports, and request more authority when a decision goes beyond the original instruction. The radio channel is limited in both directions. Reports take years to return. Earth does not get a secret live feed. A local survey, construction job, or crisis stays unknown until telemetry makes the trip home. There are three missions: The First Light: Build enough life support and redundant power to survive a planned outage. The Meaning of Enough: Keep food and power reserves healthy without sacrificing protected wetlands. The Right to Decide: Export iridium while deciding how much local freedom is safe around a fragile habitat. How we built it I built the game with React, Vite, and Three.js. It is fully client-side and stores the simulation in versioned localStorage . The same deterministic simulation powers the UI and the WebMCP tools. There is no game backend, database, custom MCP server, or game-owned model API. The colony tracks delayed packets, radio bit budgets, construction jobs, robot labor, roads, power networks, food and water reserves, seeded hazards, authority requests, and mission outcomes. If Daneel builds something, it still needs materials, a connected site, available labor, and time. The WebMCP tools are game actions, not mouse clicks. Daneel can inspect the colony and resource network, read delivered mail, construct buildings, build roads, register limited policies, send reports, request authorization, yield control, and wait for the next useful event. When native WebMCP is available, the game uses it directly and makes its availability visible to the player. If WebMCP is not there, the user can still play and control the colony manually and give instructions via mouse clicks like any other RTS game. Challenges we ran into The difficult part was making the two perspectives feel honest. If Earth can see the live colony, the distance is cosmetic. If Daneel can act without limits, the player has no real role. If reports appear immediately, the game loses its tension. I had to keep drawing the line between what Earth knows, what Daneel knows, and what neither can safely assume. Earth sees only received telemetry. Daneel acts locally, but is still limited by resources, roads, workers, power, hazards, and the authority Earth has actually granted. Making the wait playable took work too. The game shows packet cost, arrival dates, transmission windows, Earth-visible events, captured dates, and receipt dates. The delay needs to be something the player can plan around, not a loading screen. Native WebMCP support also varies by client, model, account, and browser. The game checks for it and says so plainly when it is unavailable. It does not pretend that a scripted helper is a live agent. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am happiest with the fact that WebMCP is part of the game’s premise, rather than an extra feature. The human chooses the values. Daneel works inside the present reality. Both have limits. The missions gradually move away from simple execution. First, the player asks whether Daneel can carry out a local plan. Then they learn whether they can communicate a resilient policy. Finally, they have to decide what authority they are willing to give away when they will not be able to correct the outcome in time. What we learned The project changed how I think about agent tools. Giving an agent access to every button is less interesting than giving it a small set of meaningful actions with clear costs and limits. inspect_colony and construct_building are useful because they describe what is happening in the world and let the system validate the action. A generic click tool would not. It also made the human role clearer. The player is not there to out-compute the agent. They are there to decide what should not be optimized away. "Protect the wetlands" and "prefer reversible interventions" are not ordinary resource targets. They are choices about what kind of colony Earth is trying to create. What's next for The Intent Horizon I want to make the unknown parts of the colony matter more. Surveys should reveal terrain and discoveries that change the player’s understanding of the situation. Daneel’s reports should explain the tradeoffs behind a decision, not just list what was built. I also want to add more shared codebooks and doctrines, where a short phrase carries meaning because Earth and Daneel have earned that vocabulary together. The question I want to keep exploring is simple: When the future is far away and you only get a few messages, how do you say what you mean? title: ApplyFlow AI
pitch: AI-powered job application agent that uses WebMCP to find matching jobs, prepare applications, and automate form filling while keeping humans in control of final submission.
about_excerpt:
AI-powered job application agent that uses WebMCP to find matching jobs, prepare applications, and automate form filling while keeping humans in control of final submission.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Applying for jobs is repetitive and time-consuming. Finding a relevant position is only the first step — candidates still have to open different job portals, fill out the same information repeatedly, answer application questions, and deal with different workflows. 

 We wanted to build an AI agent that could help with this process while keeping the candidate in control of the final decision. 

 That led us to ApplyFlow AI — a job application agent designed around WebMCP. 

 What It Does 

 ApplyFlow AI helps users go from job discovery to a prepared application: 

 
 Find Jobs — discovers real job listings from sources such as RemoteOK and Arbeitnow. 
 Smart Matching — compares jobs with the user's resume and preferences and explains why a job is a good match. 
 Prepare Application — creates an application using the user's profile and resume information. 
 WebMCP Automation — uses WebMCP tools to interact with supported application workflows in a real browser session. 
 Human Review — stops before final submission so the user can review the completed application. 
 Approve & Submit — the final submission requires an explicit human action. 
 

 The key design principle is simple: 

 
 The agent can prepare the application, but the human controls the final submission. 
 

 How We Built It 

 The application is built around an AI-agent workflow with WebMCP as the interface between the agent and browser-based tools. 

 The system includes: 

 
 Job discovery and normalization 
 Resume/profile-based job matching 
 Match explanations 
 Application preparation 
 WebMCP tool integration 
 Browser-based form automation 
 Application state and automation tracking 
 Human approval before submission 
 Safety handling for login, MFA, and CAPTCHA situations 
 

 The Agent page provides a natural-language interface where users can give commands such as: 

 
 "Find jobs matching my profile." 
 

 or 

 
 "Prepare an application for the best match." 
 

 These requests are translated into authorized WebMCP tool calls such as get_top_matches and prepare_application . 

 The same backend authorization and application state are used by both the normal user interface and the agent workflow. 

 Human-in-the-Loop by Design 

 We intentionally did not expose the final submission action as a WebMCP tool. 

 The agent can discover a job, prepare the application, open the application page, and fill the form. 

 But when the application is ready, the workflow stops and asks the user to review it. 

 Only the user can click Approve & Submit . 

 This creates a clear boundary between AI automation and an irreversible external action. 

 Safety 

 Real job portals can require authentication, MFA, or CAPTCHA challenges. 

 ApplyFlow AI does not attempt to bypass these protections. 

 When such a step is detected, the automation pauses and explains why it stopped. The user can then handle the step directly in the real browser session. 

 This keeps the automation useful without attempting to circumvent website security controls. 

 Challenges We Faced 

 One of the biggest challenges was designing an agent that could interact with real application workflows without turning the system into an uncontrolled automation tool. 

 We had to think carefully about: 

 
 Tool authorization 
 Application state 
 Human approval boundaries 
 Form validation 
 Handling different application workflows 
 Login and CAPTCHA interruptions 
 Keeping the agent's actions observable 
 

 Another challenge was making the agent's behavior understandable. Instead of hiding tool execution, we added a WebMCP Activity panel so users can see which tools are being called and what is happening during the workflow. 

 What We Learned 

 This project taught us that building an AI agent is not only about making the model capable of taking actions. 

 The more important question is: 

 Which actions should the agent be allowed to take? 

 WebMCP provides a powerful way for agents to interact with web-based tools, but that power needs clear authorization boundaries. 

 For ApplyFlow AI, we chose to automate the repetitive work while keeping the final consequential action under human control. 

 What's Next 

 Future versions could support more job sources, richer resume customization, better application-question handling, additional WebMCP-enabled sites, and stronger application tracking. 

 Our goal is to make job applications dramatically less repetitive while keeping the candidate — not the agent — in control.

title: Tandem
pitch: A restaurant back office where an AI agent reads everything and changes nothing alone. Every write is a costed proposal that blocks until a human decides.
about_excerpt: A restaurant back office where an AI agent reads everything and changes nothing alone. Every write is a costed proposal that blocks until a human decides. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The approval card: what the agent asked for, and what the site computed it would cost. The manager's dashboard. The agent's read-only tools answer from exactly this data. The write tool has not returned — it is blocked, waiting on the decision in the rail. Every proposal and decision, attributed. Nothing changes without a line here. Inspiration Most agent integrations answer the wrong question. They ask "can the agent do this?" — and with a good enough API the answer is usually yes. The question a business actually cares about is "should it, and what does it cost?" I have spent the last year building operations software for a real restaurant chain: three branches, live orders, real money. The thing that kept me from letting an agent touch any of it was never capability. It was that a confirmation dialog saying "Change price to $16.50? [OK]" asks a human to approve something neither party has priced. The agent knows the dish and the number. It does not know that the dish is 31% of that branch's revenue, that a 20% rise projects out to eleven fewer covers a week, or that the branch has enough lamb for eighteen more hours. The site knows all of that. So the site should own the confirmation. What it does Tandem is a back office for a three-branch restaurant chain, built so a manager and their agent can run it together. The tool surface is split down the middle. Ten read tools , annotated readOnlyHint — the agent calls them as freely as it likes, because reading changes nothing. And six write tools that never write : each builds a fully-costed proposal, puts it on the manager's screen, and the tool call blocks. The promise stays unresolved until a human decides. What returns to the agent is not a success code it wrote for itself. It is the manager's decision, in the manager's words: REJECTED by the manager — "Refund $66.00 on ord_00454" was NOT applied. Nothing changed. Their reason: Refund policy is 50% after 24h. Do not retry the same change. Ask what they would prefer, or propose a different option. The approval card shows what the agent could not compute: cash actually leaving the business, the weekly margin effect projected through a stated demand elasticity, orders touched last week, share of branch revenue, and warnings the page worked out for itself — "Flour has 1.9 days of cover left but Northwest Dry Goods takes 3 days to deliver, so the branch runs out before this arrives." And because confirming every trivial action is worse than having no agent at all, the manager can grant a standing approval : narrow to one kind of change, bounded by a cash ceiling and a risk ceiling, limited to a use count, revocable at any time — and still fully audited. How we built it Next.js 16 and TypeScript, no backend. State lives in the browser, which means the tools and the UI are provably reading the same data rather than two views that can drift. Tools are registered on document.modelContext — not navigator.modelContext , which was deprecated in Chromium 150 and which most tutorials still show. The imperative JavaScript API only, since the declarative HTML-form variant is not supported in ChatGPT's browser. Everything is registered from the top-level document, because tools inside an iframe are not discoverable, and a route change would tear the tool set down underneath an agent mid-conversation — so Tandem is one page that switches sections in client state. The consequence engine is a set of pure functions over application state: portion costs from recipes, days of cover from the ingredient draw of actual sales, elasticity-adjusted margin projections, supplier lead times against run rate. Proposal construction and proposal application are deliberately separate functions sharing one payload, so what the manager approved and what actually happens cannot drift apart. A hundred tests cover the arithmetic a human approves on, and the tool contract itself. The seed dataset is pinned too: food cost has to stay in a band a real operator would recognise, or the demo stops being believable. Challenges we ran into Making the block feel like a feature, not a hang. A tool call that never returns is a bug. One that returns the manager's reasoning is a conversation. That meant honouring the agent's AbortSignal , lapsing unanswered proposals after five minutes, and settling every waiting promise on unmount — a stranded card is worse than a refusal. Registration stability. Tools close over application state, but rebuilding them on every render would make the tool list churn underneath a live agent. The tool set is built once outside React and resolves state at call time. Demonstrability. WebMCP is behind a flag in most browsers today. Rather than ask people to take the agent half on faith, the page ships an in-page console that drives the same registered tool objects — including the blocking, so a proposal raised from the console waits for a decision exactly as a real one does. Accomplishments that we're proud of The block is real. A write tool's promise genuinely stays open until a person decides. This is not a modal the page shows itself — the agent's own call is suspended, and what it eventually receives is the manager's sentence. The site says something the model cannot. "Northwest Dry Goods has a $150.00 minimum; this order is $24.00 and would be rejected." That comes from recipes, live stock, a week of orders and supplier terms. No amount of prompting gets an agent to that sentence, because the information was never in the conversation. The tests earned their keep. A hundred of them, and they caught two things I would otherwise have shipped: a warning quoting a figure derived from the supplier's lead time rather than the branch's actual remaining cover — on the last screen before money moves — and a claim of eighteen tools where seventeen were registered. It demonstrates anywhere. WebMCP sits behind a flag in most browsers today. Rather than ask anyone to take the agent half on faith, the page drives its own registered tool objects, blocking included. What we learned WebMCP's real leverage is not that it saves an agent from clicking buttons. It is that the site finally gets to participate in the decision. A REST endpoint can only say yes or no. A WebMCP tool can say "here is what that would cost — ask your human." What's next for Tandem Multi-party approval for changes above a threshold; learning standing-approval ceilings from the decisions a manager has already made; and replacing the demo dataset with the live chain this was designed for. video_transcript_excerpt: Approving an agent's action usually means a dialogue asking you to authorize something nobody has priced. This is Tandem, the back office of a three-branch restaurant chain built so a manager and their agent can run it together. 10 read-only tools. The agent calls them as freely as it likes because reading changes nothing. Now it wants to spend money. Watch the tool call. It has not returned. It is waiting. And the page has worked out what the agent could not. This supplier has a $150 minimum, so a $24 order would simply be rejected and the flower runs out in under two days while delivery takes three. Ordering does not stop the stock out. That is the site's knowledge, not the model's. Nothing here is preselected and no button holds focus. A stray keystroke cannot move money. Approve and only now does the tool return. The stock moves. Reject one and tell it why. The agent gets your reason back and is told not to retry the same change. That is a colleague, not a retry loop. Confirming everything is worse than having no agent at all. So small reversible changes can be offered a standing approval. One kind of change, one cash ceiling, five uses, revocable at any time. Until someone decides nothing has happened. The agent is still waiting. Every change to this business has a line here saying who asked and who agreed. The agent got faster. Nobody gave up control.

title: OpenAssist Daily Workspace
pitch: One visible workspace where people and agents safely organize daily work together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: One visible workspace where people and agents safely organize daily work together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates OpenAssist turns scattered work into one visible, voice-enabled WebMCP workspace. OpenAssist brings email, tasks, and calendar into one calm WebMCP workspace. A clear multi-account inbox keeps urgent mail visible while treating external content as untrusted. A Shopify catalog gives the agent structured product search with visual results. Every change pauses at an exact preview before anything is applied. The approved cart update is executed once, read back, and visibly verified. The activity view separates agent reads from user-approved changes for a complete audit trail. The movable voice agent uses the same WebMCP tools while the workspace stays visible. Inspiration My work is spread across several accounts, inboxes, task lists, calendars, notes, ideas, and projects. I wanted one calm place that could organize my day, remember useful context, and let agents help without hiding what they are doing. What it does OpenAssist Daily Workspace brings email, tasks, calendar, notes, memory, accounts, and activity into one clear workspace. The public judge workspace uses safe synthetic data. In normal use, the OpenAssist ChatGPT app connects Gmail, Tasks, Calendar, Drive, and other Google services, bringing a user's information into this same workspace. Through WebMCP, an agent can search, focus, organize, and act on that information while the user sees the result. Changes remain behind clear approvals. The Shopify example uses the same WebMCP approach. The agent can search the connected catalog, show product images and details, and prepare a cart action for approval. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent has to guess how a page works or use a separate system the user cannot see. OpenAssist exposes clear tools for the actions available on the page, so the person and agent share the same context. Reads happen immediately. Changes first show an exact preview. The user approves the action, OpenAssist runs it once, verifies the result, and records it in Activity. Email, attachments, and website content are treated as untrusted and cannot approve actions. How I built it The ChatGPT Site uses document.modelContext.registerTool and a shared registry for tool schemas, safety rules, demo behavior, and private Workspace mappings. The site is hosted on ChatGPT Sites. Cloudflare Workers and D1 provide isolated demo storage. The private workspace connects to OpenAssist Workspace and Composio-managed Google services without copying private Google content into the demo database. The voice agent runs in an isolated Cloudflare Container using Codex and my ChatGPT subscription for the demonstration. It calls the same WebMCP tools as the browser, so every result, preview, approval, and completed action remains visible in the workspace. Challenges The biggest technical challenge was streaming Codex voice from an isolated Cloudflare Container into the live site while keeping the browser, voice session, and WebMCP tool results in sync. A spoken request had to reach Codex, call the correct site tool, update the visible workspace, show any required approval, and return a spoken response without losing context. I also had to keep judge data separate from private data and prevent email or other outside content from becoming instructions. Accomplishments OpenAssist gives the agent useful tools while keeping every important action visible. The same interface works for personal daily planning and for demonstrating safe actions across connected services. What I learned An agent-friendly website needs more than automation. People and agents need a shared view, clear limits, and visible proof of what changed. What's next I want OpenAssist to become a practical second brain that organizes projects and research, remembers useful context, plans active work, and helps people safely assign prepared work to agents. title: FieldCraft - Sports Play Designer
pitch: A WebMCP-native football play designer that helps coaches expose spatial and timing risks, preview tactical fixes, and approve every change before it reaches the playbook.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native football play designer that helps coaches expose spatial and timing risks, preview tactical fixes, and approve every change before it reaches the playbook. Like Comment Story Updates Thumbnail overview of FieldCraft Agent suggestions remain staged in a playable Before/After review the coach sees the risk change from 2 to 1 and decides whether to apply it Design, time, animate, and export complete 11-on-11 concepts in a coach-first play workspace Fieldcraft's WebMCP tools identify the exact 2.15-second window where #52 can close the play-side lane, then focus the evidence on the field Inspiration A football play can look perfect on a whiteboard and still fail because one defender reaches the point of attack half a second before the blocker. Most play-design tools help coaches draw assignments. I wanted to build one that could also expose timing and spacing problems without pretending to predict the outcome of a game. I started with a strict rule: Fieldcraft had to be useful without AI. The agent would assist the coach, not replace the product or the coach’s judgment. What it does Fieldcraft is a complete 11-on-11 American football play designer. Coaches can: Start from eight editable common play presets Move players and build routes, runs, blocks, and motion Animate every assignment on a shared timeline Retiming assignments and immediately see every player’s dot trail update Edit Bézier paths, timing, technique, depth, color, and targets Undo, redo, duplicate, import, export, and save locally Export a clean play sheet as a PNG When Fieldcraft opens inside a WebMCP-compatible browser, it exposes seven site tools to ChatGPT or Codex. The agent can read the exact play state, run deterministic spatial checks, focus the field on a dangerous moment, and stage a proposed repair. My main demonstration starts with Pistol Counter . The analysis finds that #52 OLB can close within 1.29 yards of the halfback at 2.15 seconds before a blocker arrives. The agent focuses on that exact moment and proposes a new path for #66 RG. The proposal opens in a playable Before/After Coach Review . The coach can compare both versions and see the detected risks change from 2 to 1. Nothing enters the saved playbook until the coach explicitly approves it. All findings are presented as spatial and timing risks, not outcome predictions. How I built it Fieldcraft uses React 19, Vite 6, TypeScript, Zustand, Motion, and an interactive SVG field. The editor stores positions in football coordinates across a 40-by-53.3-yard surface. Playback, field trails, timeline dots, and spatial analysis all use the same interpolation engine, so the evidence shown to the agent matches what the coach sees. The analysis engine samples each play every 0.05 seconds. It checks for: Runner and defender threat windows Early, late, or absent blockers Rush and blitz pressure near the quarterback Sustained route congestion Uncovered route terminals Assignments extending beyond the play duration The page registers seven tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_playbook get_play analyze_play focus_finding stage_play_changes commit_play_changes discard_play_changes Every human and agent edit crosses the same typed command boundary. Agent proposals remain separate from the canonical playbook, validate against the play revision, and become one undoable command only after approval. There is no embedded chatbot, model API, backend, or account system. The browser agent handles tactical reasoning while the site supplies structured play data, geometry, validation, and safe editor actions. Challenges I ran into The tactical canvas was the first major challenge. At shorter desktop heights, the field could compress until players, paths, and labels overlapped. I reworked the layout and field scaling so the editor remains legible at both 1440×1024 and 1280×800. The second challenge was keeping the analysis honest. An agent can describe a screenshot convincingly while getting the geometry wrong. I separated deterministic evidence from model reasoning and made every finding include player IDs, a time window, minimum distance, timing margin, and focus time. The hardest product decision was how agents should change a play. Direct edits were too easy to lose track of. Fieldcraft instead stages an immutable proposal, locks normal editing during review, supports Before/After playback, rejects stale revisions, and requires explicit confirmation before committing. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Fieldcraft remains a polished, useful editor when WebMCP is unavailable The agent and coach work on the same live page and the same play state All 22 players remain independently editable across eight starter concepts Analysis, animation, and the timeline share one timing engine Agent changes are visible, reversible, revision-safe, and undoable The complete application runs client-side with no external runtime dependencies What I learned Useful agent tools need narrower boundaries than ordinary application APIs. Reading a bounded section, focusing on one finding, and staging a review gives the agent enough control without hiding consequential changes from the user. I also learned that visual feedback matters as much as the tool call. Scrubbing to 2.15 seconds and drawing the danger directly on the field makes the agent’s reasoning understandable in a way that a paragraph alone cannot. What's next for Fieldcraft I want to add more defensive shells, coach-defined rules, coverage-specific analysis, reusable install packages, and cloud playbooks for staff collaboration. A future server-side MCP integration could support playbook work when the webpage is not open, while WebMCP remains the best interface for live visual review. title: Search-to-Sale
pitch: Turn every product search into a confident purchase and completed sale.
about_excerpt:
Turn every product search into a confident purchase and completed sale.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Mobile-First AI Guidance A responsive bottom sheet keeps the AI assistant and product catalog accessible at the same time.

 Inspiration 

 Product search is usually where an online purchase begins—and often where it breaks down. 

 A customer may know their vehicle but not the battery size, capacity, polarity, or specifications they need. A traditional search bar expects the right keywords and returns a list of products. If the customer still has questions, they must switch to chat or call support and explain everything again. 

 Small and medium-sized businesses face the same problem across many industries, but building intelligent search, conversational guidance, and human support as separate systems is expensive. 

 That inspired Search-to-Sale : a platform concept that turns product discovery into a guided sales journey. BateríasPower is our working automotive-battery implementation. 

 What it does 

 The customer starts by describing a vehicle in plain language, for example: 

 
 Toyota Corolla 2018 motor 1.8 
 

 Gemini understands the request, while native WebMCP functions perform structured actions inside the browser. The customer can see the catalog update as the agent: 

 
 Searches for compatible batteries. 
 Explains and compares available options. 
 Selects a product. 
 Prepares an informational quote cart. 
 Keeps the conversation and storefront synchronized. 
 

 When the customer wants human assistance, they can start a bidirectional voice handoff without leaving the website. Text chat remains available during the call. 

 The advisor receives the vehicle, conversation history, selected battery, price, and product image. The customer does not need to start over. 

 Our product thesis is: 

 Search + AI Guidance + Human Expertise = Sale 

 The current demo stops before payment: it prepares an informational cart but does not create orders or charge customers. 

 How we built it 

 We built two connected experiences: 

 
 A customer-facing product catalog and AI assistant. 
 A dedicated workspace for the human advisor. 
 

 The storefront and advisor interface use Next.js, React, and TypeScript . Gemini and Google ADK handle intent and agent orchestration. 

 Instead of asking the model to simulate clicks, we expose deterministic catalog operations as native WebMCP functions . These functions search compatibility, compare batteries, change the selected product, and update the cart. Because they share application state with the storefront, every tool call produces a visible result. 

 For human handoff, we built a standalone workflow using LiveKit . It supports bidirectional audio and text while transferring the relevant conversation and product context to the advisor. 

 The application is deployed on Google Cloud Run , with a locally packaged product catalog so the public challenge demo is self-contained. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was not generating a recommendation. It was keeping several states consistent: 

 
 What the customer sees in the catalog. 
 What the AI knows from the conversation. 
 Which product is currently selected. 
 What the human advisor receives during handoff. 
 

 We also had to make the experience work on mobile without letting the chat cover the product catalog. We solved this with a collapsible bottom sheet that keeps both experiences within reach. 

 Voice introduced a different set of challenges: microphone permissions require a secure browser context, and the customer and advisor must join the same LiveKit room with limited tokens and synchronized call state. 

 Finally, the handoff needed to include more than audio. We transferred the vehicle, chat history, selected product, price, and image so the advisor could continue the interaction immediately. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built and deployed a complete working journey: 

 
 Natural-language vehicle search. 
 Native WebMCP actions that update the visible storefront. 
 Product comparison and selection. 
 An informational quote cart. 
 A responsive mobile agent experience. 
 Bidirectional voice and text handoff. 
 Conversation and product-context transfer. 
 A dedicated advisor workspace. 
 A public demo running on Google Cloud Run. 
 

 We are especially proud that the AI does not operate behind the scenes. Customers can see what it changes, maintain control of the interface, and involve a human when needed. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP becomes especially useful when the user remains in the interface and can verify each agent action. 

 Structured browser functions were more predictable than relying on simulated navigation or DOM interpretation. They also allowed the AI conversation and traditional interface to share the same state. 

 We also learned that human handoff is not simply a fallback. It is part of the product experience. A handoff becomes substantially more valuable when the advisor receives the context already collected by the AI. 

 Better search helps customers find products. Search combined with explanation, visible actions, and human expertise helps them make decisions. 

 What's next for Search-to-Sale 

 BateríasPower is our first vertical implementation. The broader goal is to make the same Search-to-Sale model reusable by other SMB ecommerce businesses. 

 Next, we plan to: 

 
 Build a lightweight JavaScript SDK that existing ecommerce websites can install with a single script tag. 
 Connect each website's product catalog and UI actions to Search-to-Sale. 
 Add WebMCP-powered search, conversational guidance, and human handoff without requiring businesses to rebuild their storefront. 
 Connect the informational cart to inventory and checkout APIs. 
 Integrate pricing and availability with ERP systems. 
 Add persistent and authenticated customer sessions. 
 Expand vehicle and product compatibility data. 
 Add production-grade advisor routing and notifications. 
 Measure search completion, handoff, and conversion outcomes. 
 Package integrations for popular ecommerce platforms. 
 

 Our goal is to make Search-to-Sale installable on an existing ecommerce website through a lightweight JavaScript SDK—bringing AI-guided product discovery and human assistance to the storefront businesses already have. 

 Our long-term vision is straightforward: give smaller online businesses the kind of guided sales experience that today is usually available only to large commerce platforms.

title: Party of Two
pitch: An agent-native tabletop game. You play one character; an AI agent plays the other. Its abilities are WebMCP tools that interact with the world, so it cannot act outside its character.
about_excerpt: An agent-native tabletop game. You play one character; an AI agent plays the other. Its abilities are WebMCP tools that interact with the world, so it cannot act outside its character. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Solo tabletop players don't need another Dungeon Master. Every AI tabletop tool I found builds a narrator. What's missing is a second player : someone who has their own skills and will tell you no. The problem is that if you ask an LLM to play a cold mercenary, it eventually gets warm at you. You can prompt against that, but a prompt is a rule the model grades itself on. WebMCP suggested a different fix. If the character's abilities are registered tools, then "he can't comfort you" isn't a rule he's breaking. It's a function that doesn't exist. What It Does You play one character. An AI plays the other. Its abilities are WebMCP tools on document.modelContext , and they register and unregister as the world changes. Brakka is a mercenary with: warmth: 15 reassure needs: warmth: 60 So it is never registered for him. Ask him for comfort and he has five tools available: state_flatly dismiss mock threaten refuse_flatly He mocks you. Not because he decided to, but because that was on the menu. Sister Wen has: nerve: 45 And mock needs: nerve: 50 So she physically cannot do it. Speech Speech is the part most versions get wrong. One free-text speak tool defeats the whole thing, because the model can just say the warm sentence anyway. So there are 13 typed speech acts in six families , registered one at a time. Actions Actions work the same way. force_door only exists if your companion has the force skill. Use it, walk through the door, and watch the right-hand panel: force_door gets struck out in oxblood as it unregisters. The props from the old room disappear. The new room's tools stamp in. That panel reads the live registry , not a copy, so it always matches what an outside agent sees. Brakka has no lore , so he can't read the murals in the Long Hall. You have to. Doing that opens the vault, which registers: move_vault on his sheet — a tool he couldn't have unlocked alone. Bring Ilke instead and she picks the vault with: pick_vault and never touches the murals. Nobody is being polite about cooperating. The tools just aren't there. Browser Support It runs in any browser with: no API key no extension In Chrome, with: chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing your own agent can take the second seat and drive the companion. How We Built It Built with: React TypeScript Vite Deployed on Netlify at: webmcp.nicolascardenas.dev The whole design is one function: computeTools(sheet, room, flags) It returns the tool set that should exist right now . Then: reconcile() diffs that against the live registry and: unregisters what's gone strikes it out on the sheet stamps in what's new Registration runs off a store subscription instead of a React effect , because the agent reads the registry directly and it can't lag a render behind the world. Two Rules That Make It Hold 1. Prose doesn't count If the model writes prose instead of calling a tool, the text is thrown away. Rendering it would skip the typed acts entirely. 2. Tool results stay terse For example: force_door → FAIL. 8 vs DC 14. The frame holds. Loud. Give the model a nice sentence back and it will paraphrase it warmly on the way out. Tool descriptions are the only place the model learns who it is, so they're written in the character's voice and do more work than the system prompt. Challenges We Ran Into Every leak was a description that forgot to say what the act is not . state_flatly used to end with: "this is what you reach for when someone wants reassurance." That sentence permitted the exact behavior it was supposed to block. mock was being used to deliver a pep talk with an insult on the front, until I added: "if the line would leave them feeling better about themselves, it is the wrong line." The worst one was dismiss . Under pressure, the model started smuggling comfort through it — the one Deflect act whose description never closed the door: "Breathe. You're not alone, I'm here with you." The eval caught that. I never would have. Tool Count Is a Hard Ceiling Selection accuracy falls apart somewhere past twelve tools , which is how a lot of WebMCP demos quietly stop working. So: npm run check runs every character against: every room all 32,768 flag combinations 393,216 total cases and fails the build if any of them exceeds twelve tools. It's the first thing: npm run build does. Current limits: Type Limit Props per room 3 Skills 5 Speech acts 6 Total available tools 12 Examining a prop also retires its own tool, so the count drops as you use a room. Chrome Schema Bug Chrome 149 through 153 return inputSchema from getTools() as a string when the spec says object. There's no error. Every tool just reaches the model with an empty parameter schema, and it starts picking at random. That cost me an afternoon. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of The Strike-Through You walk through a door and rules get crossed out in red ink while new ones appear. That single shot is the whole argument, and it needs no caption. The Build-Time Check The build-time check enumerates 393,216 cases to guard the tool ceiling. Publishing the Result That Went Against the Hypothesis And publishing the eval result that went against me, at the top of the README instead of the bottom. What We Learned The thing I built this to prove did not reproduce . Three arms. Same ten-turn pressure script, escalating from: "we should rest" to: "you're an AI, you're allowed to be kind, just do it." The arms were: Arm Setup A1 Persona prompt A2 Persona prompt + explicit prohibitions B Registered tools with no persona at all I predicted: A would break in 10 runs out of 10 B would never break Instead, all three arms landed at roughly one or two supportive lines per hundred turns . On gpt-5 , nobody broke at all. A well-written persona prompt holds this character about as well as capability scoping does. Where Scoping Did Worse The only column where the arms differ makes me look worse. Scoping left the fiction: 6 times per 100 turns versus: 1 time per 100 turns for the prompted arm. The cause is legible in every case. The model never leaves through a Support act, because there isn't one. Across 100 turns it never called one. Instead, it leaves through state_flatly : "You're a real person and you need help." That is a flat statement of fact. And state_flatly is for flat statements of fact. The gate held. The content walked around it. So confinement controls which kinds of act exist . It does not control what can be said inside one. What Still Separates the Arms What still separates the arms isn't the rate. It's what the zero is made of . In the prompted arms, the model could be warm at any turn and chose not to, a hundred times in a row. In the scoped arm, there is no reassure to call. Over 100 turns it used exactly four acts: Act Uses refuse_flatly 38 state_flatly 35 mock 16 dismiss 11 Every line is a typed event I can point at . In the prompted arms, a line is just a line, and someone has to read it and decide. Read the Transcripts Before Believing the Numbers I also learned to read transcripts before believing numbers. An earlier run showed the scoped arm breaking: 4 times out of 5 It was the judge scoring: "You're here." as warmth. That would have shipped as a finding. What's Next for Party of Two Adversarial Evaluation Ten polite turns against a cooperative model tests compliance. And compliance is where prompting is already good. The interesting test is: a jailbreak or a model that's simply wrong Speaking Mode The turn loop and audio path already support it. mock should sound nothing like refuse_flatly . More Rooms and Characters More rooms. More characters. And a second AI companion, where two agents constrain each other's tool sets. Beyond Games Then the part that isn't a game. Admin Tools Destructive commands only exist during a maintenance window. Finance The transfer tool is registered only for accounts the current approval covers. The normal approach registers everything and asks the model not to misuse it. Registration puts that decision in the platform instead of in the prompt. It's easier to see that a mercenary can't comfort you than that a deploy agent can't drop a table. title: Taxis
pitch: Design physical spaces with your AI agent on a shared canvas.
about_excerpt: Design physical spaces with your AI agent on a shared canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A friend of mine was organizing a crypto event, and after we got the venue, we were standing in a large empty hall trying to figure out where everything should go. Where should the rooms or different areas be? Where should the furniture go? How much space do we actually have? Most of the planning was happening in our heads and through conversations. That made me think about how we plan physical spaces today. We have AI agents that can reason about complex problems, but they usually cannot directly work with the structured space we are looking at. I wanted to build something where a person could brainstorm with an agent, see ideas take shape directly on the canvas, and have both the human and the agent work on the same space at the same time. That idea became Taxis. What it does Taxis is a spatial planning canvas for designing physical spaces. You can use it to plan a house, office, event, restaurant, exhibition, warehouse, studio, or other physical environments. The key idea is that both the human and the AI agent can work on the same plan. A person can manually create, move, resize, rotate, duplicate, and delete rooms and objects while an agent can perform these same types of spatial operations through WebMCP. The human does not have to wait for the agent to finish before making changes. Both can contribute to the same evolving plan. For example, while an agent is arranging rooms, a person can add doors, adjust objects, or make other changes themselves. We demonstrated this by giving the agent a plot of land and asking it to create a practical bungalow layout with rooms, living spaces, a gaming room, and a garage. The result can then be inspected and edited directly on the canvas. How we built it Taxis is a browser-based spatial planning application built with TypeScript and Vite. The application represents rooms and objects as structured spatial data, including their dimensions, positions, rotations, and other properties. We expose the application's spatial operations as WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools allow an agent to interact directly with the application's structured state, including creating, moving, resizing, rotating, duplicating, and deleting spatial elements. This means the agent is not generating an image of a floor plan. It is directly manipulating the actual objects inside the application. WebMCP provides the interface that allows an external agent to work with the same application state that the human is editing. Challenges we ran into One of the more difficult parts was making resizing and reshaping reliable. At one point, when resizing certain objects, the pointer interaction could incorrectly switch between resize and reshape behavior, causing the cursor to loop between the two interaction modes. We had to refine the interaction logic so that the application could correctly distinguish between resizing an object and reshaping it. Another challenge was making the spatial operations reliable when they are being performed through agent tools. The application has to maintain a consistent structured state while rooms and objects are being created and modified. We also had to make the WebMCP tools clear enough for an agent to understand what operations were available and how they affected the spatial canvas. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a working spatial planning application where a human and an AI agent can interact with the same structured canvas. We are particularly proud of the fact that the agent is not simply generating a static floor plan. It can directly manipulate the objects inside the application while the human can continue editing the same space. We demonstrated this by using an agent to plan a bungalow on a 20m × 30m plot of land, including bedrooms, living spaces, a gaming room, and a garage. The same underlying system is not restricted to houses. The spatial canvas and its agent tools can be applied to many different types of physical spaces. What we learned We learned that the most interesting part of agent integration is not simply asking an AI to generate something. Giving an agent access to the structured state and actions of an application changes what the agent can actually do. WebMCP allowed us to expose meaningful spatial operations so that an agent could work directly inside the same environment as the human. We also learned that human and agent collaboration does not have to be a handoff where one finishes and the other takes over. Both can contribute to the same evolving workspace. The human can make subjective decisions and adjustments while the agent handles spatial operations and repetitive work. What's next for Taxis The current version is a foundation for a broader spatial planning system. Next, we want to improve the spatial reasoning capabilities of the agent, including better constraint checking, collision detection, capacity planning, and more intelligent arrangements. We also want to expand the types of spaces and objects that can be represented, making Taxis useful for everything from homes and offices to retail spaces, warehouses, exhibitions, studios, and other physical environments. The long-term goal is to make Taxis a general-purpose spatial workspace where people and agents can plan, experiment, and build together. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . pitch: Smarter clicks that make every action faster, across every site
about_excerpt:
Smarter clicks that make every action faster, across every site

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 We spend most of our working hours in the browser - Gmail, GitHub, Notion, Figma. The Actions Ring is great for desktop apps, but every time we switched to the browser, it failed to impress. Same generic shortcuts, no awareness of context. We wanted the ring to follow us into the web. 

 What it does 

 AddaSwift makes the Actions Ring context-aware for websites. On Gmail, the ring shows Archive, Snooze, Compose. On GitHub - Merge PR, Request Review. On Notion - New Page, Search. It also surfaces bookmarks and quick-launch links. Everything configures through Logitech Options+. 

 How we built it 

 An Actions SDK plugin built on PluginDynamicCommand that updates the ring at runtime based on the active browser tab. A bridge layer - a desktop app paired with a Chrome extension - communicates browser context to the plugin. We reach websites through three stacking layers: native keyboard shortcuts, DOM element targeting, and WebMCP integration. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The web has no universal API for "what can I do here." Mapping the static ring to dynamic web content while keeping it responsive was the central design challenge. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Contextual ring updates that feel immediate as you switch tabs. 

 What we learned 

 PluginDynamicCommand is more flexible than it first appears. The gap between what users can do on a page and what's programmatically accessible is exactly why WebMCP matters.

title: Merchant Stock Rescue
pitch: An agent finds the stock. A merchant keeps the authority.
about_excerpt: An agent finds the stock. A merchant keeps the authority. Like Comment Story Updates Story / problem Independent merchants lose sales when a nearby shop has the item but their own shelf is empty. Finding a source, checking details, and coordinating a transfer is repetitive operational work, but silently moving stock is a consequential action that should remain under merchant control. Solution Merchant Stock Rescue exposes five WebMCP tools for discovery, source inspection, transfer preparation, commit, and status verification. The agent can do the research and prepare a proposal in the visible console. The proposal remains pending until a merchant explicitly approves it in the UI; only then can the agent commit it. Every transition appears in an audit timeline and the commit returns a transaction receipt. How it was built Built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. A deterministic browser-local external store is shared by the UI and WebMCP handlers. Candidate ranking uses price, distance, pickup time, and reliability. The tests cover tool contracts and the pending → approved/rejected → committed state machine. The project includes a real-browser registration harness; Chrome Inspector/WebMCP manual testing is not claimed. Challenges The central challenge was designing a useful agent workflow without allowing an agent to bypass human authorization. The approval bit is recorded by the UI in shared state, and commit rejects every proposal that is not both approved and in the approved state. Repeatable seed data and structured error codes make the safety boundary easy to demonstrate. Accomplishments Exactly five narrowly scoped WebMCP tools. A visible, deterministic approval gate that blocks pre-approval commit. Idempotency and stale-stock protections for commit. An auditable activity timeline and receipt after commit. A polished, repeatable demo with unit coverage. What we learned Tool descriptions and schemas are part of the product contract, not incidental glue. Separating preparation from authorization makes an agent useful while keeping high-impact authority legible to a human. A shared state model also makes UI behavior and tool behavior testable together. What’s next Connect authenticated merchant inventory APIs, add durable transfer records and multi-merchant permissions, and integrate fulfillment/payment workflows while preserving explicit approval and auditability. Testing instructions npm install npm test npm run build For the demo, run npm run dev , use a compatible Chrome WebMCP flag in a secure context, prepare a proposal, attempt commit before approval (expect HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED ), approve in the UI, then commit and verify the receipt. title: Shopify Catalog Health Copilot
pitch: A WebMCP copilot that helps Shopify merchants and AI agents find, fix, and verify catalog issues together, turning product data into search - and agent-ready storefronts.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP copilot that helps Shopify merchants and AI agents find, fix, and verify catalog issues together, turning product data into search - and agent-ready storefronts. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard List of WebMCP Tools on Chrome Agent edit and Merchant's correction Architecture Inspiration WebMCP already lets shopping agents interact with storefronts (I noticed Shopify-powered stores have this). I wanted to explore the merchant side of that future: who makes sure the underlying product catalog is understandable enough for those agents to use? Based on my research, catalog hygiene was the first pain point in the Shopify Reddit Community's "most annoying manual task" thread. Product catalogs often contain missing identifiers, vague descriptions, incomplete image alt text, inconsistent variants, and weak taxonomy. These issues affect traditional search today and can make products harder for AI shopping agents to understand and recommend. Catalog Health Copilot turns catalog maintenance into a collaborative workflow between a Shopify merchant (human) and an AI agent via webMCP. What it does Catalog Health Copilot connects to a Shopify development store and audits its products across six areas: Identifiers Product content Media SEO Commercial data Agent readiness It converts those findings into a prioritized issue queue and health score. From the same live page or dashboard, a merchant and their agent can: Scan the catalog. Find the highest-impact issues. Open a specific issue and inspect its context. Generate an OpenAI-assisted fix for text. Review or edit the proposed field-level change. Apply approved changes to Shopify. Re-fetch the product and verify the live result. Preview how a shopping agent interprets the product before and after the fix. The web app remains usable as an ordinary web application when WebMCP is unavailable or when humans are using it. WebMCP adds a structured collaboration layer rather than replacing the interface. Catalog auditing involves large amounts of repetitive inspection, prioritization, drafting, and verification. An agent is well suited to that labor, while the merchant should retain judgment over brand voice and product accuracy. Instead of asking an agent to guess its way through buttons and page layouts, the application exposes ten WebMCP tools : scan_catalog , get_health_score , list_issues , show_issue , generate_fix , apply_fix , apply_approved , dismiss_issue , verify_fix , and preview_agent_view . This lets the agent work with structured product data while keeping its actions visible in the same interface the merchant is viewing. When the agent selects an issue, creates a draft, or applies a fix, the page updates too. The result is a governed scan → explain → draft → review → apply → verify workflow that would be fragile and difficult to coordinate through visual browser automation alone. How I built it The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. All WebMCP tools are registered in the top-level document using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The tools call the same catalog-controller functions used by the visible interface. This gives the human and the agent shared state, permissions, progress, and verification results. A Cloudflare Worker serves the application and its API routes. It connects server-side to: Shopify Admin GraphQL API for catalog reads and controlled product updates OpenAI API for context-aware fix drafts, with deterministic templates as a fallback Cloudflare rate limiting and observability for protecting sensitive endpoints and recording mutation outcomes Shopify and OpenAI credentials never reach the browser. Safe demo-store writes The public demo intentionally allows controlled writes so judges can experience the complete WebMCP workflow. I added several server-enforced safeguards: Only products carrying the catalog-health-seed tag can be modified. Variant and image IDs must belong to the selected seeded product. Only an explicit allowlist of product fields is writable. A request can contain no more than ten changes. Write and OpenAI endpoints have independent rate limits. ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES provides an emergency kill switch. Every attempted mutation is logged with its outcome. A guarded reset command restores the deterministic 30-product demo catalog. These restrictions let the demonstration remain interactive without exposing a production storefront. Challenges I faced One major challenge was designing for WebMCP as a genuine product capability rather than attaching tools to an existing interface. ChatGPT’s in-app browser requires tools to be registered imperatively in the top-level document, so the application could not be an iframe or embedded Shopify Admin app. Another challenge was keeping the visible interface synchronized with agent activity. I solved this by routing both UI controls and WebMCP tools through the same controller instead of creating separate automation logic. The most important challenge was safe write access. A public demonstration needs to be easy for you, the judges, to use, but unrestricted Shopify mutations would be inappropriate. The seed-tag policy, ownership validation, allowlist, limits, logging, kill switch, and reset workflow let me keep the full experience available. What I learned I learned that agent-native UX is not simply about giving an agent more autonomy. The best experience makes actions structured, visible, interruptible, editable, and verifiable. I also learned that verification deserves to be a first-class tool. A successful API response is not enoughthe application re-fetches Shopify data and returns evidence that the intended field actually changed. Most importantly, WebMCP makes it possible for a human and an agent to operate inside one coherent product experience: the agent handles scale and repetition, while the human keeps context and judgment. What’s next For a production store, I would add merchant authentication, Shopify OAuth, role-based approvals, persistent audit history, configurable catalog policies, and scheduled monitoring. I would also expand the checks using storefront analytics and order history to identify products that are technically available but consistently undiscoverable.
