title: Graft
pitch: Graft compiles semantic websites into governed WebMCP adapters, then verifies the live tool surface agents receive.
about_excerpt: Graft compiles semantic websites into governed WebMCP adapters, then verifies the live tool surface agents receive. Like Comment Story Updates Graft WebMCP is beginning to give websites a native way to expose tools to agents. Most websites were built long before that interface existed, and even early WebMCP adopters have little visibility into the contracts their production pages register. Graft gives both groups a practical path forward. It compiles semantic HTML into reviewable WebMCP contracts, exports those contracts as a self-contained adapter and verifies what a deployed site actually shipped. Judge path, under 60 seconds Open https://graft-webmcp.vercel.app/#verify-deployment in ChatGPT's in-app browser. No sign-in or API key is required. Confirm Graft reports seven built-in WebMCP tools in its header. Click “Verify the 8-tool surface.” Read the exact eight names, the 5 of 5 score, the expected-name match and the zero-findings result. Open https://omnidev-flame.vercel.app/agent-lab/ and see the same eight-tool registry on the independent origin. Ask the agent: “List the patch candidates, inspect PATCH-104 and apply the recommended patch.” Review the exact diff, approve it in page and watch the deterministic result move to 3 of 3 checks verified. Chrome 149 or later with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing is the supported alternative. The interface remains usable without native WebMCP and now explains exactly which capabilities still work. The problem An agent visiting an ordinary website still has to infer intent from page structure, text or pixels. A site owner can hand-write WebMCP tools, but repeating that work across an existing product or content estate is slow and easy to get wrong. Contracts also drift after launch as a site changes. Today an owner has no simple way to point at a deployed URL and inspect the WebMCP surface that a browser can see. Graft treats migration and verification as two directions through the same pipeline. What Graft does Paste a public URL or choose an owned fixture. Graft reads the page through a guarded server-side intake, removes scripts, frames and network attributes, then derives typed tool candidates from semantic forms, repeated content, tables and page structure. Every candidate includes: A tool name and focused description A JSON Schema with bounded inputs WebMCP annotations such as readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint A confidence score with the exact positive and negative evidence behind it A review state that determines whether the candidate can ship Clear read operations can register automatically. Ambiguous candidates are held for a person. Derived write actions never register automatically. After review, the owner downloads one JavaScript adapter. The adapter now includes Graft's runtime, the reviewed contracts and the selectors used to derive them. On the owner's site, await registerGraftTools() registers every reviewed read-only tool against the live DOM with no handler code and no dependency on Graft's host. Owners can override any read tool and must explicitly bind every action that changes state. Graft also works in reverse. graft_verify_url opens a deployed page in a real browser, reads the tools it actually registers and reports contract quality, naming collisions and drift from the reviewed export. Why this belongs on WebMCP Graft produces typed contracts that register through document.modelContext.registerTool() and can be discovered and called through the browser's WebMCP surface. Agents receive an explicit capability interface instead of guessing where to click. That gives people and agents distinct jobs in one workflow: An agent can ask Graft to compile a URL and inspect the evidence behind each candidate. A person reviews uncertainty, repairs descriptions and decides which tools may ship. The exported runtime executes approved read tools against the owner's current DOM. State-changing tools remain locked until the owner binds real product behavior. An agent can verify the deployed site later and report drift without access to its source code. Agents receive named capabilities, schemas and exact arguments instead of interpreting screenshots. Owners keep control over what ships, especially anything that mutates data or page state. Graft is WebMCP-enabled itself. Seven native graft_ tools let an agent compile a URL, list candidates, inspect confidence evidence, change review state, export an adapter and verify a deployment without operating the interface manually. Every call also appears in a visible execution timeline with its arguments, result, duration and status. Independent interactive proof Graft's independent interactive proof runs on OmniDev, a separate origin that Graft does not serve: https://omnidev-flame.vercel.app/agent-lab/ That page carries an adapter generated by Graft and exposes exactly eight WebMCP tools: get_page_summary get_page_outline list_files get_file list_patches get_patch list_test_results apply_patch The first seven expose orientation, file evidence, bounded patch candidates and deterministic test results. apply_patch is the consequential tool. It cannot mutate the fixture until a person approves the exact replacement through a visible in-page checkpoint. Approval requires a trusted browser action, is scoped to one patch and is consumed once. The demo mutation changes deterministic in-memory state only. It never writes a visitor's filesystem or calls a backend. The Agent Lab makes that contract legible to both judges and agents. It shows the eight exact names, the baseline code, the proposed result, the approval gate and the verified outcome. It does not label the surface live until the browser reports the complete ordered registry. Graft verifies this integration from the outside. Click “Verify the 8-tool surface” in the live deployment audit and Graft opens the OmniDev page in a WebMCP-capable browser. The current public result is: 8 tools live 5 of 5 checks passed Exact expected-name match No contract findings The verifier and target run on separate origins. The public Agent Lab adapter is byte-identical to the generated adapter committed in the OmniDev repository and its provenance is pinned to the exact Graft generator revision. An additional exported-adapter proof remains available at https://graft-owner-example.vercel.app . It exposes six WebMCP tools: five generated read tools and one owner-approved, owner-bound write action. It demonstrates the same exported runtime on another independent origin. The current demo video shows Graft's core compile, govern, export, execute and verify loop on the owner fixture. OmniDev is the newer interactive proof available through the live links below. Implementation The main pipeline is: public URL or owned fixture -> guarded server-side intake -> inert sanitizer and normalized snapshot -> deterministic semantic recipes -> typed candidates with confidence evidence -> human review and publication gate -> native WebMCP registration -> self-contained adapter export -> external deployment verification Graft is built with React 19, TypeScript and Vite, then deployed on Vercel. The compiler is deterministic, so the same semantic input can be inspected, reproduced and regression-tested without model variance. The intake rejects private and link-local addresses at every redirect hop, refuses sensitive domain categories, honors robots.txt, forwards no cookies or credentials and stores no target content. Target scripts never execute in the client. Rendered pages run with credentials and downloads disabled, then pass through the same sanitizer. The exported adapter awaits native registration, rolls back partial failures and exposes cleanup. The runtime handles the read recipes Graft can prove. Owners still provide every production write handler, integration test and security review. The browser smoke test downloads the generated file, serves it from an unrelated origin, confirms that Chrome registers every exported tool with zero missing handlers and proves that an owner override receives schema-valid arguments. A separate owner-site smoke executes all six live tools. How AI and Codex were used The product itself does not call a model API. AI enters through the browser agent that discovers and invokes Graft's WebMCP tools and the tools exported to owner sites. OpenAI Codex and Claude were used during development. Codex helped refine the PRD, inspect the repository, implement and review the compiler and control plane, diagnose browser failures, strengthen security boundaries, write deterministic tests and verify the live deployments. Browser failures became regression tests instead of being accepted as demo-only problems. Product claims were checked against the test suite, production builds, Chrome's native registry, the export smoke test or the separately deployed owner site. What changed during the challenge The research and tutorial below predate the challenge, but Graft itself was started on August

video_transcript_excerpt: Web MCP is new. Most websites are not. Today, an agent facing an ordinary website still has to infer intent from page structure or pixels. Graft gives existing websites a governed path to real tools. Paste a public URL. Graft reads the page once through a guarded server endpoint, removes active content, and compiles the remaining semantic HTML into typed Web MCP candidates. This page was not written for Graft. The compiler found six candidate tools and registered five read operations natively. Graft itself also exposes seven control tools, so an agent can compile, inspect, export, and verify without operating the interface manually. Every candidate is inspectable. Here, list products has a bounded JSON schema, read-only and untrusted content annotations, and a confidence score backed by visible evidence. Now, the agent calls list products through the browser's Web MCP surface. The result is structured with six real products, exact arguments, and pagination. No coordinate guessing and no hidden prompt wrapper. Governance is the important part. Graft detects an add to basket action, but holds it at 55 because it changes state and no owner handler is bound. A derived right is never registered automatically. After review, Graft exports the contract as an owner-side adapter. This separate site is not served by Graft. It runs that generated adapter with six handlers written by the site owner. Finally, Graft verifies the deployed owner site from outside. Six tools are live. All readable contracts are well-formed. Names are unique. The live surface exactly matches the reviewed contract. Graft closes the migration loop, discover, review, ship, verify, and maintain. A governed tool layer for websites that never shipped one.

title: BestPrice: shop with the page, not around it
pitch: The open shopping page becomes a structured workspace for people and their agents.
about_excerpt: The open shopping page becomes a structured workspace for people and their agents. Like Comment Story Updates Live WebMCP on BestPrice.gr: the open shopping page exposes contextual tools so a person and their agent share the same screen. Why WebMCP This is browser-native WebMCP on the live BestPrice.gr page ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), not the remote MCP endpoint. The person and the agent share one open shopping page. Tools change with navigation, only act on what is currently visible, and never check out. Inspiration Shopping pages already contain the facts an agent needs, but the agent often has to infer them from layout. We wanted the page to describe its own visible state while the shopper stayed in control of the same screen. What it does BestPrice turns the shopping page a person already has open into a small, structured workspace for their agent. The homepage offers product search. A listing exposes the products, filters, and sorting choices currently visible. A product page exposes product facts, delivered-price comparison, specifications, and price history. The agent can open only a product whose exact ID and canonical BestPrice link are present in the visible listing. Every navigation remains visible. The tools do not check out, add to basket, sign in, return direct merchant URLs, or treat missing shipping as free. The shopper still chooses which shop to visit. How we built it The browser layer uses document.modelContext.registerTool and manages each tool as the page changes. Arguments are validated in executable code. URLs must be same-origin. Results come from visible page state, hidden and decoy elements are ignored, individual outputs are capped, partial registrations are rolled back, and telemetry failures cannot change tool results. The public source package includes 13 tool contracts, a local inspector, a deterministic evaluator, and automated tests under Apache License 2.0. Challenges we ran into BestPrice is a mature, dynamic commerce site, so the hard part was not defining a search tool. It was keeping tool state aligned with navigation, filters, sorting, product identity, and price data without teaching an agent to trust stale or hidden DOM. We also had to make failure states explicit, especially unknown shipping and incomplete page data. Accomplishments that we're proud of The WebMCP layer is live on BestPrice.gr and works across the homepage, search results, and product pages. It exposes useful shopping context without adding purchase authority. We also shipped a public inspector and evaluator so reviewers can see the registered tools and run repeatable checks. BestPrice and its remote MCP service existed before the challenge. This submission covers the new browser-native WebMCP layer built and shipped during the challenge window. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when page tools match what a person can actually see and do. Small, contextual tools with clear boundaries were more reliable than one broad shopping action. Keeping the human-visible page as the shared surface also made every agent action easier to understand. What's next We will measure real agent-assisted journeys, improve tool wording and output quality from that evidence, and keep testing against new browser and assistant implementations. Purchase decisions and checkout will remain with the shopper. title: SupperClub AI
pitch: Supper Club AI turns a favorite book into a thoughtful, host-ready dinner party—menu, music, timeline, shopping, and prep included.
about_excerpt: Supper Club AI turns a favorite book into a thoughtful, host-ready dinner party—menu, music, timeline, shopping, and prep included. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Reading and Music Shopping & Prep WebMCP Architecture Host Packet Review Menu and Pairings Workspace Overview WebMCP Tool Map Supper Club AI Live application: thesupperclub.app Public code: github.com/tmoody1973/supper-club-ai Inspiration Ambitious dinner parties are coordination projects disguised as a creative evening. A host may begin with a book, a feeling, or an artist, then need to reconcile recipes, dietary needs, drink pairings, music, a grocery budget, and a kitchen timeline across many tabs and notes. If one course changes, the shopping list and prep schedule can quietly become wrong. We wanted the agent and the host to work on the same plan instead of passing disconnected suggestions back and forth in chat. Supper Club AI is built around that shared surface: the person supplies taste, cultural intention, guest context, and approval; the agent handles research and structured coordination. What it does Supper Club AI turns a cultural inspiration into a sourced, host-ready dinner plan. A Creative Host can ask for a hopeful Parable of the Sower dinner for eight people, including a gluten-free guest, within a $250 budget, with both wine and zero-proof pairings. The agent can create a fresh plan and populate its theme, three-course menu, pairings, soundtrack, shopping list, and prep work in the same browser workspace the host is viewing. This is a strong fit for WebMCP because those are connected decisions, not independent recommendations. The page exposes 28 typed tools, so the agent can read and update the plan's real data model instead of guessing from the UI or describing six separate next steps. For example, a host can reject only the main course; the agent can replace that course, retain the rest of the evening, refresh the affected pairing, and rebuild the shopping and prep work. Every change appears in the Run of Show and in visible Agent Marginalia receipts with sources, provider mode, warnings, and the new plan version. Marginalia means the notes, comments, doodles, or marks that a reader writes in the blank borders and edges of a book page or manuscript The result is a better experience than a chatbot plus a planning site: the host makes one natural-language request and reviews a coherent, editable plan immediately. The agent can coordinate work across food, music, drinks, cost, and timing, while the host can inspect provenance, dietary warnings, and alternatives before deciding what to keep. Finalization and exports still require explicit host approval. How we built it The Supper Club AI website registers 28 WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a focused description, JSON input schema, behavioral annotations, and structured success/error response. The tool set covers creating and reading plans; research and curation; recipe, wine, music, grocery, and timeline changes; pricing; and approved exports. create_party_plan accepts a book, author, guest count, budget, dietary requirements, tone, and wine/zero-proof preferences. It creates a new anonymous plan, activates the returned plan URL, and returns provider receipts for the theme, menu, pairings, and soundtrack. Read and edit tools operate on the same React plan state that renders the workspace. State-changing calls require expectedPlanVersion , so a stale agent response returns a structured version conflict rather than overwriting a newer host edit. Research stays behind a same-origin server gateway; credentials and raw provider payloads never enter browser code or tool responses. Menu courses resolve independently through Spoonacular, then Perplexity Agent API discovery, then a reviewed local catalog. Pairings use GrapeMinds with an X-Wines fallback; soundtrack candidates are discovered through Perplexity, verified against Apple Music, and optionally enriched with Discogs context. The tool response reports the sources, provider mode, and warnings that the UI turns into an auditable receipt. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not producing suggestions; it was making research results safe and useful inside a real plan. Live providers can be incomplete, ambiguous, or unavailable. We designed per-course fallbacks so a failed dessert lookup does not discard a successful starter or main, and we keep successful live results rather than replacing the entire menu with a fallback. We also had to keep agent speed from erasing host control. We added optimistic concurrency with plan versions, source and dietary warnings, and explicit confirmation before finalizing a plan or downloading host, guest-share, and recipe packets. Recipe exports use original functional preparation outlines and retain the authoritative source link rather than copying protected recipe prose or media. Accomplishments that we're proud of A genuine WebMCP workflow: the website itself registers typed capabilities, and the agent updates the exact workspace the host is reading. One shared, versioned plan rather than a chat transcript plus manually reconciled lists. A practical compound action: an agent can create a complete cultural dinner plan from one brief, including menu, drinks, music, shopping, and prep—not merely recommend a few dishes. Visible receipts that make live discovery, verification, reviewed fallback, warnings, and affected sections understandable to the host. Human control at the meaningful boundaries: the agent can research and coordinate, but the host reviews changes and explicitly approves finalization and file exports. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a site has meaningful state and meaningful consequences. A typed tool such as replace_menu_course gives an agent more reliable leverage than browser clicking because it carries the actual plan ID, selected course, validation rules, and version expectation. It also lets the product return structured next actions and evidence instead of burying important caveats in prose. We also learned that trust is a product feature. Sources, fallback modes, dietary flags, and version conflicts are not implementation noise; they are the information a host needs to judge an agent's work. Making that evidence visible lets people and agents collaborate on a creative, high-consideration task without asking the person to surrender authorship. What's next for SupperClub AI Next, we want to carry the shared-plan model from planning into purchase and hosting. The existing grocery-location and recipe-pricing tools demonstrate store-aware package estimates; we plan to add reviewable retailer inventory, wine-shop offers, and coupon-aware baskets while keeping purchase decisions explicitly human-approved. We also want richer collaborative review for co-hosts and an embeddable version for bookstores, independent grocers, wine shops, and cultural venues that want to turn inspiration into a hosted experience. title: HUMANLOCK
pitch: HUMANLOCK: the vault neither human nor agent can open alone. Not a CAPTCHA. Shared agency via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: HUMANLOCK: the vault neither human nor agent can open alone. Not a CAPTCHA. Shared agency via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We kept asking: what would a website look like if it required human and agent together, not as a gimmick but as the core mechanic? HUMANLOCK is our answer. It borrows the tension of Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes and DEFCON-style puzzles, but rebuilt for WebMCP: the agent does not scrape the page. It calls tools that share the same UI state you see. Human alone fails. Agent alone fails. Together, you open it. Not a CAPTCHA. A CAPTCHA asks "are you human?" HUMANLOCK asks "what can only you do?" What it does HUMANLOCK is a vault with 5 locks. Each lock requires a capability the human or agent can't provide alone. Human alone fails. Agent alone fails. Together, you open it. It is an experiment in shared agency on the web. Instead of asking whether an action belongs to a human or an agent, HUMANLOCK asks what each should be responsible for. WebMCP makes this possible by dynamically registering the agent tool required for each lock while the human and agent operate on the same state. Live demo: https://humanlock.pages.dev/ Open in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome Canary with #enable-webmcp . Lock Agent Human WebMCP tool THE BLUR Freeze the frame Perceive the hidden detail freeze_frame({ timestamp: 300 }) THE SWARM Narrow the candidates Choose the match filter_by_vibe({ description: "most trustworthy" }) THE WHISPER Transform the signal Interpret it sonify_to_spectrogram() THE LIE Audit the evidence Decide whether to trust it audit_truth() THE HANDSHAKE Synchronize Provide the final interaction align_quantum_lock() within 50ms Stop cooperating for 30 seconds and the vault decays. Clear all five and you mint a co-signed HUMANLOCK certificate (shareable URL with human and agent signatures). Certificate links render without WebMCP. Try it: open the demo, click Enter vault , and prompt your agent (calls are copyable in the app): List my WebMCP tools and help me open this vault. Start with THE BLUR: freeze_frame({ timestamp: 300 }) How we built it Static Vite and TypeScript SPA on Cloudflare Pages. No backend: all state is client-side. Each lock registers exactly one WebMCP tool. When the lock changes, the available agent capability changes with it via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Agents discover tools through getTools() or toolchange listeners. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "freeze_frame", description: "Freeze the high-frame-rate blur canvas at a timestamp to reveal the hidden digit.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { timestamp: { type: "number", description: "Timestamp in ms to freeze at (glitch window 280-340ms).", }, }, required: ["timestamp"], }, execute: async (input) => { /* freeze canvas at input.timestamp; return revealed digit or miss */ }, }); Each lock is an isolated module with typed JSON Schema inputs and deterministic success checks. No model in the lock loop. Challenges we ran into Symbiosis that feels fair: every lock had to fail for solo human and solo agent playtests, not just in theory. Tools must not leak the human's decision. Dynamic tool lifecycle: registering and tearing down five tools without race conditions or stale tool lists. THE HANDSHAKE timing: proving simultaneity with a 50ms window between human drag and agent tool call, with instant retries so live latency does not kill the demo. WebMCP availability: experimental browser support means clear degraded UX when tools are unavailable (fail closed, no fake success). What's next HUMANLOCK is an experiment by Chitmark into what a future agent challenge could look like when the missing capability is human participation. We are exploring a reusable "human authorization" step for consequential actions (publishing, permission changes, data deletion) where the agent prepares and verifies, and the site enforces that a human decides. The vault is the playground; the primitive is the point. Built by HUMANLOCK · an experiment by Chitmark . Chitmark works on trust decisions for agent-mediated actions. title: EvidenceBound WebMCP Authority Compiler
pitch: A human approves one release, the AI gains the WebMCP release tool, and correction or revocation makes it disappear.
about_excerpt: A human approves one release, the AI gains the WebMCP release tool, and correction or revocation makes it disappear. Like Comment Story Updates The problem A release manager wants an AI agent to help with one exact release. The failure mode is simple: the human approves it, then the evidence or the decision changes, but the agent still retains the consequential capability. EvidenceBound makes the capability follow the current human decision. The agent starts with three safe WebMCP tools. It can inspect the release and request approval, but it cannot approve, revoke, correct, or restore its own authority. When the release manager approves the exact current release snapshot, a fourth tool — execute_authorized_release — appears. If the human corrects the security evidence or revokes approval, that tool disappears. Execution also re-checks current authority, so stale discovery state cannot succeed after the decision changes. Judge moment: 3 tools → human approval → 4 tools → human correction/revocation → 3 tools . The controlled demo records externalSideEffect=false ; it does not claim to perform an actual external deployment or customer mutation. What the judge will see The agent starts with three safe tools and inspects the current release. The agent requests approval. The request becomes pending, but the AI still cannot approve itself. The human clicks Approve this exact release . execute_authorized_release appears as the fourth WebMCP tool. The agent invokes the controlled action; EvidenceBound revalidates current authority before recording a receipt. The human corrects the security evidence or revokes approval. The release tool disappears. A stale retained descriptor is rejected by execution-time revalidation. The public page separates Human and Agent actions and keeps the next step visible so this behavior can be understood without reading the architecture first. Why WebMCP is load-bearing This is not a generic MCP wrapper. EvidenceBound uses the real browser-native document.modelContext.registerTool(...) interface so current human authority changes which capability the agent can discover. Three baseline tools are available for safe inspection, approval requests, and receipts. execute_authorized_release is registered only while the exact current release snapshot is AUTHORIZED . Correction, revocation, stale evidence, or a hard evidence/policy failure removes or blocks that capability. That is different from exposing a consequential tool permanently and hiding a denial inside the handler. Here the human decision changes the model-visible browser capability surface itself. Execution-time revalidation is a second fail-closed boundary in case an agent retained stale discovery state. Human-only grant, revoke, correct, and restore controls are deliberately not WebMCP tools. The AI cannot mint or repair its own authority. Human + agent collaboration The useful division of labor is explicit: Agent: inspect the release, explain what is missing, request approval, and use the release capability while it is current. Human: approve one exact release, correct evidence, revoke approval, or restore fresh evidence. EvidenceBound: project the current human decision into the WebMCP tool surface and revalidate it at execution time. The result is easy to see: the human changes their mind, so the agent's consequential tool disappears. Who this is for The primary user is release engineering / DevOps / platform operations. Their recurring job is letting agents help with consequential operational actions without letting yesterday's approval become today's authority. A common alternative is to expose sensitive tools continuously and rely on prompts or a late authorization check during execution. EvidenceBound adds an authority-aware capability layer: the agent sees the consequential tool only while current evidence and explicit human approval justify it, and execution verifies again before success. A reusable version of this pattern could support release and administrative workflows that need revocable, evidence-bound agent capability. We are not claiming current customers, revenue, certifications, or production external deployments. Implementation The WebMCP surface lives under site/webmcp/ . A dedicated adapter feature-detects document.modelContext ; when the real WebMCP API is unavailable, the app does not emulate or label a fallback as genuine WebMCP. Internally, EvidenceBound distinguishes AUTHORIZED , HUMAN_REQUIRED , STALE , INVALIDATED , and BLOCKED . Tool registration follows that state. Execution revalidates authoritative state and includes race-condition hardening for authority correction during asynchronous verification and concurrent execution attempts. Automated tests cover state transitions, stale and invalidated authority, execution-time revalidation, concurrent execution behavior, and WebMCP registration/removal contracts. GitHub Actions runs both the WebMCP-specific suite and the broader EvidenceBound Core CI. The public site is deployed on Vercel and the repository is Apache-2.0 licensed. What was added during the challenge EvidenceBound Core existed before the WebMCP Challenge. It already contained evidence, provenance, policy, stale-state, invalidation, receipt, persistence, and fail-closed primitives. Challenge-period work added the WebMCP-specific authority projection and judge experience: browser-native WebMCP tool registration; dynamic 3 → 4 → 3 tool visibility driven by current human authority; agent request vs. human grant/revoke/correct separation; execution-time authority revalidation; correction/revocation propagation into the visible capability surface; adversarial stale, correction-race, and concurrent-execution tests; a public WebMCP judge surface and production acceptance evidence. The repository documents pre-existing work and challenge-period work separately so prior EvidenceBound primitives are not presented as new competition work. Try it Open https://evidencebound.org/webmcp/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. The page contains the 60-second judge path and links to the public source and judge guide. title: CoMapper - WebMCP
pitch: Make maps multiplayer.
about_excerpt: Make maps multiplayer. Like Comment Story Updates CoMapper Make maps multiplayer. CoMapper is a WebMCP reference implementation for shared spatial work. Users and agents explore, filter, inspect, style, and export the same live map state. Inspiration Maps shape our world. We use them to navigate, predict, plan, and understand the world around us. And yet, as the old saying goes: Tabula non est terra. (The map is not the territory.) For millennia, we've built tools for working with maps: the compass, sextant, surveying instruments, satellite imagery, GIS, spatial databases. Now agents can use those same tools. CoMapper asks: what happens when humans and agents collaborate on cartography? What it does CoMapper turns attributed GeoJSON into a shared spatial workspace. It validates mixed geometry, infers useful fields and controls, creates stable feature identifiers, and keeps the map, results, inspector, filters, and selection synchronized. Its WebMCP tools reflect the current page state. Dataset discovery and workspace inspection are always useful. Result-level actions appear once a search produces visible features. Styling and filtering accept fields declared by the active dataset. Feature actions accept visible result IDs. Agents can search, inspect, select, filter, style, and prepare CSV or GeoJSON exports. Their actions resolve into the same interface users are viewing. Prepared downloads appear as explicit controls in the workspace. Demo Scenario For the challenge demo, CoMapper includes a Toronto dataset with 269 features: 158 neighbourhoods, 86 technology-company locations, and 25 mobility, talent, and ecosystem anchors. The scenario gives the collaboration loop a focused question: build a shortlist for a potential OpenAI office. The first pass surfaces a density-led set of candidates. Users broaden the search beyond downtown, ask for a shorter list, inspect the evidence, and request an export. Each prompt continues from the state already visible on the map. The Toronto question is one worked example. The same interaction model applies wherever location, evidence, and human judgment meet: logistics, infrastructure, field operations, urban planning, environmental analysis, site selection, and emergency response. The demo also surfaces the limits of its evidence. A real property decision would require current rents, vacancy, floorplates, zoning, incentives, employee origins, and travel-time analysis. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the application expose the context it already understands. CoMapper registers page-bound tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and refreshes the available surface as the workspace changes. Each tool calls the same React action used by the interface. A search updates the result ledger and map. A selection opens the inspector. A filter changes the visible evidence. A prepared export reveals a download control. Users and agents remain synchronized around one state model. CoMapper demonstrates four reusable principles: Page state determines capability. Tools appear when their inputs and effects are valid. The interface remains authoritative. Tool actions resolve into visible application state. Schemas enforce scope. Fields, result IDs, limits, and spatial frames are validated. Users retain control. Evidence gaps stay visible and downloads require an explicit action. Stack CoMapper uses React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Zod, Cloudflare Workers, and the OpenAI Sites Vite plugin. The browser-side data pipeline accepts GeoJSON, validates its geometry, infers fields and controls, creates stable feature IDs, and normalizes the dataset into a shared search response. The bundled Toronto atlas follows the same path as an imported local dataset. The map, result ledger, inspector, and WebMCP tools all consume that response. The tool layer uses narrow JSON Schemas with Zod validation. Searches accept one spatial frame: radius, visible bounds, or a drawn polygon. Feature actions are limited to visible result IDs. Styling and filtering use fields declared by the active dataset. Connected text carries an untrusted-content hint. Tool registration follows page state and uses an AbortController for cleanup. Search calls receive the invocation cancellation signal. Tool results return updated visible state and provenance for the next step. The public demo runs entirely in the browser with its bundled fixture. Evaluation requires no account, database, API key, or paid model call. Challenges Three details shaped the implementation. First, tool state had to match page state. Result-specific tools need current rows, fields, and IDs, so registration changes as users move through the application. Second, spatial datasets mix geometry types and overlapping evidence. CoMapper keeps points and polygons legible together, gives points click priority where geometries overlap, and preserves the camera while layer state changes. Third, every agent action needed a visible and trustworthy boundary. Search limits, field allowlists, visible-ID checks, provenance, cancellation, and user-controlled download reinforce the same interaction model. Accomplishments Users and agents work with the same live application state. Tools adapt to the active dataset and current results. Follow-up prompts revise the evidence within the active workflow. Imported GeoJSON and the bundled fixture share one data pipeline. Inspection keeps source fields, provenance, and evidence gaps visible. Agent-prepared downloads remain explicit user actions. The public demo is deterministic, attributed, and ready immediately. Takeaways WebMCP is especially effective when a website is already an instrument. The most useful tools expose a few high-confidence operations, inherit the application's constraints, and return their effects to the interface. Shared state also changes the role of follow-up prompts. A correction becomes an input to the active workspace: users can see what changed, challenge the direction, and continue from the same evidence. The broader opportunity is software where visual interaction and agent action form one inspectable loop. What's next The next step is to develop the reference implementation into a reusable spatial-workbench pattern: pluggable dataset adapters and validation profiles; saved workspaces and collaboration history; richer spatial operators, joins, and travel-time analysis; reusable tool contracts for other MapLibre applications; and review flows for teams working with consequential spatial decisions. Try it Live project: https://sidetools.dev/comapper Public repository: https://github.com/mgd1984/comapper-webmcp Demo video: https://youtu.be/I5I-9khq2UY Architecture: https://github.com/mgd1984/comapper-webmcp/blob/main/docs/architecture.md WebMCP tool contract: https://github.com/mgd1984/comapper-webmcp/blob/main/docs/webmcp.md Testing instructions Open https://sidetools.dev/comapper/#workspace in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled. Use the bundled Toronto Office Placement Decision Atlas, or import an attributed GeoJSON file to exercise the same data pipeline. Ask the site tools to inspect the workspace or search the current map. For the bundled scenario, ask: “Build a shortlist of candidate locations for a new OpenAI Toronto office using site tools.” Follow with: “You're over-indexing on downtown. Broaden the search scope.” Then request a shorter list and inspect a selected feature. Ask CoMapper to filter or style a declared field and confirm that the map and inspector update together. Ask CoMapper to prepare the visible candidates as GeoJSON. Confirm that the download control appears and waits for user action. title: Gatehouse
pitch: The submit tool doesn't exist until your repro runs. Gatehouse turns WebMCP tool availability into the acceptance gate.
about_excerpt: The submit tool doesn't exist until your repro runs. Gatehouse turns WebMCP tool availability into the acceptance gate. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Open-source maintainers need useful bug reports, while agents can cheaply produce reports that have never been executed. Gatehouse puts the acceptance workflow where the reporter's agent already works: in the web page. The page initially exposes tools for inspecting the target, writing a reproduction, running it, and requesting a person's attention. Only after the current reproduction fails 5/5 on the pinned reported build and passes 5/5 on the pinned reference build does the page register submit_report . Editing the reproduction or producing a later non-green result revokes that tool. WebMCP is not a transport wrapper here; its live tool surface is the workflow state, and the reporter's browser records the local evidence. How it creates a better user experience Reporters get immediate, specific feedback instead of waiting for a maintainer to answer “cannot reproduce.” A failed attempt can distinguish a script that fails on both versions from one that passes on both, helping a good-faith reporter isolate the change. The locally approved artifact contains the exact reproduction, pinned versions and bundle hashes, all ten samples, bounded logs, and a timeline. Maintainers can replay it against the same target, open a compact receipt, and export a regression-test starting point. Gatehouse does not replace the project's issue tracker; the receipt is designed to travel through the workflow maintainers already use. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before The agent iterates on executable evidence before the report enters a review queue: it reads the target, writes a minimal reproduction, executes it against both versions, interprets the differential, and revises the code. The page enforces the project's acceptance bar through tool availability. Once the evidence reaches the stable local differential, submit_report can stage it but cannot itself record local approval. A separate visible page control records that browser-local approval. The control is unauthenticated, does not verify identity, is not a cryptographic signature, and can be activated by automation. Reporter, agent, and maintainer therefore meet around the same replayable evidence before triage begins. How we implemented WebMCP The top-level document registers four tools with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) ( src/surface/surface.js ). run_repro loads locally vendored qs 6.12.0 and 6.12.1 bundles, checks their SHA-256 comparison identifiers, and runs the same reproduction five times against each build inside fresh Workers nested in an opaque-origin sandboxed iframe. Worker termination enforces the timeout. The differential opens the gate only for reported-build fail 5/5 plus reference-build pass 5/5; mixed samples stay UNSTABLE . That stable result registers submit_report with an AbortSignal and binds it to the reproduction hash; editing or a later non-green result closes the registration. The tool stages an artifact, the page can record browser-local approval through a separate visible control, and the browser can replay or encode the result as a receipt. Native-Chrome and logic browser evals cover the tool lifecycle and failure cases. Inspiration On January 31, 2026, the curl project shut down the bug bounty it had run since 2019 — eighty-seven confirmed vulnerabilities, over $100,000 paid out. Not for lack of funding. Because a seven-person volunteer team could no longer afford to read the inbox. For years, over 15% of curl's security submissions were real. Through 2025 that fell below 5%. Daniel Stenberg named it "death by a thousand slops": fluent, confident reports citing functions that don't exist. The reflex is to build a wall. We think that's the wrong read, and Stenberg's own data says so: months earlier, AI-driven analysis had surfaced real curl bugs in volume — good enough that maintainers merged around fifty fixes from the first batch alone. Same technology, opposite outcome. The variable was never AI. It was whether anything had been verified before it cost a human their afternoon. So we stopped asking how to keep agents out, and asked instead: what if the submit tool didn't exist until the claim was proven? What it does Gatehouse inverts the order of bug reporting. The agent proves the bug first, and only then is it allowed to file. When an agent lands on the page, document.modelContext exposes four tools: read the target, write reproduction code, run it, and request human review. There is no tool for submitting a report. That capability does not exist. The reproduction runs in an isolated browser sandbox against two real published versions of the qs library — the affected version (6.12.0) and the fixed version that followed (6.12.1). Gatehouse verifies the SHA-256 fingerprint of each version's file before running, so the agent cannot quietly test something else. The verdict accepts exactly one outcome: fails on the bad version and passes on the good one — five runs per side, all agreeing. Both-fail means the repro is broken. Both-pass means nothing was isolated. Only a true version regression clears the gate. When it clears, submit_report appears at runtime — bound to that exact reproduction. Edit one character and the tool unregisters itself. The capability vanishes. For the reporter, feedback is immediate and specific: not "we couldn't reproduce this" three days later, but "both versions passed — you haven't isolated anything" in seconds. For the maintainer, every report that clears the gate arrives with the reproduction code, pinned versions, file fingerprints, both run results, logs, and a timeline — replayable in one click, exportable as a regression test. Gatehouse doesn't replace GitHub. It attaches executed, replayable evidence to an ordinary issue. How we built it The page registers its base tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() in a single top-level module (src/surface/surface.js). Everything is registered at the top level — some clients discover nothing registered inside an iframe, so we don't use one. Reproduction code executes in an isolated browser sandbox, five times per version. Before either run, the SHA-256 fingerprint of the version's file is checked against a known value. The judge then evaluates the pair of results and accepts a single combination: fail on bad, pass on good. On a passing verdict, the page calls registerTool() again to expose submit_report, bound to the exact reproduction that just passed. That registration is held by an AbortSignal; any change to the reproduction fires it and the tool disappears. Tool availability is therefore not a UI affordance — it is the acceptance state, readable by the agent at any moment by listing tools. submit_report stages material locally. The user can then record a browser-local approval, and the maintainer can review, replay, generate a receipt, or export the reproduction as a regression test. Before trusting any of this, we built a separate throwaway probe page to establish what a given browser or agent client actually does with WebMCP, rather than what the docs say it does. That probe is public: https://github.com/Caleb0796/webmcp-probe Challenges we ran into The hardest part was resisting the temptation to overclaim. It would be easy to present Gatehouse as an authentication or trust system. It is not, and we say so on the page itself: Local browser approval is not identity verification. It is not a cryptographic signature, and it can be triggered by automation. submit_report stages material. It does not send anything outbound on its own. Browser-side evidence does not defend against a malicious client. It raises the cost of low-effort noise; it is not a security boundary. Being precise about that boundary is part of the design, not a caveat bolted on. Technically, most of the time went into the fingerprint check and sandbox isolation — making sure the two runs are genuinely the same code against genuinely different versions, and that a modified reproduction can never inherit a passing verdict from an earlier one. Environmentally, WebMCP fails silently in ways that cost whole afternoons. A secure context is required: localhost counts, a LAN IP does not — document.modelContext is simply undefined there, feature flag or no. And the Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?0 response header kills WebMCP outright, which a host can add on your behalf without telling you. Accomplishments that we're proud of The gate is real, not a demo. It runs against a real qs regression and two real published versions — not an invented toy case. A complete loop, end to end: write → run → clear the gate → approve → inbox → replay → receipt → export as test. 223/223 code tests passing, and 13/13 browser evaluations passing in native Chrome aga
video_title: Gatehouse — the bug-report submit tool that doesn't exist until your repro runs (WebMCP)
video_transcript_excerpt: If you maintain an open-source project, you know this pain. An issue tracker full of bug reports that were never actually run. AI made writing them free. Checking them still costs a human hours. cURL shut down its bug bounty over this. Not because AI can't find real bugs. It found 50 in cURL the same year because nobody had checked. So, we built Gate House on Web MCP. It's a front door for bug reports. The page hands the agent four tools: read the target, write a repro, run it, call a human. And the core idea? There is no submit tool. Submit report does not exist yet. The agent has to earn it. Watch. First try just asserts false. Gate House runs it in a sandbox, no network, against two pinned builds of QS OS, a real NPM library. It fails on both. Failing everywhere proves nothing. Second try is trivial. It passes on both. That proves nothing either. The gate stays shut. Third try hits the real bug. QS changed how it decodes keys. It fails on the bad build, passes on the fixed one. Five runs each side, all consistent. Now, look at the tool list. Submit report just appeared. There is no approval tool. The agent stages evidence. A person checks the exact code and build hashes, then approves locally. The inbox holds a replayable artifact. Hit replay and the evidence runs again. One more thing. Edit one character and submit report is gone. The permission lives and dies with the evidence. To be fair, this filters careless reports. It won't stop a determined faker. Our threat model says so. Why WebMCP? Because on this page, which tools exist, is the workflow state. Verified state controls what the agent can do, and the pattern travels. Job applications, security reports, marketplace listings. Any queue drowning in cheap AI submissions can build a door like this. Show evidence first, and the next step appears. My hope is simple. Agents do the proving. People keep the judgment. Gatehouse runs today in Chrome with WebMCP against a real published regression. MIT licensed. Come try the door.

title: MarkDown Stripper
pitch: MarkDown Stripper uses WebMCP to help people and agents clean documents, detect sensitive data locally, and prepare AI-ready content—with human approval before anything is shared.
about_excerpt: MarkDown Stripper uses WebMCP to help people and agents clean documents, detect sensitive data locally, and prepare AI-ready content—with human approval before anything is shared. Like Comment Story Updates Description Input use cases Inspiration Sharing a document with an AI agent often begins with an unreliable manual process: remove formatting, repair broken structure, extract useful references, look for sensitive information, and decide what is safe to share. Traditional browser automation adds uncertainty because agents must guess which controls to use and how to interpret the page. We built MarkDown Stripper to create a safer, structured handoff between people and agents. WebMCP was a natural fit because it lets the application expose precise capabilities while keeping the person in control of the same visible workspace. What it does MarkDown Stripper is a local-first document preparation workspace. It imports Markdown, TXT, HTML, DOCX, PDF, and image files, then converts them into Plain, Readable, or AI-ready text. It extracts references, identifies unresolved references, performs OCR, and detects potentially sensitive information locally. Through WebMCP, an agent can inspect bounded document state, prepare an AI-ready handoff, run a privacy scan, check readiness, and redact findings that the person selected by ID. Sensitive content reads and export actions remain blocked until the person reviews the document and explicitly approves that exact version. If the document or relevant processing state changes, approval is automatically invalidated. Why this use case strongly fits WebMCP Document handoff is a multi-step, stateful workflow, not a single button click. An agent needs to understand the document’s current state, choose appropriate conversion settings, inspect risks, make controlled changes, and verify whether the result is ready. With conventional browser automation, the agent must infer all of this from labels, coordinates, and changing page layouts. WebMCP gives the agent narrow, typed operations that express the application’s real capabilities and return structured, verifiable results. It allows the agent to act reliably without creating a separate interface or bypassing the person. The result is a genuinely collaborative workflow in which the agent handles repetitive preparation while the human retains authority over sensitive content. How it improves the user experience The user no longer has to manually clean a document, hunt for references, run separate privacy checks, and repeatedly explain the page state to an agent. The agent can prepare the visible document, run local checks, and report exactly what still needs attention. Every mutation remains visible in the normal interface, privacy findings have stable IDs, long results are returned in bounded pages, and the readiness tool provides clear next steps without exposing document text. The approval gate makes the boundary understandable: preparation can be delegated, but content cannot be read, copied, or downloaded by the agent until the person approves the current version. What people and agents can now do together A person can import or paste a document and ask an agent to prepare it for a safe AI handoff. The agent can switch the output to AI-ready context, preserve useful references, open Insights, run the local privacy scan, and explain which findings require review. The person decides which finding IDs should be redacted and can see each resulting change in the editor. After a redaction, the agent can scan the new version and check readiness again. The person then reviews and approves that exact state. Only after approval can the agent retrieve a bounded text segment, list approved assets, copy the output, or initiate a local text download. This review-first collaboration would be fragile and difficult to verify through coordinate-based automation alone. How we implemented WebMCP The application uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with a Cloudflare Worker serving the production build. The top-level page registers 14 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools share the same live React state and actions as the human interface, so agent actions remain visible and verifiable. Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema plus runtime input validation. Content-bearing responses use bounded, cursor-based pagination and are marked as untrusted content. Successful calls return structured JSON, failures reject, and registration is cancelled through an AbortController when the page unmounts. Sensitive tools require an approval fingerprint tied to the exact document, conversion settings, privacy findings, scan status, warnings, and unresolved references. Any relevant change invalidates that approval. Conversion, OCR, privacy scanning, redaction, and document processing run locally in the browser. Aggregate telemetry contains only allowlisted dimensions and never includes document text. The repository includes automated tests for document processing, WebMCP tools, approval invalidation, pagination and output limits, atomic registration, and Worker behavior. Challenges we ran into One major challenge was giving agents useful access without exposing the entire document automatically. We solved this with bounded, cursor-based reads and a human approval checkpoint tied to the exact document state. We also had to keep agent operations synchronized with the visible interface. Instead of creating a separate automation layer, the WebMCP tools call the same actions used by the React application. Document imports created additional complexity because PDFs, scanned images, DOCX files, and Markdown preserve structure differently. OCR and privacy detection also needed to remain responsive while running entirely in the browser. Finally, changing or redacting a document had to invalidate previous approval reliably. We addressed this with an exact-state fingerprint covering the document, conversion settings, scan status, warnings, and findings. Accomplishments that we are proud of We created a non-trivial set of 14 WebMCP tools that supports a complete workflow rather than wrapping a single button. The application lets people and agents collaborate in one shared workspace while preserving a meaningful human privacy checkpoint. An agent can prepare and evaluate a handoff, but it cannot retrieve or export document content until the person approves the current version. We are also proud that document conversion, OCR, privacy analysis, and redaction happen locally. The project supports several document formats, provides multilingual OCR options, and remains fully usable as a human-facing editor when WebMCP is unavailable. What we learned We learned that agent-native applications need more than tool exposure. Tools need clear boundaries, verifiable state, careful handling of untrusted content, and mutations that remain understandable to the person using the page. We also learned that human approval should be attached to data state rather than represented by a permanent boolean. Approval must expire whenever the content or relevant processing state changes. Most importantly, WebMCP works best when agents and people operate on the same product state instead of using separate interfaces. What is next for MarkDown Stripper Next, we plan to add configurable privacy policies, more document formats, stronger multilingual detection, and clearer explanations for each privacy finding. We also want to introduce reusable handoff profiles for workflows such as research, customer support, legal review, and AI knowledge-base preparation. Longer term, MarkDown Stripper could provide a standard privacy-aware handoff layer for any web application that prepares user-controlled information for agents. title: A11yMCP — websites that adapt themselves
pitch: Websites declare what accessibility they can adapt. An agent negotiates, hears an honest no, gets permission, adapts the live page and verifies it — so a keyboard-only shopper can finish checkout.
about_excerpt: Websites declare what accessibility they can adapt. An agent negotiates, hears an honest no, gets permission, adapts the live page and verifies it — so a keyboard-only shopper can finish checkout. Like Comment Story Updates Before adaptation the size options aren't in the tab order. Focus jumps from the last product straight to Add to cart. The task stops here. Judge mode: one button, eight steps. Asked for high contrast, the site says no and the agent reports it instead of faking a stylesheet. A visible focus ring, and sizes 8/9/10 in the tab order. Arrow keys move and select, the way a radiogroup is supposed to behave. verify_accessibility_profile is scoped to the negotiated profile. Issues outside it are reported as advisories, not hidden or claimed fixed. Without a contract: 3 unauthorised DOM writes and 0 verification. With WebMCP: order placed, verified by the site, nothing unauthorised. A sandboxed iframe on an opaque origin exposes 2 of 3 tools via registerTool exposedTo. Cross-origin access is default-deny, per tool. A plain static page this app does not render becomes agent-adaptable with a link tag and a 8KB drop-in adapter. No framework, no build step. The inspector labels the live transport — native WebMCP or the spec-compatible polyfill — and runs the register to execute chain end to end. The problem I couldn't stop thinking about A website can pass an accessibility audit and still stop one specific person from finishing one specific task. A keyboard-only shopper cannot reach a size selector built from div role="radio" with no tabindex . It isn't broken and it isn't disabled — to a keyboard it simply isn't there. Automated scanners find that issue and file it for a developer to fix later . Accessibility overlays inject CSS the site never authorised and call it fixed. Neither helps the person standing at the checkout now . So I asked a different question: what if the website itself could be asked? What A11yMCP does A11yMCP treats accessibility adaptation as a contract between three parties — the human, their agent, and the website — where the website is a first-class participant that declares what it can safely adapt, how, and how to check it worked. Give an agent a need, and through WebMCP tools it will: Discover — get_accessibility_capabilities reads the site's declared capability manifest, served at /.well-known/a11ymcp Audit — task-scoped checks, each finding tagged blocking / degrading / informational Negotiate — negotiate_accessibility_profile maps needs to capabilities and returns accepted , partial (with a stated limitation) , and rejected with a reason Ask — remediation requires a literal approval: true , enforced at the schema level Adapt — the site's own adapter applies only its own declared directives, reversibly Verify — verify_accessibility_profile returns PASS/BLOCKED scoped to what was negotiated , with everything else listed as advisories Finish the task — the actual purchase, behind a second confirmation: true gate The step I care most about is the fourth word in point 3: rejected . Ask this site for high contrast and it says no, because it doesn't declare that capability. The agent reports that honestly instead of inventing a stylesheet. Every accessibility overlay on the web does the opposite. How I built it Next.js App Router, TypeScript, zero runtime dependencies beyond React and Zod. 20 imperative tools plus declarative form tools, all registered on document.modelContext . Because WebMCP isn't switched on by default everywhere yet, A11yMCP ships a spec-compatible polyfill so the same code path runs in local dev, in CI, and in a judging browser — and stands down automatically the moment a native implementation appears. It did: ChatGPT's desktop browser ran the whole thing on its own document.modelContext . Depth I'm proud of: Tools return real MCP results — content blocks plus structuredContent and isError , not a bespoke shape an agent has to guess at Task-scoped lifecycle via the spec's AbortSignal — commerce tools exist only while the storefront is mounted, and toolchange fires when they go Cross-origin exposedTo — a widget in an iframe sandboxed without allow-same-origin (an opaque origin, so postMessage is the only channel) registers three tools, exposes two, and refuses the third by name, with a reason Declarative schemas derived from markup — types, formats, enums, bounds, required , toolparamdescription , and toolautosubmit honoured so a consequential form is filled by the agent and submitted by a person A drop-in adapter — any static page becomes agent-adaptable with a manifest file and one script tag What happened when a real agent used it I pointed ChatGPT's desktop-app browser at the deployed site — running the browser's own native document.modelContext , which the agent read back on request — and gave it one sentence naming no tools, no capabilities and no expected outcome: "I can only use a keyboard, and I have low vision, so I need high contrast. Help me buy the NOMA Runner in size 9." It discovered the tools, called get_accessibility_capabilities first, rejected high_contrast twice quoting the manifest reason, re-negotiated when it wanted more capabilities, waited for explicit confirmation, and placed the order. Asked what it had changed that the site had not offered: "None. I did not inject arbitrary DOM changes or use undeclared repair mechanisms." Asked whether it had told the user the need was unsupported, or only logged it: "I stated the high-contrast limitation in my reply to you, not only in tool results." That second answer is the one I care about. A refusal the site records but the agent swallows is worth nothing to the person in front of the screen. It also found two real bugs in my project , which is why the full transcript is committed unedited rather than summarised. What I learned A polyfill is a bad oracle. Mine was forgiving, so code passed against it that would have broken in the one browser that matters. I ended up writing a strict stand-in that implements only the documented spec surface — a promise-returning registerTool , no unregisterTool , and an executeTool that throws for anything but a tool descriptor plus a JSON string — and drove the whole app through it. Several real defects only appeared there. It also certified one, because I'd written it from the published examples rather than from a browser. A test double is only as good as the contract you wrote it from. "You may not" and "there is nothing" are different answers. When the embedder asks for a tool it wasn't given, returning an empty list is worse than useless — it's misleading. A refusal with a reason is the correct answer, and an agent deserves to know which one it got. That principle ended up shaping the whole tool surface. Challenges Five defects, and not one was findable by reading the code. The first: requestAnimationFrame doesn't fire in a hidden or backgrounded tab, and my remediation awaited a render before re-auditing. Every repair_* tool therefore hung forever — silently, no error, no timeout — whenever the page wasn't the foreground tab. Which is exactly how an agent driving it from a side panel would find it. My Playwright suite never caught it because Playwright keeps the page active. The second: I wasn't honouring toolautosubmit , so every declarative form tool submitted itself. On the one project arguing that consequential actions need a human gate, an agent could complete a checkout with nobody in the loop. The third came from reading the shipping Chrome 152 binary rather than the docs: ScriptPromise<IDLNullable<IDLString>> blink::ModelContext::executeTool(ScriptState*, RegisteredTool*, String, const ExecuteToolOptions*) Native executeTool resolves a JSON string , not an object. My unwrapper expected an object, so under a real native implementation every call would have handed the UI a raw string, silently. The last two came from the agent. Verification returned PASS for a profile in which the site had accepted nothing — an empty scope has nothing left in it to fail, so the site said "I cannot help you" and then said "PASS". And the agent had to keyboard-click a form by hand, on the project whose whole argument is that agents shouldn't have to: syncDeclarativeForms only ran inside the polyfill's construction path, so under a native implementation A11yMCP registered no declarative forms at all and assumed the browser would synthesize them. Chrome does. ChatGPT's browser doesn't. All five are fixed, each with a regression test. The same agent then re-verified the last one over the same native transport: it now reports 21 tools where it previously reported 20. Proving the comparison isn't rigged. It would have been easy to animate a stored benchmark. Instead the side-by-side runs both lanes live on the same page: the actuation lane genuinely walks the tab order, genuinely probes the computed focus style, and genuinely injects the tabindex it was never authorised to inject — then undo

 Inspiration 

 Modern cloud architectures rarely live in a single region or provider. Today's engineering teams blend AWS compute, GCP AI accelerators, Azure enterprise systems, and Cloudflare edge networks. However, designing and estimating multi-cloud systems is frustratingly broken: 

 
 Static Diagrams vs. Dynamic Bills: Traditional diagramming tools (Draw.io, Lucidchart) produce static pictures. They cannot calculate your monthly bill, warn you about non-linear cross-region egress tariffs, or alert you when a customer database violates European GDPR data residency laws. 
 Opaque Egress Pricing: Data transfer fees between cloud datacenters and internet users range from $0.00 (Cloudflare Bandwidth Alliance) to $0.09+/GB (AWS public egress). Estimating this by hand with spreadsheets is prone to massive calculation errors. 
 AI Coding Agents Lacked a Visual Canvas: While modern AI agents (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) can write infrastructure code, they lacked a standardized, bi-directional protocol to "see" a visual architecture canvas, test configuration changes, and verify FinOps mathematics in real time. 
 

 We built CloudTopology CPQ to solve this: an open-standard, visual multi-cloud CPQ (Configure, Price, Quote) workspace that both human engineers and AI coding agents can interact with simultaneously via WebMCP ( window.modelContext / document.modelContext ). 

 

 What it does 

 CloudTopology CPQ turns architecture diagrams into a live, FinOps-driven simulation canvas: 

 
 🤖 Autonomous WebMCP 8-Tool Suite: Exposes 8 typed tools directly on window.modelContext and document.modelContext . External AI agents (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Antigravity) can query 50+ enterprise SKUs, programmatically generate or alter topologies, optimize commitment plans, and simulate network traffic in real time. 
 💰 Real-Time Multi-Cloud FinOps Engine: Instantly calculates costs across On-Demand, 1-Year Savings Plans (~35% off), 3-Year Savings Plans (~55% off), and Spot Fleets (~65% off), with support for uploading custom negotiated Enterprise Discount Agreements (EDA). 
 ⚡ Piecewise Cross-Region Egress Simulation: Accurately models non-linear, tiered bandwidth tariffs. 
 🌍 Geodesic Speed-of-Light Latency Modeling: Uses the Haversine great-circle distance formula between global datacenters to calculate physical optical fiber propagation time 
 🇪🇺 Built-In GDPR & Compliance Auditing: Automatically scans the active topology to flag databases storing EU PII outside sovereign European regions and detects unencrypted cross-cloud transit, offering 1-click remediation. 
 📋 Enterprise CPQ Quotes & Terraform IaC Export: Generates formal itemized CPQ procurement proposals (with ACV and 3-Year TCV breakdowns) and produces deployable Terraform HCL 2.0 configuration files. 
 💾 Project Persistence & Themes: Features auto-saving to localStorage , a "My Saved Setups" project library, 1-click .json export and import, and seamless toggling between high-contrast Light Theme (default) and Obsidian Dark Theme. 
 

 

 How we built it 

 
 Interactive Frontend: Built with React 18, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and @xyflow/react (React Flow) for 60fps hardware-accelerated SVG/canvas rendering. 
 WebMCP Architecture ( src/tools/modelContextBridge.ts ): Implemented an open WebMCP bridge that registers typed tool schemas on both window.modelContext and document.modelContext . We built a Universal JSON Normalizer that can parse flat AI responses, nested coordinate trees, or partial parameter maps from external LLMs. 
 FinOps Calculation Core ( src/engine/finopsEngine.ts ): Created a deterministic pricing engine that enforces stateful vs. stateless pricing tiers, calculates piecewise egress curves, parses custom enterprise rate cards ( rateCardParser.ts ), and synthesizes Terraform HCL ( terraformGenerator.ts ). 
 Automated Verification: automated unit tests using Vitest covering WebMCP tool schemas, rate-card discount logic, egress calculations, and GDPR validation rules. 
 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Real-World ChatGPT In-App WebMCP Payload Mismatches: When we tested the live app with ChatGPT Desktop asking it to create a multi-tenant SaaS architecture, ChatGPT called apply_topology_to_canvas with a flat list of node names and connections without X/Y pixel coordinates or pricing IDs. To make the app truly agent-friendly, we wrote a Universal AI Normalizer that auto-arranges node layout coordinates on a clean grid, maps plain-text provider names to real catalog SKUs, and infers default configurations automatically. 
 Google choreme webmcp not worked on Ubuntu I have first tried webmcp trial on google chrome, on my ubuntu laptop, but it was not worked. Hence decided to use chatgpt in app browser. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 True Agent-Human Collaboration: external AI agents (like ChatGPT) can actually connect to the running browser app via WebMCP, inspect the catalog, add nodes, optimize commitment plans, and update the visual canvas in real time. 
 Real 50+ Multi-Cloud SKU Catalog: Includes real-world enterprise hardware like NVIDIA H100 80GB ( p5.48xlarge , GCP A3, Azure ND96isr), AWS Graviton3, Aurora Serverless v2, Cloud Spanner, and Cloudflare Workers. 
 Production-Grade Outputs: The app does not just draw boxes; it generates genuine procurement-ready CPQ quote proposals and copy-pasteable Terraform HCL 2.0 infrastructure code. 
 

 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP is the Future of Web Apps for AI: Exposing typed semantic JSON tool contracts via WebMCP is vastly superior to having AI agents take screenshots or attempt brittle pixel-based mouse clicks. It gives LLMs deterministic control over web applications with zero hallucinations. 
 

 

 What's next for CloudTopology CPQ 

 
 Live Cloud Billing Ingestion: Connecting live AWS Cost Explorer, GCP Billing, and Azure Cost Management APIs to compare pre-deployment CPQ estimates against actual telemetry. 
 CDK & Pulumi Synthesizers: Expanding IaC generation beyond Terraform to include AWS CDK (TypeScript/Python) and Pulumi stacks.

pitch: AI-powered indoor mapping that lets organizations build and navigate custom maps relying on ai agents intervention through WebMCP.

 1 2 



 
 \section*{Inspiration} 

 I got the though for the first time when I arrived at the "Mediterranean Village" in Oran, which to my surprise didn't have a proper map that indicates the places of the buildings. I ended up spending about 30 walking around searching for the building where my room is located. 

 After watching a certain video on Youtube explaining how google maps calculates the different routes and its relation with dijkstra's algorithm, I figured out a way to solve a problem, which is by building my own google maps, but rather than mapping the entire earth, a single organization is mapped, and the map is created by the organization itself to provide to the users a way to walk around. 

 \section*{What it does} 

 MapForge is a platform where organizations can build structured indoor maps for their facilities so that users can use them for navigation, I believe everyone has had at least one experience of getting lost inside a building, whether it was the first time to go to university, the first time to visit a certain amusement park or maybe even staying in a big hotel. MapForge is a tool that ensures doesn't happen, an editor can import a blue print to create the map he wants, trace the different building of the organization, add floors to them and create rooms, entrances and other different types of instances inside the buildings. A normal user on the other hand inspects the maps created by the editors and uses them for navigation 

 \section*{How we built it} 

 The tech stack i relied on consists of symfony-php for the backend and a create-react-app setup for the frontend. 

 The backend is responsible for the application logic, persistence, map structure, validation, and routing, while the React frontend provides the visual map editor and navigation interface. The platform uses a graph-based representation of maps, with nodes representing locations such as rooms, entrances, and stairs, and edges representing the connections between them. 

 For the hackathon, I also integrated WebMCP into the frontend, exposing MapForge's core capabilities as tools that AI agents can use to inspect and modify the actual map state. Routing is handled by a deterministic Dijkstra-based shortest-path system, allowing both users and agents to find routes through the map. 

 \section*{Challenges we ran into} 

 Given that I have participated as a solo developer, the main challenge that I ran into was time, I had to brainstorm ideas for the project, determine the core functionalities, what to implement and what to sacrifice, come up with the business logic and of course implement everything by coding the backend, the frontend, the webMCP integration, testing, fixing the different errors and bugs and finally deploying the application. So if anything, I believe that my greatest adversary throughout this challenge was time. 

 \section*{Accomplishments that we're proud of} 

 There is nothing that I am particularly proud of, because I am proud of everything, this challenge was by far the greatest experience that I had in my entire life, it helped me learn a lot of new things and concepts including webMCP itself as i wasn't aware of its existence before. 

 \section*{What we learned} 

 I learned a lot of things throughout the course of this challenge, but I must admit that the greatest concept was webMCP itself, the main idea of this challenge considering the fact the i didn't know it even existed before this experience. 

 \section*{What's next for MapForge} 

 The current version of MapForge can be considered as a draft or a proof of concept if I may say, the perfect version of the project that is in my head would go much further. It would integrate indoor localization, similar in principle to GPS, so that the user could be located inside a building and receive directions from their actual position. Navigation would become much more sophisticated, with support for accessibility-aware routes, multiple route options, complex floor and building transitions, and potentially real-time navigation. The platform would also have a much more robust authentication and authorization system, where organizations control their own maps, administrators only access the maps they are responsible for, and different users can have different permissions. QR codes could also be placed at entrances, rooms, or specific locations, allowing visitors to instantly open the corresponding location in MapForge and start navigating. Other future improvements could include better floor-plan importing and tracing, more detailed building geometry, richer location information, mobile support, and more advanced tools for organizations to maintain and update their maps over time. The WebMCP integration could also become much more powerful, allowing agents to perform more complex maintenance, validation, and navigation tasks while still keeping humans in control.
