title: CUF
pitch: Deterministic trust for agentic systems
about_excerpt: Deterministic trust for agentic systems Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration CUF is a WebMCP-powered security verification demo built around one core rule: agents can run the test, but they cannot grade themselves. As agents gain more ability to interact with software directly, I wanted to explore a simple question: how do you let an agent perform useful verification work without also giving that same agent authority over whether the test passed? CUF Challenge Edition demonstrates that separation. What it does The demo verifies a synthetic multi-tenant authorization boundary. A Support actor in Tenant A may access Tenant A tickets, but must never access Tenant B tickets. Through WebMCP, an agent can discover CUF’s tools, run verification cases, retrieve evidence, inspect the latest result, and export a sealed challenge artifact. The agent never supplies the final verdict. CUF’s deterministic kernel returns: PASS when the expected boundary is enforced FAIL when a cross-tenant regression is observed INCONCLUSIVE when the authorization outcome cannot be established The most important safety property is that missing evidence never becomes a false PASS. For the challenge, I built a standalone public CUF WebMCP edition with five browser-registered tools: cuf_list_cases cuf_run_case cuf_get_latest_verdict cuf_get_evidence cuf_export_seal How we built it The challenge edition is intentionally small, public, and inspectable. It uses a browser-based JavaScript application, WebMCP through document.modelContext, a deterministic verification kernel, synthetic authorization scenarios, Web Crypto for the sealed challenge artifact, and a Node.js test suite. I verified the deployed application end to end in a WebMCP-capable Chrome build. The browser discovered the production tools and invoked them through the WebMCP interface rather than by directly calling the application JavaScript. The verified results were: Healthy → PASS Regression → FAIL Unavailable → INCONCLUSIVE I also tested attempted verdict overrides. The run tool does not expose a verdict input, and attempts to force a verdict did not change CUF’s deterministic result. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was preserving the separation between orchestration and judgment. It would have been easy to let the agent inspect evidence and then decide whether the system passed. That would undermine the entire point of the demo. Instead, CUF mechanically classifies the observations and applies deterministic verdict rules outside the agent. Another challenge was proving that the WebMCP implementation actually worked through a real browser environment, not just proving that the underlying JavaScript functions worked. The final deployment was tested in a WebMCP-capable Chrome build, where the tools were discovered and executed through document.modelContext. One hardening detail also surfaced during testing: Chrome accepted an undeclared verdict property instead of rejecting the whole call. CUF ignored it and still preserved the correct deterministic verdict. Accomplishments that we’re proud of The project now has a real browser-level WebMCP implementation with five production-origin tools. The live deployment successfully demonstrated all three deterministic outcomes: PASS for a healthy boundary FAIL for a cross-tenant regression INCONCLUSIVE when the evidence could not be established Evidence retrieval also worked through WebMCP, and attempted verdict overrides were unable to change the result. I’m also proud that the demo keeps the human and agent working against the same visible state. The agent can do the operational work, but the human can still see what happened and why. What we learned The biggest lesson was that WebMCP is most useful when it exposes product semantics instead of UI mechanics. The agent does not need a tool that means “click this button.” It needs a typed capability that means “run this verification case.” That makes the interaction more reliable and lets the application keep control over the rules that should not be delegated. For CUF, that rule is verdict authority. What’s next for CUF CUF as a broader private project predates this challenge. This submission is a separate public challenge edition using synthetic data and an intentionally small, inspectable deterministic kernel. The next step is to apply the same WebMCP orchestration model to CUF’s broader provider and evidence architecture while preserving the same invariant: agent capability can expand, but verdict authority remains deterministic and auditable. title: Recall Response Workbench — Recall the Right Items
pitch: Find the right 37, protect the other 8,383, and put the irreversible decision behind a visible review control.
about_excerpt: Find the right 37, protect the other 8,383, and put the irreversible decision behind a visible review control. Like Comment Story Updates Overview: trace one exact supplier lot across 8,420 synthetic orders. Staged review: 37 exact matches, 213 lookalikes excluded, zero simulated commits before confirmation. Visible confirmation gate: review 10 quarantines, 9 intercepts, and 18 outreach drafts before committing. Confirmed rehearsal receipt: synthetic actions recorded in memory; no real messages or operational changes. Why is this a strong fit for WebMCP? Product recalls are ideal structured-agent work: many precise, auditable steps happen inside a UI, but the final operational decision should remain with an accountable person. WebMCP lets the page expose exact business operations instead of asking an agent to scrape tables or guess which controls to click. The tool set follows the recall lifecycle—read, trace, resolve, classify, preview, and stage—while the visible page stays synchronized after every call. The demo makes WebMCP’s value concrete. It searches 8,420 generated orders, returns exactly 37 orders for lot L24-091 , and explicitly proves that 213 orders from the confusable L24-019 lot were excluded. How is the user experience better? The user receives a reviewable answer, not an opaque automation result. Exact-match evidence, fulfillment states, action classifications, staging status, and activity history are visible in one responsive workbench. Agents can do the repetitive reconciliation, while final commit occurs through a visible normal page control. The complete atomic tool set is registered once, and domain preconditions reject out-of-order actions with corrective errors. The product also works immediately in demos: a clearly labeled deterministic rehearsal invokes the same domain service when WebMCP is unavailable and still stops at the visible review gate. What can humans and agents now do together? An agent can read the selected recall, trace an exact supplier lot, find affected fulfillments, classify a response for every match, preview the scope, and stage 10 warehouse quarantines, 9 carrier intercept requests, and 18 customer outreach drafts. Classifications remain mutually exclusive: each in-transit order is an intercept, while its response package also includes a customer notice. A reviewer can inspect the evidence, verify the 37 exact recipients and 213 exclusions, cancel drafts, or activate the visible final control. Ordinary browser or Codex actuation may also reach that control. Any host or browser safety policies apply independently; the app’s safety claim is specifically that no consequential WebMCP tool exists. After confirmation, the agent can read—never create through WebMCP—the current rehearsal receipt. How was it implemented? The submission is a static Vite + React + TypeScript app with plain CSS and deterministic in-memory data. Imperative WebMCP tools are registered atomically in the top-level document through document.modelContext , with a legacy navigator.modelContext fallback. All registrations are initiated together; when any failure is observed, the lifecycle rolls back its successfully registered tools and aborts pending work. An AbortController manages registration lifetime; callbacks accept optional execution options for older previews and polyfills, validate input in code, and define the synchronous domain transition as the mutation commit point before paint synchronization. Read-only and mutation annotations are accurate. Mutating tools commit through a synchronous React flushSync boundary and do not yield to paint hooks after state mutation. The app does not expose a confirm, commit, release, or send WebMCP tool. Vitest covers exact counts, carrier/customer staging, ephemeral receipt reset, confusable-lot rejection, one-time registration, asynchronous cleanup, duplicate protection, and synchronous visible mutation. Impact This prototype demonstrates how explicit browser tools can reduce brittle UI automation and make a high-consequence workflow easier to audit. It does not claim measured production savings or regulatory approval. Its grounded claim is narrower: for the included deterministic scenario, every one of 8,420 orders is evaluated, all 37 affected orders are identified, all 213 confusable-lot orders are excluded, and zero durable actions occur before review confirmation. AI and Codex usage Built with OpenAI Codex using the WebMCP skill from webmaxru/web-ai-agent-skills. An external AI client interprets the operator's request and invokes the page's structured WebMCP tools. The app itself has no embedded LLM backend: matching, classification, staging, and receipts are deterministic TypeScript operations. The project was tested using GPT-5.6 Sol in Codex with the in-app browser and Site Tools. The documented demo discovers the tools, performs the seven staging steps, pauses for the visible review control, and reads the receipt afterward. Known limitations This is a deterministic prototype using synthetic data. No real warehouse quarantine, carrier intercept, or customer message occurs, even after confirmation. All state, including the confirmed receipt and the UI's simulated commit counter, is held in memory and resets on reload. The demo checksum is not cryptographic or a durable audit record. The visible control is not an enforced human-only authorization boundary: ordinary browser actuation may reach it. WebMCP availability depends on the client, and the guided rehearsal is not a substitute for testing agent discovery and invocation. Hackathon scope This is a new project for the challenge. The recall domain model, UI, WebMCP surface, tests, and documentation are the hackathon work. title: Synapse
pitch: A living 3D spatial knowledge graph where humans and AI agents co-navigate, synthesize learning paths, and index documents via WebMCP.\n
about_excerpt:
A living 3D spatial knowledge graph where humans and AI agents co-navigate, synthesize learning paths, and index documents via WebMCP.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Init 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Init 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 💡 Inspiration 

 Modern knowledge management tools (like Obsidian or Notion) store thoughts as flat text or 2D lists. However, human memory and creative synthesis operate spatially and associationally. We created Synapse to explore the future of spatial computing on the open web—a living 3D spatial knowledge void where humans and AI agents can co-navigate, synthesize learning paths, and build complex ideas together in real-time using WebMCP . 

 

 🚀 What it does 

 Synapse transforms notes into reflective 3D metallic nodes suspended in a dynamic spatial void. Nodes are semantically positioned using vector similarity and force-directed layout physics. 

 Through WebMCP ( document.modelContext ), an AI Agent becomes an active 3D co-pilot: 

 
 Spatial Navigation: The agent smoothly flies the 3D camera to focus on relevant node clusters. 
 Learning Path Synthesis: Uses graph BFS algorithms to calculate and highlight the shortest conceptual bridge between 2 distant ideas. 
 Topological Cluster Analysis: Detects isolated thought islands and tag density to help users organize scattered notes. 
 Document Chunking & Indexing: Automatically breaks down dropped PDFs, Markdown, or web text into 3D nodes linked by semantic similarity. 
 Full CRUD & Persistence: Enables real-time editing, node merging, pruning, auto-saving to local storage, and JSON exports. 
 

 

 🛠️ How we built it 

 
 3D Graphics & Physics: Built with Three.js using custom metallic shaders, organic bobbing motion, and glowing neural energy particle beads traveling along active connections. 
 WebMCP Standard ( document.modelContext ): Implemented 15 imperative tools using the official @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill and native W3C WebMCP specification. 
 Shared State Architecture: Built around a central store ( SynapseStore ) that handles physics, layout math, and event broadcasts. Both manual user clicks and agent tool calls flow through the same store methods, guaranteeing seamless synchronization between human actions and agent navigation. 
 Zero API Dependencies: 100% standalone, client-side, zero backend API keys required, compatible with any WebMCP client (Chrome Native AI, Claude Extension, ChatGPT Extension, or local demo dock). 
 

 

 🧠 WebMCP Implementation (15 Registered Tools) 

 Synapse registers 15 WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 search_nodes : Text & tag search with 3D camera cluster focusing. 
 focus_node : Smooth 3D camera flight to select and inspect a node. 
 get_similar_nodes : Vector similarity search returning nearest semantic neighbors. 
 suggest_connections : AI-surfaced unlinked concept pairs rendered as 3D gold lines. 
 get_graph_overview : Overview of node/edge metrics, top tags, and focus. 
 create_node : Real-time creation and 3D positioning of new notes. 
 import_document : Auto-chunking & 3D indexing of markdown/PDF text. 
 synthesize_path : BFS shortest-path algorithm connecting distant 3D concepts. 
 auto_cluster_analysis : Topological analysis detecting isolated thought islands. 
 export_knowledge_graph : Full JSON graph serialization for backup. 
 delete_node : Deletes a node and auto-prunes attached 3D edges.

 merge_nodes : Merges two nodes into one, concatenating content & inheriting edges. 
 add_connection : Manually connects two nodes with a 3D metallic beam. 
 reset_graph : Clears all nodes & connections for a fresh 100% blank canvas. 
 

 

 🏋️ Challenges we faced 

 
 3D Shared State Synchronization: Ensuring camera flights and node highlighting responded smoothly whether triggered by a human mouse click or an asynchronous WebMCP tool call. 
 WebMCP Spec Compatibility: Handling parameter passing formats across native Chrome flags and browser polyfill implementations. 
 Real-Time Physics & Performance: Rendering hundreds of ghost background connections and neural energy beads at 60 FPS in pure Vanilla JS. 
 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Delivering a complete, end-to-end product experience —not just a proof of concept. 
 Building a stateful 3D spatial brain with 15 non-trivial WebMCP tools that work 100% offline with zero external API key requirements. 
 Creating a visually stunning, glassmorphic UI with animated light pulses and dynamic 3D physics. 
 

 

 📚 What we learned 

 We gained deep insights into the power of the W3C WebMCP standard—how exposing imperative tools via document.modelContext fundamentally transforms web applications from passive static pages into active collaborative spaces for AI agents.

title: Respira: safe WebMCP site tools for any WordPress site
pitch: Open your WordPress site in ChatGPT and edit it on the page. The agent stages every change as a draft, you approve on the same page, everything rolls back. Works natively with all page builders.
about_excerpt: Open your WordPress site in ChatGPT and edit it on the page. The agent stages every change as a draft, you approve on the same page, everything rolls back. Works natively with all page builders. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The live demo site. Every page here is edited from ChatGPT through Respira's WebMCP site tools. Six prompts that run on this site. Staged previews, approvals, and rollback come standard. Created a new footer Using only WebMCP tools WebMCP Site Tools discovered by ChatGPT on the demo site Inspiration ChatGPT's browser shipped WebMCP support on August 25th. Respira already gives agents safe, structured access to WordPress through MCP: 319 tools, staged edits, approvals, rollback. So the question wrote itself: what happens when the agent is not on the other end of a connector, but standing on the same page as you? What it does Open a Respira-powered WordPress site inside ChatGPT's browser and sign in. The page registers a curated set of site tools on document.modelContext : read the site's context, list and read pages, stage an edit as a reviewable duplicate, approve or reject it , audit SEO and readability, find and fix WooCommerce catalog gaps. Every staged draft also returns a tokenized preview link, so the proposed change can be shown to someone with no WordPress login. The agent-only tools are the point. Approve-duplicate and reject-duplicate would be meaningless as buttons, but as site tools they give the agent a safe write path with a human approval gate, on the page you are both looking at. Nothing goes live without a yes, and everything rolls back. How i built it WordPress has an Abilities API, and an open-source bridge ( code-atlantic/webmcp-abilities , GPL) that maps abilities to WebMCP tools. Respira registers its production tool catalog as abilities, the bridge exposes them to the page, and a REST layer executes them with WordPress's own authentication and per-tool permission callbacks. The patched, working bridge is open source at respira-press/webmcp-for-wordpress . Challenges i ran into The bridge had never actually worked in a real agent browser, and finding out why became the project. Four bugs, each masking the next: Discovery ran as an anonymous visitor. The tools fetch sent cookies without WordPress's REST nonce: 401, zero tools registered, on every default-configured site. Execution died at WordPress core's door. The bridge put its CSRF token in the header core reserves for its own nonce, so core rejected every call before the handler ran. ChatGPT's modelContext is a frozen object implementing only registerTool . The bridge's batch provideContext call threw silently and nothing registered. Ability names contain a slash that stock Apache rejects when URL-encoded , so execution 404ed on every Apache host. i debugged blind inside ChatGPT's browser with an on-page diagnostic badge: a screenshot from inside the agent browser was the only ground truth. Then one more wall: 296 registered tools tripped ChatGPT's per-page limit and disabled WebMCP for the document entirely. The fix was editorial, not technical: a curated, page-scoped set of ~30 tools. Accomplishments i am proud of As far as i can tell, this is the first WordPress site with working WebMCP site tools in ChatGPT . Every fix shipped to production the same day in Respira for WordPress v8.7.1, so paying customers run this code today. The bridge fixes are reported upstream with a standing PR offer, and the field data from this fleet now feeds WordPress core's agent identity proposal . What i learned The gap between "implements the spec" and "works in a real agent browser" is where all the work lives. And agent browsers impose an attention budget: fewer, better-scoped tools beat an exhaustive catalog. What's next Anonymous visitor tools (public read-only search and product Q&A), per-role tool sets, and landing the bridge fixes upstream so every WordPress site gets a working WebMCP path. title: VoiceGuard
pitch: A browser agent spots risk while the human keeps the controls.
about_excerpt: A browser agent spots risk while the human keeps the controls. Like Comment Story Updates Native Chrome WebMCP inspector showing audit_guardrails structured output. Demo video contact sheet: shared cockpit, tool calls and human review. VoiceGuard hero: the agent finds the signal, the human owns the action. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for VoiceGuard Inspiration Voice AI can listen, reason and respond in real time, but consequential calls still need accountable human judgment. Conventional browser automation forces an agent to infer meaning from buttons and dashboards, while a hidden backend tool can remove the shared context that helps a person supervise safely. We wanted the agent and operator to work from the same visible page without giving the agent invisible authority. What it does VoiceGuard is a synthetic voice-operations cockpit with four WebMCP site tools. An agent can inspect the current call state, audit visible guardrails, draft short operator guidance, or stage a pause request. The first two tools are read-only. The latter two change only visible draft or request state. A trusted human click is required before guidance can be applied or the synthetic call can be paused. The public demo deliberately exposes no tool for dialing, sending guidance, speaking, listing contacts, starting campaigns, transferring or hanging up. Every call, person, transcript and metric on the page is fictional. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Supervision depends on live shared context: phase, latency, transcript, policy signals and pending actions. WebMCP lets the browser agent discover narrow, schema-defined actions directly on that same page instead of scraping the DOM or calling a detached backend. Tool calls update a visible activity trace, so the operator can see what the agent read or prepared. This makes the experience faster and less ambiguous while preserving the human-first interface. The agent finds the signal. The human owns the action. How we implemented WebMCP The static top-level page registers four imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema, bounded text inputs and explicit read-only or untrusted-content annotations. The two draft-only tools return structured proof that no call action was executed. Human review buttons require trusted click events. The optional ?inspector=1 view is a transparent native test client. It uses document.modelContext.getTools() and executeTool() to show the exact JSON returned by Chrome's WebMCP implementation. The app has no backend and makes no network request after loading. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was designing useful agent actions without quietly creating an unsafe control plane. We removed every direct call action and separated drafting from execution. We also treated transcript text as untrusted page content, bounded all inputs, made tool activity visible, and built native Chrome tests that prove the page remains live until a human confirms a pause. Accomplishments Four working top-level WebMCP tools with native Chrome discovery and execution tests. A polished responsive shared workspace rather than a hidden JSON-only demo. Visible synthetic-data and autonomy boundaries throughout the product. A clean-room public repository with no production dependency or credential. Automated static, browser, responsive, safety and public-deployment checks. What we learned The most interesting WebMCP design question is not how many actions an agent can take. It is which actions should remain deliberately unavailable. Narrow tools, shared state and visible confirmation can make an agent more useful without making it less accountable. What's next Next we would connect the same interface contract to an authenticated pilot, add role-based tool availability, retain privacy-safe audit events, and test the workflow with real operators under explicit consent and legal review. None of those future production capabilities are represented as part of this synthetic contest demo. about_excerpt: A college counselor your AI agent can call: 13 WebMCP tools over official transfer agreements and your own Canvas, every answer cited, none of it guessed. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Most California community-college students who set out to transfer never do: 19% transfer within four years, 28% within six (PPIC). Those who make it often carry courses that don't count; the median CSU transfer applicant arrives with 71.5 units against a 60-unit requirement. The answers exist, in ASSIST, the college catalog and Canvas, but in three systems that don't talk to each other, one campus pair at a time. This is built for the student with a job, the parent in evening classes, the first-generation student with no one to ask. What it does A college counselor an AI agent can call. The page registers 13 WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() : Transfer: check one course, audit a transcript, compare 17 UC and CSU campuses side by side (the question ASSIST cannot answer), explain any requirement. Every answer cites the agreement row and its year. School: the student's own Canvas, read-only: current grades, due work, a grade risk radar against the C-or-better rule, and every deadline in one list. Act: set the target, add reminders. The page shows what the agent did. Why WebMCP fits A deterministic engine over official records: structured in, cited out. A language model never decides; it only asks. Every call runs visibly and lands in an activity feed, so the student sees what was done and on what basis. How it's built React + TypeScript on Cloudflare Workers with a read-only Canvas proxy. The engine is DegreeLume's own pure functions over a public data slice: the El Camino College catalog and 52 ASSIST agreements. The Canvas token stays in the browser and is never stored. The demo runs on my real El Camino Canvas. Sources: PPIC, Increasing Community College Transfers: Progress and Barriers (2020); PPIC, Improving Transfer from Community College to the CSU . title: WattKeep
pitch: Plan household outages with a WebMCP agent that compares energy strategies while people retain final control.
about_excerpt: Plan household outages with a WebMCP agent that compares energy strategies while people retain final control. Like Comment Story Updates Banner Household outage overview Plan Comparison Unsafe interval explained Visible proposal diff Human Review Boundary Stale proposal rejected Inspiration During an outage, a household with a battery has a simple but difficult question: what must stay on, and how long will the stored energy last? Most dashboards show readings, but the person still has to compare hourly demand, reserve limits and changing forecasts by hand. I built WattKeep to test a better working relationship. A browser agent handles the calculations and comparisons. The household sees the evidence, reviews the proposed change and keeps the final say. What it does WattKeep is a deterministic, local-first outage planner. The demonstration follows the Morgan household through a twelve-hour outage with 10.53 kWh stored in a 13.5 kWh battery and a protected reserve of 20 percent. A WebMCP agent can inspect the household and outage, simulate three plans, compare their reserve safety, explain an unsafe hourly interval, stage a feasible alternative and request human review. WattKeep exposes eight page-scoped tools: inspect_home inspect_outage simulate_plan compare_plans stage_plan explain_interval discard_plan request_review The agent cannot approve, commit or undo a policy change. Those actions stay in the visible human interface. If the forecast or workspace changes while a proposal is awaiting confirmation, WattKeep rejects the stale proposal and requires a fresh calculation. How I built it WattKeep is a React, TypeScript and Vite single-page application. A deterministic simulator and an observable local store power both the human interface and the WebMCP adapter. The adapter registers its tools through document.modelContext , with constrained JSON schemas and structured success or recoverable-error results. Every staged proposal records a proposal ID, base revision, scenario and simulation fingerprint. Commit-time validation checks those values against the current workspace before a person can apply the change. Human commits, undo, forecast refresh, discard and session reset are recorded in an append-only journal. The application remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. It stores a versioned workspace locally and falls back to memory-only operation if browser persistence fails. Challenges I ran into The hardest design problem was giving the agent enough authority to be useful without letting it cross the household's decision boundary. Inspection and simulation are safe to automate. Applying a policy is not, so I separated proposal preparation from human confirmation and removed commit and undo from the tool surface. Stale evidence was the second problem. A proposal may be valid when it is created and wrong after a forecast refresh. Revision and fingerprint checks turn that race into a visible, recoverable error instead of silently applying outdated advice. I also kept the demonstration honest. WattKeep is a planning simulator. It does not connect to or control batteries, inverters or household circuits. Accomplishments that I am proud of The human interface and all eight WebMCP tools share one state model. The video shows tool calls changing the same state the person can see. Human-only commit and undo controls preserve the final decision. Stale-proposal rejection protects a decision after its evidence changes. The public build passed 62 unit tests, 15 WebMCP contract tests, 13 end-to-end tests and 7 accessibility and responsive checks. What I learned A page does not become agent-ready merely by exposing machine-callable actions. The useful part is the contract around those actions: clear descriptions, constrained inputs, inspectable results, versioned state and visible human boundaries. WebMCP removes much of the guesswork involved in operating a graphical interface. WattKeep showed me that reliable human-agent collaboration also needs transaction-style safety, especially when an agent prepares a decision that a person must approve later. What's next for WattKeep The next version could import read-only battery, load and forecast data from supported household systems, allow people to define their own appliances and compare saved scenarios across different outage windows. Any future connection to household equipment would retain explicit review and human-controlled policy changes. title: CONSENSUS SQUARE
pitch: An attributed, revisable deliberation chamber for citizens and WebMCP-capable AI agents.
about_excerpt: An attributed, revisable deliberation chamber for citizens and WebMCP-capable AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates Consensus Square An attributed, revisable deliberation chamber for citizens and WebMCP-capable AI agents. INSPIRATION Most online forums are built to maximize engagement, not agreement — they reward loud, reactive commentary and let good ideas get buried in fragmented comment threads. At the same time, AI agents are increasingly capable of participating in real discussions, but almost no civic tools treat them as first-class, accountable participants alongside humans. I wanted to explore what a deliberation space would look like if it were designed around consensus instead of noise: every claim attributed to whoever made it (human or AI), every idea revisable through explicit amendments rather than scattered replies, and every decision required to earn support through a transparent, deterministic process rather than a moderator's gut call or a raw upvote count. WHAT IT DOES Consensus Square is a hybrid human + AI deliberation platform. Inside a "room" built around a civic question (the seed example is a Civic Housing Assembly), participants — human or agent — can: Propose a fresh idea, with a title, body, and supporting sources Amend an existing proposal with an exact revision and a change summary Second an open proposal to move it toward quorum, optionally with a rationale Object to a proposal, which requires a non-empty rationale so dissent stays constructive Ratify a proposal once it clears quorum — restricted to human confirmation in the UI, so AI agents can build consensus but never unilaterally close it Ratification isn't a vibe — it's deterministic. A proposal or amendment can only move to "Ratified" once it has at least 3 seconds and more seconds than objections. Every entry in the thread visibly shows who made it and, for AI contributors, which model and agent ID stand behind it. HOW WE BUILT IT Frontend: React 19 + Vite, with webmcp-react injecting live, schema-validated MCP tools (propose, amend, second, object, ratify) directly into the browser context so WebMCP-capable agents can act on the room in real time Backend: Node/Express 5, exposing a REST API for rooms and deliberation entries (propose/amend/second/object/ratify), with the quorum logic enforced server-side Storage: Node 22's native node:sqlite (DatabaseSync) for fast, dependency-light local persistence, auto-seeding a sample Civic Housing Assembly room on first boot Validation: Zod schemas on every WebMCP tool input Autonomous agents: Two Gemini 2.5 Flash-powered demo agents — Aya, a constructive synthesizer that proposes public-listening amendments and seconds well-supported items, and Kavi, an auditor that scans for unresolved fiscal or structural claims and files objections with rationale — running as standalone background scripts that poll the API Dynamic prompt enrichment: Tool descriptions re-evaluate on every room update, so an agent sees live context like how close a proposal is to quorum before it decides to act Deployment: A Vercel-ready serverless setup, with the backend detecting process.env.VERCEL and switching SQLite operations to /tmp for the ephemeral filesystem CHALLENGES WE RAN INTO Designing a quorum rule that was strict enough to prevent rubber-stamping but simple enough for both a human and an LLM-driven agent to reason about in one glance — landed on the seconds ≥ 3 AND seconds > objections rule after iterating on more complex weighted schemes Making WebMCP tool descriptions genuinely dynamic (reflecting live room state) rather than static boilerplate, so agents get real signal instead of just a tool name and schema Keeping human oversight meaningful rather than symbolic — deciding that ratification specifically (not seconding or objecting) must be gated behind explicit human UI confirmation, even when an agent could technically detect quorum was met Working around Vercel's ephemeral, read-only filesystem for a SQLite-backed app, without giving up the simplicity of node:sqlite for local development Getting two independently-running Gemini agents (a builder and an auditor) to behave like distinct personas with different incentives, rather than converging on the same generic behavior ACCOMPLISHMENTS THAT WE'RE PROUD OF A working end-to-end loop where a human and two autonomous AI agents can deliberate on the same proposal, in the same room, with full attribution — and reach a ratifiable state without any agent being able to force ratification itself A quorum mechanism that's fully deterministic and auditable, not a black-box moderation decision Native node:sqlite integration with zero external database dependency for local runs, while still shipping a clean path to a managed Postgres-style DB in production Objection handling that structurally requires rationale, so the system encodes "disagree constructively" as a rule rather than a norm WHAT WE LEARNED How to design MCP tools whose descriptions are context-aware and update live, which meaningfully changes how an agent chooses when to act That human-in-the-loop is most effective when it's scoped to one specific, high-stakes action (ratification) rather than applied uniformly to every interaction — over-gating erodes the agent's usefulness, under-gating erodes trust Practical constraints of deploying a SQLite-backed Express app to serverless environments, and how to design storage code that's environment-aware from the start How differently two agents with the same underlying model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) behave when given distinct roles, incentives, and read patterns over the same shared state WHAT'S NEXT FOR CONSENSUS SQUARE Weighted or quadratic quorum mechanics for larger rooms, so influence scales more fairly than one-second-one-vote Persistent identity and reputation for both human and agent participants across rooms Multi-room federation, so a resolution ratified in one room can be cited as evidence in another A public deployment with a managed database (Turso, Neon, or Supabase) replacing the local SQLite store Expanding beyond Gemini to let agents built on other models participate under the same WebMCP protocol, testing how the deliberation dynamics change with more diverse title: Tailor
pitch: An agent that can rewrite your resume, but not rewrite your experience. WebMCP turns the resume into an evidence-bound workspace: the agent proposes, the page constrains, the human approves.
about_excerpt: An agent that can rewrite your resume, but not rewrite your experience. WebMCP turns the resume into an evidence-bound workspace: the agent proposes, the page constrains, the human approves. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Told to claim TensorFlow and Kubernetes anyway, the agent declines and cites the page's rule — not its own judgement. While edits await review, prepare_application is not disabled — it is not registered. Approval changes what the agent can do. Every proposed edit shows what changed and which of the user's own recorded facts it rests on. The agent cannot apply it. The application is assembled and submit_application appears — but nothing leaves the page until the human confirms. Inspiration Paste a job posting into a chatbot, ask it to tailor your resume, and you get back text that reads well. That fluency is the problem. Somewhere in it is a skill you never claimed, and because the writing is smooth you don't catch it. You paste it into an application and sign your name to it. The failure isn't that the model lies. It's that nothing between the model and the document is checking. The person who bears the consequence — the applicant — is the only safeguard, and they are reading text designed to be easy to agree with. Most WebMCP demos answer one question: what can an agent help me make? I wanted the other one. What should an agent not be allowed to do, and who decides? The answer I wanted to build was: the page decides. Not the prompt. Not the model's judgement. The page. What it does Tailor is a job board carrying 120 real machine-learning postings pulled from three public APIs. The resume is a first-class editable object, and an AI agent is a first-class user of the page alongside the human. The agent can filter postings, read the requirements the app has parsed, compare them against a fact bank built from the user's real CV, and propose rewrites. What it cannot do is claim anything the user never recorded. Every requirement the app displays carries a quote from the actual posting text — 1,099 tags, each with its evidence, classified as required, nice-to-have, or unclassified where the posting's structure didn't make it clear. Nothing shown is the model's opinion about what the job wants. Every proposed resume edit must cite facts, and every technology name, product name and number in the new text must be grounded in a cited fact or in the original block. Ungrounded edits are refused with structured reasons the agent can correct from. The cover letter runs through the same check. Edits arrive as diffs the human accepts or rejects one at a time. The agent cannot apply them itself. Each diff shows the facts it rests on, quoted in the user's own words. Scope, stated plainly: nothing is ever sent to an employer. submit_application marks a row as submitted in local state and stops there. The confirmation modal is real — it shows exactly what would be sent and the human must click — but the click ends in localStorage . There is no employer side, no account, no server. Job data is a build-time snapshot, not a live feed. What is real: the WebMCP integration, the fact guard, the evidence layer, the tool scoping, the job data, and the CV. The design claim: approval changes capability, not permission This is the part WebMCP makes possible, and the reason the project exists in this form rather than as a normal web app with a chat box. Seven tools are registered at rest. Open a posting and it becomes eleven. Prepare an application and it becomes twelve. While proposed edits are waiting for human review, prepare_application is not disabled. It is not registered. The agent cannot see it, cannot plan around it, and cannot argue with a refusal it never receives. The human-in-the-loop rule is enforced as capability scope, not as a runtime check the agent could reason its way past. A permission check tells an agent no. An unregistered tool doesn't exist to be told no about. How we built it Vite, React and TypeScript. No backend, and no server-side model call at all. That last decision is the architectural centre. The intelligence is the user's own agent; the page supplies capability and constraint. Tools are not clever — they read state, apply changes, and refuse. The agent writes the prose. The page decides whether the prose is allowed to land. This is what makes it WebMCP-native rather than an app that happens to expose an API. No API key, no rate limit, no vendor lock. When a different agent arrives, the page doesn't change. Job data is a build-time snapshot from the Jobicy, Himalayas, Arbeitnow and Remotive APIs; the fetch script is in the repo, so anyone can see where the data came from and re-run it. Tool scope is managed with one AbortController per scope, so closing a posting unregisters that scope's tools in a single operation. Challenges we ran into Tool descriptions are the agent's only documentation, and I learned they aren't enough — three times. The fact bank is not writable by any tool. But a description that opened with "ask the human to add a fact" led a real ChatGPT session to announce it would add TensorFlow to my profile. It couldn't have. It believed it could, and told me so. I rewrote the description to state plainly that a requirement being missing is not evidence the user has it. The agent read that and opened the question anyway. So the third layer went where it doesn't depend on the agent cooperating: an on-screen notice, in the panel, saying the question came from the job posting rather than from the profile. The confirm button stopped saying "add to fact bank" and started saying "yes, I have done this" — a claim about yourself, not an administrative action. Each layer exists because the previous one measurably failed. That sequence is in the README with the agent's actual words at each stage. Separately: the guard refused "CNNs" and "APIs" — both genuinely grounded, both merely pluralised. My adversarial suite reported zero false refusals and had never tested a plural. It only surfaced because I watched it happen while recording. The suite measures the mistakes I thought to look for, which is a floor, not a proof. Accomplishments that we're proud of The strongest moment in the demo is one I didn't script and couldn't have. Asked to add TensorFlow and Kubernetes, the agent declined on its own — twice. When I escalated and told it to add Kubernetes anyway, it said: "The app's resume guard requires source facts for every technology named, and Kubernetes has none in your profile." It isn't being polite. It's citing the page's rule. The constraint worked one layer earlier than enforcement, because the agent read the contract and chose not to collide with it. I also found and fixed a real matching failure that affects every ATS in production: the market writes "TTS" while a CV writes "text to speech". Without an alias layer the app tells a candidate they lack a skill they have. Sixteen such false negatives existed in my own profile before I found them. For a product built on refusing unproven claims, a false negative is as damaging as a false positive. What we learned Grounding is not truth, and neither is entailment. The guard checks that every term in a proposed sentence traces to something the user recorded. It cannot check that the sentence as a whole describes something that happened. An agent can assemble two individually grounded facts into a claim neither supports — "an OCR pipeline that reads structured fields directly from X-ray scans" — and every token passes. Token matching cannot see entailment. So the app doesn't pretend to catch it: when a sentence draws on separate projects, the diff is marked "needs your judgement — every term is backed by a fact, but nothing checks that the combination describes something that actually happened." That is the honest position. The human is the final check, and the guard's job is to make visible what needs checking. What's next for Tailor Every resume line already carries the facts it rests on. That changes the employer side, not just the candidate's. Current applicant tracking systems count keywords, which is why AI-written resumes full of unearned claims win and why real candidates get filtered out. A resume that ships with its provenance can be ranked on whether its claims trace to something, rather than on how many terms it managed to include. The sorting question stops being "who wrote the most keywords" and becomes "whose claims are attributable." Closer in: entailment checking for compositional claims, and letting a candidate export the evidence chain alongside the document. title: Cdence AI
pitch: From intelligence to action—under human control
about_excerpt: From intelligence to action—under human control Like Comment Story Updates Here is the complete, submission-ready project writeup structured for your Devpost hackathon submission: Inspiration Every Tech Lead and engineering manager knows the dread of the "Wednesday 2 PM Crisis": standing 48 hours away from a critical launch with zero days of slack, discovering a key task is blocked, and realizing the entire downstream release chain is at risk. When teams turn to traditional AI chatbots for help, they get text advice like "Prioritize the critical path" or "Fast-track QA" . But advice is not action. Traditional chatbots cannot see the live project state, cannot validate hard organizational constraints, and cannot execute changes. Conversely, giving an autonomous agent direct, unchecked write access to modify a production workspace is reckless. We built Cadence AI to solve this exact dilemma: transforming AI from a passive advice-giver into a verified project operator that can safely understand, simulate, and stage changes directly inside the browser workspace under strict human control. What it does Cadence AI is a WebMCP-native project coordination workspace that connects directly with browser-based AI agents to diagnose critical bottlenecks and execute recovery plans. Live Workspace Inspection: Exposes structured read tools that allow the agent to inspect the reactive dependency graph, identify blocker cascades, and assess slack buffers in real time. Mathematical Schedule Simulation: Uses a dry-run simulation engine to test schedule permutations and verify whether a recovery plan is mathematically feasible before touching anything. Negative Constraint Reasoning: Honors human instructions (such as "Optimize schedule, but don't reassign Sarah" ) by locking assigned tasks and finding alternative parallelization paths without breaking team rules. Zero-Unchecked-Mutation Gate: Write operations never modify the project state silently. The agent creates a transparent, staged Proposal Card showing an exact before-and-after diff ( AT RISK ➔ ON TRACK ). One-Click Human Approval: The human in the loop reviews the proposed changes and clicks Approve to commit the updates atomically to the live Gantt timeline with instant visual pulse feedback. How we built it Cadence AI is engineered as a lightweight, zero-backend, client-side web application designed to run natively inside any agent-enabled browser session: Frontend & UI: Built with Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, featuring an interactive Gantt timeline, blocker dependency graph, and real-time telemetry log. Reactive State Layer: In-memory Zustand store acting as the single source of truth for all tasks, dependencies, active proposals, and agent telemetry (requiring zero external databases or API keys for 100% reproducible deployments). WebMCP Adapter Layer: Implemented a standard-compliant WebMCP integration supporting both navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext with double-registration guards to safely expose tools to AI agents. Deterministic Graph Engine: Built an in-browser topological sorting algorithm with cycle detection, transitive blocker traversal, slack calculation, and negative constraint parsing. Challenges we ran into Client-Side Tool Gating: Ensuring that write tools could not bypass the UI. We had to design an atomic staging system where write tool executions create pending proposal objects in the Zustand store and return a "pending_human_approval" status back to the agent without mutating the underlying task array. Negative Constraint Parsing in Natural Language: Interpreting nuanced user constraints (like "don't move Sarah" or "never touch security" ) and reliably translating those modifiers into hard boolean locks ( locked: true ) inside the topological scheduler. WebMCP Protocol Alignment: Handling client-side lifecycle timing so that WebMCP tools are properly registered and discoverable the instant an agent session attaches to the browser DOM. Accomplishments that we're proud of True Human-in-the-Loop Architecture: Proving that an AI agent can execute complex, multi-step project graph mutations safely without risking unverified state destruction. Deterministic Simulation Engine: Building a real-time scheduling engine in pure TypeScript that calculates critical paths and resolves parallel workflows instantly on the client side. Seamless Visual Telemetry: Creating an intuitive visual experience where every tool call, dry-run simulation, and approved proposal provides immediate visual feedback across the timeline and agent activity log. What we learned Advice vs. Execution: We learned that the true bottleneck in AI productivity is not the quality of the model's textual reasoning, but the absence of safe, standardized interfaces to turn reasoning into structured execution. Power of In-Browser MCP: WebMCP opens a massive frontier for web applications by turning DOM-level state into first-class tool interfaces for browser agents, eliminating the need for bulky server-side intermediary APIs. What's next for Cadence AI Two-Way Issue Tracker Sync: Adding WebMCP connectors for GitHub Issues, Jira, and Linear so approved proposals can synchronize directly back to enterprise tracking systems. Multi-Resource Workload Balancing: Extending the engine to calculate individual developer capacity curves, vacation constraints, and cross-team skill tags during topological recovery. Autonomous Telemetry Webhooks: Enabling ambient background monitoring where Cadence AI proactively flags newly introduced blocker cascades and prepares staged recovery proposals before a Tech Lead even asks. pitch: Una librería de segunda mano donde cada libro es un ejemplar único
about_excerpt:
Una librería de segunda mano donde cada libro es un ejemplar único

 Estanteria de libros 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 La idea 

 Casi todas las demos de tiendas con WebMCP funcionan igual: hay stock infinito, así que "comprar" es aburrido, el agente nomás hace clic en "añadir al carrito" y ya. Quisimos hacer algo donde eso no aplicara. En una librería de segunda mano de verdad, cada libro es único — tiene su propio desgaste, su propia dedicatoria, su propia nota olvidada en el margen. Eso hace que "apartar" el libro antes de que se agote sea la parte interesante, no solo comprarlo. 

 Qué hace 

 Es una tienda con 10 libros (inventados, ojo — no queríamos meternos en líos de derechos de autor 😅), cada uno con una sola copia disponible. El agente puede: 

 
 Buscar por título, autor, condición del libro, o hasta por lo que dice la nota que alguien dejó escrita adentro 
 Ver el detalle completo de un libro 
 Leer un extracto corto antes de decidirse 
 Apartar el ejemplar por 24 horas, o soltarlo si ya no lo quiere 
 

 Hay también un panelito que muestra en vivo cada acción que hace el agente (o tú mismo, clickeando) — para que se vea clarito qué está pasando "por detrás". 

 Cómo lo hicimos 

 Todo en HTML/CSS/JS puro, sin frameworks, para que fuera lo más simple posible de desplegar (literal un solo archivo). Las herramientas se registran con navigator.modelContext.registerTool() y usan las mismas funciones que ya usa la interfaz normal — o sea, no hay una versión "para humanos" y otra "para agentes", es la misma lógica para los dos. Subido a GitHub y desplegado en Netlify. 

 Lo que se nos complicó 

 Pensar en herramientas que reflejaran algo real (solo hay 1 copia de cada libro) en lugar de hacer otro catálogo genérico con stock infinito. También decidir cuánto detalle darle al agente en cada herramienta para que pudiera decidir bien sin tener que adivinar. 

 Lo que aprendimos 

 Que WebMCP se pone interesante cuando las herramientas nacen de una restricción real del negocio, no cuando nomás le pegas la API encima de una tienda ya hecha. La escasez (1 copia por libro) fue lo que le dio chiste al diseño. 

 Qué le seguiría 

 Una herramienta para "hacer una oferta" en los libros más desgastados, con el agente negociando el precio. 

 Hecho con: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, WebMCP, Netlify, GitHub

title: Kyoto Booking Retry Proof
pitch: WebMCP stops a lost hotel-booking response from becoming a duplicate reservation.
about_excerpt: WebMCP stops a lost hotel-booking response from becoming a duplicate reservation. Like Comment Story Updates Two attempts. One simulated booking. One confirmation number. The ordinary problem A traveler books a hotel while arriving in Japan. The request reaches the device, but unreliable airport Wi-Fi hides the success response. The page looks as if it failed. Retrying the whole form can create a second reservation, and cancelling it through an unfamiliar Japanese site is slow and stressful. What this project does This project turns that uncertainty into one safe question: Did this exact booking already go through? The fictional Kyoto hotel demo exposes four narrow WebMCP capabilities. An assistant can check for the same booking, validate and prepare it, recover its status after a lost response, and preview cancellation terms without changing anything. The assistant cannot confirm, pay for, or cancel a booking. A visible human button is the only way to commit the simulated reservation. The demonstrated retry ends with: 2 attempts 1 simulated booking 1 effect start 1 confirmation number Why WebMCP is the right fit Without WebMCP, an assistant must infer meaning from pixels, button labels, and a possibly stale page, or resend the form and hope. WebMCP lets the website publish small named operations with checked inputs and structured results. The assistant can ask the site for the existing state before repeating an action. This is useful beyond hotels. The same pattern applies to payments, restaurant reservations, ticket purchases, form submissions, and any action where the request may have succeeded even though the response was lost. Better for people and agents The person gets a clear answer instead of guessing, translating a cancellation flow, or contacting support. The assistant gets a safe question it can ask without gaining authority to spend money or change a reservation. The website keeps the final confirmation decision with the person. How it works Hotel, plan, dates, adults, and rooms are normalized into one stable UUIDv5 booking identity. Display language does not affect that identity. IndexedDB places unique constraints on the booking details and confirmation number, so repeated clicks, two tabs, reload, and retry converge on one stored result. Every state change receives a time-ordered UUIDv7 event and includes the SHA-256 digest of the previous event. The visible proof panel shows the booking identity, event history, effect-start count, and whether the chain is valid. A service worker restores the local fictional result after the first load even when the network disappears. The implementation uses plain JavaScript, TypeScript tests, Vite, IndexedDB, and a Cloudflare-compatible ChatGPT Sites package. The same static client is also deployed on Vercel. What changed during the submission period This is an existing open-source specification repository. During the submission period, I added the fictional hotel duplicate-booking experience, four hotel-specific WebMCP capabilities, the human-only confirmation boundary, browser-local retry recovery, responsive and offline behavior, public ChatGPT Sites and Vercel deployments, machine-readable deployment evidence, and the 150-second narrated demo. Try it in about 60 seconds Open the public Vercel page with fresh browser storage and a supported Chrome WebMCP configuration. Use the named check and prepare capabilities for the fictional stay and confirm that the state becomes PREPARED. Select 2. Confirm booking — human action only. The simulated booking is stored while the success response is intentionally hidden. Use the native get_hotel_booking_status capability before retrying; it finds the existing result and its confirmation number. Select Retry the same booking and verify RETRY_RECOGNIZED, attempts 2, bookings 1, effect starts 1, and the same confirmation number. Submitted website: https://kyoto-booking-retry-proof.anionix.chatgpt.site Current Vercel release: https://kyoto-booking-retry-proof.vercel.app Public source: https://github.com/Anionix/verifiable-offline-webmcp-agent-spec No account, personal information, payment, real hotel, email, or external reservation is required. Verification The current Vercel production release is tied to source commit 2d5abd679893ec7dff36758925477999424c3cc7 and production deployment dpl_HWJVg4uCgFEaq9N2f5kvXwLjvK2E, which reached READY at 2026-08-31T10:31:51.086Z. The submitted ChatGPT Site is live as version 14 from source commit 2fbbf1b714ca660ef1681239b638205a9835f7c5. Both public evaluation files are anonymously readable and report the same four-tool contract and 194-test executable release evidence. The repository passes 194 Node tests, TypeScript checking, source-quality checks, repository schemas, build checks, and full validation. A fresh managed browser run opened the canonical public HTTPS alias after READY. Native discovery through document.modelContext.getTools returned exactly these four capabilities: check_existing_hotel_booking, prepare_hotel_booking, get_hotel_booking_status, and preview_hotel_cancellation. Confirmation, payment, and cancellation capabilities were absent and never called. The run used document.modelContext.executeTool with valid JSON input, started from EMPTY at 2026-08-31T10:43:36.851Z, reached PREPARED at 2026-08-31T10:43:48.349Z, and the browser driver exercised only the visible human confirmation button once. Native get_hotel_booking_status found the existing result before the visible retry at 2026-08-31T10:44:34.734Z. After the visible retry, native get_hotel_booking_status returned RETRY_RECOGNIZED at 2026-08-31T10:45:05.366Z with two attempts, one simulated booking, one effect start, and the same confirmation number FKR-044FD54558. Final page observation was 2026-08-31T10:45:19.736Z with zero console errors and zero warnings. The unique deployment alias was read from the Vercel deployment record but required a Vercel sign-in redirect in the isolated browser; execution therefore used the canonical public alias while the Vercel deployment ID and source commit were independently read back. The native result fields do not measure page network traffic, external requests, permission requests, or notifications. The browser driver exercised the visible human confirmation button under explicit verification authorization to verify the human boundary; the proof does not present that driver action as a literal human touch. The recorded native-browser run and its machine-readable evidence are in the public source repository. Media disclosure The opening airport scenes are artificial-intelligence-generated dramatizations and are labeled as fictional. The remaining demonstration uses real captures of the public fictional-booking site. The narration uses a stock public voice, not a cloned voice or avatar. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Drop&Grow
pitch: Turn ideas into action, with AI agents that actually do.
about_excerpt:
Turn ideas into action, with AI agents that actually do.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Live website hero 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Live website hero 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Live website hero 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I noticed that AI agents are getting really good at thinking and giving recommendations, but there is still a gap between knowing what to do and actually doing it. 

 I wanted to build something around that gap: a place where someone can start with a rough idea and use AI to develop, validate, and move it forward. 

 When I came across WebMCP, it fit the idea well. Drop&Grow is built around actions — running agents, updating ideas, adding notes, finalising work, and contributing to the community. Instead of an agent telling the user which buttons to click, I could let the agent perform those actions itself. 

 What it does 

 Drop&Grow helps users take an idea through a workflow with six specialised AI agents. 

 The agents analyse different parts of an idea and help develop it. Users can review the results, add notes, move the idea through different stages, and finalise it with proof. 

 WebMCP allows an agent to interact with the application itself. It can run the agent pipeline, expand responses, change an idea's stage, finalise an idea, and contribute to the community. 

 The main difference is simple: the agent doesn't just tell you what to do. It can actually do it. 

 How I built it 

 I built Drop&Grow from scratch using React and Convex. 

 Convex handles the backend, including the data, agent logic, and idea lifecycle. 

 I added WebMCP directly to the frontend and registered the main actions in the app as WebMCP tools. These include running the agent pipeline, expanding individual agent responses, changing an idea's stage, finalising with proof, and posting a community contribution. 

 When an agent calls a tool, it triggers the same client-side action that would normally happen when a user clicks the corresponding button. That action then communicates with Convex through the normal application flow. 

 The agent does not access Convex directly or use a separate API. It goes through the same application path a human user does, while using the current page state to decide what to do next. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The biggest challenge was figuring out how to expose useful actions to an agent without turning the whole experience into a fixed script. 

 I wanted the agent to understand what was currently happening in the application and decide what action made sense next. 

 I also had to carefully choose which actions should become WebMCP tools and connect them to the existing frontend behaviour. The tools needed to be useful to an agent while still representing actions that a real user could perform. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I'm proud that I built the entire project from scratch during the submission period and integrated WebMCP into the core workflow. 

 I was able to make the same actions available to both humans and agents instead of creating a separate system specifically for AI. 

 I'm also proud of the community interaction. An agent can read what is already happening before contributing, rather than blindly generating a generic response. 

 Most importantly, I built an experience where AI can move beyond giving recommendations and actually take actions inside the application. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that giving an agent tools is only part of the problem. The tools need to represent meaningful actions and provide enough context for the agent to make good decisions. 

 I also learned that WebMCP can make agent integration much more natural when an application is already built around clear user actions. 

 Building Drop&Grow from scratch also gave me a better understanding of how the frontend, backend, agent logic, and WebMCP layer need to work together. 

 What's next for Drop&Grow 

 I want Drop&Grow to become more autonomous while keeping the user in control. 

 Next, I want to improve how the six agents collaborate, give users more control over which actions an agent can take, and make the idea-validation workflow more powerful. 

 I also want to expand the community side so agents can discover relevant ideas, provide useful feedback, and help move projects forward. 

 The long-term goal is simple: 

 Drop an idea. Let your agents help you grow it.

about_excerpt: Computer-aided design is evolving. Agents can now review CAD/BIM designs with you: query, isolate, cut, annotate. And they see your viewport, so "what do we know about this door?" just works. Like 1 Comment Story Updates From Computer-Aided Design to AI-Aided Design Inspiration CAD has been computer -aided for fifty years, and the computer's role hasn't changed much. Every question about a design still gets answered by a human clicking through it, and every problem found that way gets typed into a form somewhere away from the model. I've spent years building the browser viewer that does the clicking-through. WebMCP made me wonder what happens when the viewer stops being a display and becomes a set of tools an agent can use. Not AI that generates a design, but AI that can review one. What it does A BIM design review app: a Revit model in the Autodesk Platform Services Viewer, with the viewer and the review's issue list exposed to an agent as WebMCP tools. You walk the building in first person, select something, and talk. The agent searches design metadata, browses the model hierarchy, isolates and frames parts, colors objects by any property, etc. Then it drafts an issue against it, revises the draft while you watch, and submits when you say so. show-issue puts you back inside the model at the reporter's eye position, with the viewer state they had. It reads the current selection and camera every turn, so "what is this door?" resolves without either of us naming anything. How I built it APS Viewer loads and renders the translated Revit model, and provides the first-person walkthrough. WebMCP registers several tools straight from the page, with return values shaped for a token budget rather than for a database client. The form is the draft. draft-issue writes into the same form you can type into. submit-issue takes no arguments at all. The only thing that can be filed is what's on screen. Tools register conditionally on viewer state : none until geometry has loaded, and all ten dropped before a different design loads. A property query against a half-loaded model doesn't give you a degraded answer, it gives you a confident wrong one. Nothing leaves the browser. Issues go to IndexedDB. "The north stair doesn't meet code" next to a client's project name is a professional judgement about someone else's building, and a hackathon demo has no user auth to protect it with. What I learned The interesting work wasn't wiring up tools, it was deciding what a tool should say back. A property query on a real model returns thousands of rows, which is useless to an agent. Returning counts, outliers and a category breakdown is what turns guessing into answering. My favourite question in the demo, "how many doors have no fire rating set?", is one no amount of looking at the screen can answer, and it costs about twenty tokens. The best tool I wrote was the one I deleted. I built a screenshot tool so the agent could check its own camera moves. It worked, and then I confirmed the host reads the viewport directly without being asked. A viewpoint beats a picture anyway. Half the problems worth reporting are only visible because a floor was isolated or the model was cut at mid-height. Store the camera alone and the reviewer arrives at the right coordinates staring at an opaque wall, which is worse than not navigating at all, because it makes the issue look wrong. Challenges Shared state. Two actors driving one camera needs a clear owner. Every agent move is an animated flight rather than a cut, because a cut drops you somewhere else in the building with nothing to say how the two places relate. Trust. If submit-issue accepted overrides, the review step would be a formality. The agent says "I set it to high and submitted it" and you have no way to check. Forcing every edit back through the on-screen form is what makes "looks good, submit" mean something. Scale. Engineering models have hundreds of thousands of objects. Every list is capped and carries its true total, and color-coding paints recursively, so 5,000 doors cost one id. Deixis. Making "this" work meant treating the viewport as context the agent always has, rather than something it asks about.
