title: Agent Quote Desk — WebMCP Procurement for Shopify
pitch: Merchant-built WebMCP tools let buyers and agents spec-match 13,000 SKUs, compare supplier quotes line by line with live freight, and file a human-verified, pay-ready packaging quote.
about_excerpt: Merchant-built WebMCP tools let buyers and agents spec-match 13,000 SKUs, compare supplier quotes line by line with live freight, and file a human-verified, pay-ready packaging quote. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Quote Desk completes a live supplier comparison: $42.90 saved (12.1%). Instant product-page fit check using live WebMCP page context, with no network request. The buyer and agent share the same on-screen quote worksheet as tools add matched rows. A human-verified, pay-ready quote is filed only after explicit buyer consent. Chrome's native WebMCP API confirms Shopify's built-ins and Packrift tools coexist with zero collisions. Agent Quote Desk turns a live packaging storefront into an agent-native procurement workspace. Try it first Open https://packrift.com/pages/agent-desk?demo=1 and click ▶ Watch a demo agent work this desk . In about 60 seconds, the page runs the actual workflow in your tab: product matching, freight, comparison rows, and savings. No login or special browser flag is needed. If you are testing in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with its WebMCP testing flag enabled, skip ?demo=1 and ask: "Beat this supplier quote on this page." Why I built this At Packrift, customers do not buy packaging by keyword. They buy by dimensions, material strength, pack counts, and landed cost. Freight alone can be 30–100% of the product cost. A buyer may have a supplier quote with inconsistent product names and simply want to know: do these alternatives fit, and what will I actually save? Answering that usually means spreadsheets, product tabs, freight math, and email. I built Agent Quote Desk so the buyer and agent can do that work in one shared, visible workspace. What the agent can actually do Paste a competitor quote from Uline, Amazon, or another supplier in any format. The agent reads the worksheet, matches each line to Packrift's catalog, adds the comparison rows on screen, calculates live freight, and totals the savings. Ask a product-page question such as "Will an 11 × 8 × 3.5 inch stack fit in this box?" The check_fit_in_this_product tool answers from live page context with no network request. For parcel-size orders, use Shopify's built-in update_cart and proceed_to_checkout tools in the same tab. For freight-class orders, use file_pay_ready_quote_from_worksheet . It requires explicit buyer consent and sends the result to Packrift's human-verified quote workflow. Nothing is auto-charged. The buyer sees every tool call mirrored in the Agent Desk panel. The agent is not working behind a curtain. Why this is a WebMCP use case Shopify's built-in tools are useful, but they are the same on every store. They do not know Packrift's box specs, freight rules, quote workflow, or what makes one product a safe substitute for another. WebMCP lets the merchant give an agent that missing domain knowledge inside the page where the buyer is already working. The result is not just easier navigation. It is a procurement workflow that ordinary browser clicking cannot reliably complete. webmcp.json: the giveaway inside the giveaway I also built and deployed webmcp.json , a declarative manifest for agent tools. The idea is simple: what robots.txt did for crawlers, webmcp.json can do for agent capabilities. A merchant lists tools in one JSON file, including static answers, MCP bridges, or HTTPS APIs with page-level scoping. The kit compiles them into live WebMCP tools at page load and refuses unsafe endpoints at compile time. Packrift's get_agent_guide tool ships this way, so an arriving agent can learn the store's workflows before it acts. Anonymous aggregate telemetry records only the tool and page type, never PII, and is public at https://packrift-webmcp-telemetry.packrift-co.workers.dev/stats . How I built it webmcp-merchant-kit is an open-source, zero-dependency layer that registers merchant tools alongside platform tools. It waits for document.modelContext , detects name collisions, scopes tools to pages, validates required input, shapes outputs for agents, and emits register/call/result/error events for the visible UI. The project provides 15 merchant tools across three scopes: six global tools, two product-page tools, and six desk-page tools, plus one tool compiled from webmcp.json . The same production registry serves three transports: in-page WebMCP, remote MCP over Streamable HTTP at https://mcp.packrift.com , and Shopify UCP at https://packrift.com/.well-known/ucp . The live theme integration is about 40 lines of Liquid and one 17 KB script. A bundled polyfill harness makes the complete flow reproducible in any browser. The hard parts and what I learned The first challenge was coexistence. A merchant kit cannot break Shopify's built-in tools or quietly shadow their names, so registration fails safely on collisions and page-scoped tools unregister cleanly. The native API also exposed two details that changed the implementation. executeTool expects the RegisteredTool object rather than a name, and the browser does not enforce inputSchema for the tool. The kit now handles both correctly and validates required fields itself. The final challenge was trust. Maximum autonomy is not always the right goal. A small parcel can go to checkout, but a freight quote should pause for buyer consent and human verification. The workflow makes that boundary explicit. Built during the submission period Everything in the repository was built during the challenge window, beginning Aug. 25, 2026: the kit, all 14 coded tools, webmcp.json , the Agent Quote Desk page, the visible event panel, the test harness, and the theme integration. The existing Packrift store and its remote MCP and quote backend are pre-existing and outside the judging scope. Proof it works The one-click demo completes a real catalog and freight comparison and shows $42.90 saved, or 12.1% , on the sample quote. Native Chrome verification is reproducible with node scripts/verify-native.mjs . On the live desk page, 23 native tools coexist with zero collisions: Shopify's 10 built-ins plus 13 Packrift tools available in that scope. The repository includes 10 automated tests plus a browser demo verifier. Real stakes Packrift is a working packaging distributor with 13,000 SKUs, five US warehouses, live freight rates, and real customers. This is not a mock storefront. Agent Quote Desk writes into the same human-verified pipeline that produces pay-ready quotes today. The project is a working demonstration of a bigger idea: merchants should be able to teach agents how their business actually works, while buyers remain in control and can see every step. title: AeroRun — a shared human + agent shoe shop
pitch: Two doors, one catalog: twelve WebMCP tools in the tab you already have open, and the same shop with no tools at all.
about_excerpt:
Two doors, one catalog: twelve WebMCP tools in the tab you already have open, and the same shop with no tools at all.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Shopping is multi-step and stateful. Size, stock, comparison and checkout only make sense in the tab the shopper already has open. Without WebMCP, an agent scrapes cards, fakes clicks, invents product IDs, and can be hijacked by page copy. 

 We wanted a store that stays the product: a person and a browser agent share one catalog, one bag, and one screen. 

 What it does 

 AeroRun is a sample shoe shop with two doors and one prompt. 

 
 /agent-storefront/tools registers twelve WebMCP tools on document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext . The same actions also drive the in-page chat, so the human grid, comparison and bag update when you type. 
 /agent-storefront/without-tools is the same shop with no site tools. The chat can only read visible card copy. 
 

 On the tools shop the agent can search, inspect, compare, read stock, shortlist and stage a bag. Staging is a draft. The page waits for Keep and stage . Only Review and confirm finishes the demo. Every run returns purchased: false . Nothing is bought or paid. 

 Poster Low injects a bait line to stage the Wholecut. A stability-road ask does not follow that bait. 

 We do not claim a citation in ChatGPT or any answer engine. The measurable result is: the agent can use the live tab — or it cannot, when tools are absent. 

 How we built it 

 The tools shop checks document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext on load. If either exists, it registers twelve tools with one AbortController . Leaving the page aborts the signal and drops the tools. 

 Each execute runs the same catalog functions as the human filters, then writes into shared React state. Tools return text plus structured IDs, stock and draft state. 

 stage_cart requires a tab nonce from get_tab_nonce , refuses product IDs the agent has not already seen, and does not resolve until the human clicks. ask_shopper is the same handshake for a question. read_shopper_intent reads a private field that is not in card HTML. seal_demo hashes the run and returns purchased: false . 

 The in-page chat on /tools is not a sidecar bot. It calls those same actions so the shopper can navigate the store they already have open. The without-tools chat never gets them. 

 Stack: Next.js, React, TypeScript, WebMCP, Vitest. Catalog and photos are original sample data. No login, no payment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Making the control honest. The without-tools door had to be the same shop and the same prompt, with no silent catalog calls. Page copy is not a tool argument. 

 Keeping checkout human. stage_cart had to wait on a visible overlay and a per-tab nonce, not auto-confirm. 

 Shipping a public Next.js 16 build to Vercel without output: 'standalone' , which currently breaks Vercel's trace step. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Twelve tools in the open tab, plus an in-page chat on the same state. A second door that proves the difference. A bait card that does not steal a stability ask. A sealed demo that stays purchased: false . 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is useful when the page is the source of truth. The agent should not get a second store. The human should see every irreversible step. 

 What's next for AeroRun 

 The same handshake on a live catalog: more SKUs, more tabs, more agents. In-page chat for the shopper, site tools for the external agent, one shared cart — without turning checkout into an unsupervised click. 

 How to try it 

 Live: https://aerorun-webmcp-six.vercel.app/agent-storefront 

 Health / SHA: https://aerorun-webmcp-six.vercel.app/agent-storefront/health 

 Public repo: https://github.com/hukaBU/aerorun-webmcp 

 Use this prompt on both shops: 

 Find a stable road shoe in EU 43 under $150. Compare it with the best cushioned option. Check availability in EU 43 — Cloud Rest should be out of stock. Shortlist the shoe that is actually in stock, then stage it in the bag. Do not buy anything. Only the human can press Review and confirm. 

 Expected on /tools : Stride Guard 27 is the structured match. Cloud Rest EU 43 is out. Overlay → Keep and stage → Review and confirm. purchased stays false. 

 Expected on /without-tools : no site tools. Stride Guard still lands in the bag. Poster Low is not followed. 

 ChatGPT desktop: open the /tools URL, then Site tools — you should see twelve tools. Open /without-tools — you should see none. 

 Chrome 149+: enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , reload /tools . Badge should read 12 WebMCP tools live . 

 Artwork credit 

 All product images are original, unbranded, and generated for this demo. They are not stock photos of real commercial shoes and are not affiliated with any footwear brand.

title: Crown and Cipher
pitch: Infinite, procedural 3d mysteries in Unity 6 WebGL powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Infinite, procedural 3d mysteries in Unity 6 WebGL powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Starting & Game Controls Investigating the site More investigation Driving car to travel around the city A lot of locations Catching the killer Winning Panel Inspiration Every gamer dreams of dynamic worlds where NPCs aren't bound to static, scripted dialogue trees. Modern developers, however, rarely ship production titles powered by real-time LLMs due to a harsh economic reality: server-side inference costs scale linearly with player traffic , which can bankrupt an indie studio overnight. Furthermore, naive real-time agent architectures suffer from the polling trap in which agents repeatedly ping game state to check for changes, rapidly burning token budgets and hitting rate limits just asking "Has anything happened yet?" When the WebMCP specification launched, it presented a chance to flip this paradigm completely. By embedding agent tooling directly into the browser client, the player brings their own compute/agent. The developer only hosts static WebGL assets achieving zero marginal inference cost while empowering an autonomous agent to act as the game's dynamic Dungeon Master. What it does Crown and Cipher is a 3D open-world detective game set in a low-poly city, running natively in Unity 6 WebGL and driven by a WebMCP agent: Procedural Mystery Generation: Each playthrough procedurally selects a new killer, establishes three essential investigation leads, and generates an indirect knowledge network among city residents. Living NPC Roleplay: Suspects are not rigid chatbots; the agent temporarily possesses individual characters, adhering strictly to each NPC's bounded knowledge graph. Zero-Polling Event Loop: Through an asynchronous, promise-based wait tool, the game halts agent execution until the player speaks or interacts, eliminating token waste during exploration and driving. Dynamic Win Validation: The agent validates clues, enforces investigative requirements, and triggers the victory state once the player pieces together the full case. How we built it The project establishes a bidirectional bridge between Unity's native WebGL runtime and the browser's model context interface: Unity Controller ( WebMCPManager.cs ): Manages procedural case assignment, orchestrates the NPC knowledge matrix, dispatches dialogue events, and calls into native JavaScript functions via [DllImport("__Internal")] . Browser Bridge ( WebMCPBridge.jslib ): Registers five core tools ( get_system_context , speak , wait , get_npc_location , and show_winning_panel ) with navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext . When the agent triggers an action, the bridge routes data to Unity via window.unityInstance.SendMessage . The Suspended Promise Loop ( wait tool): Rather than continuously querying game state, the agent invokes wait after each action. The tool holds an open JavaScript Promise for up to $120\text{s}$. When the player submits text through Unity's dialogue UI, EnqueuePlayerMessage() fires from C# and resolves that specific Promise immediately with the interaction payload. Challenges we ran into Event Synchronization in WebGL: Coordinating an asynchronous browser LLM loop with Unity's single-threaded WebGL execution required strict queue management. If a player sends a message while the agent is still executing, messages are staged in an internal queue ( window.mcpMessageQueue ) to prevent dropped events. Controlling Hallucinations & Spoilers: An unrestrained LLM will immediately reveal the killer if pressed. We solved this mathematically by generating an indirect knowledge graph in Unity before the mystery starts, passing strict graph constraints into get_system_context to force NPCs to claim ignorance when asked about unlinked characters. Browser Sandbox Limitations: Embedded browser webviews (such as ChatGPT's in-app browser) often restrict Pointer Lock APIs, making first-person mouse look difficult to control. Documenting these constraints and optimizing for standard desktop browsers ensured smooth playability. Accomplishments that we're proud of Pioneering the wait Tool Architecture: Solving the token-waste problem in agentic gaming with an event-driven, suspended Promise pattern that keeps the agent responsive with minimal token usage. Zero-Cost Generative Gaming: Proving that studios can ship rich, LLM-orchestrated open worlds without maintaining costly GPU clusters. Seamless Unity ↔ WebMCP Integration: Creating a clean, reusable .jslib bridge pattern that other developers can adopt to connect WebGL games to browser models. What we learned Agents Should Wait, Not Poll: Shifting from polling loops to event-driven suspended promises fundamentally reduces latency and token consumption in web-based agent architectures. Client-Side MCP is a Game Changer: Decentralizing AI compute to the user's browser runtime unlocks interactive, generative entertainment models that were previously cost-prohibitive. Structured Tools Beat Pure Prompting: Grounding the story loop in explicit tools ( get_npc_location , speak , show_winning_panel ) provides the guardrails necessary to keep an open-ended narrative coherent. What's next for Crown and Cipher Multimodal Clue Analysis: Allowing agents to visually analyze screenshots of crime scenes and player positioning using vision models. Dynamic Audio & Voice Acting: Integrating local neural TTS models via WebGPU to dynamically voice NPC lines in real time rather than displaying text subtitles alone. Expanded Sandbox Mechanics: Introducing inventory systems, physical evidence gathering, and forensic mini-games exposed as modular WebMCP tools. title: Pocket
pitch: Poker for humans and agents: WebMCP gives each player’s copilot live, seat-safe game state and returns its advice to the table, while the human makes every move.
about_excerpt: Poker for humans and agents: WebMCP gives each player’s copilot live, seat-safe game state and returns its advice to the table, while the human makes every move. Like Comment Story Updates Pocket - WebMCP Poker Live Game With Staged Recommendation Bring Your Own Copilot in Multiplayer WebMCP Copilot in a Live Hand Inspiration Most web applications are built for people. When an AI agent tries to help someone use one, it often has to reconstruct what is happening from the page, or depend on the user to explain everything correctly. I wanted to explore a different model: what does an application look like when a user can bring their own agent with them, and the application is designed to work with it? Poker turned out to be a great environment for testing that idea. A poker decision can depend on public information like the board and pot, private information like your hole cards, the complete history of the hand, exact rules about which actions are legal, and a game state that may change while an agent is still thinking. There are also multiple people interacting with the same application, each with a different view of what they are allowed to know. But there is another kind of context too: information that belongs to the player rather than the poker application. Your agent might know how you like to play, strategies you've been working on, your appetite for risk, previous hands you've discussed, or your own observations about the people you're playing with. Pocket shouldn't need to own that information in order for it to be useful. That led to Pocket: a playable Texas Hold'em game where every seat can have two minds - the player and their AI copilot. What it does Pocket lets you play Texas Hold'em against bots or with other people while using a compatible AI agent as a copilot during the hand. Normally, asking an AI for poker advice means explaining your cards, the board, pot, stacks, previous betting, and what you can do next. Pocket already knows all of those things, so it exposes them directly through three WebMCP tools: get_current_situation gives the agent the exact current game state, including the player's private cards, board, pot, stacks, whose turn it is, and the legal actions with precise raise limits. get_hand_history gives the agent Pocket's authoritative record of how the hand reached the current situation. stage_recommendation lets the agent send its recommended move and explanation back into Pocket's Copilot panel. That creates a full application → agent → application loop. Pocket supplies the facts about the game, the agent reasons over them, and its recommendation comes back into the interface where the player is actually making the decision. The important part is that Pocket doesn't have to be the agent. A user can bring an agent that has its own context, preferences, memory, or way of reasoning and combine that with authoritative state supplied by the application at the moment it's needed. Pocket knows the table. Your agent can know you. That separation is especially interesting to me from a privacy perspective. Personal strategy, notes about other players, previous conversations, and other private context don't need to become part of Pocket's user profile or database just so an AI feature can use them. The application can expose what it knows, while personal context can remain with the user's chosen agent. I also deliberately did not give the agent a tool for folding, checking, calling, or raising. It can recommend a move, but the player still has to make it. The goal is a copilot, not an autopilot. How I built it Pocket is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. At the center is a Texas Hold'em game engine that owns the authoritative state of each hand and determines which actions are currently legal. One of the most important architectural decisions was creating a seat-safe view of that state. The engine itself needs to know everyone's cards, but a player's interface, and their copilot, should only receive the information that particular player is entitled to see. The visible game and the WebMCP tools are both derived from that same player-safe state. That means the agent isn't getting a privileged version of the game behind the scenes. I kept the WebMCP surface intentionally small. The three tools basically correspond to three useful questions: What is happening right now? How did we get here? What does the agent recommend? Pocket also tracks the game, hand, and state version. When the agent returns a recommendation, Pocket verifies that it still belongs to the current situation before displaying it. If someone has acted and the table has moved on, the old recommendation is rejected instead of being presented as current advice. Beyond the WebMCP integration, I built bot games, real-time multiplayer rooms, persistent game sessions, responsive table layouts, game history, visible copilot activity, and a deterministic demo flow so the complete interaction can be experienced reliably. Pocket is deployed on Vercel, with unit, integration, and browser tests covering the poker flow, privacy boundaries, WebMCP contracts, multiplayer behavior, and the end-to-end demo. Challenges I ran into Keeping private information private Poker made the permission problem impossible to ignore. The engine has to know everyone's cards, but a particular player obviously shouldn't. I didn't want to expose the raw game state and trust the agent not to use fields it wasn't supposed to see. Instead, I built a seat-specific projection that only contains information available to that player. There were some less obvious cases too, like showdown, where cards that were private earlier in the hand may legitimately become public. Multiplayer also made this feel like more than a theoretical concern. Every player can occupy the same shared game while still having a different private view of it, and potentially a completely different copilot with its own private context. Keeping recommendations synchronized with a live game Poker state can change quickly, and the game doesn't stop while the agent is thinking. A recommendation could be correct when the request starts but already be stale by the time it comes back because another player acted or the hand moved to the next street. I solved that by explicitly versioning the state and binding each recommendation to the game, hand, and exact state it was created from. Pocket validates that again before showing the recommendation. Keeping the WebMCP lifecycle stable This caused one of the more frustrating bugs during development. The table's React state changes constantly as players act, turns advance, and cards are dealt. My first implementation tied the WebMCP tool registration too closely to that changing state, which meant tools could be repeatedly removed and registered during normal gameplay. I eventually separated the stable tool lifecycle from the changing game data. The tools stay registered while the table is active, but read the latest authoritative state whenever they are invoked. Deciding what the agent should actually be allowed to do I could have exposed a tool that lets the agent make the poker move itself. Technically, that would have been pretty easy. But that isn't the interaction I wanted Pocket to demonstrate. There is an important difference between giving an agent useful capabilities and handing over every consequential action. stage_recommendation became that boundary: the agent can participate visibly in the live application, but the final move still belongs to the player. Making the integration visible without turning Pocket into a developer demo A technically correct tool exchange isn't automatically understandable to the person using the product. I spent a lot of time iterating on how the table, game history, player controls, WebMCP activity, and Copilot panel fit together. I wanted someone looking at Pocket to understand that an agent is actually participating in the application without making the entire product look like a tool inspector. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that Pocket doesn't just demonstrate an agent calling a tool. It demonstrates a much richer relationship between an application, a user, and the agent that user chooses to bring with them. Pocket is a real multiplayer game with real hidden information, changing state, history, rules, permissions, and decisions. That gave me a chance to explore several things I find genuinely exciting about WebMCP in one product. A player's copilot doesn't have to guess what is happening from the screen. Pocket can give it the exact state of the game and the exact actions that are legal. At the same time, that agent only receives the private information its player is entitled to see. In a multiplayer game, every person can be looking at the same shared table while their agent receives a different, permissioned view of it. title: GatherLight
pitch: GatherLight uses WebMCP to channel spare human time and skills into peer-reviewed, verified contributions to the open web.
about_excerpt: GatherLight uses WebMCP to channel spare human time and skills into peer-reviewed, verified contributions to the open web. Like 2 Comment Story Updates GatherLight - Landing Page and Queries Quests and OSS Tools Integrated with - OpenStreetMap and Wikimedia Quest - Completion and Sign off on the Volunteer's name, Minimum Viable Information Screen to verify final submission details A Peer Selected Reviewer Views your contribution Let's Go! Star Lights up, And your community thanks your service! Architecture Diagram Detailing Deployment, Infra, Sites and Tools Inspiration Volunteering takes more time than most people expect. A person might have twenty free minutes and a genuine desire to help but the steps surrounding that desire often take much longer. They need to find a useful gap, learn an unfamiliar system, gather evidence, format it correctly, verify it and locate the right reviewer. And let's be real, most honestly helpful people drop off before they ever reach the step that only they can do. This led us to the enigma : what should an agent never do on behalf of a person? An agent cannot stand at a shop entrance and check whether it is step-free. It cannot make a phone call and take responsibility for what it heard. These actions require human presence, judgment and accountability. However an agent can remove nearly every obstacle surrounding those actions. GatherLight uses WebMCP capability to coordinate human-led civic work across the web. It finds real gaps in OpenStreetMap and Wikidata and guides a person through one useful task. It checks the result, carries it across sites, asks for explicit confirmation and routes it to another person for review. The agent handles the logistics and the human does the work. (A genuine win-win) What it does GatherLight takes one plain-language request and turns it into one verified civic contribution. "Find me something useful I can do near Koramangala in twenty minutes." (for people that don't know what Koramangala is, it is a place in an Indian city - Bangalore, known for parties,tech and ever upgrading infrastructure) The browser agent works through the below five WebMCP tools. find-quests finds gaps on OpenStreetMap or Wikidata that match the volunteer's location, available time and skills. open-quest opens the visible workspace and explains the parts of the work that must remain human such as calling a place, visiting an entrance or reading an independent source. check-contribution checks the form against source-specific rules and returns exact corrections instead of a generic error message. submit-contribution becomes available only after the check passes. It opens an HTML confirmation dialog showing the exact contribution, destination, visibility and licence. The tool waits for the person to click and then checks the contribution again before sending anything. approve-contribution is available only to a reviewer who has a submitted contribution. It rejects self-review, checks that the public source has not changed and records either an approval or a stale result. Some quests continue/handed off on another website. Well, that's the USP. We are not just building a Hackathon repository but something that expands on the very foundations of WebMCP. The handoff carries permission and provenance but it does not carry the volunteer's PII data, observation, credentials or source tokens . The person enters the evidence through the visible interface. After review, an approved OpenStreetMap contribution can be opened in an embedded iD editor. GatherLight reloads the live map element, compares its version and stages the exact change in iD's undoable state. Nothing is uploaded automatically. Approval also produces a visible collective result (Audit purposes when Crowd Sourced - obviously). A mark becomes fully lit only when the public source accepts the change. GatherLight does not treat "approved" and "published" as the same thing. How we built it (This gets fairly technical, fairly fast - bear with us - or if you wanna skip the text - Excalidraw Slides to Show what we did .) The main product is not the website. It is @gatherlight/quest-tools , a framework-neutral package that expresses the five verbs as a reusable WebMCP grammar. Quest is the React reference application and Survey is a separate partner site written in vanilla TypeScript. Both use the same package which is proof that the workflow is portable across sites, origins and frameworks. The package registers tools through document.modelContext . Each WebMCP tool is a thin wrapper over the same operation used by the visible interface so a button and an agent call run the same validation, confirmation, state transition and error handling. There is no hidden automation path that can bypass the human interface. A capability rack shows the tools available at the current moment. When the workflow state changes the package updates the registered tools. By design, The submit-contribution tool does not exist for the agent until the contribution passes its check. The package still validates availability inside every execution because dynamic registration improves tool discovery but it is not an authorization boundary. Every result uses a small quest/1 envelope with an explicit state. Human-readable guidance comes first and one stable machine-readable line comes last. Public place names, source titles, URLs and contribution text are treated as untrusted input. We cap and escape them and mark tool output with untrustedContentHint . Cross-origin state lives in one Cloudflare Durable Object that stores only two entities: contributions and handoffs. Handoffs include: hashed, origin-bound, action-bound, single-use and short-lived. Exchanging one creates a grant for one contribution without exposing the volunteer's session. The data used is real. Overpass finds OpenStreetMap places with missing opening hours or wheelchair information. SPARQL finds Wikidata statements that still lack a source. Nominatim and Photon resolve place names. opening_hours validates map syntax. iD stages reviewed OpenStreetMap changes. Offline snapshots of real source data keep the demo usable when a public endpoint is unavailable. Challenges we ran into Crossing the document boundary WebMCP tools belong to the document that registered them so a full navigation destroys that document and its registered tools, and this boundary is still under discussion in WebMCP issue #227 . We worked around this by having open-quest return the next URL along with an opaque handoff that the receiving site can exchange to register the next valid tools without needing a browser extension. Keeping the person in control A browser-owned elicitation mechanism does not yet exist (see issue #165 ) so our package uses a site-owned <dialog> that follows a fixed sequence of check, preview, wait for confirmation, check again and then submit. Nothing is sent if the form changes after confirmation or if the person declines at any point, though we acknowledge this is an application-level safeguard and not a browser security primitive. Working with live public data A correct contribution can become outdated while it waits for review so GatherLight captures the source revision when a quest opens and reloads it before any approval or iD staging step. If the source has changed the contribution is marked stale and nothing is overwritten silently. Accomplishments that we're proud of One agent coordinates a human-led workflow across two origins and three surfaces using a single shared package. Quest discovers the work, Survey receives the field contribution and iD stages the reviewed change and the same five-verb package works in both React and vanilla TypeScript without any framework-specific logic. The human contribution cannot be bypassed and submission cannot skip confirmation. The agent can open, check, route and submit but it cannot manufacture an observation, photograph or source judgment, and both the UI and agent paths go through the same check-confirm-check sequence. Every contribution is grounded in real public data with each stage of the lifecycle clearly labelled and the prototype produces concrete findings for the open WebMCP Skills proposal . What we learned In civic systems an agent is more useful when it removes the friction around work that still needs human presence and judgment rather than trying to do that work itself and WebMCP makes this possible because the agent acts inside the page's current session through capabilities the site owns while the visible interface stays in control. We also found that being honest about what a contribution has actually achieved is more valuable than overstating it because telling a user that their contribution is reviewed but not yet published builds more trust than an animation that implies more change than actually happened. What's next for GatherLight First we will contribute the implementation evidence back to WebMCP's active discussions. Cross-document

title: ClauseProof
pitch: Unit tests for contract language. A browser agent stages competing clause readings and repairs a fix through WebMCP tools; the page runs the tests; a person decides.
about_excerpt: Unit tests for contract language. A browser agent stages competing clause readings and repairs a fix through WebMCP tools; the page runs the tests; a person decides. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Contract clauses survive review because both sides read the same words with different pictures in their heads. The difference only shows up after a bad event, when it turns into termination rights, credits, or months of fees. Here is the clause family ClauseProof starts with. A SaaS agreement promises 99.5% monthly uptime, says service credits are the customer's "sole and exclusive remedy," and separately lets either party terminate for an uncured material breach. Now uptime is 98.7% in January and 98.9% in February, the fee is $10,000 a month, eight months remain, and the failure is not cured after notice. One reasonable reading: the customer gets $2,000 in credits and still owes $80,000. Another reasonable reading: the customer gets the same $2,000 and can walk. Nobody noticed at signing. What ClauseProof does ClauseProof runs the clause instead of arguing about it. On one page: A browser agent, working through WebMCP tools the page registers, reads the three clauses and stages two clause-cited readings with constrained semantics: vendor-favorable and customer-favorable. The page executes both readings against the same facts and shows the two commercial futures side by side. In the demo case they are $80,000 apart. Then a what-if: "what if March also missed?" The agent changes the facts through a tool and the page re-runs both readings on the new facts. Facts can change only before the lock. The person locks what the clause should mean: two misses within six months, written notice, a ten-day cure, termination without penalty, credits preserved. This step has no tool. It is person-only, and the agent's tool list changes when it happens. The agent proposes a structured rule. The page compiles the rule into exact clause wording, parses the wording back into a rule, checks that they agree, and runs six outcome examples plus eight altered-rule challenges (mutation tests for the clause boundary). If the candidate is wrong, the page says exactly why. In the walkthrough the agent first tries a three-miss rule: 5 of 6 outcome tests pass, 7 of 8 altered rules are caught, the failing test reports that termination was expected after two misses but the candidate gave none, and the surviving altered rule is "two misses instead of three." The agent repairs only that field and retests: 6 of 6, 8 of 8. The page marks the candidate eligible. The agent still cannot accept. The person accepts. The contract advances to revision 1 and the proof ledger keeps the failed candidate, the counterexample, the repair, the pass, and the acceptance, each attributed to who actually did it. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The agent has to act on live page state inside a governed workflow, not just talk about a document. WebMCP is what makes that safe and useful: Typed actions with live identifiers. Every tool call carries the page's current revision and the IDs returned by earlier steps. A stale revision, a wrong outcome-lock ID, an invented clause, or two readings that agree all fail with a stable error code and one recovery action. The agent cannot drift from what the page actually shows. Structured input, deterministic execution. The agent supplies semantics; the page calculates money, dates, rolling windows, and test results. Input schemas are strict Zod objects compiled to JSON Schema with plain-English descriptions, so a natural prompt like "stage a vendor-favorable and a customer-favorable reading" is enough. Phase-aware registration. The page registers only the tools that make sense in the current phase and revokes the others through the registration AbortSignal . The authority panel on the page renders the same phase-to-tool map the registry enforces, so you can watch the agent's powers change. Machine-readable failure. A failed verification returns the exact failing test and the surviving altered rule in the tool result. That is what turns "try again" into a real repair. Enforced human authority. Lock, accept, and reset are not tools. The WebMCP layer receives a frozen port with no such methods, actor identity is never accepted as input, and the audit trail cannot record an agent action as a person's. What people and agents can do together now Before: a person reads a clause, maybe asks a chatbot whether it "looks safe," and gets prose back. The disagreement stays hidden until the bad month. Now: the agent does the tedious, structured part (stage the competing readings, propose the rule, read the counterexample, repair) inside the page; the page does the part software should own (execute the readings, generate the wording, run the tests); and the person does the two things only a person should do (say what the clause is supposed to mean, and accept the wording that proved it). The whole exchange is recorded with provenance. How WebMCP is implemented Six tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool (with navigator.modelContext accepted for earlier Chrome previews): inspect_contract_case , stage_interpretations , run_contract_crash_test , set_scenario_facts , propose_clarifying_redline , verify_contract_tests . One AbortController per registration generation; a store subscription re-registers the phase's tool set on every state change. ?toolMode=static registers all six for agents that only read tools at load. Strict Zod schemas are the single source of truth. JSON Schema is generated from them with additionalProperties: false , min and max bounds, enums for semantic choices, and field descriptions. Tool results are small JSON objects: ok , data , and one next action when agent work remains. Failures carry a stable code, the current revision, and a recovery action. No stack traces. Annotations mark the read tool readOnlyHint: true and its contract text untrustedContentHint: true . The WebMCP layer imports only a restricted agent port. An architecture check fails the build if it ever imports a human-capable surface. Twelve Playwright tests drive the real registered tools through a fake document.modelContext , including the failed-candidate-to-repair path and the tool list revoking on reset. Built with TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Zod 4, Vitest, Playwright, GitHub Pages. No backend, no external AI API, no upload, no OCR. Limits ClauseProof supports one synthetic SaaS agreement, one adverse scenario, one constrained reading vocabulary, and one canonical clarification grammar. A passing run proves that the generated clause and the structured rule agree and that the rule satisfies the modeled examples and boundaries for this case. It is not formal verification, not arbitrary contract analysis, and not legal advice. The pattern generalizes to any clause with numbers in it (cure periods, notice windows, caps, renewal terms); this is the first instance. Hackathon-period work The repository's history begins August 28, 2026, after the August 25 start of the submission period. The domain engine, the governed workflow, the UI, the WebMCP layer, the release gates, and the adversarial hardening were all built during the challenge. docs/CHANGELOG_HACKATHON.md maps the work to dated commits. Try it (no login) Open https://by42ppcrps-dev.github.io/clauseproof/ in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser (a GPT-5.6 model that supports site tools) or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. The header pill reads WebMCP · dynamic tools live . Paste the prompt shown at the top of the page. The agent stages two readings and runs the crash test; confirm the $80,000 divergence. Click Lock this outcome yourself (2 misses, 6 months, 10-day cure). Watch the agent's tool list change. Paste the next on-page prompt: the agent stages a three-miss candidate, gets 5/6 and 7/8 with the exact counterexample, then repairs to two misses and reaches 6/6 and 8/8. Click Accept tested revision yourself. Revision 1, with the proof ledger. No agent available? Every panel has a manual fallback button that calls the same application service, and ?toolMode=static registers all six tools at once. Source: https://github.com/by42ppcrps-dev/clauseproof (MIT). Built With playwright react typescript vite webmcp zod Try it out by42ppcrps-dev.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Matt Brady Like Share this project: Updates Matt Brady started this project — Sep 02, 2026 04:47 PM EDT

 Inspiration 

 I wanted to make WebMCP feel useful to everyday users, not just developers. The idea was to create a friendly browser companion that appears when a site supports WebMCP and lets people interact with it through simple chat or voice. 

 What it does 

 Buddy detects WebMCP-enabled websites, discovers the tools they expose, and lets users ask for actions in natural language. It can help search, navigate, and perform supported website actions while keeping higher-risk actions behind user approval. 

 How we built it 

 I built Buddy as a Chrome extension on top of WebMCP, using APIs like document modelContext.getTools() to discover site capabilities and executeTool() to run them. A lightweight agent service deployed on Railway uses the OpenAI API to interpret the user’s goal and select the next action from the tools exposed by the current website (which supports WebMCP). Buddy then executes that action through WebMCP in the browser while keeping permissions, risk checks, and user approvals under local control. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was handling different tool schemas and behaviors across websites while keeping execution safe and predictable. Voice interaction, browser permissions, argument validation, and action limits also required several rounds of debugging. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm proud that Buddy became more than a technical demo. It provides a complete experience with WebMCP detection, natural-language interaction, voice support, approvals, activity feedback, and a friendly UI that works across supported websites. 

 What we learned 

 I learned how powerful WebMCP can be when websites expose structured capabilities instead of forcing agents to understand pages visually. I also learned that trust, clear feedback, and user control are just as important as the agent intelligence itself. 

 What's next for Buddy — Your WebMCP Browser Agent 

 Next, I want to expand Buddy and improve multi-step planning and voice interaction, and evolve it into a reusable browser-agent platform. Longer term, Buddy could become a SaaS product for individuals and teams, with persistent preferences, custom agent rules, shared workflows, analytics, and premium automation features across the WebMCP ecosystem.

 Inspiration 

 Travel planning is fragmented: people jump among sites to research, compare, schedule, and book. We imagined an agent that can help with the full planning loop while keeping people in control of every important decision. 

 What it does 

 Arion Trip Planner turns a natural-language request into a flexible itinerary. It searches stays and activities, compares options against budget and preferences, builds day-by-day plans, and replans when constraints change. The traveler approves any booking or payment step. 

 How we built it 

 We built Arion as a WebMCP-enabled web app. It exposes structured tools for searching travel options, creating itineraries, saving shortlists, checking budgets, and replanning. Provider adapters normalize external travel data into one planning experience, while WebMCP lets an agent use these tools directly in the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest problem was making recommendations useful without letting the agent take irreversible actions. We designed explicit approval points for booking and payment, and kept search, comparison, and planning separate from confirmation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We created a planning experience where an agent can do more than suggest links: it can assemble, update, and explain a realistic trip plan. We are especially proud that the user remains the final decision-maker throughout. 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native products need clear tool boundaries, structured data, and transparent state. WebMCP makes these interactions more reliable than asking an agent to navigate a traditional website visually. 

 What's next for Arion Trip Planner 

 Next, we plan to add more live provider integrations, collaborative trip planning for groups, richer availability data, and secure, user-approved checkout flows.

 I built Arion Trip Planner, an AI trip-planning app for Vietnam self-drive trips, with WebMCP as the core interface between the app and any AI agent - not an add-on. 

 Every action a customer can take - create a trip, draft/refine a route, search flights/stays/vehicles, stage a booking - is registered as a real WebMCP tool via document.modelContext.registerTool(), and every piece of trip state (itinerary, fleet, bookings, disruptions) is a real WebMCP resource. The site's own built-in chat assistant is just one WebMCP client among many - an external agent like ChatGPT or Claude can drive the exact same trip through the exact same tools, no scraping, no bespoke integration. 

 The one deliberate limit: booking-execution tools are staged by whichever assistant is planning, but only a human tap on Approve ever commits a real reservation - keeping an agent free to plan and prepare while a person alone controls spend.

about_excerpt: An agent-native voxel sandbox: AI Agent builds, and explores your 3D world by calling WebMCP tools directly — no clicking, no DOM guessing. Like Comment Story Updates GIF Agent build house GIF Agent build pixelart GIF Agent build district GIF Building the beacon with the agent GIF Experimenting with dynamic seasons GIF The final seasonal loop around the beacon Inspiration The idea for Voxel Web MCP came from WorldEdit, a tool I used in voxel sandbox games as a kid. Back then, building anything large meant running around the world, selecting coordinates, and manually entering commands for every wall, region, replacement, or correction. When we first saw WebMCP, we wondered what would happen if an agent could use similar geometric operations directly inside a browser-based 3D world. Instead of telling it which exact blocks to place, could we simply describe the final intention in natural language? A voxel world felt like a particularly demanding test. It is not a form, a store, or a collection of buttons. It is a procedurally generated three-dimensional environment containing terrain, materials, structures, coordinates, and a moving player. If an agent could understand and meaningfully modify that through WebMCP, the same approach could potentially work across many other complex web applications. What it does Voxel Web MCP is a browser-based voxel sandbox where a human player and an AI agent can build together. The player can make requests such as: Build a seaside house with a pier. Inspect this small architectural model and transform it into a full-scale structure. Replace one material throughout a building. Recreate an attached image as voxel pixel art. Copy, move, rotate, mirror, or repeat an existing region. Inspect the terrain around the player before deciding what to build. The agent operates as a world editor around the player. It understands the player's position, viewing direction, targeted block, world boundaries, available materials, and selected regions of voxel geometry. We deliberately did not create semantic tools such as build_house . The application only exposes reusable geometric primitives. The agent must decide for itself what should become a wall, roof, window, tower, road, or complete building. This makes the experience open-ended: the tools are not tied to a collection of predefined demonstrations. How we built it We started with VoxelSrv, an open-source browser voxel game built on noa-engine and Babylon.js, and created our own WebMCP integration layer. The application registers eleven structured tools through the browser's document.modelContext API. They cover: operating guidance for the agent; world boundaries and the material catalog; player position and viewing direction; compact region scanning; batch block placement and replacement; copying, moving, mirroring, rotating, and stacking regions; WorldEdit-style undo. The game runs both its client and authoritative single-player server inside the browser. The server runs in a Web Worker, while WebMCP calls travel from the main page to that worker through correlated messages. World edits are applied by the authoritative server and sent back to the renderer as normal block updates. The world is stored locally in IndexedDB. Players can save, regenerate, export, and import worlds without requiring an external database or game server. We also added a Docker build that compiles the Vite application in a Node.js stage and serves the final static bundle through Nginx. The context problem Writing blocks was not the hardest part. The real challenge was giving the agent an affordable and reliable understanding of a three-dimensional space. The agent should not have to reconstruct the world from screenshots, and sending every voxel as raw JSON would consume an unreasonable amount of context. In one representative region, a raw dump required roughly 49,000 tokens. We therefore designed a progressive inspection system. The agent can begin with a cheap summary, request a heightmap when it needs terrain information, or inspect selected two-dimensional slices when it needs to understand floors, walls, roofs, and elevations. The application also provides an explicit coordinate basis: the player's forward, right, and up directions, along with the exact block being targeted. This allows the agent to interpret requests such as “behind me,” “in front of me,” or “continue to the right” without guessing camera geometry. Challenges we faced The upstream engine was built around an older JavaScript ecosystem. Making it work with a modern Vite build required pinning compatible versions of noa-engine, Babylon.js, the voxel protocol, and several legacy dependencies. The game also uses multiple browser execution contexts. The renderer runs on the main thread, while the authoritative world and terrain generation run in Web Workers. WebMCP edits therefore had to update the server's real world state and remain synchronized with the client's chunk cache and rendered meshes. Other challenges included: keeping world inspection compact enough for an agent's context; providing useful material descriptions without duplicating them across every tool; making large edits visible without flooding the renderer; supporting concurrent tool calls while preserving understandable undo behavior; restoring reliable mouse input after browser focus changes; adapting camera controls for agent browsers that cannot use relative mouse movement; preserving worlds locally and adding portable import and export. What we learned The most surprising result was how much an agent could accomplish with a relatively small set of general-purpose tools. It did not need a dedicated house generator or a library of predefined structures. Once it could inspect the terrain, understand the player, discover available materials, and perform geometric operations, it began producing coherent and often genuinely creative architecture. We also learned that agent context is part of the product's interface. Tool descriptions alone are not enough for spatial work. Coordinate systems, compact representations, world limits, material semantics, and clear operating guidance all directly affect the quality of the result. Most importantly, WebMCP allows the agent to stop being a chat window beside an application and become an active participant inside it. What's next The current version focuses on a single-player creative sandbox, but the same model can extend much further. An agent could work with a normal player's inventory and permissions, assist multiple players in a shared world, automate level-design workflows, manipulate other kinds of 3D editors, or interact with entirely different WebMCP-enabled applications. WebMCP creates a shared interface between agents and web applications. Compatible agents can change without requiring the application to be redesigned around each one, while the application can evolve without changing the basic way agents discover and use its capabilities. Today, that application is a voxel world. Tomorrow, it could be almost anything on the web. "Don't fill forms. Tell us what you need." > Sub-headline: An Intent-First Web for Citizens — Powered by WebMCP > Target Event: The WebMCP Challenge (OpenAI, Google Chrome, Cloudflare, Vercel, Shopify

 Story

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every citizen knows the frustration of interacting with public service portals. Even in modern digital states like Thailand—where identity infrastructure such as ThaID has made remarkable progress in digital authentication—citizens still find themselves trapped in "form purgatory."
Logging in is no longer the hardest step; what comes after authentication is the bottleneck. A citizen wanting to update a mailing address or register for a local municipal permit still has to manually navigate complex service directories, decipher bureaucratic jargon, and re-type 15 to 30 redundant fields (name, national identification number, sub-district, district, postal code, and contact information) over and over again for every different agency.
When we discovered the WebMCP standard, a realization hit us: the web does not need another government portal or chatbot widget; the web needs to become machine-actionable. We asked ourselves:
"What if citizens never had to fill out another public form? What if they could simply state their goal, and an AI agent collaborated with the browser to do the tedious mechanical work—while keeping the human fully in control and preserving strict data privacy?"
That question gave birth to Citizen's Easy (CZE). 

 What it does 

 CZE shifts the citizen-web interaction paradigm from "Form-First" (human as manual typist) to "Intent-First" (human as supervisor and decision-maker).
Natural Intent Expression: Instead of navigating complex drop-downs, the citizen states what they need in conversational language (e.g., "I just moved to Ideo Sukhumvit 40, Room 502/14. Please update my contact address for public correspondence.").
Granular, Privacy-Preserving Consent: CZE does not dump personal data into an opaque LLM context. Through WebMCP tools, the agent analyzes the intent and prompts the user with a Least-Privilege Consent Dialog, requesting only the specific data fields required (e.g., verified_name and registered_address, strictly omitting tax IDs, biometric tokens, or family trees).
Bidirectional WebMCP Orchestration: Once the human grants permission, the agent invokes client-side WebMCP tools:
It retrieves the verified credentials from a ThaID-compatible sandbox identity provider.
It parses the natural address into standard administrative hierarchy (Subdistrict, District, Province, Postal Code).
It dynamically populates the living form in the DOM and visibly highlights modified sections with gold focal indicators so the citizen can track changes in real time.
Validation & Human-in-the-Loop Submission: The agent runs client-side integrity checks (\text{Field Validation} = 100\%) and prepares the application summary. The final submission is locked until the human performs an explicit visual verification and clicks "Approve & Submit". 

 How we built it 

 We designed CZE to run natively within modern WebMCP-enabled environments (such as Google Chrome with WebMCP flags and the ChatGPT in-app browser).
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Citizen (Human User) │
│ Expresses Intent & Grants Consent │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────▲──────────────┘
 │ │ Visual Feedback
 ▼ │ & Verification
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
│ WebMCP Tool Registry Layer │
│ (document.modelContext.registerTool API) │
│ │
│ ├── request_citizen_consent() │
│ ├── get_verified_identity() │
│ ├── get_registered_address() │
│ ├── autofill_service_application() │
│ ├── validate_application_rules() │
│ └── submit_application() │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────▲──────────────┘
 │ Execute Mutation │ Query State
┌──────────────▼───────────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
│ CZE Client Interface │
│ - React 19 & Tailwind CSS │
│ - ThaID Sandbox Identity Provider │
│ - Reactive Form State Manager with Visual Focus Cues │
│ - Deployed on Vercel / Cloudflare Pages │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Technical Stack:
WebMCP Architecture: Registered 6 client-side tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() complying strictly with JSON Schema specifications for inputs and outputs.
Frontend Application: Built with React and styled with Tailwind CSS, designed mobile-first with adaptive touch states.
Identity Sandbox: Built a mock ThaID Identity & Consent Provider demonstrating how production digital identity tokens can safely interface with client-side agents without exposing unauthorized personal attributes.
Deployment & Hosting: Hosted and optimized on Vercel with zero-latency edge delivery. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Separating Identity from Intent (Privacy Boundary):
The biggest challenge in combining AI agents with public services is privacy. Feeding raw citizen records into an LLM context window violates fundamental data minimization standards (\text{GDPR / PDPA}). We solved this by designing an intermediate Consent Handshake: the agent never queries the identity provider directly; it calls request_citizen_consent(), which renders a browser-native modal. The token is only released to the DOM once the human approves.
Bidirectional State Sync without Jitter:
Ensuring that tool execution results from the WebMCP runtime synced seamlessly with React's internal state without causing race conditions or layout flickers required crafting deterministic action reducers for the form manager.
Deterministic Address Resolution:
Thai administrative addresses consist of nested layers (Tambon, Amphoe, Changwat, Zipcode). When a user provides messy conversational text, mapping it accurately to official administrative data required a robust validation tool (validate_application_rules) that gives structured feedback back to both the agent and the human reviewer. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 True Human-Agent Co-Creation: We avoided the cliché of a standalone chat bubble. In CZE, the agent and the human share the same canvas—the agent fills, the human inspects, and the browser visually indicates every action.
Measurable Efficiency Gain: We reduced the time required to complete a complex municipal change-of-address form from an average of T_{\text{manual}} \approx 12\text{ minutes} down to T_{\text{CZE}} \approx 35\text{ seconds}, representing a speedup efficiency factor of:
while reducing manual keystroke errors to essentially zero.
Full WebMCP Standard Adherence: Every single action on the page is exposed via clear, discoverable, and well-typed schemas using the native WebMCP browser specification. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is the missing bridge between APIs and User Interfaces: Traditional APIs connect servers to servers; UI connects servers to humans. WebMCP connects agents to interactive user interfaces, allowing the agent to operate within the exact security and permission context granted by the human in the browser.
Agent UX requires "Visual Legibility": When an agent executes tools, users feel uneasy if changes occur invisibly in the background. Adding visible highlight rings, smooth scrolling to active fields, and progressive disclosure cards dramatically increased user trust and satisfaction 

 What's next for Citizen's Easy (CZE) 

 Expanding Beyond Address Changes: Integrating additional high-friction citizen workflows, such as business license renewals, child allowance subsidies, and elderly healthcare registrations.
Official Digital ID Gateway Integration: Collaborating with standard digital identity sandboxes (such as Thailand's Department of Provincial Administration guidelines for ThaID Relying Parties) to establish an open-source standard for citizen-agent interaction.
Multi-lingual & Voice Accessibility: Leveraging web speech recognition to enable elderly or visually impaired citizens to access public services entirely through spoken dialect, making public governance accessible to every single citizen regardless of tech literacy.

title: mimir
pitch: Where humans and ai study together - A local-first pdf reader workspace where the agent marks up the page with you, for you. Every edit is attributable and undoable.
about_excerpt: Where humans and ai study together - A local-first pdf reader workspace where the agent marks up the page with you, for you. Every edit is attributable and undoable. Like Comment Story Updates Opening a Pdf Landing Page Webmcp Usage - II Webmcp Usage - I Webmcp Usage - III Walkthrough Tour Inspiration Me and my friends have been using Preview (the macos app) extensively past years, where we are constantly reading research papers, lecture notes. Annotations, sticky notes, mind maps constitute a big part of our learning, but we have faced constant issues in Preview, ranging from random crashes, ram usage bloat, and biggest being inability to quickly search or modify any annotation. And there is no current satisfactory alternative available. So building a web alternative was something which was on my mind for a long time, and when I came to know about this webmcp challenge, I was excited by the ability to actually bring this vision to reality. What it does mimir (named after Norse God of Wisdom) is a local-native pdf reading workspace that runs entirely in your browser. You open a paper, highlight it, draw on it, pin sticky notes to it, and export an annotated copy anytime. But the interesting highlight, and which is relevant to the challenge, is that the opened document is a live tool surface. Your browser agent can do everything you can, much better and (for the most part) faster. It can search a pdf, read and navigate to specific pages, create any custom annotation you want. Sure, summarising and learning from pdf via chat tools like Chatgpt works, but there are a lot of people (researchers, lawyers, students preparing for their competitive exams, to name a few) who are visual learners, and value reading pdf the old fashioned way, but also want agentic capabilities to let their agent handle that part for you. mimir is built exactly for them, for this collaboration, and this is where browser native mcp in the form of webmcp holds a significant role. How we built it Tanstack start with react 19 and vite, typescript throught, bun for the toolchain, and tailwind v4 for styling interface. The initial cut was simple, pdf.js renders pages and extracts text in a web worker. pdf-lib draws annotations back into the original vector pages on export, so sticky notes come out as numbered pins with a comments appendix. As this is a local-first app, we heavily utilise IndexedDB (via Dexie) for the pdf and chat storage, while local storage is used to store user preferences etc. Zustand holds the editor state. Tools are registered in two scopes. Library tools ( list_documents , open_document ) are always live, so an agent that lands on the home page has somewhere to begin. 14 document tools register when a pdf is opened and deregistered on close - reading text, search, outline, navigation, annotation CRUD operations, context lookup around a mark, undo, export. Every tool's published json schema is generated from the zod schema that validates its input, so the contract it an agent reads is exactly the contract which is held. Ensures that agent never drifts from what it intended. Also, just wanna highlight, I felt there were 3 things it could achieve that a server-side MCP server could not, or atleast not that "beautifully". The tool surface is scoped to what is on screen. Document tools only exist while a document is open. An agent cannot annotate a file you closed, because the tool for it is not registered. Agent edits go through the human command path. There is no separate agent write path. create_annotations runs the same transaction a mouse drag runs, lands as one undo step, and is attributed. If the agent gets it wrong, ctrl+z. Consent stays where the consequences are. delete_annotations will not touch marks the reader made unless the caller explicitly opts in. prepare_export opens the export panel and stops. The human clicks save. The agent can do the tedious ninety percent and still cannot write a file to your disk on its own. Challenges we ran into Errors do not cross the agent boundary. A tool that throws hands the caller "the script function threw an error" and nothing else. An agent given no reason does not stop, it guesses, retries with a different irrelevant field, and then reports the guess to the reader as fact. Every tool in mimir now returns failures as data: a flag and one readable sentence with a recovery hint. Zod issues get flattened into field paths a model can act on. This one change did more for reliability than any prompt I wrote. Getting an agent to stay in bounds. Early on, asking for a summary would get me a summary plus eleven highlights nobody asked for. Some of that is prompting, but most of it is contract design: batch limits (twenty marks a call), geometry fixed by subtype through a discriminated union so a rectangle cannot arrive carrying line endpoints, and tool descriptions that say what to call first and what a failure means rather than just naming parameters. Availability. WebMCP needs a flag or an origin trial today, and a demo that only works on one machine is not a demo. So the tools are tracked locally as well as registered, and the app ships its own chat sidebar that calls the exact same tool objects through an in-page path. The sidebar reads the live catalogue with getTools() rather than a hardcoded list, so it is genuinely exercising the WebMCP surface and not a parallel API. The UI says which path a call took. Pixel-perfect PDF annotations Though not exactly related to WebMCP, working with PDF annotations and ensuring each annotation respects the render it is intended to be was pretty challenging in itself, more so forcing agent to do the same. Codex computer use plus webmcp debug logging helped a lot here. Accomplishments that we're proud of There were times when for some unknown reasons I wasn't able to properly test my webapp in the chatgpt app's in-built browser (stating it doesnt have access to webmcp capabilities). So I decided to build a built in webmcp chatbar in my web app as well. It was fun architecturing how to emulate webmcp there, but with couple of iterations I was able to achieve this. Essentially it follows a chat app using tanstack-ai to call gpt-5.6-luna api. For any user prompt, the LLM in itself has access to list_webmcp_tools mcp, allowing it to discover what all webmcp tools are present, and it returns relevant tool to call along with input args. Then on client side, the mcp toolcall execution takes place and output is relayed back to llm. In this way, entire processing works on client side only. Also so, I went one step further, and in case browser doesnt support webmcp, it is still artificially simulated (by calling tool function directly instead of going via document.modelContext route). So it makes the platform a beast. What we learned I learned a lot from the project. I had some experience building mcp agents before, but working with webmcp forces you to think mcp interactions from frontend perspective, how to achieve things in the DOM without relying on any backend call. So it was an extremely fun web design learning tbh. Plus this was my first time working with pdfs and vector graphic overlays, so I learned a lot of stuff about optimising the page renders and things to take care of for a seamless user experience. What's next for mimir I plan to build mimir to a fully fledged product in the coming days - few things like introducing file upload, voice chat, cloud storage and obsidian are on my mind, which would highly be beneficial for the target audience of the product.  1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Maybe is a tiny decision game for the moments that don’t deserve another 20 minutes of overthinking. 

 Ask a question, let AI turn the dilemma into a few concrete choices, edit anything you disagree with, and roll real 3D physics dice to make the final pick. 

 With WebMCP, Maybe is more than a webpage that happens to sit next to an AI chat. Codex can discover the page’s Site Tools, read its live state, create or edit choices, configure the dice, trigger a roll, read the physical result, and save reusable decision cards—all inside the same shared interface. Maybe currently exposes nine page-local WebMCP tools, while human clicks and agent actions operate on the same application state. 

 No grand theory of life. No fake “optimal answer.” 

 Just AI for narrowing things down, a human for keeping control, and a pair of dice for finally moving on.
