title: FableCut
pitch: A browser video editor your agent can drive. FableCut exposes its whole timeline as WebMCP tools, you and your agent cut the same edit, live, in the same tab.
about_excerpt: A browser video editor your agent can drive. FableCut exposes its whole timeline as WebMCP tools, you and your agent cut the same edit, live, in the same tab. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Agent moves the playhead, selects a clip, splits it, then undoes it. The edit lands on your undo stack, so Ctrl+Z reverses it You select a clip with your mouse. The agent reads it with get_selection. No clip ids, no filenames, no describing what you mean. A real non-linear editor in the browser. Three video tracks, four audio, transitions, keyframes, all exposed to an agent as WebMCP tools. GIF Just after split_at_playhead. One V2 clip became two and the length dropped 2.60 to 1.20. The agent made this edit, not the human. The full demo timeline. Vector shots on V1, titles on V2, one grade across everything on V3. Either of you can edit any of it. Inspiration I wanted to edit video without paying for it. Premiere Pro is a subscription, and Palmier Pro needs macOS, so between the two of them the door is shut for a lot of people who just want to cut clips. That felt wrong for a community that mostly runs on free and open tools. So I built FableCut. The WebMCP part came later, out of a limitation I already knew about. FableCut could be driven by an agent over MCP, but the agent was always editing a file on disk while I was sitting in front of a timeline in a browser tab. Two views of the same edit, held together by a file watcher. WebMCP closes that gap, because the tools live inside the page the human is already looking at. A video editor is about the best possible thing to put WebMCP into, since the whole session is already live in the tab. What it does FableCut is a browser based, zero dependency video editor that an AI agent can drive. Three video tracks, four audio tracks, trimming, splitting, keyframes, transitions, real waveforms, and export, all running in the browser off one node server.js. The original idea was that project.json is the interface. The entire timeline is one JSON document, so any agent that can read and write JSON can edit video, and the open tab hot reloads in about 150ms. That still works and it is still how the MCP server operates. For this challenge I added a WebMCP layer, and it does something the file based approach cannot. It registers 11 tools on document.modelContext that talk to the running editor instead of the file. The interesting ones are the ones that have no on disk equivalent at all: get_selection reads what you have selected right now and where your playhead is. You point at a clip with your mouse and say "tighten this". No ids, no filenames, no describing what you mean. get_frame_context reports what is actually composited at a given instant, topmost first, with transforms. The flat clip list cannot answer "what does the viewer see here". set_playhead and select_clips let the agent move your cursor and your selection, so it can show you what it means before it changes anything. And the piece that makes it actually usable: every tool that changes something calls pushUndo() first. The agent's edits go onto the same undo stack as yours. Ctrl+Z reverses the agent exactly the way it reverses you. There is no separate "review the AI's changes" panel to approve or reject, because there is one timeline, one history, and two people editing it. How we built it FableCut itself was built before this hackathon. No third party libraries, no dependencies, free, and drivable by agents from day one. We used Claude Code to build it over a weekend and posted it on a random Thursday. For this challenge the new work is a single file, webmcp.js, plus one line in index.html to load it. The repo is deliberately structured so you can see exactly that. The first commit is an unmodified export of FableCut as it stood before the submission period, containing zero WebMCP code. Every commit after it is challenge work, so git diff against that first commit is the submission. WEBMCP.md spells this out. One thing that cost real time was figuring out which API to write against. The spec and Chrome's own docs say document.modelContext.registerTool(), but most of the tutorials and blog posts still in circulation show navigator.modelContext with a batch provideContext() call, which is an older draft shape. We could not control which build a judge would open it in, so the layer feature detects both and prefers the spec form. Challenges we ran into Frame rendering and clip transitions were rough early on, and got fixed in a recent build. Clips and audio were not really consumable by an agent. It could see that a clip existed but not what was in it, so we had to start transcribing audio and placing beats and effects against volume peaks and drops. For the WebMCP layer, the hard problem was reversibility. An agent that edits your timeline and cannot be undone is worse than no agent. Routing every mutating tool through the editor's existing undo stack solved it and turned out to be the best part of the whole thing. Testing was its own problem, since WebMCP needs Chrome 149 with a flag or the ChatGPT in app browser. We ended up exposing the tool set on window.FableCutWebMCP so every tool can be executed and verified in a normal browser without the flag. Accomplishments that we're proud of FableCut hit the Show HN front page with 98 points and sat at #2 for a whole day, and picked up 200 GitHub stars in the first 5 hours. It is listed in the official MCP registry and has been written up on several blogs, tech news sites, and social platforms. We also got a repost from Marcos Rico Peng, founder of Palmier Pro, on a post comparing FableCut with the existing tools in that space. The repo is past 640 stars and still climbing, with people contributing regularly. Most of that happened before this hackathon, so we are not claiming it as challenge work. We mention it because it means agent native editing has somewhere real to land. There are already people using this thing every day. What we learned SSE, a lot of ways to edit video, and how to reimplement an existing production clip or ad from scratch. Building MCP servers for free and open source agent tooling pulled us into context sharing and tool calling as a field. WebMCP added a distinction we had not thought about before. There is a real difference between an agent editing your document and an agent editing your session. The first one needs you to describe everything. The second one can just look at what you are pointing at. What's next for FableCut More features, and simpler prompts for complex edits A library/marketplace of media built specifically for FableCut: SVGs, SFX, effects, and transitions Built With canvas css html javascript mcp node.js sse web-audio-api webcodecs webmcp Try it out ronak-create.github.io github.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Ronak Parmar shekhar parmar Kalpit Padhiyar Like 2 2 people like this: Share this project: Updates Ronak Parmar started this project — Sep 03, 2026 06:27 AM EDT

title: Corsen Context
pitch: One owner-controlled WebMCP contract for the existing web: four read-only tools, governed extensions, deployed live across eleven stacks.
about_excerpt: One owner-controlled WebMCP contract for the existing web: four read-only tools, governed extensions, deployed live across eleven stacks. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Corsen Context gives an existing website an owner-controlled WebMCP read layer without replacing the human interface. The page registers explicit tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ; every call executes against a bounded, same-origin MCP endpoint (protocol 2025-11-25) and returns canonical public URLs and clean Markdown. Four read-only core tools are shared by every integration: search_site , get_page_content , list_content and get_sitemap . Live flagship: https://webmcp.corsen.ai (WordPress). Source: https://github.com/CorsenAI/corsen-context (MIT). Built by Corsen AI , France. Why WebMCP fits Browser agents currently parse interfaces built for people, guess which page is authoritative, and cannot tell what a site allows them to do. With Corsen Context the website itself exposes a small, typed, owner-selected capability layer. The capabilities live with the page instead of being reverse-engineered from the DOM, and the site owner decides what is exposed and can revoke it without touching the human pages. What people and agents can do together A person states a goal ("compare the editions, tell me what you may buy for me and what I must do myself"). The agent reads the owner's rules, calls the tools and returns grounded answers with sources. Governance is explicit and per product on the flagship store: the ten per-stack editions (9 EUR) carry agentPurchase: allowed : an agent acting for its user may complete the ordinary checkout; the production licence (29 EUR, slug corsen-context ) carries agentPurchase: forbidden with the owner's reason, so the agent hands that URL back to the human; the only write-shaped tool, request_expert_call , is annotated non-read-only and is refused server-side for every agent call ( human_only ) before anything is stored or emailed. The person keeps the decisions; the agent does the reading. How WebMCP is implemented A language-neutral tools.manifest.json declares tool names, JSON schemas and WebMCP annotations ( readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint ). The generated browser bridge registers each tool with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and forwards execute() to the same-origin MCP JSON-RPC endpoint; the browser never reimplements a tool and sends no cookies, credentials or API key. A TypeScript core (npm @corsenai/corsen-context 2.0.1 with Next.js and Astro adapters) and an independent PHP implementation (WordPress plugin 1.5.16 on WordPress.org) are checked against the manifest by parity tests. Eleven public deployments run the same four-tool core: the WordPress flagship, Express, Next.js, Astro, static HTML, Ghost, Strapi, Directus, Wagtail, MediaWiki and a Netlify template. A public verifier checks the ten stacks against one SHA-256 contract hash ( 3786c5d0d401cb9862291c9e3903ff0bd35925326b7dbc9be75f15ded2604ef4 ). The WordPress flagship adds five owner-toggled extensions ( get_product , get_sections , get_structured_data , check_agent_access , request_expert_call ), a Control Center, an audit log and a per-product agent policy published in llms.txt , on /for-agents/ and in every tools/list response. Shopify's own WebMCP, Storefront MCP and UCP surfaces are not reimplemented: a separate read-only verification kit checks them without installing an app. Integration shapes, stated honestly WordPress is a native plugin (one checkbox, no code). Next.js and Astro are published adapters with reference apps. Express and static HTML are reference servers. Ghost, Strapi, Directus, Wagtail and MediaWiki are deployable Node bridges over each CMS's public API, not native plugins. Every standalone repository ships install steps, a deployment guide, tests and CI. How to test it Open https://webmcp.corsen.ai in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Google Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and Chrome restarted. No account is needed. The page registers nine tools: the four core tools plus the five WordPress extensions ( request_expert_call is non-read-only and human-only). Ask: "Read this site's rules for agents, list the products with prices, and tell me which editions an agent may buy for me and which one it must hand back to me, with source URLs." Expected: eleven products; the ten 9 EUR editions are allowed ; the 29 EUR production licence is forbidden with the owner's reason; request_expert_call is not called. Optional: open any other live deployment listed on https://webmcp.corsen.ai/integrations/ and press Run live trace ; the four core tools answer from that site's own endpoint. Optional, repository: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm test && pnpm verify:live (expects VERIFIED: 10/10 ). Existing project and challenge delta Corsen Context existed before the challenge as an open-source MCP + llms.txt layer (baseline commit 73ecaee , 2026-08-06). Everything WebMCP was built during the submission period, starting at commit 8cedb8c (2026-08-30): the manifest-backed registration bridge, same-origin execution, WordPress owner controls and Control Center, per-product agent policy, the five WordPress extensions, framework handlers, parity and browser tests, the eleven public deployments, the twelve standalone repositories, the live verifier and the demo-store governance. Tested clients ChatGPT in-app browser (shared session: https://chatgpt.com/s/cx_6a99cd8a5ff48191ad323da4ca98a166): discovered the nine flagship tools, listed the eleven products, read the per-product policy and verified initialize , tools/list and the four-tool live trace on all eleven hosted deployments. That browser host exposed no document.modelContext , so the session proves endpoints and bridge definitions rather than native registration. Native WebMCP registration: verified in Chrome 152 with the WebMCP flags (nine tools registered on the flagship) and in the Codex desktop in-app browser. What we learned A governed contract beats a clever scraper: once a site publishes what an agent may read and may do, agents stop guessing, owners stop fearing, and the same four calls work on a WordPress store, a Django CMS and a static folder alike. title: WebMCP-QCG: Quantum Call Gate
pitch: A browser-native HITL gate that inspects a Q# request, recommends the next safe action, and records evidence before quantum execution.
about_excerpt: A browser-native HITL gate that inspects a Q# request, recommends the next safe action, and records evidence before quantum execution. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Quantum developers already have capable frameworks, simulators and hardware services. The risky moment often comes before execution: an AI agent can prepare a technically valid-looking call before the human has verified the artifact, target evidence, limits, scientific intent or authority to spend. I built WebMCP-QCG to make that moment inspectable. Its promise is simple: review before you run. What it does WebMCP-QCG is a browser-native, human-in-the-loop quantum preflight workbench. A human imports a local Q# artifact. QCG keeps the source in session memory, computes a SHA-256 digest over the exact bytes, compiles it locally with the pinned Q# WebAssembly runtime and freezes a dated target-profile snapshot. Its deterministic policy returns exactly one recommendation: reuse_result reject recompile simulate_first ready_for_external_execution The agent can use four progressive WebMCP tools: inspect_quantum_experiment evaluate_quantum_call run_bounded_qsharp_simulation export_quantum_evidence_report The first two appear only after a human-loaded artifact is ready. A bounded simulation tool appears only after a valid simulate_first recommendation and visible human acceptance. Its one-use consent is consumed after invocation. QCG exports a JSON or Markdown evidence receipt binding the artifact, target snapshot, recommendation, human choice and measured effects. The MVP never submits a provider job, uses a provider credential or calls a QPU. Its QPU counter remains zero. Live application: https://qcg.securedme.ca/ Source and reproducible evidence: https://github.com/SeCuReDmE-main-dev/webmcp-hackathon-2026 How I built it The application uses React, TypeScript and Vite. Strict Zod contracts reject unknown properties and bound artifact size, shots, qubits and timeouts. qsharp-lang@1.31.0 runs inside a Web Worker so compilation and the published Bell simulation remain local and cancellable. Raw Q# stays out of WebMCP responses and IndexedDB; only evidence receipts persist locally. All human buttons and WebMCP tools call the same service layer. Tools are registered through document.modelContext with AbortSignal cleanup. The retained HTTPS origin serves the required WebMCP and security headers, the Worker and the pinned WebAssembly asset. Challenges I ran into The hardest design problem was separating three different things: an agent recommendation, a human authorization and an actual effect. Treating them as one state would make a convenient demo and a weak control system. The first live smoke run also exposed a real browser race: the inspection tool could be discovered before the initial WASM analysis finished. I changed the registration lifecycle so artifact tools stay absent until the manifest exists, then repeated the full test on the public origin. A second challenge was restraint. A multi-provider quantum router is an attractive future direction, but the hackathon proof needed one narrow, falsifiable vertical slice. Accomplishments I am proud of A real Q# file produces a byte-exact manifest and zero-diagnostic compiler evidence. Five falsifiable requests exercise all five decisions. The human can accept, defer or override with visible provenance. One accepted Bell simulation returned 64 correlated shots with the Bell invariant passing. The simulation tool disappeared after its one-use consent was consumed. The evidence export contained no raw Q#, local path, secret or provider error. Vitest passes 17/17 tests, including exact-versus-near reuse and false-ready regressions. Official WebMCP smoke evaluation passes 2/2 on the retained HTTPS origin. The live trace records one local simulation and zero QPU submissions. What I learned WebMCP adds value when the agent needs a compact capability that is absent from the visible DOM and shares the same state transitions as the human interface. Progressive registration is part of the product contract, not decorative plumbing. I also learned that a refusal, reuse decision or request for better evidence can be a useful outcome. Quantum tooling does not become safer by executing more calls; it becomes clearer when every proposed call has a reason, an authority boundary and a receipt. What's next I will test the frozen cases with quantum developers, measure false-ready decisions, refresh target-profile evidence and refine the visual workbench. Future adapters may normalize evidence from additional ecosystems while preserving their native semantics. Provider submission and paid execution remain outside this MVP and would require a separate authorization design. Built With indexeddb q# react typescript vite web-workers webassembly webmcp zod Try it out qcg.securedme.ca github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I originated WebMCP-QCG and serve as its solo architect, researcher, developer, and technical writer. I defined the problem, compared the candidate directions, designed the four-tool quantum preflight contract, audited the relevant quantum ecosystems, implemented and verified the QDK WebAssembly spike, and maintain the public evidence journal. Codex supports this work as my research partner for mapping, source comparison, quality assurance, and deliverable preparation; I retain authorship, technical judgment, and responsibility for every project decision.  AI Assistant WebMCP — Project Story 

 Inspiration 

 Small clinics, counseling centers, and SMBs have websites, but no AI to answer the basic questions visitors ask around the clock — booking, pricing, location. General-purpose chatbots don't know the business's actual information and end up hallucinating. We wanted to give every small business an AI assistant that actually knows their site, without requiring any engineering effort from them. 

 What it does 

 WebMCP is a fully automated AI-assistant SaaS. You paste a URL, and it: 

 
 Crawls the site (sitemap-based, multi-page) 
 Generates industry-specific Q&A with an LLM 
 Builds a widget (5 themes, voice input, quick-menu) 
 Ships a paste-and-go embed ( /embed/<id>.js ) 
 

 Visitors then chat with an AI that answers from the site's real knowledge — with off-topic screening and hallucination guards built in. 

 How we built it 

 
 Nuxt 3 (SSR) console + Django 5/DRF backend + vanilla JS widget (single loader embed) 
 Celery-free polling worker — select_for_update + lock-expiry auto-recovery for restart resilience 
 Dual LLM engines — Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite for real-time chat (low latency + off-topic guard), OpenRouter gpt-oss-120b for batch Q&A (~$0.00196/run) 
 Multilingual silos — ko/en fully separated across DB, containers, prompts, and UI 
 3-stage deployment — Docker Compose → self-hosted server (nginx + Let's Encrypt) → Render Blueprint (IaC) 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Passive → proactive AI — the ideal is the widget JS dynamically scanning and injecting into site forms (no owner-side changes), but form structures vary wildly. We deliberately deferred form control and focused on chat automation. 
 Crawling engine trade-off — plain HTTP parsers fail on WAF/SPA sites; browser crawlers are too heavy. Solved with a dual engine (httpx + browser-header fallback). 
 Off-topic questions — solved with system-prompt bounding + cached Q&A similarity matching (≥0.6), verified stable on Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite. 
 Multi-tenant security — Origin allowlist + publicId auth, per-tenant keys, global IP-allowlist switch. 
 Platform quirks — Render misread a dockerCommand chain as a filename, crashing the worker in a loop. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 End-to-end automation — URL in, working widget out, validated all the way to the cloud. 
 Cost engineering — batch Q&A at ~$0.00196/run using OSS models, with similarity caching to cut expensive calls. 
 Structural multilingualism — language mixing blocked at the architecture level, not via translation keys. 
 45 documented test records (T-001~T-045) and a troubleshooting FAQ that prevent repeat mistakes. 
 

 What we learned 

 
 Scope selection is the essence of automation — one feature done end-to-end beats many half-done features. 
 Combine models by purpose — cost-effective OSS for batch, low-latency Gemini for real-time. 
 The prompt is a security layer — off-topic filtering via prompt bounding, at zero extra cost. 
 Security should be a switch, not a default — environment-adaptable controls are what make them practical. 
 

 What's next for AI assistant WebMCP 

 
 Proactive form integration — the widget JS dynamically scanning and injecting into site forms (booking, contact), so the AI can complete actions, not just answer. 
 Broader language silos — Japanese, Chinese, and more, following the existing 4-step extension path. 
 Deeper model routing — per-tenant model selection and cost controls at scale. 
 

 

 AI 어시스턴트 WebMCP — 프로젝트 스토리 

 Inspiration (영감) 

 소규모 병원·상담센터·중소기업은 웹사이트는 있지만, 방문자가 24시간 궁금해하는 기본 질문(예약, 요금, 위치)에 답해줄 AI가 없습니다. 범용 챗봇은 그 업체의 실제 정보를 몰라 환각을 일으킵니다. 우리는 엔지니어링 노력 없이도 모든 소규모 사업체가 자기 사이트를 진짜 아는 AI 비서를 가질 수 있게 하고 싶었습니다. 

 What it does (하는 일) 

 WebMCP는 완전 자동화 AI 비서 SaaS입니다. URL만 붙여넣으면: 

 
 크롤링 (sitemap 기반 멀티페이지) 
 업종별 Q&A 생성 (LLM) 
 위젯 빌드 (5종 테마, 음성 입력, 빠른메뉴) 
 붙여넣기 임베드 배포 ( /embed/<id>.js ) 
 

 방문자는 사이트의 실제 지식을 바탕으로 답하는 AI와 대화합니다 — 오프토픽 스크리닝과 환각 방지 가드가 내장되어 있습니다. 

 How we built it (구축 방법) 

 
 Nuxt 3(SSR) 콘솔 + Django 5/DRF 백엔드 + vanilla JS 위젯 (단일 로더 임베드) 
 Celery 없는 폴링 워커 — select_for_update + 잠금 만료 자동 복구로 재시작 내성 확보 
 LLM 이중 엔진 — 실시간 채팅은 Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite(저지연+오프토픽 가드), 배치 Q&A는 OpenRouter gpt-oss-120b (1회 약 $0.00196) 
 다국어 사일로 — ko/en을 DB·컨테이너·프롬프트·UI까지 완전 분리 
 3단계 배포 — Docker Compose → 자체 서버(nginx+Let's Encrypt) → Render Blueprint(IaC) 
 

 Challenges we ran into (직면한 도전) 

 
 수동적 → 능동적 AI — 이상은 위젯 JS가 사이트 폼을 동적으로 스캔·삽입하는 것(소유자 수정 불필요)이지만, 폼 구조가 천차만별이라 의도적으로 폼 제어를 미루고 채팅 자동화에 집중했습니다. 
 크롤링 엔진 트레이드오프 — 단순 HTTP 파서는 WAF/SPA를 못 읽고, 브라우저 크롤러는 너무 무거움. 이중 엔진(httpx + 브라우저 헤더 폴백)으로 해결. 
 오프토픽 질문 — 시스템 프롬프트 바운딩 + 저장 Q&A 유사도 매칭(≥0.6)으로 해결, Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite에서 안정 동작 확인. 
 멀티테넌트 보안 — Origin 화이트리스트 + publicId 인증, 테넌트별 키, 전역 IP 화이트리스트 스위치. 
 플랫폼 특이점 — Render가 dockerCommand 체인을 파일명으로 오판해 워커가 크래시 루프에 빠짐. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of (자랑스러운 성과) 

 
 엔드투엔드 자동화 — URL 입력 → 동작하는 위젯 출력, 클라우드까지 검증 완료. 
 비용 엔지니어링 — OSS 모델로 배치 Q&A 1회 약 $0.00196, 유사도 캐시로 고비용 호출 절감. 
 구조적 다국어 — 번역 키가 아닌 아키텍처 레벨에서 언어 혼용 차단. 
 45건의 테스트 기록 (T-001~T-045)과 트러블슈팅 FAQ로 재발 방지. 
 

 What we learned (배운 점) 

 
 자동화의 본질은 범위 선택 — 하나를 끝까지 완성하는 것이 여러 개를 반쯤 하는 것보다 낫습니다. 
 모델은 용도별 조합 — 배치는 가성비 OSS, 실시간은 저지연 Gemini. 
 프롬프트가 보안 계층 — 오프토픽 필터링을 프롬프트 바운딩으로, 추가 비용 없이 해결. 
 보안은 스위치로 설계 — 환경에 맞게 조절 가능해야 실용적입니다. 
 

 What's next for AI assistant WebMCP (다음 단계) 

 
 능동적 폼 통합 — 위젯 JS가 사이트 폼(예약·문의)을 동적으로 스캔·삽입해, AI가 답변을 넘어 행동을 완수 하도록. 
 더 넓은 언어 사일로 — 일본어·중국어 등, 기존 4단계 확장 경로를 따라 추가. 
 고도화된 모델 라우팅 — 테넌트별 모델 선택과 대규모 비용 통제.

title: Nonprofit Pass
pitch: Nonprofit Pass helps youth-led organizations outlive graduation by enabling founders, successors, and AI agents to discover opportunities, prepare applications, and complete handoffs together.
about_excerpt: Nonprofit Pass helps youth-led organizations outlive graduation by enabling founders, successors, and AI agents to discover opportunities, prepare applications, and complete handoffs together. Like Comment Story Updates Home Page Throughout high school, I led a nonprofit that impacted more than 20,000 people. Building the organization was one of the most meaningful experiences of my life, but when I moved to college, I could no longer give it the time and attention it deserved. I began trying to transition the organization to a new leader, only to discover how difficult nonprofit succession can be. The organization’s knowledge, relationships, documents, and responsibilities were spread across different places, and there was no simple way to prepare another student to take over. In college, I was selected to attend one of America’s premier youth service summits. At the conference, I met other young nonprofit founders who were experiencing the same problem. They had created organizations that were making a real difference, but graduation, college, and new responsibilities made it difficult for them to continue leading. Their nonprofits were not ending because their missions were no longer important. They were at risk because they did not have an effective way to find, prepare, and support their next leaders. That experience inspired me to build Nonprofit Pass, a WebMCP-powered platform that helps student-led nonprofits survive leadership transitions. The platform gives founders, potential successors, and AI agents a shared space in which they can plan and complete a responsible handoff. A student interested in becoming a successor can use Nonprofit Pass to discover leadership opportunities, search and filter organizations, save nonprofits to a shortlist, compare opportunities, and prepare an application. A founder can evaluate whether an organization is ready for succession, identify missing documents or institutional knowledge, create a structured 30-day transition plan, and leave important notes for the next leader. Both people can see the same transition progress, creating continuity between the person who built the organization and the person who will lead it next. I built the project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with browser-based storage to preserve user progress. I integrated WebMCP through the document.modelContext API, allowing AI agents to understand and interact with the application through structured tools. The project includes 11 WebMCP tools that can search for nonprofits, retrieve organization details, maintain a shortlist, compare opportunities, prepare and review applications, assess handoff readiness, update transition tasks, add shared notes, and summarize transition progress. My goal was not simply to let an agent click buttons. I wanted the agent to become a useful collaborator. An AI agent can organize information, identify gaps, prepare drafts, and recommend next steps, while people remain responsible for consequential decisions. Submitting an application and approving a final leadership handoff are intentionally human-only actions. This makes the agent helpful without allowing it to make irreversible decisions on someone’s behalf. One of the greatest challenges was determining how much authority an agent should have. Leadership succession affects real organizations and the communities they serve, so completely automating the process would be irresponsible. I addressed this challenge by separating assistance from approval. Agents can help people understand their options and prepare their work, but final decisions stay with the founder and successor. Another challenge was designing the application for two users with very different needs. Successors need a simple way to discover and evaluate opportunities, while founders need tools for documentation, readiness assessment, and transition planning. I created role-specific experiences for each person while connecting them through a shared transition workspace. I also added visible activity tracking so users can understand which actions were completed by a human and which were assisted by an agent. Building Nonprofit Pass taught me that an agent-native application requires much more than exposing existing interface controls to AI. It requires carefully deciding what context agents receive, which actions they may perform, how their contributions are communicated, and where human judgment must remain mandatory. I also learned that succession is not a single moment when one leader replaces another. It is an ongoing process involving trust, documentation, training, shared memory, and accountability. In the future, I hope to connect Nonprofit Pass with real nonprofit opportunities and verified organizational accounts. The platform could eventually include document integrations, mentor verification, founder-successor introductions, transition health monitoring, and long-term impact tracking. My goal is to ensure that a student’s graduation does not have to mean the end of an organization. Young founders create projects that address meaningful needs, and those projects deserve the opportunity to continue. By helping founders, successors, and AI agents work together, Nonprofit Pass creates a path for a nonprofit’s mission and impact to outlive its original founder. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: BeatScope Director
pitch: An in-browser WebMCP music workspace where AI agents can inspect timing, find visual moments, compare sections, and control playback using BeatScope’s deterministic local audio analysis.
about_excerpt: An in-browser WebMCP music workspace where AI agents can inspect timing, find visual moments, compare sections, and control playback using BeatScope’s deterministic local audio analysis. Like Comment Story Updates GIF WebMCP Director focusing and comparing measured visual ranges inside the BeatScope player. Inspiration BeatScope started from a simple problem: music visualizations often look impressive, but the timing logic behind them is usually locked inside one demo. I wanted to turn musical timing into reusable, deterministic data that could drive different visual systems — and also be understood by coding agents. The WebMCP Challenge made it possible to take that idea one step further: instead of making an agent inspect the DOM or guess how the player works, BeatScope can expose its musical state directly as structured browser tools. What it does BeatScope Director adds an in-browser WebMCP collaboration layer to BeatScope. An AI agent can inspect the loaded track, query timing and energy at any moment, read bounded musical events, find visually interesting ranges, compare sections, focus the timeline, control playback, and create loops — all inside the same player the user is watching. It currently exposes eight WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() , including: get_project_context get_state_at_time get_events find_visual_moments compare_ranges focus_range control_playback set_loop_range The agent does not receive the source audio. It works from BeatScope's already-computed analysis, while the user's normal local upload and playback workflow remains unchanged. How I built it I kept BeatScope's existing architecture and analysis pipeline intact and added WebMCP as a separate browser integration layer. Both the existing stdio MCP server and the new WebMCP Director read the same Rhythm IR and deterministic runtime, so they describe the same track with the same semantics; only the transport and lifecycle are different. The WebMCP layer is split into schemas, queries, actions, responses, and registration lifecycle code. Read-only tools are explicitly separated from tools that modify the page. Agent actions are visible in the UI and can be reversed by the user. I also built a reproducible WebMCP demo with rights-safe synthesized audio, browser smoke tests, snapshots, benchmarks, and CI coverage. Challenges The hardest part was keeping the agent useful without letting it invent musical meaning. BeatScope deliberately reports measurable facts such as beats, transients, frequency-band energy, and neutral structural repetition. It does not pretend that an onset is a kick or snare, or that a repeated section must be a verse or chorus. Another challenge was browser control. Playback actions have to respect autoplay restrictions, variable-tempo timing, cancellation, page lifecycle, and user ownership of the final state. I also wanted WebMCP to fail gracefully: if document.modelContext is unavailable, BeatScope still behaves like the normal player instead of breaking. What I learned WebMCP works best when it is not just a wrapper around buttons. The most useful tools expose the application's actual domain model. In BeatScope, that means giving the agent direct access to deterministic rhythm, structure, energy, and playback state instead of forcing it to reconstruct those concepts from the interface. I also learned that human-agent collaboration feels much safer when agent actions are visible, bounded, and reversible. The user still owns the player; WebMCP simply gives the agent a structured way to participate. title: λ-SPEC WebMCP
pitch: Resilience you can delegate. Evidence you can audit.
about_excerpt: Resilience you can delegate. Evidence you can audit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Rich analytical web apps are easy for humans to use but brittle for agents. A browser agent normally has to infer intent from forms, synthesize clicks, and scrape charts back out of the DOM. λ-SPEC explores a better contract: a scientific web application that exposes its real domain capabilities directly to an agent while keeping the human in the same visible workspace. What it does λ-SPEC measures observed system–environment coupling and asks what remains when environmental support is progressively withdrawn. It computes coupling λ, complementary fragility Φ, rolling λ and dλ/dt, an environmental-withdrawal stress envelope, ranked measured environmental drivers, confidence, limitations and exportable evidence. For the WebMCP Challenge, λ-SPEC was extended with eight typed WebMCP tools. An agent can discover datasets, load and configure a demo, run the resilience analysis, inspect the current evidence, inspect the withdrawal envelope, ask an evidence-bounded interpreter and run an end-to-end collaboration workflow. Why WebMCP is essential The agent is not clicking buttons or scraping charts. document.modelContext.registerTool(...) exposes the underlying analysis contract with constrained JSON schemas, read-only annotations and explicit validation. Tool calls update the same in-page state the human sees. A person can manually change the method, rolling window or column roles and then ask the agent to continue from that exact revised state. That human→agent handoff is the core improvement: both sides operate on one visible scientific state instead of maintaining separate hidden automation contexts. How we built it Challenge-specific implementation lives in lambda_spec/static/webmcp.js . The registered tools are: list_resilience_demos load_resilience_demo configure_resilience_analysis run_resilience_analysis get_resilience_state inspect_environmental_withdrawal ask_resilience_evidence run_resilience_collaboration Inputs are bounded with enums, limits, uniqueness constraints and validation against the active dataset. WebMCP progressively enhances the app: if document.modelContext is unavailable, λ-SPEC still works normally for a human. Existing project vs. challenge work λ-SPEC v1.2 existed before the challenge with its analysis engine, demos, charts, CSV workflow, exports and evidence interpreter. The WebMCP layer was added during the challenge period beginning at commit b40ec1f6ff4d2ff2f506b08331f69fe678754499 . Subsequent challenge commits add tool registration, shared human/agent state, tests, deployment configuration and judge materials. How to test Open the live app in a WebMCP-capable browser/runtime and ask: Analyze the orbital telemetry demo. Tell me whether measured coupling is strengthening or weakening, inspect the environmental-withdrawal envelope, identify the strongest measured environmental drivers, and tell me what to investigate next. Stay within the measured evidence. Then manually change the coupling method or rolling window and ask: Inspect the current resilience state again and continue from the state I changed. The floating WebMCP · human + agent workspace panel reports agent activity visibly. Scope and limitations λ-SPEC measures observed coupling. It does not establish causality, provide clinical diagnosis, certify engineering safety, make financial suitability determinations, or guarantee forecasts. The withdrawal curve is a controlled signal-removal stress envelope, not a literal simulation of every real-world intervention. I designed the human-agent interaction model so AI agents can understand available web capabilities, execute structured actions, and return useful results while preserving human oversight. I focused the platform on health and education use cases, translating complex workflows into accessible, explainable, agent-ready experiences. I also coordinated the project positioning, technical narrative, public demo, and final Devpost submission. title: CharDesk
pitch: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI agents are fluent in text, but people understand complex ideas faster when they can see structure, position, emphasis, and relationships. Existing collaboration tools usually force one side to compromise: people work through visual interfaces while agents imitate mouse clicks, or agents produce plain text that people must mentally reconstruct. We wanted a medium native to both. CharDesk began with a simple idea: What if the canvas were visual to people, but still made of tokens an agent could read and edit precisely? What CharDesk does CharDesk is a shared visual workspace for humans and AI agents. An agent can create or update a Blackboard through WebMCP. The result immediately appears as a live Unicode canvas that a person can inspect, navigate, and continue discussing with the agent. The same canvas can combine: Unicode and ANSI art Markdown and fenced code Mermaid diagrams Tables, JSON, and YAML Mathematical expressions Scientific plots and Vega-Lite Spatial layouts and character-based slides This makes CharDesk useful for explaining concepts, visualizing research, mapping systems, designing interfaces, presenting stories, and maintaining a shared project workspace. For example, someone can ask: “Explain how a GPU renders one frame.” The agent can turn that request into a structured visual scene containing a pipeline diagram, memory relationships, annotations, and styled interface elements—not just another long answer in chat. Why it is better with WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would need to guess how to operate the interface or manipulate individual canvas cells. CharDesk instead exposes focused workspace tools for discovering, creating, reading, writing, patching, deleting, and validating Blackboard files. The source remains authoritative; the canvas is a live projection of it. This gives each participant the representation they work with best: Human sees relationships, hierarchy, and visual emphasis ⇅ CharDesk Blackboard ⇅ Agent reads and edits structured, diffable text Agents can also call chardesk_read_materials to learn the visual language from worked examples. The tool teaches not only how to call the API, but how to compose an effective scene. How we built it CharDesk has a protocol-neutral tool layer shared by two thin host adapters: Standard WebMCP for compatible Chrome environments The imperative WebMCP capability supported by ChatGPT Site Tools Both adapters expose the same underlying Blackboard operations, so product behavior does not depend on a particular browser integration. A Blackboard stores source files and layout metadata. Changes are compiled through a shared rendering pipeline into a fixed character grid. This pipeline handles Unicode width, CJK characters, Nerd Font glyphs, ANSI styles, structured diagrams, and multidimensional layouts. The browser keeps the latest valid canvas mounted while an agent edits the source. If an intermediate update is invalid, CharDesk returns diagnostics without replacing the visible scene with a broken or empty state. The same format also works outside the browser through the CharDesk CLI, making projects portable, inspectable, renderable, and friendly to normal version-control workflows. Challenges we faced One unexpected challenge was tool ownership across browser tabs. Opening several CharDesk pages could cause identical tools to be registered multiple times, leaving the agent unable to choose a target. We built an origin-level gateway lease so only one page exposes the tools, with automatic takeover when that page closes. Chrome and ChatGPT also expose different subsets of the evolving WebMCP API. Instead of spreading compatibility checks throughout the product, we isolated those differences behind capability adapters backed by one canonical tool definition. Another challenge was timing: some hosts inject WebMCP after the application has already loaded. CharDesk therefore uses an adaptive registration handshake rather than assuming the API exists at startup. Finally, we learned that exposing tools is not enough. An agent may know how to write a file without knowing how to create a compelling visual explanation. Embedding CharDesk’s materials and examples as a callable tool gave browser agents the missing creative context. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-native design is not simply automation layered onto an existing UI. A better pattern is to give agents a precise, structured representation while giving people a rich visual projection of the same underlying artifact. WebMCP makes that relationship discoverable directly from the website, without requiring agents to reverse-engineer the interface. CharDesk explores what becomes possible when the web page is no longer just something an agent operates, but a shared medium in which the human and agent can think together. title: PromptFlow.ai — AI Software Architect
pitch: Describe it. Watch it architect. Build it.
about_excerpt: Describe it. Watch it architect. Build it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Judge Mode deliberately breaks, diagnoses, heals and re-tests the architecture before producing a production verdict. 49 WebMCP tools let an AI agent discover and operate PromptFlow directly. PromptFlow.ai — AI Software Architect Describe it. Watch it architect. Build it. PromptFlow.ai is an AI-native software architecture workspace where humans describe systems in natural language and AI agents operate the live architecture through WebMCP. Instead of treating architecture as a static diagram, PromptFlow treats it as a living system that can be designed, analyzed, deliberately broken, diagnosed, hardened, re-tested, built, executed, and verified. Why WebMCP? WebMCP is the core interaction layer between the AI agent and PromptFlow. A normal visual architecture tool requires an agent to understand the application's UI and manually figure out how to manipulate it. PromptFlow exposes structured, typed WebMCP tools so an agent can discover capabilities, reason about the user's intent, construct an architecture plan, and invoke deterministic operations directly. PromptFlow currently exposes 49 WebMCP tools: 37 Agent OS tools 12 atomic architecture tools For a complete product brief, the primary agent workflow is build_and_verify_system . The calling AI agent owns open-ended semantic reasoning. PromptFlow owns validation, state mutation, deterministic architecture intelligence, project generation, browser-native execution, and verification. Humans + Agents The human provides the product idea and constraints. The AI agent interprets the intent and decides which PromptFlow capabilities to use. WebMCP carries the structured tool calls into the live application. PromptFlow validates the agent-authored architecture plan, updates the live graph, analyzes the system, simulates failure, applies hardening, generates the project, executes it in a browser-native WebContainer, and produces a final production verdict. This collaboration makes it possible to move from: Natural-language intent → architecture → failure analysis → implementation → executable proof without requiring the human to manually construct every node and connection. The Core Verification Loop PromptFlow's Judge Mode orchestrates: Brief → Reason → Architect → Break → Diagnose → Heal → Re-test → Build → Execute → QA → Verdict The system intentionally injects failure scenarios into the architecture instead of only demonstrating a successful happy path. It then: identifies bottlenecks and failure propagation, diagnoses the affected architecture, applies bounded hardening, re-runs the same failure scenario, generates the implementation workspace, executes the generated project inside WebContainer, runs Production QA, produces a final release verdict. The result is an architecture workflow that demonstrates not only what the system looks like, but how it behaves under failure and whether the generated project can actually execute. Real WebContainer Execution PromptFlow uses WebContainer as a browser-native Node.js runtime. The generated project goes through: Generate → Mount → Install → Test → Build → Diagnose → Heal → Re-run → Verify The generated source is not executed directly by the host page. The production demo successfully verifies the real execution loop, including: mounting, dependency installation, testing, building, runtime verification. Architecture Intelligence PromptFlow evaluates architecture across: Reliability Scalability Performance Security Resilience Observability It also provides: deterministic architecture audits, heuristic stress testing, Architecture DNA, failure simulation, digital-twin analysis, implementation readiness, implementation contracts, project blueprints, migration planning, architecture versioning. These are explicitly planning and review signals, not security certifications, production load-test guarantees, or infrastructure capacity guarantees. Production QA The final Production QA gate checks the actual application state, including: architecture integrity, generated artifact safety, WebMCP registry coverage, browser isolation requirements, generated project readiness, real WebContainer execution state, architecture checkpoint integrity. The final demo produced: 100/100 architecture score 86 → 100 compute-failure survivability +14 recovery 100/100 Production QA 11/11 Judge Mode stages completed 5/5 real execution steps passed What Makes PromptFlow Different Most architecture tools stop at visualization. PromptFlow connects the full lifecycle: Describe → Architect → Break → Diagnose → Heal → Re-test → Build → Execute → Verify The architecture itself becomes an active system that can be reasoned about, challenged, repaired, and proven. PromptFlow's central idea is: Architecture should be a living system, not a static diagram. Implementation PromptFlow is built with: React TypeScript React Flow Zustand Vite WebMCP WebContainer Netlify WebMCP tools are registered directly in the browser using the WebMCP model context API. The application does not require a PromptFlow backend for the core architecture execution flow. The architecture graph remains in browser state, while the WebMCP layer provides the agent-facing execution contract. Demo Live application: https://promptflow-webmcp.netlify.app/ The demo video shows: AI agent discovery of PromptFlow WebMCP tools Agent-authored architecture planning Live architecture generation Judge Mode failure injection Diagnosis and hardening Re-test and recovery Real WebContainer execution Production QA Final production verdict WebMCP Challenge Work PromptFlow was meaningfully extended for the WebMCP Challenge submission period. The WebMCP-specific work includes: WebMCP tool registration and discovery Agent OS architecture tools 49 agent-facing WebMCP tools structured agent-authored architecture plans build_and_verify_system orchestration deterministic architecture execution WebMCP execution telemetry Judge Mode integration failure injection and diagnosis architecture hardening and re-testing project generation browser-native WebContainer execution Production QA final production verdict production WebMCP deployment configuration The repository history documents the WebMCP implementation work added during the challenge period. Safety & Boundaries PromptFlow intentionally keeps semantic reasoning and deterministic execution separate. The AI agent can reason about arbitrary product requirements, but PromptFlow validates all structured operations before applying them. Simulation tools are non-destructive. Generated code is executed only inside the isolated WebContainer runtime. Architecture Intelligence, Digital Twin, and Production QA metrics are clearly presented as deterministic or heuristic planning signals rather than guarantees of real-world production performance, security, or availability. title: Patchwork WebMCP- let people and AI agents discover projects
pitch: Turn good intentions into neighborhood action. Patchwork lets people and AI agents discover projects, build plans while keeping them human-approved. Use any AI browser to query it, like ChatGpt.
about_excerpt: Turn good intentions into neighborhood action. Patchwork lets people and AI agents discover projects, build plans while keeping them human-approved. Use any AI browser to query it, like ChatGpt. Like 2 Comment 1 Story Updates 1 Patchwork WebMCP Small actions. Shared momentum. Patchwork is an open-source neighbourhood planning workspace where people and browser agents discover opportunities, build practical plans, and draft new community needs together—while every publication or commitment remains under human control. Project links Live application: https://patchwork-webmcp.pages.dev/ Source repository: https://github.com/lsantos2000/patchwork-webmcp Demo video: https://youtu.be/so9sDOxzeJY Browser testing guide: resources/docs/browser-test.md Visual evidence: README.md#visual-evidence License: MIT Created by Leonardo Santos-Macias as an individual submission to the WebMCP Challenge. Inspiration People often want to help their neighbourhoods but struggle to turn good intentions into a practical plan. Finding opportunities, comparing them, and deciding what fits into a free afternoon takes effort. The push to actually build it was personal. Our newborn, Ellie Victoria, arrived premature—a fighter from the first day—and is growing into a wonderful child. Watching my wife become a mother, with our other children and our family around us, changed how I think about spare time: it stopped being an afternoon and became the gaps between feeds, school runs, and appointments. That is what most volunteering asks you to have, and what a new parent never does. So Patchwork starts from a smaller question: what if an agent did the searching, comparing, and fitting-it-together work, and handed back something small enough to actually do—while the person kept every decision that mattered? Small actions. Shared momentum. What it does Patchwork is a WebMCP-powered neighbourhood action prototype. People can explore example community projects, filter opportunities, and assemble a plan that fits their interests and available time. A compatible browser agent can work with the same project data and the same visible plan through structured tools. Instead of merely describing what someone could do, it can help organize those opportunities inside the application. The Discover tab covers intent-aware project search, an editable weekend plan, device-local persistence, community-project drafts, and draft-only pledges. Plan together adds negotiated planning: the person sets a time budget, selects and pins projects, and reviews the agent's proposed before-and-after revision. Action history records accepted and rejected planning actions without pretending a real-world pledge was sent. The boundary is deliberate: preparing a plan is not making a commitment. An agent can propose changes, draft a new local need, and prepare a pledge draft, while approval remains a separate step in the interface. The prototype does not send pledges to real organizations. Why WebMCP This workflow maps naturally to declared website capabilities: search project records, combine selected IDs into a plan, inspect a shared workspace, propose a revision, structure a new community need, and prepare a pledge draft. Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer meaning from visual pages, scrape text, or automate fragile click sequences. Patchwork instead exposes typed operations and structured results through the website itself. The agent works with the application's real records and constraints, while its results update the same interface the person is viewing. This creates a continuous human-agent experience. A person can inspect an agent-created plan, adjust it manually, preserve a pinned choice, reject a proposed revision, approve a community-project draft, or undo an accepted workspace change without transferring information between a chat response and another form. How I built it I built Patchwork with React and TypeScript, using Vinext for the Cloudflare Pages production build. Project-domain helpers provide deterministic catalogue search, planning, constraint checks, and persisted-data validation. A reusable React hook registers WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool({...}), falls back to navigator.modelContext, and unregisters tools during cleanup. Each handler validates or normalizes its input, calls the relevant domain helper, updates shared React state, and returns a structured response—so agent actions and manual interactions stay connected. The WebMCP integration exposes six tools, scoped to the active workflow. Discover provides: search_neighborhood_projects build_action_plan propose_neighborhood_project pledge_support Plan together and Action history provide: get_workspace propose_plan_revision Proposal results include revision information and a before-and-after comparison. Stale revisions and impossible constraints produce explicit conflicts rather than silent compromises. The human-control boundary is built into the results. propose_neighborhood_project returns human_approval_required with published: false; only the visible approval control adds the draft to the browser-local catalogue. pledge_support returns confirmation_required and never delivers a pledge. Local browser storage preserves the Discover plan between visits on the same device. I also added automated tests, browser-testing instructions, screenshots, and submission documentation. The source is publicly available under the MIT license. Challenges I ran into One challenge was making agent actions understandable. A successful tool response is not enough—the person needs to see what changed and keep the ability to review it. WebMCP handlers therefore update the same React state as the human controls, so both participants share one visible source of truth. Another was distinguishing discovery from planning: finding projects that each fit a time limit does not automatically produce a combined plan within that limit. State synchronization also required care. A plan must stay consistent when it is edited manually, created through a WebMCP tool, restored from local storage, or revised in the negotiated workspace. The implementation validates persisted records and uses workspace revision numbers so a stale agent proposal cannot overwrite a newer human choice. I also fixed production styling problems and state disappearing after navigation. Throughout, I worked to distinguish actual browser evidence from automated tests and edited demonstrations. Accomplishments I'm proud of I'm proud of building a shared interface where people and agents work with the same plan, rather than two separate experiences. Patchwork demonstrates why WebMCP is useful here: structured tools let an agent use the application's own data and actions without relying on fragile page scraping. Review and consent are part of the design, alongside persistence, testing, and documentation. A deployed, open-source WebMCP application that stays fully usable without an agent. Six structured tools across two scoped workflows. Explicit approval, rejection, conflict, and undo behaviour. Device-local persistence with validation and graceful storage-unavailable messaging. A responsive interface with production styling on Cloudflare Pages. Automated coverage plus separately recorded native WebMCP evidence. Clear prototype boundaries: demonstration data, browser-local publication, and no real pledge delivery. What I learned I learned that useful agent integration depends as much on clear boundaries as on capability. An agent should understand what an action changes, what stays a draft, and when approval is required. WebMCP is most compelling when it exposes meaningful domain actions rather than recreating low-level clicks. Small, well-described tools give an agent enough structure to help while keeping the application's rules in the application. Honest constraints also improve the agent experience. A structured conflict response is more useful than silently dropping a pinned project or exceeding a time budget, and revision tokens protect a person's newer decisions from stale proposals. I also learned that a convincing demonstration must make those distinctions visible. Good documentation and reproducible tests help explain both what works and what remains a prototype. How AI tools were used Patchwork does not embed its own model or chatbot. It exposes browser-local WebMCP tools that a compatible external agent can discover and invoke. Codex assisted with React and WebMCP implementation, debugging, automated testing, documentation, browser evidence, and demo production. Google Gemini was also used during the project. Piper generated the synthetic narration for the demo, and FFmpeg assembled and validated the final video. ChatGPT WebMCP discovery query A ChatGPT conversation was used to query the live application with the request: Discover tools at https://patchwork-webmcp.pages.dev/ The query identified six WebMCP tools across Patchwork's workflows. title: Vivid
pitch: Vivid turns any dashboard into an agent editable surface - no MCP server, no vision model, just the browser tab exposing its own governed webmcp tools.
about_excerpt: Vivid turns any dashboard into an agent editable surface - no MCP server, no vision model, just the browser tab exposing its own governed webmcp tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept seeing the same demo of "agentic BI": a headless MCP server that spits out a chart, or a vision model squinting at a screenshot to figure out where to click. Neither one understands the chart it's looking at, and neither lets a person and an agent actually work on the same dashboard together. WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool offers a different answer — the page exposes its own tools, the tab itself becomes the tool surface, nothing in between. I built Vivid to see if that holds up on something real: a six-panel B2B SaaS revenue dashboard, not a toy chart. What it does Vivid is a live analytics workspace with two dashboards — a six-panel revenue report (Northbeam) and a product-usage report (Activity OS) — that an agent can read and edit right in the same tab a person is looking at. No MCP server behind it, no model reading screenshots. The agent can pull live report context, set filters (segment, region, plan tier, channel, contract type, account), and reshape specific charts. ARR bridge and NRR/churn retention take a validated patch to their underlying state — never a raw spec. ARR mix, top accounts, and net-new logos only let the agent swap between a couple of approved presentations, like donut vs. bar. A semantic layer — Cube Cloud over 7 real Postgres tables — grounds open-ended questions ("MRR by region") in real metric definitions instead of guessed column names. And it's genuinely shared: every edit, person or agent, goes through the same validation, persists to a room, syncs live to everyone on that room's link, can be undone, and lands in one activity log with both actors in it. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript. Two report surfaces, each with its own filter state and its own WebMCP tools, registered only while that tab is open. The two agent-editable charts (ARR bridge, retention) are Vega-Lite specs rendered via vega-embed, but the spec is derived from a small "knob" object, never written directly. Everything else is plain SVG/CSS. A lighter contract ( set_report_chart_contract ) later opened up three more panels — ARR mix, top accounts, net-new logos — to an allow-listed presentation swap, still no direct spec access. The tool layer is document.modelContext.registerTool calls made from the page: read-only ( get_report_context , list_report_options , find_field_values ) and mutating ( update_chart_spec , set_report_filters ), each validating input before touching state. Every call returns { ok: true, data } or { ok: false, reason, error } . Persistence is one JSON snapshot per room, mutated only through a Supabase Edge Function and a Postgres RPC that checks a capability digest, compare-and-swaps the version, and writes state plus an activity-log row in one transaction. RLS blocks direct table writes — no shortcut around validation. The semantic layer is Cube Cloud over those same 7 tables, reached only through an Edge Function proxy — the API token never touches the browser. Two more tools, get_business_definitions and query_business_metric , answer questions unrelated to either report's charts. Challenges I ran into document.modelContext is a draft API — I didn't have a browser that ships it. So I injected a minimal registerTool polyfill through devtools and added a re-entry point ( window.__vividRegisterTools() ) to still exercise the real execute functions end to end: discovery, validation, re-render, persistence, activity log. Not a live agent, but as close as I could get without one. Making "never dual-axis" actually true took longer than expected. Telling an agent not to do something is easy; making the schema incapable of expressing the bad state is harder. I kept finding invariants that were still just conventions until I pushed them into the validator. Adversarial input was its own problem once I accepted an agent writing state needs the same suspicion as a hostile user — oversized values, SQL-looking field names, injection attempts, spoofed capabilities, UUID reuse. A dedicated test suite covers all of it; the rule was every one has to fail cleanly, never a crash or a silent partial write. Keeping Revenue and Product Usage independent without duplicating everything was a constant judgment call — separate filters and tool sets, but one shared wire protocol and undo pattern underneath both. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A full WebMCP tool contract — discovery, reads, validated writes, real error reasons — running end to end with nothing mocked, verified without a shipping WebMCP browser in hand. Invariants that hold because the validator won't let them break, not because a tool description asked nicely. An adversarial security pass that throws real hostile input at every mutation path and degrades cleanly every time — no crashes, no silent writes. Multiplayer that isn't faked for the demo: agent and person edits share one path, one sync, one log. A semantic layer with zero shared imports back into the chart code — it'd survive being lifted into a different app. Something live at vividdata.pages.dev a judge can actually click through. What I learned Chart-as-data instead of chart-as-code is what makes this trustworthy. I could've let the agent send a raw Vega-Lite spec — I didn't. Every editable chart runs off a small typed object, and the spec is derived from it. That's the decision that made invariants real instead of aspirational. MCP and WebMCP aren't rivals — they're two stages of the same job. MCP gets you a fast first draft: a headless server hands an agent the data, it produces something in one shot. But getting a draft right after that is visual and iterative — "make the bars wider," "try it as a donut," "now filter to EMEA" — and a headless server has nothing on screen to see or touch for that. WebMCP picks up right there. A semantic layer changed what "grounded" meant in practice — real metric definitions instead of guessed column names made the gap between a correct answer and a confident wrong one a lot more visible. Multiplayer forced honesty about state. Once edits sync live into a shared log, you can't hand-wave version tracking — it's a real compare-and-swap, or two edits eventually stomp on each other. What's next for Vivid Right now this proves the idea on one dashboard. I want chart-as-data to stop being specific to Northbeam and become a pattern other people's dashboards use. That means pulling the governed-presentation contract and the knob-based chart state out of this codebase into something closer to a spec — small and documented enough that any team could implement it over their own charts without re-deriving these invariants from scratch. I also want Vivid to stop being a demo of one dashboard and become a place people actually work. Connect Data already proves the generic version — point at any Postgres table, get an agent-editable chart through a validated contract — I want that to be the default onboarding, not a hidden tab. The semantic layer should scale past one Cube deployment over 7 tables — the same shared-key discipline tying a chart's knobs to its metric definition could stretch across multiple warehouses. I like the idea of more than one agent in a room at once — a drafting agent proposing something, a review agent checking it against governed invariants, a person steering both — on the same activity log and undo stack that already treats a person and an agent as peers. Before any of that touches real data: real tenancy. The bearer-link model is deliberately bare-bones; authenticated rooms and real capability revocation are what turn this from a convincing prototype into something a company could point at its own numbers. And longer term — every BI vendor is racing to ship its own locked-in MCP server. My bet runs the other way: WebMCP means any agent, not just the vendor's own, can reach into a live chart. title: Overloaded
pitch: A real-time strategy game that keeps more depth than one player can manage, because your agent playsalongside you through its own interface instead of your screen.
about_excerpt: A real-time strategy game that keeps more depth than one player can manage, because your agent playsalongside you through its own interface instead of your screen. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Strategy games are simplified down to what one player can handle. Options get buried in submenus and whole systems get cut before release, and the limit is never the simulation. It is how much a person can look at while the clock is running. A model does not have that limit, which means the depth can stay in and the game does not have to be flattened to be playable. What it does Overloaded is a Napoleonic real-time strategy game. You raise infantry, cavalry and artillery, group them into named formations, and fight over supply depots against a clock. The whole live match is published as nineteen WebMCP tools, so your agent reads the field and gives orders in the same tick you do, from the same match state, without a screenshot and without taking your pointer. It can also write standing orders — instructions the army carries out on its own, with no model involved. How we built it TypeScript with no game engine. Every unit and building is assembled from primitives in three.js, the terrain is painted to a canvas at load, and every sound is synthesised through the Web Audio API, so nothing is loaded from an asset file. The tools call the same command layer the interface calls: issue is what a right-click runs and add_rule is what the panel's new-order button runs, so both sides drive one match object. Challenges we ran into A tool call takes seconds and the game runs at twenty ticks a second, so an agent that only reacts is always acting on information that has already changed. That is what standing orders are for: the agent writes a rule once, and the game runs it the moment the thing it watches reports. The second problem was discovery. The tools published one flat vocabulary while the interface filtered its dropdowns per formation, so an agent had to infer that a battery cannot charge. It now reports, for every formation and base, exactly which orders it can be given. Accomplishments that we are proud of Two people can command the same battle at once without either waiting for the other. And add_rule is a tool whose effect outlives the call it was made in — once written, the order runs with nothing in the loop. What we learned An agent surface is not just the list of things it can do. It is what the page tells the agent about what is possible right now, for this object. A capability that is technically available but not reported is one the agent will never use. What is next More arms and terrain, and a shared match where each side is commanded by a different person and their agent.
