title: DrawCMS
pitch: AI changes code fast, but its system impact is hard to see. Our WebMCP-native diagram editor lets agents turn changes into animated architecture and workflow diagrams—reviewed and refined by people.
about_excerpt: AI changes code fast, but its system impact is hard to see. Our WebMCP-native diagram editor lets agents turn changes into animated architecture and workflow diagrams—reviewed and refined by people. Like Comment Story Updates Generate with ChatGPT's in-app browser DrawCMS Editor Playing Steps Inspiration AI-made code changes are fast, but understanding their architectural and business-process impact is often not. Animated diagrams are still tedious to create by hand, and most diagram tools are inaccessible to AI agents. WebMCP changes that. We built the first browser-based diagram editor that speaks MCP natively, letting agents turn code changes into living, animated system diagrams. What it does DrawCMS is an open-source editor for animated technical diagrams (architecture, sequence, BPMN, etc.) built on React Flow + GSAP. It registers 8 WebMCP tools via navigator.modelContext , so an AI agent (e.g., ChatGPT agentic browsing) can build, animate, and narrate diagrams directly on the live canvas . no API keys, no servers, no simulated mouse clicks. Humans and agents co-edit the same canvas; every agent edit is one undoable Cmd+Z batch. How we built it Next.js 16 + React 19 + React Flow v12 for the canvas, GSAP for motion. The agent layer exposes tools like drawcms_replace_diagram , drawcms_set_motion , and drawcms_set_story through the browser's native navigator.modelContext API (with legacy fallback), backed by a visual grammar registry (~100 elements: including UML, ER, BPMN, and AWS/GCP/Azure icons) so agents know what to draw and how to animate it. Local-first storage, PNG/GIF export. the site deployed to Cloudflare worker. Challenges we ran into Designing tool schemas that give agents enough structure to produce good-looking animated diagrams (visual grammar + auto-layout + sensible motion defaults) while keeping edits incremental and reversible. Also handling the browser WebMCP API gracefully, non-supporting browsers just render the ordinary editor. Accomplishments that we're proud of A single prompt like "Build an animated diagram of a checkout request flowing through API gateway, queue, and database" makes a real animated diagram build itself before your eyes, and it runs with zero backend. Fully keyboard-accessible, 360 green tests, one-click deploy buttons for Vercel/Netlify/Render/Cloudflare. What we learned Exposing tools natively from the web app (WebMCP) makes agent integration almost free compared to scraping or browser extensions and the same tools double as a cleaner programmatic API for the product. title: OpenCast
pitch: Edit video by editing words — you and your AI agent cut, clip, caption, swap backgrounds, and drop in visuals together, live in one editor, via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Edit video by editing words — you and your AI agent cut, clip, caption, swap backgrounds, and drop in visuals together, live in one editor, via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates OpenCast Inspiration Two ideas collided. The first: tools like Descript proved that the transcript is the best interface for editing talk-heavy video — you delete a sentence, the footage follows. The second: WebMCP proposes that a web page should hand agents typed, callable tools instead of making them guess at buttons. Put together, they describe the same product. If editing is already "operate on words," then an agent that speaks in words is a native editor, not a bolted-on chatbot. I wanted to build the version of that idea where the human and the agent aren't in separate worlds — they look at the same live page , pull the same levers , and every change lands in the same undo stack. Editing a podcast felt like the sharpest possible test: it's real work, it's language-shaped, and you can see whether the collaboration is real. What it does OpenCast is a transcript-first podcast/video editor. Upload a recording; the transcript becomes editable in about a minute; then you — or your agent, through 47 WebMCP tools — cut filler words and silences, fix mis-transcriptions, assemble named compositions (hooks, clips) from timeline ranges, turn on live captions, layer timed images over or under the footage, remove the background with in-browser ML, and export a finished MP4 with everything burned in — rendered entirely in the browser. How I built it The architecture is three layers, and it's the part I'd defend in any design review: Page state — a Zustand store holding words (with per-word timestamps), sources, compositions, overlays. One shared action hub — every edit is a narrow verb: cutWords , renameSpeaker , addToComposition , removeOverlay … Two front ends to the same hub — buttons for humans, and WebMCP tools ( document.modelContext.registerTool — a name, a JSON schema, a callback) for agents. Same verbs; nobody gets a special door. Tools return what changed , so the agent can verify itself, and destructive ones require explicit confirmation. Around that core: a Next.js app on Vercel; a Fly.io Docker worker that takes resumable 16 MiB upload chunks straight to a volume, extracts audio with ffmpeg, and runs a words-first pipeline — Whisper word timings through a bounded concurrent pool unlock the editor fast, while speaker diarization runs as a background enrichment that relabels the live transcript when it lands (and multi-track projects skip ML diarization entirely, because the track is the speaker). Exports use a canvas compositor: play the kept ranges once, draw background layer → footage (MediaPipe selfie segmentation for background removal) → B-roll layer → captions, and record it with the source audio via MediaRecorder to MP4. Challenges I ran into The silent five-minute ceiling. Long diarization calls kept dying with a cryptic Headers Timeout Error : Node's fetch (undici) aborts any request whose response headers take over 300s — and retried the doomed request forever. Diagnosing that, giving OpenAI calls a real deadline through an explicit dispatcher, and then restructuring to words-first (never let the slow model block the editable transcript) was the single biggest turn in the project. Embedded browsers are a different planet. ChatGPT Desktop's browser is narrow, blocks programmatic downloads without a user gesture, and can't be trusted with a GPU delegate. That forced real fixes: on-screen layers scoped to the footage's aspect ratio instead of the pane, a CPU fallback for segmentation, and layouts audited at 480px. Canvas taint. Recording a canvas fails if any drawn image isn't CORS-readable — one bad overlay URL could poison a whole render. Locally uploaded images are compressed into data URLs (always safe); non-CORS remote images are skipped rather than killing the export. Building on a moving spec. WebMCP is pre-standard; API names have already shifted. Keeping the tool layer thin over the action hub meant the churn only ever touches one file. What I learned Design tools as narrow verbs with clear side effects that report what changed — agents chain small verbs better than they wield big ones. Words-first beats complete-but-slow: shipping the editable thing early and enriching in the background changed how the product feels more than any feature. And the deepest one: the trust problem with agents isn't solved by logs or promises — it's solved by a shared screen , where every mutation happens in front of you and your undo key still works. What's next Program-cut-aware multicam rendering on the worker, cross-chunk speaker identity stitching, and a consent surface for tool calls that's worthy of the spec this is all betting on. title: SHIPGATE
pitch: SHIPGATE aligns agent capability with release evidence, ensuring WebMCP tools dynamically unlock shipping only when tests and human approvals pass.
about_excerpt: SHIPGATE aligns agent capability with release evidence, ensuring WebMCP tools dynamically unlock shipping only when tests and human approvals pass. Like Comment Story Updates Evidence becomes capability. BLOCKED REVIEW REQUIRED Human authority stays outside the agent SHIPPED SHIPGATE's release state and authority model Inspiration SHIPGATE started with one question Should an agent have access to a consequential action before the conditions for that action are satisfied? Most agent systems expose tools continuously and rely on the model to decide when not to use them. I wanted to test a different model where trusted application state changes what the agent can actually do. That became SHIPGATE. Evidence becomes capability. Instead of keeping deployment authority permanently available, SHIPGATE changes the browser's WebMCP tool surface as release evidence and human decisions change. What SHIPGATE does SHIPGATE turns release state into agent authority. A release moves through four states BLOCKED → REVIEW_REQUIRED → READY → SHIPPED In BLOCKED , the agent can inspect evidence and request evaluation, but ship_release is not registered. When the hard evidence passes, request_signoff becomes available. The agent can request approval, but it cannot approve itself. Human confirmation stays outside WebMCP. Only after human approval does the release become READY and ship_release appear as a registered WebMCP capability. After shipping, that capability retires and temporary rollback_release authority appears. Two rules shaped the project. The agent can request evidence, but it cannot author the evidence. The agent can request authority, but it cannot grant authority to itself. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the mechanism, not an interface added afterward. SHIPGATE uses the browser's actual tool inventory to represent the agent's current authority. BLOCKED → ship_release absent REVIEW_REQUIRED → request_signoff available READY → ship_release available SHIPPED → ship_release retired and rollback_release available temporarily This improves the experience for both sides. People can see what authority the agent currently has and what evidence or human decision is still missing. Agents do not need to reason over a deployment tool that should not yet be available. The collaboration is explicit. The agent gathers evidence and asks for judgment. The human contributes authority the agent cannot give itself. The application turns those inputs into the capabilities that exist. How I built it The core architecture is: trusted evidence → application state → capability → runtime recheck → verified effect SHIPGATE is built with JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Node.js, Netlify, and native WebMCP. Tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Six tools remain permanently available for inspection and evaluation get_release_state get_release_policy inspect_check compare_to_baseline list_evidence_gaps run_check_group Three capabilities appear only when the release contract allows them. request_signoff during REVIEW_REQUIRED ship_release during READY rollback_release after SHIPPED while rollback remains valid I also separated requesting evidence from creating evidence. run_check_group lets the agent request an evaluation, but the agent cannot supply PASS or FAIL, choose the evidence source, change the candidate identity, or provide human confirmation. The evaluator owns the result. Evidence is tied to the current candidate and its provenance. Stale or untrusted evidence cannot satisfy the release contract. Human approval is deliberately outside WebMCP. Tool availability also is not the security boundary. Consequential tools recheck the contract when invoked. Tool availability narrows the action surface. Runtime validation remains the enforcement boundary. Challenges I faced Dynamic tool registration The first challenge was making authority change safely at runtime. ship_release needs to disappear when authority is lost and later return under the same name without duplicate registrations or race conditions. I implemented a registration lifecycle. HIDDEN → REGISTERING → ACTIVE → RETIRING → HIDDEN SHIPGATE waits for registration or retirement to settle before the same capability can reappear. A native Chrome race condition The hardest bug appeared only during native WebMCP execution in Chrome 152. ship_release could successfully move the release to SHIPPED, but immediate retirement of that tool could cancel the still-running executeTool() promise with an UnknownError . The release had succeeded, but the browser call looked like it had failed. I fixed this by separating policy authority from physical registration retirement . The policy changes immediately, so another ship attempt already fails its runtime precondition. The browser registration retires only after the active invocation finishes. That distinction made the native WebMCP lifecycle reliable. Evidence authority I also had to prevent the agent from creating the evidence that would unlock its own capability. The solution was simple but important. The agent can request an evaluation. The evaluator decides the outcome. That separation became one of the central design principles of SHIPGATE. Testing I tested both the application logic and the real browser capability surface. SHIPGATE has 20 passing automated tests covering release transitions, evidence provenance, stale and untrusted evidence, human approval boundaries, runtime enforcement, conditional registration, same-name registration, and in-flight retirement. I also tested the complete lifecycle in Chrome 152 using native document.modelContext WebMCP without mocks or stubs. The browser confirmed the intended progression. BLOCKED → ship_release absent REVIEW_REQUIRED → request_signoff appears pending approval → release does not advance READY → ship_release appears SHIPPED → ship_release retires and rollback_release appears rollback → temporary rollback authority retires For me, this was the important proof. SHIPGATE does not only change a button in the interface, but also changes the capability the browser exposes to the agent. Demo candidate SHIPGATE gates a real browser-game release candidate called FAKE LEFT. FAKE LEFT provides the behavioral and regression evidence used in the demo release contract. FAKE LEFT is the candidate being evaluated. SHIPGATE is the system deciding which capabilities become available around that candidate. What I learned The biggest lesson was that agent judgment and agent authority are different product problems. I began by thinking about whether an agent could correctly decide that a release was safe. Building SHIPGATE changed the question. Even if an agent can reason correctly, why should a consequential capability remain available before the surrounding evidence and human judgment are complete? WebMCP let me make that distinction concrete. The agent can inspect, evaluate, and request. The human provides judgment the agent cannot give itself. The application translates both into the authority that actually exists. I think this pattern can extend beyond deployment to infrastructure changes, administrative actions, sensitive data access, financial operations, and other workflows where agent authority should follow trusted state. What's next The next step is connecting this capability model to real operational evidence. The current demo uses deterministic evidence so every state transition is reproducible. I would next connect SHIPGATE to CI pipelines, evaluation systems, production monitoring, approval workflows, deployment infrastructure, and rollback systems. The long-term idea is straightforward. Consequential agent capabilities should follow trusted real-world state rather than remain permanently exposed. title: Openings — Agent Native Job Discovery
pitch: A workspace where you and an in-browser AI agent work the same job board resolving official career portals, extracting real openings, and scoring them against your resume, all via WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
A workspace where you and an in-browser AI agent work the same job board resolving official career portals, extracting real openings, and scoring them against your resume, all via WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Openings — Agent-Native Job Discovery 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Openings — Agent-Native Job Discovery 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Openings — Agent-Native Job Discovery 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Job hunting is a two-surface problem. Aggregators like Naukri and Indeed are great at telling you which companies are hiring — but they surface only a fraction of each company's roles and bury the link to the company's own careers page, where the complete, current list actually lives. Bridging those two surfaces — take a company name, find its official portal, extract every matching role, repeat, twenty times over — is exactly the repetitive, multi-step web work a human dreads and an agent is good at. 

 We wanted to see what happens when an AI agent and a human work the same job board, live, on the same page — not a chatbot bolted on the side, but an agent driving the app's real functions. That's the promise of WebMCP , and job discovery turned out to be a perfect fit. 

 What it does 

 Openings is an agent-native job-discovery workspace. You start from a Naukri search or just name a few companies, and Openings: 

 
 Resolves each company's official career portal — skipping aggregators, going straight to the source (e.g. stripe.com/jobs , ramp.com/careers ). 
 Extracts the real, current openings from that portal via a server-side crawl and structured extraction. 
 Scores every role 0–100 against your resume , with honest strengths, gaps, and tailored bullet rewrites that reframe your real experience — never fabricated. 
 Keeps everything on one shared board with a live activity feed . 
 

 The key idea: nothing is "agent-only" or "human-only." Every WebMCP tool is a thin wrapper over the same store action a UI button calls, so the human and the agent drive identical code and see one shared state . Paste companies and click Import, or ask the agent to do it — the outcome is the same. The agent handles the breadth (opening twenty portals in seconds); the human keeps the judgment (shortlisting, accepting resume edits). 

 How we built it 

 
 Frontend: Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS — a split-screen workspace (pipeline board on the left, resume canvas + activity feed on the right). 
 State: a framework-agnostic observable store ( src/store.ts ) shared by both the UI and the agent, persisted to the browser's localStorage . 
 WebMCP: five tools registered on document.modelContext.registerTool(...) — import_from_naukri , discover_company_jobs , add_job_to_board , match_with_resume , list_board_jobs . Each is a thin wrapper over a store action, and registration no-ops gracefully when WebMCP is absent, so the app still works as an ordinary web app. 
 Serverless: Netlify Functions handle portal resolution, career-page crawling, structured extraction, and resume scoring — so no API key ever touches the browser, and the SPA and functions share one origin (which WebMCP requires). 
 AI: a pluggable provider facade — Mistral ( mistral-small-latest , default) or Google Gemini ( gemini-3.6-flash ) — behind one generateJson contract, swappable with a single env var. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 JS-only career SPAs that can't be crawled. We added a knowledge-based fallback that returns the model's best-known roles, clearly flagged unverified in the activity feed so the user is never misled. 
 Structured-output reliability. Gemini's JSON mode could stall, so we built a circuit breaker : structured output is throttled independently, and if it trips, the helper falls back to plain-text JSON and skips the slow path on later calls. 
 Bounded latency. SDK retries are capped and every attempt is timed out, so a request never hangs for minutes during a live demo. 
 One-origin constraint. WebMCP requires the SPA and its functions on the same origin — we run everything through netlify dev locally so the tools connect exactly as they do in production. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A genuinely shared human–agent surface : one code path, one board, no "demo-only" wiring. 
 Going past aggregators to the official source for every role, with a direct link on every card. 
 Honest resume scoring with truthful bullet rewrites — sharpening real experience, never inventing it. 
 A backend that stays resilient even on free API tiers, so the demo doesn't fall over. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes how you architect an app: the moment your UI actions and your agent tools are the same functions , "agentic" stops being a bolt-on and becomes the natural shape of the code. The hard part isn't exposing tools — it's designing a store clean enough that a button and an agent can safely share it. 

 What's next for Openings — Agent Native Job Discovery 

 
 More ATS adapters (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby) for deeper, verified extraction. 
 Application tracking and status stages on the board. 
 Multi-resume profiles and per-role tailoring. 
 Swappable persistence (Netlify Blobs) so a board can sync across devices.

title: CommonGround Travel
pitch: CommonGround lets an agent reconcile every traveler's budget and must-haves through 27 WebMCP tools, then select a fair hotel and prepare a human-reviewed booking draft.
about_excerpt: CommonGround lets an agent reconcile every traveler's budget and must-haves through 27 WebMCP tools, then select a fair hotel and prepare a human-reviewed booking draft. Like Comment Story Updates Codex explains trade-offs, selects a zero-violation hotel, and prepares a reviewable draft using CommonGround’s Site Tools. The agent prepares a €380 hotel draft and stops at human approval. Nothing is booked, purchased, or charged automatically. Live workspace with 27 WebMCP tools, traveler constraints, visible agent activity, conflicts, and fair hotel rankings. Inspiration Planning a group trip rarely fails because there are too few hotel options. It fails because the important details are scattered across messages and held by different people. One traveler needs step-free access. Another has a hard nightly limit. A parent needs a suitable family room. Someone else cares most about reviews, location, or a gym. The organizer ends up acting as a human spreadsheet, and the loudest preference often wins. We built CommonGround to make that negotiation explicit, fair, and inspectable. The goal is not to let an AI choose a holiday for everyone. It is to let people and an agent work on the same decision, while preserving each traveler’s constraints and keeping the final commitment with a human. What it does CommonGround is a shared hotel decision workspace for groups of up to 30 travelers. Each person has a budget, preferences, and locked must-haves. The workspace detects conflicts, normalizes hotel inventory, and scores options under three transparent strategies: Group Consensus, Best Value, and Balanced Compromise. An attached agent can use 27 WebMCP Site Tools to read the live workspace and act on it. In one request, the agent can: identify every traveler by name; read their budgets, preferences, and locked requirements; explain concrete conflicts between them; search the available hotel inventory; compare all three decision strategies; select the fairest zero-violation result; and prepare a complete booking draft for human review. In the public Lisbon demo, that flow considers Maya’s step-free requirement, Diego’s €130-per-night limit, Sana’s family-room requirement, and Leo’s higher-budget preferences. It identifies budget gaps of €80, €100, and €140, then selects Pensão Lumen at €95 per night—€380 for four nights—with zero locked must-have violations. The agent stops there. The final Approve draft button remains untouched. CommonGround has no autonomous purchase path, and the tool response reports purchaseOccurred: false . Why WebMCP is essential A screenshot or scraped page is not enough for this problem. The agent needs structured access to shared state: who owns a requirement, whether it is a preference or a lock, which hotels violate it, which scoring strategy is active, and what the agent is permitted to change. WebMCP turns the website itself into the agent interface. The agent and the travelers use the same workspace, the same scoring logic, and the same visible controls. There is no separate chatbot database that can drift away from the page. When the agent selects a scenario or prepares a draft, the board changes in front of the group and the action appears in the activity and telemetry surfaces. This replaces a multi-screen, copy-and-paste workflow with one auditable request. More importantly, it gives the agent useful power without hiding its actions or surrendering human control. How we built it CommonGround feature-detects document.modelContext and registers 27 typed Site Tools. Every tool has a strict JSON schema, read/write annotations, cancellation support, and structured success or error results. Eight read tools expose workspace identity, onboarding and collaboration state, invitations, named traveler constraints, normalized inventory, scenario comparisons, and conflict explanations. Nineteen permission-aware action tools cover workspace creation, scoped invitations, trip and capacity settings, traveler-profile changes, priorities, locks, vetoes, scenario and hotel selection, and booking-draft preparation. The tools call the same React state transitions and scoring functions as the human interface. Writes are immediately visible. Invitation tokens are scoped to a traveler and stored as hashes. Supplier responses are treated as untrusted data. There is deliberately no reservation or payment endpoint behind the draft action. The application is built with React, TypeScript, Vite/vinext, Zod, Cloudflare Workers and D1, and Codex Sites. Vitest and automated browser verification exercise the scoring, permissions, tool contracts, state synchronization, and the no-purchase safety boundary. For a reliable judging experience, the deployed challenge build uses six clearly labeled curated Lisbon hotel records. The inventory layer is provider-based, so a licensed TravelWithWadjet, Booking.com Demand, Expedia Rapid, or other hotel supplier adapter can replace the demo provider without changing the consensus model or the WebMCP interface. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering tools; it was keeping three things synchronized: the state returned to the agent, the state visible to people, and the permission boundary between reading, changing, and committing. We also had to make subjective fairness explainable. A single “best hotel” score hides who is being asked to compromise. CommonGround therefore shows individual satisfaction, hard violations, group conflicts, and the effect of each scenario rather than presenting an unexplained recommendation. Browser support for an emerging technology was another practical challenge. We added capability detection, clear connection status, deterministic demo data, strict tool outputs, and a Chrome verification path so a judge can distinguish a product problem from a missing browser capability. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that CommonGround is a complete shared product experience rather than a chatbot wrapped around a static demo. A real external Codex agent can discover 27 typed Site Tools, identify four travelers by name, explain their specific conflicts, compare three decision strategies, choose a zero-violation hotel, and prepare a human-review draft in one request. The same actions immediately update the board the travelers are looking at. We are especially proud of the safety boundary. The agent is useful enough to complete the difficult research and negotiation work, but it cannot quietly cross into a purchase. The interface shows zero autonomous purchases, the draft explicitly says that no purchase is made, and the final approval remains a deliberate human action. We also built beyond the single demo path: organizers can create private workspaces for up to 30 travelers, invite people with scoped links, configure the trip, manage priorities and locks, and follow a guided onboarding flow. Automated tests and browser acceptance checks cover the tool contracts, permissions, fairness scoring, state synchronization, and booking-draft boundary. The result is something judges can use as a coherent product, not merely inspect as a technical prototype. What we learned Agents are most useful when they can operate on the same structured state as people—not when they merely describe what appears on a page. We also learned that visible actions are a product feature, not debugging decoration. People trust an agent more when they can see what it read, what it changed, why it made a recommendation, and where its authority ends. What's next for CommonGround Travel The next step is to connect licensed live hotel inventory through the provider adapter and carry the same model into flights, itineraries, and group expense decisions. The larger opportunity is a reusable negotiation layer for any shared decision where several people have different constraints and an agent should help without taking control away from them.  1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Working in cloud consoles like AWS, Azure often turns a simple task into a scavenger hunt across services, settings, documentation, and browser tabs. When I get stuck, I usually leave the console to ask ChatGPT or Claude for instructions. Sometimes the steps are accurate; other times they are outdated, incomplete, or based on a console layout that has already changed.
Even with the right answer, I still have to return to the console, locate every resource, and translate those instructions into clicks myself. The AI can describe the maze, but it cannot see where I am or work through it with me. Sightline was inspired by the idea that an agent should operate inside the console’s real context—helping navigate and prepare work while the human remains in control. 

 What it does 

 Sightline makes complex operational consoles like AWS, Azure and related, easier to use. It connects every service, resource, and setting involved in a task into one clear path that a person and an AI agent can navigate together, while the human retains control over final changes. 

 How we built it 

 We connected ten WebMCP tools directly to Sightline’s shared console state. Agents can search resources, trace dependencies, navigate between services, and prepare coordinated changes while each action appears instantly in the interface for human review. Only the human can apply the final changes. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was designing tools that were useful without giving agents too much control. We also had to handle stale revisions, invalid patches, sensitive values, and clear separation between prepared and applied changes. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 We can now turn a complex operational request into one clear path across multiple services, resources, and settings. 
 Agents can find dependencies, explain their impact, and prepare coordinated changes without applying them. 
 Humans can review every proposed action inside the console and retain control over the final change. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP works best when tools expose meaningful product actions instead of mirroring buttons. Stable resource IDs, clear schemas, and visible feedback make agent behaviour safer and easier to understand. 

 What's next for Sightline 

 Next, we want to connect Sightline to real cloud APIs, authentication, authorization, and audit systems, then test it with larger infrastructure environments and more operational workflows.

title: CloudSwarm: Agent-Native Cloud Infrastructure CAD
pitch: Humans and external LLMs co-design AWS/Azure/GCP topologies in real-time. Powered by WebMCP, CloudSwarm compiles production Terraform and executes live SecOps/FinOps audits with zero race conditions.
about_excerpt: Humans and external LLMs co-design AWS/Azure/GCP topologies in real-time. Powered by WebMCP, CloudSwarm compiles production Terraform and executes live SecOps/FinOps audits with zero race conditions. Like Comment Story Updates 💡 Inspiration Modern cloud architecture is trapped between two disconnected silos. On one side, solutions architects sketch static boxes on visual whiteboards (like Miro or Lucidchart) that are non-executable, drift from reality within days, lack cost awareness, and cannot be programmatically audited. On the other side, DevOps engineers spend weeks authoring thousands of lines of Terraform in text editors, reviewing complex infrastructure pull requests without spatial context—leading to silent security misconfigurations and budget blowouts. When the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) was introduced, the missing link became obvious to me: What if the web browser itself became an agent-native cloud workstation where a human engineer and external LLMs co-architect multi-cloud systems in real time? Instead of brittle DOM-scraping or slow sequential click-bots, WebMCP enables external models to discover typed tools, inspect live spatial canvas state, and execute atomic architectural mutations right alongside human engineers. 🚀 What it does CloudSwarm is an enterprise multi-cloud architecture CAD workstation built entirely around the WebMCP standard. Simultaneous Human + AI Co-Design: Human architects drag primitives from a 108-item multi-cloud catalog (AWS, Azure, GCP) and wire dependencies with the mouse. Simultaneously, external LLMs (via ChatGPT Desktop or Claude) can inspect state, provision GPU clusters, attach WAF shields, and route fabrics over WebMCP JSON-RPC. 4-Agent Concurrent Swarm: I natively route multi-agent workflows across specialized roles: Atlas (Compute/Infra), Breach (Security/WAF), Forge (Storage/Data), and Cost (FinOps). Organic Hardware-Accelerated Cursors: AI cursors glide across the canvas displaying concise task badges (e.g., Linking 800G Fabric ) letting humans watch the AI's physical workflow in real-time. Bidirectional Terraform HCL2 Sync: Canvas topologies continuously compile into production-ready HashiCorp Configuration Language. Modifications to the live code editor automatically update the visual topology in real time. FinOps & Zero-Trust Verification: Live multi-cloud rate cards compute hourly and monthly spend, while a continuous CIS Benchmark 1.5 engine audits security posture (e.g., 100/100 A+ ) with automated remediation. Time-Travel Decision DAG: Every architectural change is an immutable commit in a Directed Acyclic Graph. You can rewind history, fork experimental branches, or view visual A/B diffs. ⚙️ How I built it WebMCP Protocol Engine: I implemented 35 registered WebMCP tools over both window.modelContext and a high-performance local HTTP/SSE bridge ( :3001/mcp ) supporting JSON-RPC 2.0. 64-Stripe Entity Lock Manager: To prevent race conditions and "last-write-wins" corruption when human architects and multiple external LLMs modify adjacent resources simultaneously, I built a highly-concurrent lock manager. Optimistic State Engine: Mutations are evaluated as atomic RFC 6902 JSON-Patch transactions. Failed constraints or security violations roll back in microseconds without interrupting the human workflow. Frontend Stack: Built with React 19, TypeScript Strict Mode, and Tailwind CSS. ⚡ Challenges I ran into Single-Threaded State Contention: Coordinating simultaneous user mouse interactions and high-throughput external LLM tool batches without freezing the UI. I solved this with my 64-stripe fine-grained entity locking. Cursor Lifecycle & Perception: Preventing AI cursors from flashing or unmounting prematurely. I engineered a persistent lifecycle where cursors glide smoothly ( cubic-bezier CSS transitions) and display readable task badges before gracefully fading out to idle states. Bidirectional AST Synchronization: Compiling unstructured graph topologies into clean, idempotent Terraform HCL2, while parsing raw text edits back into deterministic visual graph nodes. 🏆 Accomplishments that I'm proud of True Multi-Agent Concurrency: Up to 4 external ChatGPT Desktop sessions can manipulate the exact same canvas simultaneously without deadlock or state corruption. Zero Frontend API Keys: A fully sovereign architecture. The workstation holds zero API keys; external LLMs bring their own intelligence over the open protocol. Massive Enterprise Catalog: 108 accurate, multi-cloud CAD primitives providing complete coverage across AWS, Azure, and GCP. Production-Grade Reliability: Backed by 38 test suites and 510/510 passing unit tests (100% green) covering adversarial stress, CAS rollbacks, and multi-cloud compiler accuracy. 🧠 What I learned WebMCP transforms autonomous agents from simple conversational assistants into active, spatial teammates. When AI models can observe live interface state and execute fine-grained tools over an open protocol, the boundary between human design and autonomous synthesis disappears. Giving an LLM a physical cursor in a CAD environment fundamentally changes how humans trust and verify AI actions. 🔮 What's next for CloudSwarm Direct Cloud Deployment: Adding 1-click terraform apply executions via ephemeral runner containers to actually spin up the drawn infrastructure. Live Reverse Ingestion: Importing existing AWS/Azure environments via terraform plan or CloudFormation into interactive, editable canvas DAGs. Global Multi-Tenant WebSockets: Expanding from local WebMCP bridges to distributed cloud rooms so global engineering teams and AI swarms can collaborate in the same browser session. title: Mandate
pitch: Mandate turns updatable fields into temporary mandates — a live WebMCP tool compiled from what one person chose, expiring on its own, and re-checked by the server on every call.
about_excerpt: Mandate turns updatable fields into temporary mandates — a live WebMCP tool compiled from what one person chose, expiring on its own, and re-checked by the server on every call. Like Comment Story Updates GIF See it working live alongside ChatGPT. GIF The agent deliberately stops and lets human fulfill the apply step. Inspiration When people talk about giving an AI agent access to their software, the conversation almost always turns to scopes: how narrowly can you define what it's allowed to touch? We followed that path for a while before noticing it answers a question nobody is really asking. Scoping is a solved problem. OAuth scopes, per-resource API keys, read-only tokens, role-based access control — you have been able to say "this credential may read invoices in this one project and nothing else" for years. What you cannot do is grant that permission at the moment it becomes relevant. Every access-control system we use is configured in advance. Someone sets it up, usually an administrator, usually weeks earlier, and almost never the person who will be sitting there when the agent actually does something. Then it stays configured. The credential outlives the task by default, and revoking it is a separate act of housekeeping that somebody has to remember to perform. Now think about how you delegate to another person. A colleague offers to cover for you while you're out. You don't hand over your login. You say something much smaller and much more specific: yes, go ahead and update those two accounts, just the status and the next step, and only until I'm back. That sentence is already a complete permission. It names the records, it names the fields, and it has an expiry built into it. The remarkable thing is that it has nowhere to go. No software takes a request made in the moment and turns it into authority that a machine will hold, enforce, and then let run out. WebMCP is the first place we've seen where it could. Because the tools live inside the page rather than behind a remote API, they already have the session, the current selection, and whatever the person has half-finished on screen. The authority behind them doesn't have to be provisioned ahead of time and sized for every case it might one day need. It can be exactly as small, and as short-lived, as the moment that produced it. What it does Mandate turns delegation into something you do explicitly, watch happen, and can take back — inside the application you were already using. The demo host is a CRM. It's deliberately generic; it exists so there's something for the layer to be installed into. Open it and Mandate is present but holding nothing at all: a small badge in the corner, and that's the whole of it. Selecting rows does nothing, and this is the first thing worth being pedantic about, because it's the distinction most permission interfaces blur. Clicking customers narrows what you could delegate, but it grants nothing, and a selected row and a delegated row never look the same on screen. What happens to be highlighted has no bearing on what an agent is able to do. Delegation is a separate, deliberate act. You name the records, you name the fields, and you choose a duration — two accounts, two fields, ten minutes. What comes out is a mandate: versioned, revocable, and counting down from the moment it's granted. Then the part the project is actually about. The page registers WebMCP tools whose schemas are compiled from that mandate. The record-id parameter is an enum containing exactly the records you delegated. The field parameter is an enum containing exactly the fields you named. An agent reading that tool description is reading your decision back to you, in the only vocabulary it has. Narrow the mandate and the tool narrows with it. Revoke it and there is nothing left to call. An agent that calls the tool can stage changes, which appear against the record where you can see them, but it cannot commit them. There is no apply tool, no apply route reachable from the agent's path, and no argument that could reach the apply method from that side. Human edits and agent edits land in the same staged change with provenance marked for each, so a change you both touched says so. Underneath all of it is one rule: the schema communicates, the server enforces. The narrow enum is a courtesy to a well-behaved caller, telling it where the edge is. But a caller that ignores the schema entirely gets exactly as far as one that respects it, because every mutating request is re-checked against the live mandate before anything happens. How we built it The front end is React and Vite, the API is Hono on Vercel, and sessions live in Redis. The WebMCP adapter prefers provideContext where a browser offers it and falls back to registerTool otherwise, reporting honestly which one it got rather than assuming. The part we'd point at is the server core, because it's where the idea either holds up or doesn't. Nothing in the policy, service or capability modules knows what a customer is. A mandate is a set of resource ids crossed with a set of field names, and enforcement is string comparison against those two sets. That sounds almost too simple to be a security model, which is the point: there is very little domain-specific logic available to get wrong. We proved that to ourselves by making the host application data. One file describes what the app is — what its records are called, what fields they have, which fields may never be delegated, which contain untrusted external content. Point the same compiler at a second such file and you get a deployment console instead of a CRM. The records become services, the fields become replica counts and feature flags, and the tool the agent is offered renames itself accordingly. Not one line of the server changes. There is no LLM, model proxy or agent harness anywhere in the product. We locked that decision early and never relaxed it. The demo narration is synthesised locally with Kokoro — 82 million parameters, on CPU, from a file on disk, with no network call — and it is build tooling that never runs in the app. The film is recorded by Playwright in Chrome launched with --enable-features=WebMCP , and the recorder refuses to film anything unless document.modelContext is actually present, so every agent action on camera is a real tool call. Challenges we ran into The API isn't where the documentation says it is. It's on document , not navigator . That sounds trivial and cost us more than it should have, because once we had written the wrong noun down it propagated — into the gate copy that tells users how to enable the feature, into the capability inspector, and into the README. Finding it meant grepping the whole tree for the old claim rather than fixing the one place we happened to notice. The shapes aren't what you'd guess. inputSchema comes back as a JSON string rather than an object, and executeTool wants the tool object plus a JSON string rather than a parsed argument bag. Neither is documented in a way that would have saved us the discovery. You cannot unregister a tool. There is no withdrawal in the API at all, which is genuinely awkward for a product whose whole premise is that authority expires: a stale registration can outlive the mandate that produced it and sit in the browser's registry looking perfectly valid. We couldn't fix it, so we did the next best thing and made the inspector say so on screen. It changes nothing that matters, because a call the mandate no longer covers is refused by the server regardless of what the registry still lists. Vercel does not bundle api/*.ts , and a default export never answers. This one hurt. The API shipped broken to production while every check on our machines was green, because the deployed function is a committed bundle and ours had gone stale. The gate now rebuilds that bundle on every run and fails if the result differs from what is committed. node-redis cannot be bundled for that runtime , so the RESP client is hand-written. It is about two hundred lines and easily the least glamorous file in the repository. Three minutes. The video has a hard limit and every claim in it costs seconds that it has to earn. We rewrote the narration several times, and the version that shipped is shorter than the one before it while explaining more. Accomplishments that we're proud of The genericity claim, pressed rather than asserted. Two host applications out of one compiler, where the tool an agent is offered renames itself between them and the server is untouched. It is easy to say a mechanism is domain-agnostic; it is harder to point at two domains and a diff. A verifier that runs against the deployed origin rather than a local build, and checks fifteen things a judge would otherwise have to take on trust — including that POST /api/tools/apply returns 404, and that no compiled tool descriptor is named apply. And twenty-eight seconds of the real thing. ChatGPT's desktop app with site tools enabled, driving the deploye
video_title: Mandate — a compiler from human intent to a live WebMCP tool contract
video_transcript_excerpt: Fine-grained access control is a solved problem. A token can be limited to one project, or to read-only. What is much harder is temporary delegation at the moment the work happens: a person deciding, right now, that an assistant may touch these records, through these fields, for the next ten minutes. This CRM is the host application. The layer underneath turns that decision into a permission an agent can be held to. Here I select two customer records. Nothing has been delegated — selecting something in the interface does not change what an assistant may access. It only defines the scope I am about to offer. Now I grant it: these two accounts, only these two fields, for ten minutes, with the countdown starting immediately. That is a mandate. The moment I approve it, three things happen. The delegated records are marked. The panel reads the exact scope back to me, so I can check what I allowed. And the permission is compiled into a live WebMCP tool — one that did not exist before the grant, exposing only the records and fields this mandate covers. The assistant can now call it. Its first request is inside the mandate, so the server accepts it and stages a change against the record — visible, but not committed. Then it asks for a record that was never delegated, and the call is rejected. Enforcement does not rest on what the tool advertises: every call reaches the server carrying its mandate, and the scope is checked again before anything happens. There is a second boundary. The assistant can prepare a change but cannot commit one — no apply tool is registered for the agent at all, and the inspector makes that absence explicit. The final action stays with the person who granted the permission. This panel exists only to explain what is happening; a real user needs none of it. The production interface is a persistent badge while a mandate is live, and an indication on each record of what the agent proposed — a running delegation must never become invisible. The mechanism is not specific to CRM software. This is the same layer inside a deployment console: the resources are services, the permitted properties are replica counts and feature flags. The generated tool changes because it is derived from what the host declares. The delegation model does not. So far this has been the mechanism from inside the application. Here it is from the agent's side: ChatGPT Desktop, using this site's actual WebMCP tools, making real calls against the permission I granted a minute ago. Which is how delegation works between people too. If a colleague covers for me I don't hand over my account — I tell them what they may handle, how far it goes, and when it ends. The decision already exists. A mandate is what turns it into something a machine can enforce. So: a person defines a temporary scope at the moment it is needed, the system compiles that intent into a live WebMCP contract, and re-validates it on every request. Today I granted that from inside the application. The next step is to move the decision into the agent's own conversation — it asks for the access it needs, the person approves a temporary mandate there, and no broader credential ever changes hands.

title: WebMCP Trust Gateway
pitch: WebMCP Trust Gateway is a security checkpoint between an AI agent and the tools that websites give it.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Trust Gateway is a security checkpoint between an AI agent and the tools that websites give it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Trust Log Agent task approval Home screen Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a structured way to expose tools to AI agents. Instead of relying on fragile screen automation, an agent can directly call actions such as list_active_subscriptions or cancel_subscription . That capability is powerful, but it also creates a new trust problem: how can users know that a website's tool is safe, that its returned data is not manipulating the agent, and that the agent is not sharing unnecessary personal information or performing irreversible actions without permission? We built WebMCP Trust Gateway to explore the security and consent layer that an agent-powered web will need. What it does WebMCP Trust Gateway sits between an AI agent and the tools exposed by websites. It applies five controls: Tool metadata inspection — scans tool names, descriptions, schemas, and annotations before allowing a tool to be used. Output injection protection — scans returned tool data before it reaches the agent. Parameter minimization — removes optional sensitive fields that are unnecessary for the requested task. Human approval for mutations — pauses state-changing actions until the user explicitly approves them. Transparent auditing — records registrations, calls, blocked attacks, transmitted parameters, and consent decisions in a visible Trust Log. We demonstrate these controls through a subscription auditor. The user connects simulated providers, audits recurring spending, and receives recommendations for subscriptions that appear unused. Nothing is cancelled automatically. Before cancellation, the gateway displays exactly what the provider accepts, what the agent needs, and what will actually be transmitted. One approval authorizes only one call. Why WebMCP is the right fit A normal subscription assistant would scrape pages or automate button clicks. That approach is fragile and gives the agent little structured information about an action's inputs, permissions, or consequences. WebMCP provides explicit tool names, descriptions, input schemas, annotations, and execution functions. The gateway can therefore inspect and govern actions at the tool boundary. This creates a better experience for both people and agents: Agents receive reliable, structured capabilities instead of guessing how a page works. People can understand what an agent intends to do before it acts. Sensitive information can be minimized before transmission. Dangerous or suspicious tools can be quarantined. Every decision leaves an understandable audit trail. Together, a person and an agent can investigate spending, prepare actions, adjust decisions, and safely execute approved changes as shared structured state—something that is difficult to achieve reliably with ordinary browser automation. The security demonstration The project includes three simulated providers: StreamBox — a legitimate streaming subscription. FitSite — a legitimate gym membership that has not been used recently. DealDrop — a deliberately malicious provider used to demonstrate attacks safely. DealDrop contains two separate attack paths. The first is tool-description poisoning . Its tool description attempts to override previous instructions, access billing history, send sensitive information to an external destination, and hide the action from the user. The gateway detects the suspicious patterns and quarantines the tool before execution. The second is tool-output injection . A different DealDrop tool has a clean-looking description, but its returned data contains malicious agent instructions. The gateway scans the output, blocks it before it reaches the agent, and reports that zero sensitive bytes were sent. How we built it The application registers three browser-facing tools using document.modelContext.registerTool : trust_gateway_get_status trust_gateway_preview_subscription_audit trust_gateway_prepare_cancellation The cancellation preparation tool never performs the mutation itself. It returns minimized parameters with an awaiting_human_approval status. The security engine is separated from the interface into deterministic TypeScript functions. It evaluates tool metadata, scans serialized outputs, identifies unnecessary sensitive parameters, and enforces single-use consent. The WebMCP Activity inspector shows which tools were called, their parameters, whether they were read-only or mutations, and whether the gateway allowed, blocked, or paused them. The Trust Log provides filters for allowed calls, warnings, blocked attacks, and consent decisions. Challenges we faced One challenge was protecting both sides of a tool call. Inspecting a tool description is not enough because a clean-looking tool can return poisoned content after execution. We added a second inspection boundary for tool outputs. Another challenge was making privacy minimization visible. Silently removing a field would be secure but difficult to demonstrate. We created a parameter-diff view that shows the provider's complete schema, the agent's intended arguments, the arguments actually transmitted, and the fields that were omitted. We also needed to balance agent autonomy with user control. Read-only investigation should remain convenient, while mutations should require explicit consent. We solved this with a single-use approval gate that rejects calls without consent and prevents approval replay. Finally, we wanted the attack demonstration to be safe and reproducible. Instead of connecting real financial accounts, we created deterministic provider fixtures containing known legitimate and malicious behavior. What we learned We learned that WebMCP security is not only about deciding whether a website itself is trusted. Trust must be evaluated for every tool, every parameter, every returned result, and every attempted action. We also learned that good consent requires more than an approval button. Users need to see the specific action, the destination tool, the exact transmitted parameters, the omitted information, and whether approval can be reused. Most importantly, WebMCP's structured interface makes this level of control possible. Because tools have explicit schemas and execution boundaries, security decisions can be more precise and understandable than with traditional screen automation. Testing The project includes eight automated security tests covering: Allowing legitimate metadata Warning about optional sensitive parameters Blocking poisoned tool descriptions Blocking poisoned tool outputs Rejecting mutations without consent Transmitting only required parameters Preventing approval replay Keeping provider fixtures deterministic All eight tests pass, and the production build completes successfully. What is real and what is simulated The WebMCP registration, metadata scanning, output scanning, parameter minimization, consent enforcement, activity inspector, audit log, and automated tests are implemented. StreamBox, FitSite, and DealDrop are simulated providers created for a safe and repeatable demonstration. No real subscription, billing account, or personal information is used. This is a hackathon reference implementation. Its deterministic rules demonstrate the required enforcement points, but a production gateway would combine policy rules with stronger semantic analysis, signed tool manifests, reputation signals, and organization-specific policies. What's next The gateway could evolve into a reusable browser component or WebMCP policy SDK. Future versions could add signed manifests, configurable organizational policies, risk scoring, permission history, schema-based information-flow controls, and integrations for shopping, banking, healthcare, travel, and software-maintenance agents. Our larger vision is simple: as websites become actionable by AI agents, users should not have to choose between automation and control. title: Thought Amplifier — Evidence Workspace for WebMCP
pitch: Turn a messy brain dump into a source-grounded, inspectable, human-approved decision with your existing browser AI.
about_excerpt: Turn a messy brain dump into a source-grounded, inspectable, human-approved decision with your existing browser AI. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can clarify difficult decisions, but a chat answer is easy to detach from its source, blur facts with assumptions, or accept without a reviewable trail. We wanted a shared workspace where an agent can reason, the application enforces structure and freshness, and the human keeps the final word. What it does Thought Amplifier is a subject-independent WebMCP decision workspace for bounded plain-text brain dumps. A compatible browser agent invokes real page-defined tools to read the current source, revision, and fingerprint, then stages a structured amplification: objective, success criteria, facts grounded in exact source excerpts, assumptions, unknowns, options and trade-offs, a recommendation, reversal condition, and next actions. The result appears in the same visible page. The app validates the payload, binds it to the source revision, records the tool transition, rejects stale writes after the source changes, and exposes no agent approval tool. Only the human-facing UI can approve the exact displayed proposal. Our demo makes the product test itself: it analyzes the real decision between three challenge ideas—an MCP-readiness auditor, a residential concept coordinator, and Thought Amplifier. The workflow itself is general and supports clarify, decide, plan, diagnose, create, and learn modes. How we built it We built a React and TypeScript client with imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool. Three typed tools share live application state: read_thought_source, stage_amplification, and read_thought_workspace. Closed schemas and runtime validation reject unexpected, malformed, duplicate, or out-of-bounds data. Every staged proposal must match the current source revision and fingerprint; changing the source invalidates the old result. Human approval remains outside the WebMCP tool surface. The public repository includes architecture and tool-contract documentation, a reproducible real-host verification receipt, a demo runbook, screenshots, tests, and an MIT license. Challenges The hardest part was making the integration genuinely useful without turning WebMCP into an unrestricted write channel. We also had to make the manual and agent paths converge on the same state, keep evidence and inference distinct, and ensure a plausible result based on an older source could never silently replace newer work. Accomplishments A compatible browser host discovered and invoked all three real page tools in a local end-to-end run. It read the exact live source, visibly staged a complete proposal, read it back, and received STALE_SOURCE when an old payload was replayed after an edit. The registered tool surface contains no approval, publication, submission, or arbitrary-action endpoint. What we learned Useful agentic browsing is not just more autonomy. It is precise semantic operations inside software that owns state, validates transitions, exposes provenance, and preserves a human authority boundary. Structured reasoning becomes more credible when the source, transformation, freshness check, and approval are visible together. What's next Next: source-span citations, multiple text sources, private document and image ingestion with visible extraction provenance, persistent branches and locks, exports, and permissioned collaboration. This submission deliberately remains a focused prototype: plain text only, session-local state, no embedded model, no autonomous approval, and no claim of production or universal browser certification.  Inspiration 

 Brow started because I wanted to experiment with WebMCP inside a real Chrome session. 

 While building it, I became convinced that WebMCP represents something much bigger than browser automation. 

 The Web is currently designed mainly for humans. Websites expose their capabilities through HTML, buttons, forms, menus, and visual interfaces. Agents do not fundamentally need that presentation layer. They need structured access to what an application can actually do. 

 A website already knows that it can send a message, create a document, search for a flight, add something to a cart, or execute a query. Agents should not always have to rediscover those capabilities by interpreting pixels or reverse-engineering the DOM. 

 I believe the future Web should expose two interfaces: one for humans through HTML and UI, and one for agents through structured tools. 

 I am confident that agents will represent an increasingly large share of Web interactions, potentially more than direct human interactions in the long term. That is why I hope WebMCP becomes part of the standard Web platform and eventually reaches broad W3C adoption. 

 Web applications across every domain should be able to expose native interfaces for agents. 

 How I built it 

 That initial experiment became Brow, an open-source agentic stack running directly inside Chrome. 

 Brow operates in the user's real browser session instead of launching a separate automation browser. 

 It combines WebMCP page tools, remote MCP servers, semantic browser automation, reusable Skills, memory, and workflow demonstrations. 

 For websites that support WebMCP, the agent can use structured capabilities directly. For the rest of the Web, Brow falls back to semantic browser automation. 

 I also wanted Brow to remain model-independent, with support for OpenAI-compatible models, Claude, local models, and future providers. 

 The agent runtime is built with LangGraph.js and runs alongside a Chrome side-panel interface. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest thing I learned is that browser automation and browser understanding are very different problems. 

 Clicking an element is easy. Understanding what it means, whether it is still valid, what changed after an action, and what the application is capable of doing is much harder. 

 I also learned that raw HTML is not a great interface for agents. Modern pages contain huge amounts of implementation detail that models do not need. 

 This is why Brow uses semantic browser snapshots and structured information rather than simply sending the full DOM to the model. 

 Another important realization was that interoperability matters more than any individual model. Models and agent frameworks will change, but an open interface between applications and agents could remain. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was dealing with constantly changing browser state. Modern applications update dynamically, elements become stale, forms change, and single-page applications can completely change state without a page reload. 

 Another challenge was combining multiple tool systems — browser actions, WebMCP tools, MCP servers, Skills, and memory — into one coherent environment for the agent. 

 Chrome extensions also have strong security and execution boundaries, which makes coordination between the side panel, background worker, content scripts, page context, and agent runtime more complex. 

 What's next 

 The Chrome extension is only the beginning. 

 I eventually want Brow to give the agent its own secure development environment: a sandbox, container, or VM where it can create files, write code, install packages, execute commands, start servers, build applications, test them in the browser, and iterate autonomously. 

 This is difficult to do cleanly within the limitations of a standard Chrome extension. 

 One longer-term direction is therefore to move Brow toward a Chromium-based browser where agent capabilities can become first-class features rather than being layered on top through an extension. 

 The goal would be to combine the browser, WebMCP, MCP, Skills, memory, and an isolated computing environment into one agent-native platform. 

 Brow started as an experiment to test WebMCP. 

 It became an experiment around a bigger question: 

 What should the Web look like when many of its users are agents acting on behalf of humans? 

 I believe agents should not always have to pretend to be humans to use the Web. 

 HTML gave humans a universal interface to the Web. WebMCP could help give agents one.

title: WebMCP Zero-Trust Vault
pitch: Zero-trust context vault for WebMCP featuring WASM/SIMD sanitization, WebCrypto isolation, and Edge policy enforcement with sub-15ms latency.
about_excerpt:
Zero-trust context vault for WebMCP featuring WASM/SIMD sanitization, WebCrypto isolation, and Edge policy enforcement with sub-15ms latency.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 WebMCP and browser-native AI context integration introduce security risks regarding prompt injection attacks and indirect PII exfiltration. As LLM agents gain direct read access to DOM state and model context APIs, sensitive user data becomes vulnerable to rogue contextual payloads. WebMCP Zero-Trust Vault enforces a strict boundary between raw DOM data and the context fed into AI execution environments. 

 What it does 

 WebMCP Zero-Trust Vault is a security middleware that intercepts context calls ( navigator.modelContext.getContext() ), sanitizes DOM input, and encrypts sensitive payload data using WebCrypto isolation: 

 
 Context Interception & Filtering: Captures visible DOM nodes via viewport-aware TreeWalker inspection. 
 Lexical Sanitization (SIMD Rust/WASM): Neutralizes indirect prompt injections and maps PII patterns to volatile UUID tokens. 
 Worker-Isolated Encryption: Encrypts context payloads using non-exportable AES-GCM-256 keys inside an isolated Web Worker thread. 
 Edge Policy Enforcement: Distributes declarative security policies globally via Cloudflare Workers KV with sub-10ms distribution latency. 
 Web3 Provenance: Signs context hashes using EIP-4361 (SIWE) and EIP-191 standards for auditability. 
 

 How we built it 

 The system follows a modular architecture: 

 
 Core Engine: Rust compiled to WebAssembly with SIMD vectorization ( core-wasm/ ). 
 Cryptographic Layer: WebCrypto API utilizing non-exportable AES-GCM keys managed in a Dedicated Web Worker ( worker-crypto/ ). 
 Client SDK: TypeScript interceptor library wrapped as an ESM module ( sdk-client/ ). 
 Edge Layer: Cloudflare Workers handling policy fetches and signature verification ( edge-worker/ ). 
 Browser Sandbox: Chrome Extension built under Manifest V3 ( extension-chrome/ ). 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Performance Constraints: Meeting the Alignment Control Framework (MCA) target of total latency $\Delta t \le 15.00\text{ ms}$ while executing SIMD sanitization and WebCrypto operations. 
 Zero Memory Persistence: Guaranteeing $T_{\text{mem}} = 0.00\text{ bytes}$ retention in localStorage , IndexedDB , or cookies post-session required explicit memory scrubbing routines ( purge_memory() ) across the WASM heap and Worker context. 
 Zero-Copy Transfers: Passing context state across thread boundaries without memory duplication using ArrayBuffer transfers. 
 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Achieved 0.00% PII exfiltration rate across standardized indirect prompt injection test vectors. 
 Kept total static SDK footprint under $15.00\text{ KB}$ ($S_{\text{SDK}} < 15\text{ KB}$). 
 Verified local execution time $\le 15.00\text{ ms}$ per context extraction cycle. 
 

 What's next for WebMCP Zero-Trust Vault 

 
 Integration with emerging browser-native LLM APIs as WebMCP standards evolve. 
 Automated ZK-proof generation for zero-knowledge context policy compliance.

 Inspiration 

 Orish’s World began with my six-year-old son, Orish. I wanted to create a safer, imaginative learning world where children do not simply watch content — stories can lead into real activities, learning and conversations with their families. 

 As a mum building this independently, I have been learning the technology while developing the project. The Too-Fast Rocket became our first working story and teaches a simple lesson: STOP. LOOK. LISTEN. THINK. THEN TRY. 

 What it does 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I created an AI-ready layer for Orish’s World. 

 The demo uses WebMCP to expose structured learning actions directly from the webpage to compatible AI agents. Instead of an AI having to guess what a page offers, the website can describe useful actions as tools. 

 The prototype includes tools for discovering an age-appropriate learning activity and accessing the Too-Fast Rocket lesson. 

 How I built it 

 The project is built for the web and deployed using Cloudflare Workers, with the source managed through GitHub. 

 The WebMCP implementation uses document.modelContext.registerTool() to register Orish’s World learning actions with compatible AI environments. 

 I deliberately connected the WebMCP experiment to a real project rather than creating a standalone technical demo. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was building and deploying this while learning the technology as I went. I also needed the normal website to remain usable even in browsers that do not currently expose WebMCP. 

 The demo therefore detects WebMCP support and explains when the browser does not support it, while still containing the real registration code. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that websites can become more than pages designed only for people to click through. WebMCP creates the possibility of websites exposing meaningful, structured actions to AI agents. 

 For education, that could eventually allow AI to help families navigate learning experiences while the website and parent remain in control. 

 What's next 

 Orish’s World is intended to grow into a wider learning universe with stories, reading, cooking, science and creative activities. 

 My next step is to expand the WebMCP tools so AI can help families move between digital stories and useful real-world learning activities.

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation.
