title: BOSAI — Governed WebMCP
pitch: Discoverable is not authorized — Human GO, single-use permits, verified readback, and replay denial for WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: Discoverable is not authorized — Human GO, single-use permits, verified readback, and replay denial for WebMCP agents. Like Comment Story Updates Discoverable is not authorized WebMCP gives agents a structured way to discover and call tools exposed by a website. BOSAI explores the next problem: tool discovery should not automatically grant execution authority. BOSAI — Governed WebMCP is a public WebMCP demo that lets an agent inspect a synthetic duplicate-charge case, propose a refund, request authorization, execute only after an explicit Human GO, independently verify the result, retrieve an evidence receipt, and deny replay of the same single-use permit. The core idea is simple: Agents can discover and propose. Humans retain authority. BOSAI verifies what actually happened. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Without structured tools, agents often have to infer actions from UI state. WebMCP makes the capability surface explicit. BOSAI uses that explicit surface to add a second layer: an authority boundary around consequential actions. The live app registers eight native WebMCP tools: inspect_case inspect_transaction propose_refund request_authorization authorization_status execute_refund verify_refund get_evidence_receipt The agent has no Human GO tool. It can reach HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED, but it cannot grant itself approval. The demo flow The challenge uses a fully synthetic EUR 49 duplicate-charge refund scenario. The agent inspects the case and transaction. It creates a bounded proposal. BOSAI stops at HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED. Before approval, the mutation count is 0. A human explicitly approves that exact proposal. BOSAI issues a single-use permit. The synthetic refund commits exactly once. Independent readback returns VERIFIED and an evidence receipt. The same execution is attempted again. The replay is denied, and the replay mutation count remains 0. No real payment is made and no customer data is used. Better human + agent interaction The user experience is not "AI asks for permission" as a loose convention. The approval state is explicit, inspectable, and bound to one exact proposal. Agent: inspect, reason, propose, request authorization, execute within the granted permit, verify. Human: retain the authority to approve or deny the exact consequential action. BOSAI: enforce the execution boundary, record the result, and deny permit replay. This makes WebMCP more useful for workflows where agents should be capable without becoming self-authorizing. Implementation The challenge surface is a standalone browser app implemented with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It registers tools through WebMCP and maintains deterministic synthetic challenge state for proposals, authorization, execution, verification, evidence receipts, and replay denial. The public challenge surface is served as static assets on OVHcloud through a scoped Caddy route. The live browser proof was run in Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP testing enabled. What was added during the challenge BOSAI existed before the WebMCP Challenge. During the challenge submission period, it was meaningfully extended with a dedicated WebMCP implementation and public challenge surface, including the eight WebMCP tools above, a synthetic duplicate-charge workflow, explicit HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED behavior, zero-mutation pre-approval enforcement, exact Human GO binding, a single-use execution permit, independent verified readback, an evidence receipt, replay denial with zero replay mutations, and a public live browser proof surface. The WebMCP challenge implementation is isolated from proprietary BOSAI internals and is being published as a standalone public-safe repository for judging. Live proof The validated live flow demonstrated 8 registered WebMCP tools, HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED before authorization, 0 pre-GO mutations, 1 authorized synthetic mutation after Human GO, VERIFIED independent readback, an evidence receipt, REPLAY_DENIED on the duplicate execution attempt, 0 replay mutations, and no blocking browser/runtime errors. Live app: https://bosai.syncguard.fr/webmcp-challenge/index.html Operating principle Intelligence is not authority. WebMCP makes agent capabilities discoverable. BOSAI demonstrates how those capabilities can remain human-governed, bounded, verifiable, and auditable. title: AutoShop
pitch: A seller-controlled authority layer for agentic commerce
about_excerpt: A seller-controlled authority layer for agentic commerce Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can act, but merchants still need to control what they are allowed to do. Shopify’s agentic-commerce direction and Visa’s emphasis on spending limits, approvals, authentication, and transparency highlighted the same gap: useful autonomy needs enforceable boundaries. AutoShop explores that problem without claiming customer validation. What it does AutoShop is a seller-controlled authority layer for agentic commerce. A seller defines a numerical mandate covering order quantity, value, discount, and remaining stock. Routine orders can proceed automatically. Orders outside the mandate stop as pending actions until the seller reviews and approves that exact exception. Our demo requests six RAM modules against a five-item limit. WebMCP returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED , prevents an immediate stock change, and allows commit_action only after visible human approval. A successful commit creates an auditable receipt recording the decision path and mandate version. Everything shown is synthetic; AutoShop processes no real payment or shipment. How we built it We built two ordinary web portals with seven role-scoped WebMCP tools: Buyer: browse_products , manage_cart , and submit_order Seller: get_mandate , list_orders , accept_order , and commit_action The frontend uses framework-free HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Netlify Functions enforce validation and authorization, while Netlify Database stores versioned mandates, orders, pending actions, inventory, approvals, and receipts. Strict schemas, page-held authorization secrets, authenticated seller sessions, atomic transactions, and idempotency checks prevent the model from expanding its own authority. We verified the complete workflow in ChatGPT’s in-app Browser and maintained 65 automated regression tests. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was making human control, agent capability, and server authority agree. Buyer and seller tools had to appear only in the correct role and disappear after logout, expiry, or navigation. Confirmation secrets also had to remain outside the model-visible tool schema. The final recording produced an honest safety test: our prompt contained a mistyped pending-action ID. The agent detected the mismatch, displayed the live alternative, and requested explicit human confirmation instead of guessing. Its browser-tool connection later expired, but it disclosed the reconnect and completed the confirmed, idempotent commit exactly once. We preserved that recovery in the demo while removing only inactive waiting. Accomplishments that we're proud of Seven deployed, role-scoped WebMCP tools Two visible human authorization boundaries Server-enforced mandate decisions and stale-state protection Token-private order submission and exception approval Atomic inventory mutation with durable receipts Seller-tool removal after logout A reproducible public demo requiring no real customer or payment data What we learned Agent safety becomes understandable when people can see and test the boundary. A written instruction is weaker than a refused tool call, and a promise to ask permission is weaker than a contract that cannot execute without current human authorization. We also learned that identifiers inside natural-language prompts must be treated as untrusted input. Detecting and confirming a correction was safer than silently rewriting the request. What's next for AutoShop Our next step is an observed test with an independent small-store order approver. After validating the workflow, we would build a narrow adapter that places the same mandate → exception → approval → receipt boundary in front of an existing merchant order API. title: AgentInbox
pitch: AgentInbox is a Gmail manager that exposes WebMCP tools so any AI agent can read, organize, and reply to your email — inside your own authenticated browser session, with no API keys shared.
about_excerpt:
AgentInbox is a Gmail manager that exposes WebMCP tools so any AI agent can read, organize, and reply to your email — inside your own authenticated browser session, with no API keys shared.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Today, giving an AI agent access to your inbox usually means one of two things: handing over a personal API key to a third-party service, or trusting a closed chatbot with full access to your private data. Both approaches break the trust boundary that should stay with the user. WebMCP offered a different model — register tools directly on the page, inside the user's own authenticated session, and let any compliant agent discover and call them. AgentInbox is our exploration of what that looks like for one of the most personal apps people use every day: email. 

 What it does 

 AgentInbox is WebMCP powered Gmail manager. You can sign in with Google , view your inbox , read messages, mark them as read and reply. Built as normal website with FastAPI for backend, PostgreSQL for DB, and html/css/js for frontend 

 What makes it different is that every core action is also registered as a WebMCP tool with document.modelContext.registerTool(): 

 list_emails — retrieve the user's messages, optionally filtered to unread only
get_message_detail — fetch the full content of one message (subject, sender, date, body, read status)
mark_as_read — mark a message as read
reply_to_email — send a reply within the correct Gmail thread (using proper In-Reply-To/References headers) 

 Any WebMCP-compatible AI agent running in the user's browser can discover these tools with getTools() and call them with executeTool() — no separate integration, no API key handed to a third party, and no action taken outside the user's own real, authenticated Gmail session. 

 How we built it
Backend: FastAPI (Python), with a layered architecture — routers → services → repositories → models
Database: PostgreSQL via SQLAlchemy 2.0
Auth: Google OAuth2, JWT stored in an HttpOnly cookie
Email: Gmail API (list, get, mark-read, reply — with correct thread headers)
Frontend: plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript, no framework — served directly by FastAPI from the same origin as the API
WebMCP: four tools registered with the imperative API (document.modelContext.registerTool()), verified end-to-end via getTools()/executeTool() — including real Gmail reads and a real reply sent inside the correct thread
Deployment: live on Render (single service, backend + frontend together)
Challenges we ran into
WebMCP is a very new, fast-moving spec — the tooling ecosystem around it (browser extensions, inspectors) is still immature, and some third-party inspector extensions didn't reliably detect our imperative-API tools. We worked around this by verifying everything directly through the browser console (getTools() / executeTool()), which is exactly what an agent does internally.
Google's sensitive Gmail scopes mean full app verification wasn't realistic within the hackathon timeline, so the app runs with a whitelisted Test Users list and demo credentials for judging (see Testing instructions).
Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A complete, working product — not just a proof of concept — with real OAuth, a real database, and four WebMCP tools that actually call a real Gmail account and produce real results, deployed live. 

 What we learned 

 How the WebMCP imperative API actually behaves end-to-end in a real Chrome build: tool registration, discovery via getTools(), and execution via executeTool(), including the JSON string in/out data flow. 

 What's next for AgentInbox
Improving WebMCP tools. Making UI more better and user-friendy. Adding real AI agent.

pitch: An invoice-reconciliation dashboard humans and AI agents use together — agents query receivables, point at rows in your view, and draft chaser letters you review, via 8 WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An invoice-reconciliation dashboard humans and AI agents use together — agents query receivables, point at rows in your view, and draft chaser letters you review, via 8 WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates GotPaid dashboard — 8 WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool Agent calls a tool live — the human sees exactly what their agent just did Inspiration I run a Thai agri-export company that invoices Chinese buyers in USD/CNY. Every month a deposit lands with the wrong amount and a useless reference — "INWARD REMIT REF 88213" — and I have to guess which invoice it was, work out how much the bank silently skimmed, and remember which client always pays like this. I already built GotPaid to fix that. For this challenge, I asked a narrower question: reconciliation questions ("which buyer is slipping?", "why did this deposit match that invoice?") only really make sense pointed at a real row on a real screen — so what if the agent helping me could act inside the dashboard I'm already looking at, instead of just answering in a disconnected chat window? What it does GotPaid reconciles cross-border invoice payments against messy bank deposits — tolerant of hidden fees, batched payments, and split payments — learns each buyer's payment behavior over time, and surfaces what's still unpaid. The WebMCP layer adds 8 tools so a human and an AI agent can work the same dashboard together: the agent reads structured data (no screen-scraping — an embedded JSON island), switches tabs and flashes the exact row it's talking about in the human's own view, and drafts a chaser letter that opens on screen for review. Nothing is ever sent automatically — the agent proposes, the human decides, both looking at the same thing. That's the gap WebMCP closes: before, an agent could only describe what's on screen; now it can point at it. How we built it Python renders a static dashboard ( dashboard.py ) with all data baked into an embedded JSON script tag. On top of that, 8 tools are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() : 5 read-only ( list_companies , list_unpaid_invoices , get_buyer_profile , explain_match , get_dashboard_totals ) and 3 UI-action tools ( show_company , highlight_invoice , draft_chaser_letter ) that manipulate the DOM the human is looking at. Every tool call is echoed to an on-page "Agent activity" log so the human always sees what their agent just did. Deployed static on Cloudflare Pages — no server, no build step. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new — Chrome support is flag-gated ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), so I had to design a graceful fallback banner rather than assume every judge has it enabled. I also had to resist just exposing raw data dumps as tools; the ones that ended up mattering most act in the human's view (highlight, draft) rather than just answering questions in text. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working execute implementation behind every tool — not stubs — verified end-to-end (filtering, cross-company lookups, a chaser letter that actually reflects a buyer's real payment history) before ever opening Chrome's WebMCP flag. And keeping the human-in-the-loop boundary hard: the letter tool drafts and opens for review, it never sends. What we learned A "reasonable-sounding" tool surface (just dump every field as a tool) is worse than a smaller set of tools that do something in the human's view. Also: sponsor sandboxes don't always match their public docs — worth verifying the live account rather than trusting documentation alone when they disagree. What's next for GotPaid Agent Desk GotPaid already plugs into my company's deployed durian-export platform (2 awards at the Nanning ASEAN summit). This WebMCP layer is the template for making the rest of that platform agent-native — inventory, grading, logistics — all queryable and actionable by an agent working alongside the person actually running the business.  1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Construction is one of the slowest industries in the world to adopt new technology. When it finally does, the first step is almost always the same one: a 3D model. Companies pay for the survey, the modelling, the coordination — and then the model's working life ends the day the project is handed over. The design team keeps it. The people who run the building for the next forty years get a PDF set and a key. 

 That is why the ROI conversation stalls. It is not that digital models are expensive; it is that we only spend them on the shortest phase of the asset's life. A model that stops at handover has to pay for itself in eighteen months. A model that keeps working never has to. 

 Drill Day is our argument for the second kind. It takes the model past design, past handover, into operations — the phase where the building actually costs money — and asks a simple question: what if the model were the thing that trains the people who run it? 

 The second half of the inspiration was WebMCP. A model is only useful in operations if a non-expert can get answers out of it, and the people we care about — a week-two technician, a firefighter who has never been in this building, a contractor arriving to isolate a valve — are not going to learn a BIM viewer. But they will talk. WebMCP lets the AI they already have reach into the live model on their screen instead of into a stale export of it. That is the missing interface.

about_excerpt:
Design and execute time-based financial scenarios that users and AI agents control together through WebMCP
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Time&Dime zoomed out inside chatGPT app's inbuilt browser. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Time&Dime zoomed out inside chatGPT app's inbuilt browser. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I am inspired by many graph makers and calculation engines. I wanted to combine their traits so calculations can be more easily visualized. Calculations with real-life timings to represent the results give the repeating arithmetic operations a practical sense. I was inspired by recurring bank interests, inflations, certain amounts added or deducted from accounts, etc. I was inspired to provide dates from milliseconds to years because real life finances can have even more detailed representations. That's how I was inspired, learning and trying to simplify domestic economic cultures to international ones through different ways. To create this project with WebMCP tools, I was inspired by one of my own projects (created years ago, to automate a website through embedded javascript running engine and creating automated flows and extra UI guiding visuals by a hosted web-app, connecting them with a backend). I found this approach more effective in current times where Users and Agents can operate web-apps together and web-apps functionality is standardized so agents don't have to look for UI clicks or other DOM elements. 

 What it does 

 With Time&Dime one can create financial scenarios such as salaries, interests, debt payments, expenses, inflations, etc. with cards. WebMCP allows the agents to create models and perform all the required actions, run tools and return values for users, and Users can also create, edit and perform all the operations on the web-app UI. Users and WebMCP tools working together provide a very effective workspace to create complex financial models . 

 With WebMCP tools implemented, it becomes easier to provide instructions to agents for creating multi-step financial models with natural text. Wherever nodes can use latest information for correct values then agents can solve this beforehand. All this creates editable UI for users to manually configure their models later. 

 From the individual card's time, performing the cards' operations (Plus, Minus, Divide, Multiply, Modulus) with card's value/percentage, and with given time limit or till project's duration or end-time, on the above card(s). 

 How we built it 

 I am using Vue.js to build this web-app. For design choice and practical user experience I am using a simple flow that I used for years on my older projects, which is cards created vertically or horizontally. Considering simple requirements, I am choosing this instead of implementing vue-flow. 

 I am using local storage to store projects, nodes and their values and watching the nodes so any change reflects updated object in the local storage. 

 Initially while working each step, I started implementing WebMCP imperative API tools for core functionalities of the web-app and then after the app had reached a point of being a viable product then I created more imperative API tools for my web-app to support all of the features through Agent. 

 I used codex 5.6 sol to work through the development step by step, creating custom design of my web-app, implementing states of the project and nodes, creating CRUD for local storage, defining WebMCP imperative API tools to execute functions directly, scaffolding JS files to perform calculations. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Creating calculation engine was taking a lot of time, First try using loops for a bit of complicated multi-operations involving project, hangs up the web-app. So I asked 5.6 sol ultra mode for planning and development, Then a hybrid calculation engine with limits was scaffolded in the JS files. 

 Then having too much metadata for WebMCP tools was making a limit hit on chatGPT internal browser, So I worked with 5.6 sol's Ultra mode again to work out this issue. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Time&Dime project is up and running, With its version one, It can visualize many scenarios and create many complicated models. The nodes/cards are extremely customizable. The projects are currently isolated. WebMCP tools are properly working with the web-app. I finally have something at hand which allows me to create graphs of calculations my way! 

 What we learned 

 I learned a lot from this hackathon. First I usually try to write 2-3 modules together and sometimes codex overdoes the work and make it more like framework style. But slowly I am learning to tame codex and use lower settings like medium to create only the structure of code that one wants at a time and then performing designing of the whole project modules interconnectivity separately and work on that one by one. If a solution requires code that will turn ambiguous unintentionally (alternative to use open-source/ready-made scripts) then have it separated and validate with custom tests. 

 I learned more about how I was designing this web-app and how it should turn out. Working with it made me more aware of nuances in flows of economics, which is still relatively small compared with what other kind of deployments exists in this subject throughout other markets. 

 What's next for Time&Dime 

 I will work towards adding more features, First will be to use an existing project inside another existing project. Then I will work towards other cooler new features which I have planned to make this web-app more exciting to use.

 1 2 3 



 
 About MCP-Siege 

 We built MCP-Siege to explore a simple question: 

 What happens when an AI agent can interact with a game through WebMCP instead of controlling it through clicks and screen coordinates? 

 In MCP-Siege, players command a medieval RTS army, while WebMCP exposes structured actions that allow an AI agent to understand units and move them directly in the game. 

 The current implementation is intentionally simple: AI can command unit movement through WebMCP. But the idea goes much further. 

 MCP-Siege shows a possible foundation for games where AI agents are not just chatbots next to the game, but actual participants inside it. 

 The same approach could enable: 

 
 AI party members in RPGs that can actually follow commands and interact with the world 
 AI commanders or teammates in strategy and tactical games 
 AI crew members in simulators 
 AI companions in survival and sandbox games 
 entirely new multiplayer experiences built around humans and AI playing together 
 

 Instead of every game creating a completely custom AI integration, WebMCP could provide a common interface between the game and the agent. 

 How we built it 

 We built MCP-Siege as a browser-based medieval RTS and exposed selected game actions through WebMCP. 

 When an agent connects, it can discover the tools provided by the game, understand their schemas, and use them to move units. This avoids fragile UI automation and gives the agent a direct, structured way to interact with game logic. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 One of our biggest challenges was deciding how much of the game should be exposed to the agent. 

 Even something as simple as moving a unit requires the AI to understand what units exist, which one should be controlled, where it can move, and how the game state changes afterward. 

 We also learned that WebMCP does not need to be limited to productivity websites or forms. 

 Games are interactive web applications too. 

 MCP-Siege is a small proof of concept, but it points toward something much larger: 

 
 WebMCP could become the interface that lets AI agents enter games as companions, teammates, and characters — not just tools outside of them. 
 

 Open source 

 MCP-Siege is open source under the MIT License . The complete source code and license can be viewed in the public GitHub repository:

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: TermLens
pitch: An AI agent reads your contract, grounds every key term to its exact source sentence, and can't save a thing without your explicit approval. Everything stays local in your browser.
about_excerpt:
An AI agent reads your contract, grounds every key term to its exact source sentence, and can't save a thing without your explicit approval. Everything stays local in your browser.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 




 
 Inspiration 

 We’ve all seen AI wrappers that extract data from long legal documents and expect us to take the output on faith. But when you’re dealing with actual contracts—auto-renewals, notice periods, liability limits—blind trust isn't an option. A single hallucinated detail can cause massive headaches. 

 I wanted to build something fast that lets AI do the heavy lifting of reading legal jargon, but gives humans complete control over what gets saved. No black boxes, no silent state changes, and no sending sensitive contracts to a third-party server. 

 What it does 

 TermLens is a browser-native legal contract verification gate powered by WebMCP: 

 
 Source Grounding: Every extracted term links directly to its exact quote in the text, highlighting confidence levels so you know where to double-check. 
 Human-in-the-Loop Control: The AI can analyze and stage proposed contract terms, but it can never write or alter state without an explicit human sign-off. 
 Local-First Privacy: Documents are processed entirely inside your browser's local memory. 
 Audit Trail: Every action, approval, and rejection is captured in an exportable audit receipt (JSON/Markdown). 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Frontend: Built with vanilla HTML, modern CSS Grid/Flexbox layouts, and JetBrains Mono for a clean, developer-focused UI. 
 Animations: Powered by GSAP and ScrollTrigger to create hero reassembly effects and visual contract sweeps. 
 Agent Integration: Connected via WebMCP for deterministic tool handling and staged write-locks. 
 Deployment: Hosted on Cloudflare Pages ( termlens.pages.dev ). 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting the UI grid layouts to feel pixel-perfect across different display widths while preserving custom GSAP animation timelines took a lot of fine-tuning. We also had to ensure that the agent state machine strictly respected write locks—blocking any unverified attempts to persist contract terms without explicit user confirmation. 

 What we learned 

 Building browser-native AI workflows requires thinking about user trust first. When you give users direct grounding alongside hard write-protection, AI tools feel less like unpredictable black boxes and more like dependable assistants. 

 What's next for TermLens 

 I want to expand support for multi-document comparisons, add automated risk-scoring presets for standard SaaS agreements, and make the WebMCP integration even easier for developers to plug into their own local workflows.

title: WebMCP Studio
pitch: WebMCP Studio turns existing websites into agent-ready experiences by discovering actions, generating structured WebMCP tools, and letting AI agents safely interact with live web apps.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Studio turns existing websites into agent-ready experiences by discovering actions, generating structured WebMCP tools, and letting AI agents safely interact with live web apps. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We were inspired by the upcoming availability of WebMCP tools and noticed that many production websites still do not expose agent-native capabilities. WebMCP Studio helps developers detect useful capabilities from existing websites, then compose them into reusable workflows. This can reduce agent tool calls and make agentic workflows easier to understand and maintain. What it does WebMCP Studio discovers native WebMCP tools and infers potential tools from a website’s semantic DOM, forms, and visible actions. Developers can review the evidence, drag actions into a workflow, generate a higher-level tool such as buy_best_product, and test it on a controlled page. The hosted Studio provides a simple judge path. An optional Chrome MV3 extension supports advanced discovery and execution on eligible live pages. How we built it We built the project in TypeScript with a dependency-light browser architecture: A discovery engine scans semantic HTML, forms, controls, Shadow DOM, and same-origin frames. A capability graph stores discovered tools, schemas, locators, evidence, confidence, and effects. A structured workflow interpreter composes primitive actions using validated JSON bindings. A hosted Studio provides the visual discovery and drag-and-drop workflow builder. A versioned postMessage bridge connects Studio to controlled commerce and travel target pages. Generated tools are registered through the browser’s document.modelContext API when WebMCP is available. External URLs remain potential-only in the hosted flow; the extension handles approved live-page instrumentation. The demo workflow searches products, filters by price, views details, and adds the selected product to a cart. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP ecosystem is still evolving. Browser support, Permissions Policy, secure-context requirements, and agent-provider capabilities vary, so successfully registering a tool on a page does not automatically prove that ChatGPT can discover and invoke it. We also had to distinguish native tools from inferred suggestions. Inferred tools may be useful, but they need evidence, confidence, schema validation, stable locators, and human review before execution. Dynamic websites introduced additional challenges, including SPA updates, Shadow DOM, iframes, weak accessibility semantics, stale elements, and potentially unsafe actions. We addressed these with bounded discovery, structured validation, explicit activation, session checks, and clear native-versus-preview states. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built an end-to-end workflow from: Discover → Compose → Generate → Inject → Test We are especially proud that the product remains honest about capability status: Native WebMCP tools are clearly separated from inferred tools. Unsupported browsers receive an explicit preview path instead of a simulated native claim. Generated workflows produce structured traces and visible page effects. The project includes unit tests, Playwright end-to-end tests, deterministic target fixtures, and an optional browser extension. What we learned We learned that making websites useful to agents requires more than finding buttons or API requests. A reliable tool also needs a meaningful name, typed input schema, evidence, permissions, stable locators, and understandable failure behavior. We also learned that page-level WebMCP registration and agent-level WebMCP consumption are separate compatibility problems. Finally, structured workflows make agent behavior more reusable and auditable than repeatedly asking an agent to perform low-level website actions. What's next for WebMCP Studio Next, we want to validate the complete native ChatGPT/browser connection in a supported environment. We also plan to improve inference accuracy, add more site-specific adapters, support more dynamic and authenticated workflows, and make generated projects easier to reuse across websites and sessions. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: PantryPilot
pitch: Meal planning a human and an AI agent do together, live through real WebMCP tools, not clicks.
about_excerpt: Meal planning a human and an AI agent do together, live through real WebMCP tools, not clicks. Like Comment Story Updates PantryPilot High-Level Architecture PantryPilot Low-Level Architecture Diagram banner Inspiration Most "AI meal planning" demos are a chatbot that describes a plan in a text box - you still have to go copy the ingredients into a shopping list app yourself. WebMCP flips that: instead of an agent guessing at button selectors or a chat window narrating what you should do, a page can expose its actual capabilities as tools an agent calls directly. Meal planning turned out to be a good fit to prove that out. It's a genuinely tedious, recurring chore with real constraints - dietary restrictions, a grocery budget, food already sitting in the fridge about to go bad - the kind of multi-step, stateful task that's tedious for a human to do by hand and awkward for a chatbot to do by description, but a natural fit for an agent that can actually read and write app state. What it does PantryPilot is a meal planner and shopping list. A household sets dietary preferences (vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, dairy-free, nut-free, or a free-form avoid-list), tracks what's in the pantry (including expiry dates), and optionally sets a weekly grocery budget. From there: Search and rank a 16-recipe catalog by pantry match ("what can I make with what I already have"), by what's about to expire, by cost, by prep time, or by calories/protein. Plan a single day, or hand the whole week to plan-week , which fills every empty day under whatever constraints you give it - tags, max prep time, a calorie/protein ceiling, the remaining budget, and a "use up what's expiring" priority - while never overriding an active dietary restriction and never repeating a recipe in the same week. Get a shopping list generated automatically from the plan, aggregated across recipes and offset by what's already in the pantry. See a per-day and weekly nutrition summary. See exactly what happened and who did it - every action is logged and tagged human or agent - and undo the most recent change with one click, by either party. All of that is exposed as 19 WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() , so a human using the page and an agent acting on it are working in the same live session, not two separate experiences. How we built it Plain JavaScript, ES modules, no framework and no build step - the whole app is static files. The core design decision was a single shared domain module, js/actions.js , that owns every mutation (planning a recipe, updating the pantry, regenerating the shopping list, undo). Both the human-facing UI and every WebMCP tool's execute() call the exact same functions in that module, tagged with who's calling ( "human" or "agent" ), so there's no separate, more-powerful "agent path" that could drift out of sync with what a human can do. State lives in a small reactive store backed by localStorage ; the UI and the tool layer both subscribe to its change event, so a change from either side re-renders the page immediately. Since this session's sandbox had no WebMCP-capable browser to test against, we built an in-page "Agent Console" that drives the identical document.modelContext tool handlers through a plain form (pick a tool, edit the JSON arguments, run it) - the same code path a real agent would hit, just reachable without the Chrome 149 origin trial or ChatGPT's browser. It became a first-class part of the app rather than a throwaway test harness, since it also lets anyone verify every tool works without installing anything. We also wrote a node:test suite (32 tests) against js/actions.js directly, covering dietary-conflict enforcement, shopping-list aggregation, budget math, and the undo system, and ran full Playwright end-to-end passes over every tab and every tool before each push. Challenges we ran into No native WebMCP runtime to test against. We couldn't rely on trying it in a real agent client during development, so correctness had to come from the domain layer itself (validation, tests, the Agent Console) - the tool registration is thin by design, and almost all of the actual logic lives in code we could run and test directly. Keeping the agent from being more powerful than a human. It would have been easy to write a fast "agent path" that skips validation for convenience. Instead every tool routes through the same functions the UI uses, which meant designing actions.js first as a proper API, not as UI glue. Undo without duplicating history. A single logical action like "add a recipe to Monday" cascades into a second internal update (the shopping list regenerating). A naive undo implementation would push a separate history entry for that cascade and undo the wrong thing. Snapshots are taken immediately before the actual mutating store.update() call inside each action, and the shopping-list regeneration that happens as a side effect of another action is marked silent and skipped by the snapshot - so one user-facing action is always exactly one undo step, verified with a dedicated test. Shopping-list aggregation. Merging ingredient quantities across multiple recipes, scaling by servings, subtracting whatever's already in the pantry, and preserving which items are already checked off across a regeneration all had to work together without double-counting or losing state. Accomplishments that we're proud of 19 WebMCP tools that are genuinely load-bearing - plan-week does real constraint-based selection (dietary safety, no repeats, budget, expiry priority), not a lookup table dressed up as a tool. An architecture where an agent provably can't do anything a human couldn't do by clicking around, because they're the same code. A working undo system - a real implementation of the reversibility idea in WebMCP's own security guidance, not just a line in the description. 32 passing unit tests plus a full Playwright pass over every tab and every tool, run before every push. Zero backend, zero build step, deployable to Netlify, Vercel, or Cloudflare Pages in minutes. What we learned WebMCP's imperative API is small on purpose - registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) is most of it - which pushes the real design work down into the domain logic underneath, where it belongs. Tools that compose ( plan-week reusing search-recipes 's own ranking logic) produce much better agent behavior than a flat pile of unrelated CRUD tools would. Trust in a page an agent can write to has to be built into the architecture - one shared code path, validation at the domain layer, and reversibility - not asserted after the fact in a description. What's next for PantryPilot Testing against a real WebMCP origin trial browser and ChatGPT's browser once broadly available, beyond the in-page Agent Console. Redo (undo is currently one level deep, with no way back). Recipe ratings/favorites and multi-week history ("plan like last week"). A substitution tool that suggests a swap when an ingredient is missing or newly avoided. Optional lightweight sync so a plan isn't tied to one browser's localStorage . Exploring WebMCP's declarative API and cross-origin exposedTo , e.g. a grocery-delivery origin reading the shopping list directly. title: 5 of 23
pitch: Fill the form. Keep the rest.
about_excerpt: Fill the form. Keep the rest. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most forms ask for more personal information than they actually need. I wanted to test a simple idea: could an agent help finish a form without getting a free pass to read an entire profile? That became 5 of 23. The name is literal. The demo profile has 23 fields, but the sample application only needs five of them and an over-18 check. The point is not to make form filling faster at any cost. It is to make the boundary visible: what is needed, why it is needed, and who gets to release it. What it does The agent can inspect the application requirements and see what is missing without receiving the raw profile. For the age requirement, it calls an allow-listed is_adult check and gets a boolean result instead of a date of birth. It then requests the five fields required by the form. The request appears in the page, but it does not grant access. I approve or reject each field in the interface. Once the approved values have been applied, the form reaches 6/6 requirements and the temporary write capability disappears. There is still no submit tool. Final review remains a separate UI action. If that review is approved, the page exposes a local packet marked submitted: false . Revoking city removes the value, clears the reviewed copy and makes the old tool handle fail because it belongs to an earlier consent version. Everything in the demo is synthetic. It does not send an application anywhere. Why WebMCP This flow depends on the agent and the person sharing the live state of the same page: requirements, missing answers, approved scope, consent version and review status. WebMCP gives the agent a semantic tool surface instead of making it scrape buttons and labels. More importantly, the page can register a capability only while that capability is valid. The available tools change with consent, and the callbacks check the consent version again when they run. That is why this is not a chat box added to a form. The agent works out what the task needs and carries out the approved part. The person controls disclosure and review. The page enforces the boundary. How I built it I built the project in React and TypeScript with Vinext and Vite. The page registers its tools at the top level with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) so a compatible browser can discover them directly. A deterministic in-browser state engine owns the synthetic profile, form progress, disclosure requests, approvals, consent versions, receipts and reviewed packet. The normal interface and the WebMCP callbacks use that same store. The schemas use narrow enums, reject extra properties and bind dynamic writes to the current consent version. The prototype has no application API, database, login, analytics, payment flow or external submission handler. That kept the build focused on the consent model rather than infrastructure. The source code is public under the MIT License . Challenges I ran into The hard part was not the happy path. It was keeping six states separate and understandable: request, approval, application, review, revocation and stale authority. Dynamic tools also needed two layers of protection. A tool has to disappear when its authority disappears, but its callback must still reject an old handle that was fetched before the change. I also had to keep the proof honest: a mocked test is useful, but it is not the same thing as a real browser discovering and invoking the final page. What I am proud of In the local end-to-end browser run, the available tool count moved 8 → 9 → 8 → 9 → 8 as consent and review changed. The minimum path completed 6/6 requirements using 5 of 23 fields and one boolean age check. The other 18 fields stayed sealed in the tool/UI flow. Revoking city returned the form to 5/6 , left 4 of 23 fields disclosed, removed the reviewed-packet tool and rejected its old handle. The deterministic suite passed 14/14 tests , along with typecheck, lint, the production build and the recorded npm audit. The demo data lives in the public client bundle, so “sealed” describes the exercised interface and tool behavior, not source-code secrecy. This is a synthetic prototype, not a claim of production-grade security or measured user impact. What I learned Tool discovery is only the start of an agent-native product. The more interesting question is when a capability should exist, how small its scope can be, and what should happen to authority the moment consent changes. I also learned that privacy needs visible negative evidence. A good demo should show not only what the agent can do, but what it cannot read, cannot approve and can no longer use after revocation. What's next I would add property-based tests around redaction and stale versions, a small policy language for purpose and expiry, and a proper accessibility review of the consent controls. The next product question is whether people clearly understand the difference between a request, a grant and a reviewed local packet. title: orano
pitch: watch videos and reels with your ai and turn them into actionable tasks.
about_excerpt: watch videos and reels with your ai and turn them into actionable tasks. Like Comment Story Updates memory page video processing home page /task tracker project page projects page your saved videos What inspired this I kept losing the same thing. Someone would send me a Reel about a tool, a recipe, or a workflow. I'd save it. Two weeks later I'd want the link, the install steps, the tool name, or the recipe's ingredient list, and the video was right there in my library useless, because to answer any of those questions I had to either re-watch it or sit there transcribing it for an agent that couldn't see it. What I built For this challenge I exposed the ORANO desk web app at oranoai.com/workspace as a WebMCP surface and added nine tools that map directly to the actions a user can already take on the page: How I built it The desk is a single static workspace/index.html that loads one JS file, js/workspace.js. On load the script checks for document.modelContext and, when it's there, calls registerWebMCP() which registers the nine tools. Each tool is a plain object: a JSON Schema, an annotations block (readOnlyHint for read tools, untrustedContentHint for evidence), and an execute function that calls the same /v1 API the human UI already uses. That was the load-bearing decision: the agent doesn't get a parallel API. It shares apiRequest(), navigate(), and renderProject() with the UI, so the page state and the agent's view are literally the same state. The backend is the same FastAPI service that runs the mobile and web apps. The endpoints (/v1/projects, /v1/projects/{id}/context, /v1/profile/tasks, /v1/search, etc.) already existed to power the UI — WebMCP just gives the agent the same endpoints with structured schemas and bounded responses. The personal MCP server at /mcp/ (FastMCP) exposes the same selector through get_project_context for accounts that prefer an MCP-style integration. One concrete example of the contract. When a tool changes what's on screen (save_video, search, list_tasks), the execute function calls navigate() or renderProject() after the API call returns, so what the user sees matches what the agent was told. There's no parallel "API response" and "UI response" — there is just the workspace, and both participants read it. What I learned A few things that changed how I think about this: Agents are users, not API clients. Treating them as a separate integration channel — a separate auth flow, a separate surface, a separate data model — duplicated evidence and made the human the bottleneck. The breakthrough was giving the agent the same code path the UI uses, and the same render path so what the agent sees is what the user sees. The hard problem was boundaries, not schemas. Once the page can ask for the transcript, you have to decide how much. A bounded character budget, an allow-list of fields, and untrustedContentHint on evidence blocks were the minimum to make this safe for a real account with real saves. WebMCP made the product more human. The agent and the user doing the same work on the same data, with the same UI affordances, is the point. Writing tight tool descriptions ("List ORANO projects… use this before opening a project") forced me to write the spec for an agent that has no other context, which also helped me explain it better to humans. Challenges I faced Optimistic loading. The workbench opens with a shimmer skeleton the same shape as the real layout, so the page never looks empty while the project bundle is in flight. Cheaper to ship than a real data-fetch waterfall, and the result feels loaded within the first paint. Click-to-play embeds. Eagerly loading YouTube and Instagram iframes on every project view is slow and noisy. The page renders a thumbnail poster with a click-to-play badge; the iframe (with autoplay=1 so the user gesture counts) only loads when the user clicks. The visible state is honest about what is and is not playing. Public lab vs. authenticated desk. Two surfaces, one product. The lab exposes six tools on a guest workspace for evaluation; the desk exposes nine tools on a real account for daily use. Both share the same evidence contract, so a workflow that works in the lab is the same workflow that works in the desk once you sign in. title: Estro
pitch: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking.
about_excerpt: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Landing Page Projects Page ChatGPT Browser Window with Estro Before vs After Project Open within Estro Inspiration Everyone has a friend who takes the same photo on the same phone and it comes out like a poster. When you finally ask how, they send you a recipe: exposure +0.95, tint -18, an S-curve, blacks +52. You understood the word "photo." Every editor puts Saturation, Temperature and Tint in front of you and assumes you already know what they mean. Most people don't, so they never touch them, and the picture stays as it came off the phone. That's the gap Estro is for. The sliders were never the problem. The words were. WebMCP fits this problem unusually well because the thing a beginner needs isn't a smarter filter, it's someone beside them who can move the control, say the word out loud, and explain it in one sentence. An agent driving the real editor through the same commands a person uses can do exactly that, and the person keeps the Undo button. What it does Estro is a photo editor that runs entirely in the browser and registers 56 tools with document.modelContext . Open it in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and the agent next to the page can use the editor the way you would. Hand it your friend's recipe and it works through the steps. Every edit lands as a card in the interface naming the control, the value, a plain-language explanation of what that word means, and an Undo button for that one step. Mine and the agent's edits sit in one History, so I can undo its saturation without undoing my crop, and it can see what I did. Where Estro doesn't have a control the recipe names, the agent has nowhere to hide it. There is no Dehaze tool, so it has to say so and tell you what it used instead. Ask it where the contrast slider is and it points at the real control without touching it, so you can drag it yourself. Ask for a before-and-after and it puts the canvas in split view. Ask it to match your other three photos from that evening to this one and each project gets its own Undo, because each keeps its own history. Underneath, it's a real non-destructive editor: layers, groups, crop, transform, masks, curves, levels, colour balance, selective colour, vibrance, sharpen, blur, grain, lens correction, presets, batch export, and a live per-channel histogram that names which channel is clipping. Nothing is uploaded. There is no server and no account. How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite on the front. Dexie over IndexedDB for project history, the origin private file system for original photos, a dedicated worker for thumbnails, resampling, histograms and hashing, and Canvas compositing on the main thread with a 256 MB LRU cache for derived previews. Zod validates every command at the boundary. WebMCP was treated as an architectural layer, not a feature. The interface and the tools call the same validated domain commands, the same history, and the same transaction path, so a dragged slider and an agent's apply_color_adjustment produce identical history entries. Tools register at module load, before first paint, via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every result is a JSON envelope carrying ok , the previous and resulting revision IDs, a transactionId , an undoToken , affectedIds , warnings, and a plain-language summary . Colour and layer commands also return an explanation of the term in ordinary words, so an agent can pass it straight back to someone who didn't know it. Every mutation accepts an optional expectedRevisionId and is refused with HISTORY_CONFLICT if the project moved on, checked immediately before the commit. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint , destructive ones destructiveHint , and anything that can return user-authored text carries untrustedContentHint . Errors carry a code , a fieldPath , a recoverySuggestion , and whether the project was preserved. The agent side is never invisible. Every tool call surfaces a card in the Activity Center, every committed revision carries its Undo, and History distinguishes the person's edits from the agent's. Challenges we ran into An agent cannot open a file. Browsers grant file access only from a user gesture. Rather than fake it, the tool focuses the Import control, reports whether an editor was open to receive that focus, and says why. A manage_project operation draws a three-frame sample scene and imports it through the same path a real file takes, so an agent arriving at an empty browser still has something to edit. Import had to be atomic across two stores. A project revision in IndexedDB and original bytes in OPFS can't share a transaction. A persisted intent record moves through prepared, committed, and deleted, and startup recovery finishes or undoes whatever a crash left, so History can never point at a file that isn't there. Adjustments bled. Brightening a rotated cut-out was brightening the background behind it, because the adjustment read a padded rectangle off the shared canvas. Each adjusted layer now renders alone on an isolated surface and is composited afterwards. WebMCP can't be tested in jsdom. 940 unit tests cover the domain, commands and persistence, but tool discovery only exists in a real WebMCP-capable browser over HTTPS, so every registration check was manual. Cutting video. Estro started as a photo and video editor. Ten days in, the video half doubled the surface and carried the least-verified code. It was removed, not hidden: roughly 12,500 lines, 14 tools, five panels, and one LGPL dependency. One thing done properly beats two things done partly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The person never loses control. Every agent action is a real, named, individually undoable edit in the same History as their own, and the explanation of the word travels with it. The honesty holds under pressure. Out-of-range values are clamped and the clamp is reported. Unavailable formats are disabled with a reason. A stale revision is refused rather than silently overwritten. There's no path by which the agent can do something to your photo that you can't see and can't reverse. Fifty-six tools, one command system, zero servers. What we learned Describing side effects in the tool description matters more than clever schemas. When a tool said exactly what it would change and what it would return, the model called it correctly first time. When it didn't, the model guessed. Returning an explanation from the tool, rather than trusting the model to write one, was the right call. The product's whole promise is that the word arrives attached to the effect. That only holds if the explanation comes from the same place the effect did. And the most useful tool in the set turned out to be one that changes nothing: the one that points at a control and explains it. Teaching isn't editing on someone's behalf. It's showing them where the thing is. What's next for Estro Local model support so the explanations can be spoken aloud for people who'd rather listen than read. Voice as an input, for the same reason. Bringing back a narrower video treatment once the photo side has been used by real people for a while. And a proper accessibility pass with screen-reader users, because a photo editor that explains itself in plain words should also work for people who can't see the slider it's explaining. Here we ask it to make a cold street photo look like a golden hour shot. We also tell it to explain every control it touches. You just talk to it like a normal person. title: QuantMCP
pitch: An agent-native quantitative research terminal where humans explore markets visually and AI agents analyze, compare, and investigate them through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An agent-native quantitative research terminal where humans explore markets visually and AI agents analyze, compare, and investigate them through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates tells us explicitly when it is connected correctly QuantMCP — a shared research workspace for human + AI market analysis QuantMCP was built for a simple problem: quantitative research often becomes a disconnected chain of charts, prompts, parameters, and spreadsheets. That makes it hard to reproduce a strategy, compare alternatives, or review the quality of someone’s work. QuantMCP turns that chain into one visible, shared workflow. A human researcher and an MCP-enabled agent work on the same active asset, timeframe, historical events, saved strategy definition, event study, trade simulation, chart focus, and research notes. What it does The workflow is intentionally ordered for transparent competition review: Select a research universe. Search feasible shared parameters with chronological out-of-sample validation. Validate the saved universal region across assets and rank them. Optionally refine the best-ranked asset. Run an event study using the saved strategy definition. Run a deterministic historical trade simulation with explicit entry, stop, target, holding-period, and OHLC collision rules. Review the strongest and weakest historical cases together. This means Event Study and Trade Simulation do not silently use unrelated conditions: they inherit the saved robust strategy configuration. WebMCP integration QuantMCP exposes 18 browser-native WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect the active workspace, query structured historical conditions, calculate indicators and forward returns, compare timeframes, run universe and parameter research, simulate trades, focus chart ranges and trades, and save research findings. The human sees the same evidence immediately in the UI. The agent does not place orders and the app is designed for historical research only. Reliability and performance The project uses real continuous-futures demo datasets across eight assets. Heavy condition scans, parameter searches, timeframe comparisons, event studies, and trade simulations run in background workers, keeping the chart responsive and showing real progress instead of appearing frozen. To make the experience practical on desktop and mobile, QuantMCP includes a fast Intraday Core preset, keeps all assets available for full validation, bounds expensive universal searches, caches datasets by asset and timeframe, and progressively renders large trade lists. What I learned The hardest part was not building individual quant calculations; it was preserving one reliable shared state across human controls and agent tool calls. I learned that a useful AI research interface needs explicit dependencies, reproducible definitions, transparent out-of-sample evidence, and a UI that makes the next correct step obvious. title: MarketBench
pitch: A reproducible WebMCP benchmark for agents making economic decisions under pressure.
about_excerpt:
A reproducible WebMCP benchmark for agents making economic decisions under pressure.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration\n\nBrowser agents can complete a task and still leave reviewers unable to answer basic questions: What actions did the agent take? Did the policy really improve the outcome? Can the result be reproduced? MarketBench makes those questions measurable.\n\n## What it does\n\nMarketBench is an interactive evaluation lab for browser-agent market policies. A visitor selects a scenario and seed, runs a 12-week simulation, and gets:\n\n- a clear business outcome and plain-language insight\n- the full WebMCP tool-call and state history\n- integrity hashes for trace and final state\n- a deterministic baseline comparison\n- three-seed aggregates with mean, standard deviation, and worst-seed results\n- downloadable evidence for audit and replay\n\n## How we built it\n\nThe app is a React and TypeScript web application deployed on Vercel. WebMCP exposes typed browser tools for configuring and running experiments. The evaluation engine uses versioned deterministic fixtures for three scenarios and three seeds, so baseline and signal-aware policy runs can be reproduced exactly. Each step records its input, tool call, output, state transition, and hash.\n\nThe comparison view aggregates the same fixed seed set rather than presenting a single lucky run. It visualizes distributions and reports mean, standard deviation, and worst seed. The repository includes tests for determinism, trace completeness, hashes, aggregate math, and export structure.\n\n## Challenges\n\nThe main challenge was making rigor understandable. A raw trace is useful to an engineer but intimidating to a first-time visitor. We rebuilt the experience around a three-step flow, visible progress, a human-readable takeaway, compact trace summaries, and expandable evidence. We also made the distinction between deterministic policy fixtures and model output explicit.\n\n## Accomplishments\n\n- Full trace, state, and history export with integrity hashes\n- Transparent baseline vs signal-aware comparisons\n- Three-seed aggregate metrics and charts\n- A first-run experience that explains the value before exposing technical detail\n- A live, reproducible demo with tested fixtures\n\n## What we learned\n\nAgent evaluation needs both observability and a decision-relevant metric. Traces explain how an outcome happened; controlled repeated runs show whether the policy actually helped. Neither alone is enough.\n\n## What is next\n\nNext, MarketBench can add imported real-world task traces, more scenario packs, signed evaluation bundles, and CI checks that compare agent-policy revisions before deployment.
