 1 2 



 
 Inspiration Well I was inspired by webmcp that list 10 people for the award that's wonderful and I believe I'd be one of the winner, that's why I joined. 

 What it does DodoLink Agent Shopping gives browser agents a structured way to help shoppers navigate a real Nigerian marketplace. Instead of scraping repetitive listing cards and guessing which actions are safe, an agent can call typed WebMCP tools to search products, discover local stores, compare prices, and prepare a purchase plan. 

 How we built it I built DodoLink Agent Shopping as a web-only WebMCP experience connected to DodoLink’s real public marketplace data. 

 The page exposes four structured, read-only tools: 

 search_products
discover_stores
compare_products
prepare_purchase_plan
Each tool is registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool, using a JSON input schema and an asynchronous execute function. The tools return real product and store information, including prices, stock status, seller details, and review links. 

 I also added a manual fallback so the experience still works in a normal browser when WebMCP is unavailable. Both the manual interface and the WebMCP tools use the same marketplace search and purchase-planning logic. 

 The system intentionally does not expose payment, checkout, or seller-messaging tools. The agent can discover and organize options, but the human must review the products and decide whether to continue. 

 Challenges we ran into An agent could describe a product, but it could not reliably distinguish listing IDs, price limits, stock, seller context, and review links. The WebMCP tools make those capabilities explicit and return bounded public data. The plan tool then turns agent work into a visible human approval step. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that DodoLink Agent Shopping is connected to real marketplace data instead of using a mock catalog. 

 We built a complete experience where an agent can: 

 Understand a natural-language shopping request.
Search real DodoLink products.
Discover relevant stores.
Compare product options.
Prepare a shortlist and purchase plan.
Hand the decision back to the human shopper.
We are especially proud of the safety boundary. The agent can help with discovery and research, but it cannot spend money, check out, or send messages to sellers. This keeps the agent useful while ensuring the human remains in control of important decisions. 

 We also created a separate public and sanitized open-source repository so judges can inspect the WebMCP implementation without exposing DodoLink’s private production infrastructure. 

 What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most useful when an application exposes focused capabilities instead of allowing an agent to guess its way through a user interface. 

 For a marketplace, structured tools are much more reliable than page scraping. A tool can clearly define the product query, price limit, product IDs, and expected response format. 

 We also learned that WebMCP tools need strong safety boundaries. Marketplace listings and seller descriptions should be treated as untrusted content, while actions such as payment and messaging should remain under human control. 

 Another important lesson was that WebMCP is page-scoped and still experimental. A user must open the WebMCP-enabled page in a compatible browser before the agent can discover and use its tools. Because of this, we made the manual experience work as a fallback too. 

 What's next for Dodolink Next, we want to make the agent experience more useful for complex shopping decisions. 

 We plan to improve product filtering with more detailed category, location, availability, and seller-reputation criteria. We also want to make comparisons more informative by including delivery options, product attributes, review summaries, and clearer trade-offs between sellers. 

 We would like to improve the human handoff so shoppers can save a shortlist, share it with someone else, open a seller profile, and continue manually when they are ready. 

 As WebMCP develops, we also plan to test DodoLink with more browser agents and refine the tool schemas based on real usage. Our long-term goal is to make DodoLink a marketplace where agents are genuinely helpful while people remain informed and in control.

title: DOGAGA
pitch: Teach a browser video editor by example, let the agent generalize, then approve the result.
about_excerpt: Teach a browser video editor by example, let the agent generalize, then approve the result. Like Comment Story Updates DOGAGA's live editor with WebMCP connected: Teach by Example, an applied agent suggestion, actual Preview, and the shared timeline. Inspiration Video editing is visual, but editing intent is semantic. Meaning lives in operations such as track order, clip timing, fades, opacity, still-image duration, canvas settings, and transitions—not only in pixels or DOM controls. AI-assisted creative tools often place an agent beside the editor rather than inside the editor's structured state. The agent may generate instructions, click the interface indirectly, or operate through a separate backend. After either side edits, the other side may no longer know the real project state or the human's intent. DOGAGA explores a page-native alternative: the open web application exposes its live semantic editing state and actions through WebMCP while the person keeps the normal visual editor and final approval. What it does DOGAGA is a compact, local-first browser video editor where the human UI and a WebMCP agent operate on the same live timeline. Its collaboration loop is: Human teaches by performing a normal edit in the visual editor. DOGAGA captures semantic meaning from the supported before/after change. The agent generalizes that treatment to analogous current assets through a reviewable Edit Plan. The human approves or rejects the proposal before the timeline changes. For example, a person can load three still images, click Teach agent , add the first image to V2, set it to three seconds with a 0.5-second fade, and stop teaching. DOGAGA exposes the completed semantic demonstration through get_project_state . When the person asks, “Do the same to the other still images,” the agent can propose the corresponding operations. The app shows that plan without mutating anything; only the person's Apply action commits it. The same live project then powers actual Preview and browser-native Export. There is no fixed hackathon scene, agent-only timeline, remote editing backend, hidden replay, or fake preview. Why WebMCP is a strong fit WebMCP lets the page define an explicit contract for agent-readable state and semantic actions. The agent does not have to infer a timeline from screenshots or guess which DOM element represents a trim, fade, track, or still-image duration. This creates a better user experience because people can communicate intent through editing itself instead of translating every creative choice into a prompt. The agent receives safe, structured meaning; it can reason over current assets and propose a generalization; the person retains visible control and final approval. This human-agent workflow was difficult with conventional UI automation. Mouse-coordinate or DOM macro replay captures mechanics, not meaning. A separate MCP server can also create a second copy of the project that drifts from the open editor. DOGAGA keeps the visual UI, agent state, Preview, and Export synchronized in one page-owned project. How we built it DOGAGA uses React, TypeScript, and Vite and is deployed on Cloudflare Pages. A single EditorController and command executor power both human editing and all WebMCP mutations. The page registers typed tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() through use-webmcp-tool . The canonical editor state contains safe asset descriptors, video/audio tracks, clips, canvas settings, transitions, and playhead state. Collaboration metadata includes a small Project Brief, the completed humanDemonstration , and a reviewable editPlan . Local File objects and object URLs are kept separately in a session-only runtime media map. They are deliberately excluded from agent-visible state. WebMCP sees only safe asset IDs and descriptors—never absolute paths, file handles, object URLs, media pixels, or private Teach by Example snapshots. DOGAGA exposes 23 WebMCP tools : 21 core/collaboration tools plus add_image_clip and set_still_duration . Direct mutation tools share the UI executor. propose_edit_plan validates a complete multi-step proposal without mutating the timeline. Human Apply revalidates and commits atomically; Reject leaves the project unchanged. Preview uses browser-native video/audio elements and canvas composition. Export uses Canvas, Web Audio, and MediaRecorder, prefers MP4 when supported, and falls back to WebM. Normal editing and export do not upload source media to a DOGAGA server. Product capabilities The submitted public app supports: local video, PNG/JPEG/WebP still-image, and audio loading multiple video and audio tracks still-image display duration and transparent PNG overlays split, trim, reorder, delete, and cross-track clip movement playback speed, visual fades, and cross dissolves track opacity/visibility, audio mute, and clip volume actual multi-layer Preview with play, pause, and seek 16:9, 9:16, 1:1, and 4:5 canvases with contain/cover fitting browser-native composited video/audio Export and download Project Brief, Teach by Example, and reviewable agent Edit Plans Challenges we ran into The hardest architectural constraint was preserving one real source of truth. WebMCP could not become a second editor state, and human actions could not bypass the same validation used by agents. Local-first privacy added another constraint: the agent needs enough structured context to edit intelligently, but local file handles, paths, object URLs, and media contents must remain private. Browser-native media also required careful synchronization. Preview and Export must reflect the same clip timing, track ordering, fades, image duration, audio mixing, and canvas settings. Still images introduced separate semantics from videos while still needing to participate in the same layered timeline and export path. Finally, Teach by Example had to capture meaning rather than input events. DOGAGA compares supported semantic before/after state, exposes only the completed safe result, and routes any generalization through the existing reviewable Edit Plan path. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real public editor rather than a challenge-only demo One shared state and executor for the human UI and 23 WebMCP tools Semantic Teach by Example with explicit human approval Actual multi-layer Preview and browser-native Export Local-first media boundaries that keep source files out of agent state Non-mutating proposal validation and atomic Apply Transparent PNG and still-image support across editing, Preview, Export, and WebMCP A reproducible public repository with MIT licensing and reviewer instructions What we learned The most useful agent interaction is not always “do this for me.” In creative work, a person may communicate intent more naturally by demonstrating one example. WebMCP can turn that visual interaction into structured semantics without reducing it to a fragile macro. We also learned that human control works best when it is part of the product state: proposals are visible, reviewable, and separate from committed edits. The agent can reason broadly while the person keeps authorship over what becomes real. What was built during the Challenge DOGAGA existed before August 25, 2026, and the public repository history documents that prior work. During the Challenge period it was meaningfully extended with the WebMCP shared-state architecture and completed compact production path, including: page-native WebMCP registration and typed command schemas agent-safe editor state and privacy boundaries actual local-media Preview connected to shared state Cloudflare Pages deployment browser-native Export canonical multi-track video/audio editing speed, fades, split, cross-dissolves, opacity/visibility, and multi-audio mixing Project Brief and non-mutating propose_edit_plan still-image and transparent-PNG support Teach by Example semantic demonstrations the final 23-tool WebMCP surface The repository's dated commit and pull-request history distinguishes this Challenge-period work from the earlier project. What's next DOGAGA is intentionally compact. Next steps include persistent project save/relink, richer timeline positioning, waveforms, captions and lyrics, image motion, and more advanced effects. The current release focuses on a small but genuinely usable local-first editor and a clear human-agent collaboration model. Try it Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled: Live app: https://dogaga.pages.dev Source and setup instructions: https://github.com/yo4e/DOGAGA Recommended flow: load three local still images, teach one 3-second faded V2 treatment, ask the agent to do the same to the other images, review and Apply the proposed plan, then Preview or Export the shared result. Built With canvas-api cloudflare-pages html5-video mediarecorder open-source react typescript vite vitest web-audio-api webmcp Try it out dogaga.pages.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo creator.

title: Tax Pundit
pitch: Tax Pundit lets people and browser agents turn scattered tax records into a cited, review-ready case to file tax return - while every consequential tax decision stays with the person.
about_excerpt: Tax Pundit lets people and browser agents turn scattered tax records into a cited, review-ready case to file tax return - while every consequential tax decision stays with the person. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP processes tax documents while results appear live in the shared workspace. Profile-based onboarding creates a personalized tax preparation plan. Transparent WebMCP audit trail showing every agent action and case revision. Pundit summarizes case progress, completed actions and the next review step. The agent pauses safely when mileage needs human confirmation. A clear review handoff showing preparation status and unresolved questions. Inspiration Tax filing often means sending the same income slips, receipts, mileage records and personal details to an accountant every year. The harder part is knowing what information is missing and which deductions or benefits may apply to your job, province or family situation. During the busy filing season, it is difficult for taxpayers and accountants to discuss every possible opportunity. We built Tax Pundit to make this preparation more organized and proactive. What it does Tax Pundit is a shared tax-preparation workspace for a person, their browser agent and their tax professional. It organizes records, identifies missing information, performs bounded calculations and surfaces relevant deductions, benefits, CRA forms and official guidance. Through WebMCP , a browser agent can work directly with the application using 15 structured tools . Each action produces a visible document, calculation or decision in the center workspace, while the WebMCP panel shows the live tool sequence. The agent can gather information, calculate vehicle expenses and prepare recommendations, but it cannot approve a tax treatment. Important decisions and final export remain human-controlled. The current demo uses synthetic Ontario and British Columbia cases and creates a cited, review-ready brief for a tax professional. It does not file a real return or calculate a complete refund. How we built it We built Tax Pundit with TypeScript, React, Vinext and Vite , then deployed it through ChatGPT Sites . The interface and WebMCP tools share one canonical case store, so human and agent actions always update the same information. We added strict tool schemas, profile-based workflows, official CRA references, visible agent activity and human approval controls. The project includes 40 automated tests covering all 15 WebMCP tools, calculations, invalid inputs, changed facts, approval invalidation, undo, reset and export behavior. Challenges we ran into Our main challenge was making agent activity easy to understand. Early versions looked like technical commands running in the background. We redesigned the experience so the current result stays in the user’s eye line while the WebMCP panel provides a transparent record of the supporting actions. We also had to manage shared state safely. Reading a case should not change it, while editing an important fact—such as mileage—must invalidate an earlier approval. We deliberately prevented the agent from approving decisions or filing anything. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created a complete human-agent workflow rather than only a WebMCP technical demo. Tax Pundit exposes 15 functional tools , adapts the preparation flow to different profiles, presents agent results visually and stops for human approval when judgment is required. The application is publicly available, requires no login for the demo and has a complete open-source repository with tests and setup instructions. What we learned WebMCP works best when tools have narrow responsibilities, strict inputs and clear limits. We also learned that users need to see what an agent produced—not just that a command ran. Most importantly, agentic experiences become more trustworthy when responsibilities are clear: the agent handles repetitive preparation, while the person retains control over facts and consequential decisions. What's next for Tax Pundit Next, we would support secure document uploads, OCR and confirmation of extracted information. We would also add persistent user accounts, more Canadian tax scenarios and an accountant portal for reviewing evidence, calculations and unresolved questions. The long-term goal is to make Tax Pundit a secure preparation layer between taxpayers, browser agents and tax professionals. pitch: You already do this by hand. You add Reddit to the search and read threads until a picture forms. VibeCheck does the reading. You decide who to believe.
about_excerpt: You already do this by hand. You add Reddit to the search and read threads until a picture forms. VibeCheck does the reading. You decide who to believe. Like Comment Story Updates VibeCheck: what people actually said Inspiration It started from a habit I didn't think about until I tried to explain it: whenever I'm deciding on something real — a laptop, a bank, a framework — I don't trust the first page of search results. I type the question, then I add "reddit" to the end of it, and I read threads until a picture forms in my head. Marketing pages tell you what a product wants to be. Threads tell you what it actually is. That habit is the whole product. I wasn't trying to build a search engine or a recommendation engine — those already exist and mostly disappoint. I was trying to build the reading part: gather what real people said, and then get out of the way while a person does the one thing a model can't do for them, which is decide who to believe. The WebMCP angle came second, but it clicked hard once I saw it: an agent helping you decide on a laptop is useless if it can't see that you already rejected one source as a shill, or that you pinned a claim as the one that actually matters to you. That state lives in your head and on your screen — not in a database, not in a prompt. WebMCP is the only way an agent gets to touch it directly, in your session, live. That's not a nice-to-have integration; it's the reason the product exists in this shape at all. What I learned The biggest lesson wasn't technical — it was that "gather opinions" is a much harder problem than "run a search." A raw discussion-source query returns a pile of ambiguity: half the results are Facebook groups and LinkedIn posts dressed up as discussion, snippets are truncated mid-sentence, and search engines match your question almost literally, so a natural question like "is the Mac Mini a good device for developers?" returns nothing while "mac mini developers" returns real threads. I ended up writing a whole normalization layer just to translate a person's actual sentence into something a search API will respect. The second lesson was about trust modeling. Early on, "support" for a claim was just a count of sources. That's wrong — three people reposting the same affiliate blurb isn't consensus, it's an echo. So the real signal isn't $n$, it's a weighted sum: $$ \text{raw}(claim) = \sum_{s \in \text{evidence}} w(s), \qquad w(s) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{rejected by you} \ 1.5 & \text{trusted by you} \ 0.4 & \text{low-signal source} \ 1 & \text{ordinary discussion source} \end{cases} $$ and the bar you see is that raw score normalized against the best-supported claim on the whole board: $$ \text{weight}(claim) = \min\left(1,\ \frac{\text{raw}(claim)}{\max_{c \in \text{claims}} \text{raw}(c)}\right) $$ The moment I had that formula, the UI basically designed itself: the support bar isn't decoration, it's the math made visible, and rejecting a source visibly collapses the segment it owned. Watching a claim go from "consensus" to "thin" in real time, just because you clicked reject on one Facebook post, is the whole pitch of the app in one interaction. How I built it The architecture is deliberately small: one state shape, one reducer, and both the UI and the six WebMCP tools read and write through it. That constraint — "nothing the agent does is invisible on screen, and nothing you do on screen is invisible to the agent" — came from a very specific failure mode I wanted to avoid: tools that quietly mutate state the human can't see, which turns "collaboration" into "surveillance." The pipeline underneath is two calls: SerpApi's google_forums engine finds the threads, and an LLM (routed through OpenRouter so it can run on a free model with a paid fallback) does three jobs in one pass — decide if a thread is actually relevant, decide if the poster sounds like they own the thing or is just relaying secondhand, and cluster the recurring points into claims with evidence attached. Everything downstream — the reducer, the support math, the UI — trusts that shaping completely, so getting it right mattered more than almost anything else in the project. Challenges Credit discipline was a real design constraint, not an afterthought. SerpApi's free tier is 250 searches a month, and every extra fallback call eats into that. I built a two-stage gather — google_forums first, alone, and only fall back to a second, broader search if the first came back too thin — plus a disk cache for local dev so iterating on the UI costs nothing. Tuning how thin is too thin turned out to be its own ongoing problem: real google_forums responses are noisier than I expected, often dominated by Facebook and LinkedIn results that read as discussion but aren't, which pushes the fallback to fire more often than I originally assumed it would. Getting the LLM to stop hallucinating specificity was harder than getting it to extract claims at all. Search snippets are cut off mid-sentence — literally ending in "…" — and the model's instinct is to complete the thought plausibly. A plausible completion that the source never actually said is a fabrication wearing a citation. I had to write explicit rules against finishing a snippet's sentence, against reusing a source's distinctive phrasing verbatim, and against letting one source's detail leak into another source's evidence line. None of that is exotic prompt engineering — it's just the unglamorous work of writing rules for every way a language model quietly lies with confidence. And the last one is the most human: making the board itself feel worth staying on, not just correct. It's easy to build something that's functionally right and viscerally forgettable — an accurate list of claims with checkboxes is not a product anyone wants to spend time in. Getting the support bar to move like something real, making rejection feel like a decision rather than a checkbox, giving the empty state a reason to click something instead of stare at a search box — that's the part with no spec, just taste, and it's the part I kept coming back to rewrite. title: WorkHub Goal Room
pitch: WebMCP lets the agent act; WorkHub keeps evidence, verification, and final authority separate.
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets the agent act; WorkHub keeps evidence, verification, and final authority separate. Like Comment Story Updates Candidate v1 retained after deterministic System FAIL; the Agent remains next to repair. Corrected Candidate v2 receives deterministic System PASS without being auto-accepted. Owner acceptance is bound to the exact candidate bytes and visible evidence. Sealed S14 is terminal and actorless; no further Agent, System, or Owner action remains. Native browser evidence: exactly six Agent-callable WebMCP tools, with no privileged Owner or System tools. Architecture: WebMCP adapter, governed reducer, deterministic verifier, Owner UI, and evidence package. From callable to accountable: Goal Room governs WebMCP; post-demo ACA binds local Git evidence. Authority: NONE. PASS is not approval. WebMCP makes a website callable. WorkHub deals with what happens after the call: keeping the agent’s work tied to the right Goal, the right evidence, and the right human decision. We built the missing control layer between an agent saying “I’m done” and a human safely accepting what it actually changed. The problem we chose Giving an agent a tool is the easy part. While building this, we kept finding the same tempting shortcut: if the agent can call the tool and the checker says PASS, the system wants to treat the job as finished. Goal Room refuses that shortcut. The agent may have the right tool but stale state, the wrong Plan version, or evidence for different candidate bytes. A green check tells us that explicit checks passed. It does not prove the work is correct, and it does not give the checker authority to accept, merge, deploy, or release anything. Goal Room puts those boundaries on the page instead of hiding them behind one vague “agent completed” message. What the Goal Room demonstrates The Goal Room is one browser-local, synthetic software-release Goal shared by three distinct actors: Agent: moves work forward through six narrow WebMCP tools; System Verifier: records deterministic PASS or FAIL for the exact candidate; Owner: confirms Goal and Plan scope and makes the final acceptance decision. The page registers exactly six browser-native Agent tools: get_goal_room_state propose_goal_contract propose_plan claim_step submit_artifact request_completion There is deliberately no Agent tool for Owner confirmation, System-verdict authorship, or final acceptance. The journey begins with owner intent. The Agent proposes Goal Contract v1; the Owner requests a revision and confirms immutable v2. The Agent proposes a Goal-bound Plan v1; the Owner revises and confirms v2. Only then can the Agent claim the admitted step and submit Candidate v1. Candidate v1 fails deterministic verification and remains in the append-only history. The Agent submits corrected Candidate v2, which passes. The Agent can then request completion—but the room still stops at the Owner. PASS does not mean accepted. The Owner accepts only the exact candidate version and SHA-256 shown in the confirmation dialog. The final S14 room is sealed: current actor none , no controls, and no legal continuation. The architecture The architecture separates four jobs that agent systems often blur together: WebMCP tool surface: lets the Agent read, propose, claim, submit, and request. Governed kernel: rechecks exact input shape, state version, idempotency, Goal/Plan/step binding, candidate digest, evidence, and the current legal frontier. System Verifier: records deterministic findings for the bound candidate but cannot change the candidate or accept the Goal. Owner UI: confirms scope and retains the final exact-candidate decision. That separation is the product. The Agent can advance the work without inheriting every power in the room. What we added after the frozen demonstration Agent Change Assurance (ACA) is genuine post-demo engineering. It is not presented as part of the frozen Goal Room demonstration. The original Goal Room demo stops at synthetic release metadata on purpose. That keeps the authority model small enough to inspect, but it leaves an obvious next problem: real code changes are messier. ACA is our bounded answer. It checks whether an agent’s claim about a real local code change matches what Git and isolated checks actually show. On an explicit local observation, ACA can: bind the observation to an exact commit, tree, base, diff, and working-tree inventory; compare what the agent says changed with the files and evidence actually observed; run admitted unit and build checks in a provider-free isolated sandbox; handle failure, mismatch, cancellation, source movement, timeout, and cleanup paths; produce a digest-linked, point-in-time evidence receipt for review. The public repository contains the merged nine-commit ACA chain in PR #1 . The successor video shows the real local ACA run and its evidence receipt after the Goal Room demonstration. The important boundary is still visible: Authority: NONE. ACA did not post a GitHub comment or review, create a native Check, approve the pull request, merge it, deploy it, or release anything. Passing checks are evidence for a later decision, not the decision itself. What we proved In the demonstrated Goal Room Chrome Canary natively returned the exact six RegisteredTool descriptors. Calls used the browser testing path getTools() → executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify(input)) . The same governed state is reflected in the Agent calls, Owner UI, System findings, and receipts. Failed Candidate v1 remains visible after corrected Candidate v2 passes. PASS leaves final acceptance pending. Only the Owner accepts the exact verified candidate. No autonomous model selected tools in this recorded native evidence. In the post-demo ACA work The public ACA implementation and its authority limits are reviewable in the merged PR. A real local, point-in-time run bound one exact Git candidate to its base, tree, diff, manifest, policy, and isolated-check evidence. Unit and build checks passed in the qualified sandbox, with cleanup confirmed. Deliberate failure, mismatch, cancellation, and source-movement paths were also exercised. This is evidence of one bounded implementation and one bounded local run. It is not a claim of production security, hostile-environment attestation, repeated model reliability, or autonomous release authority. What was hard—and what we learned The hardest bug was authority leaking across layers. The UI wanted to be helpful. The verifier wanted to sound conclusive. The evidence package wanted to tell a neat success story. Any of those could accidentally turn “the checks passed” into “the work was accepted.” We kept coming back to one rule: Tool access, evidence, verification, and acceptance are four different events. Human control means very little if the approval button is attached to a vague status. It becomes useful when the decision is attached to exact state and exact evidence. Scope and limits The demonstrated Goal Room is one synthetic, browser-local Goal. Reloading starts a fresh room. It has no accounts, backend persistence, database, credentials, production effects, payment, messaging, deployment, or release action. ACA is a separately labeled local engineering extension. Its public static view cannot observe a judge’s local repository or run the sandbox. The evidence shown in the video is a recorded point-in-time local run, not a live provider-backed service or continuing monitor. How to judge it Open the frozen Goal Room WebMCP app in a qualifying WebMCP browser. Confirm exactly six Agent tools and the absence of Owner, verifier, acceptance, deployment, or release tools. Follow Goal revision, Plan revision, Candidate v1 FAIL, Candidate v2 PASS, completion request, exact-candidate Owner acceptance, and sealed S14. Watch the successor video : Goal Room first, then the clearly labeled post-demo ACA extension. Inspect the public source and merged ACA PR for the implementation, checks, commit chain, and permanent authority exclusions. title: GridBrief TR
pitch: An agent-ready bilingual workspace that turns public EPİAŞ Transparency Platform 2.0 data into explainable market, portfolio, and planning decisions through native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready bilingual workspace that turns public EPİAŞ Transparency Platform 2.0 data into explainable market, portfolio, and planning decisions through native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Türkiye's electricity-market teams must reconcile prices, system conditions, generation, consumption, and planning data before making a shift decision. Today that work often spans operator pages, spreadsheets, and chat. Each team rebuilds the same context, while the most important questions — which source, which timestamp, which scope, and how complete is the data — are easy to lose. GridBrief TR reimagines the public EPİAŞ Transparency Platform 2.0 as a bilingual, agent-ready decision workspace. It keeps the familiar market information architecture, but makes provenance, freshness, coverage, and missing data first-class product features. What it does GridBrief TR combines: a real-data market overview; the searchable Transparency 2.0 electricity catalogue; public organization and power-plant discovery; production and consumption planning views; English and Turkish interfaces; and a native WebMCP tool surface shared by the human user and browser agents. The production walkthrough uses a completed historical day and visibly shows EPİAŞ provenance, retrieval time, scope, coverage, and warnings. Examples include market price and imbalance context, 24/24 planning coverage, the public PURE ENERGY organization view and linked UEVÇB records, and an ACARSOY plant view that honestly leaves unavailable actual generation as null. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the interaction layer, not a chatbot bolted onto a dashboard. GridBrief registers eight structured tools on document.modelContext: set_analysis_scope get_market_snapshot find_market_entities compare_plan_actual stress_test_position draft_shift_brief search_transparency_datasets get_transparency_dataset A compatible browser discovers these tools and calls the descriptor returned by getTools() with schema-bounded arguments. Successful calls update the same visible workspace used by the participant, so the agent and human share the selected date, hour window, results, warnings, and sources. Our native Chrome 152 verification discovered all eight tools. It also executed search_transparency_datasets through document.modelContext and visibly synchronized the selected catalogue item. That is separate from the real-data production evidence: during the recorded native verification run, an upstream EPİAŞ live read timed out, so the harness failed closed, recorded the failure, and skipped downstream sensitivity and brief actions. It never substituted a synthetic observation. Example agent workflow A trading agent can retrieve price and imbalance context. An operations agent can inspect generation evidence and publication coverage. A planning agent can compare KGÜP, KUDÜP, EAK, load-plan, and actual series only at valid data levels. A portfolio-risk agent can apply a transparent local sensitivity after the live price reference passes validation. A management agent can turn the sourced evidence, risks, and proposed checks into an editable shift brief. These are role-specific uses of one WebMCP contract, demonstrated by a deterministic sample agent workflow in the repository. GridBrief does not claim that the runner itself is an LLM. It exposes no market-order, trading-account, message-sending, or upstream mutation tool. How we built it The application uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Vercel. A server-only EPİAŞ gateway obtains and caches the short-lived ticket-granting token without returning or logging credentials. Responses carry provider, retrieval time, scope, quality, coverage, and warnings. Partial data preserves nulls; live errors fail closed. The browser layer registers imperative WebMCP definitions for the lifetime of the workspace. A Node/CDP verification harness launches Chrome with WebMCP enabled, checks unique tool discovery, executes native descriptors, and writes bounded sanitized evidence and screenshots. The harness accepts no username, password, token, cookie, or authorization-header argument. Challenges and learnings The hardest part was preserving market-data integrity while making the experience useful to agents. EPİAŞ reports have different scopes and publication schedules; organization filters do not turn system-level actuals into organization data; and upstream availability can change during a demo. We therefore made data level explicit, preserved missing hours, withheld full-day deviation when coverage is not comparable, and separated catalogue availability from successful observation retrieval. We also learned that the current experimental Chrome implementation requires the descriptor returned by getTools() and JSON-stringified arguments. Testing that real boundary exposed issues a mock panel would have hidden, including duplicate registration risks, inclusive-versus-exclusive hour semantics, and upstream timeout handling. What's next Next steps are formal review of EPİAŞ report semantics and terms, organization-level audit retention, role controls, shared rate limiting, richer data-quality tests, and approved connections to internal portfolio systems. We will preserve the no-execution boundary unless a separately governed product is designed and authorized. Links Live English workspace: https://gridbrief-tr.vercel.app/en Turkish workspace: https://gridbrief-tr.vercel.app/tr Source code: https://github.com/haakanergun/gridbrief-tr Demo video: https://youtu.be/5dGW_ocNZJw Disclosure GridBrief TR is an independent prototype and is not affiliated with or endorsed by EPİAŞ. It provides decision support only and does not place trades or provide financial advice. title: Procura
pitch: An agent-native procurement app where the agent can't spend without your click
about_excerpt: An agent-native procurement app where the agent can't spend without your click Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept noticing that "AI agent shops for you" demos all have the same hole in them: the agent describes what it found in a wall of chat text, and then either asks you to go do the buying yourself, or it just buys and you find out afterwards. Neither is how a person actually wants to delegate a purchase. What I wanted was an app where the agent works inside the page I'm already looking at — where it can point at things on my screen — and where the moment money is involved, it has to stop and ask me. What it does Procura is a procurement marketplace for workplace equipment with 25 WebMCP tools . A person and their agent use the same application at the same time. The agent draws its reasoning into your page. When it compares products it calls compare_products , which opens a comparison table over whatever page you're on. The agent decides which product wins each row — cheapest, best resolution, longest battery — and marks its overall pick with a badge. The app supplies only the facts; the judgment is the agent's, and it lands in your interface instead of in a paragraph you have to parse. The agent cannot spend your money. request_order_approval prices an order server-side and opens an approval panel showing exactly what will be charged. There is no tool in the app that approves an order, and the server refuses to place a proposal that isn't approved. Both layers have to be defeated, and the agent has access to neither. The agent stays responsive while it waits. That call returns immediately — it does not block on your decision. The agent then polls check_order_approval , which reports placed , rejected , awaiting , or abandoned . The app records who did what. Every cart item carries addedBy , every order placedBy and cancelledBy . The agent can read them back, so it can say "you added that one, not me." Why procurement is a good fit for WebMCP Buying for a team is research-heavy and decision-light. Someone compares a dozen monitors across resolution, refresh rate, USB-C, delivery and financing terms — then makes one decision that spends real money. The research is repetitive, structured, and safe to delegate. The spend is not. That split is exactly the shape WebMCP is good at. How I built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, PostgreSQL with Drizzle, deployed on Railway. Tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , split into 9 public and 16 account tools. Account tools are registered under an AbortController that is torn down on sign-out, so a signed-out visitor's agent never sees them at all. Tools re-register on route change so client-side navigation doesn't silently drop the agent's session. The tools and the UI share one implementation — search_products and the catalog's own search box call the same function; the comparison table and get_product_details resolve through the same intelligence layer. Challenges The agent and I were seeing different numbers. The comparison table computed product ratings with its own local formula while get_product_details used the real one. One monitor showed 4.7 out of 5 from 107 reviews on screen while the agent was being told 4.1 from 8. On a page whose entire premise is that the agent and the person share one view, that is the worst possible bug. I routed the table through the same layer the tool uses, so they cannot diverge again. Blocking the agent was the wrong design. My first approval flow held the agent for up to three minutes waiting for a click. That's fragile — many agent harnesses cap tool calls well below that — and worse, it left the agent unable to do the one thing that actually helps: tell the user to go and approve. I split it into request_order_approval and check_order_approval . Telling "still deciding" apart from "walked away." Once the agent was polling, a pending proposal was ambiguous. The fix only exists because WebMCP tools run inside the page: check_order_approval checks whether the approval panel is still in the DOM. Pending proposal, no panel, means the person reloaded or left — so the agent asks again instead of polling into the void. No server API could answer that question. The panel hung on reject. Rejection dispatched the decision and then waited for the caller to close the panel — which the non-approve path never did. Reject, the X button, and Escape all froze. Rejection needs no server round-trip, so the panel now closes itself. What I learned The interesting part of WebMCP isn't wrapping an API in tools. It's that the tools run in the page , which means they can read and change what the person is actually looking at — and that a tool's honesty matters as much as its function. highlight_products used to return success while silently doing nothing off the catalog page; now it returns NOT_ON_CATALOG and says what to do instead. An agent that is told the truth about what happened is far more useful than one that is told it succeeded. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Research Control Panel
pitch: A shared control plane where researchers and browser agents inspect evidence, run bounded experiments, and review durable results together.
about_excerpt: A shared control plane where researchers and browser agents inspect evidence, run bounded experiments, and review durable results together. Like Comment Story Updates The problem AI agents are becoming useful research collaborators, but their work is often trapped in chat history or scattered across repositories, schedulers, and local artifacts. Giving an agent direct access to all of that machinery is expensive, brittle, and difficult for a researcher to supervise. Research Control Panel (RCP) keeps the research graph, evidence, conversations, bounded autonomous episodes, artifacts, and human decisions in one durable workspace. WebMCP gives that workspace a native agent interface, this serves dual purpose: inspection and control, the agent can inspect already structured research graph and dispatch RCP-managed research workflow, such as running an experiment, with just one webMCP tool call. The useful unit for a research agent is a bounded operation a researcher already understands: inspect this exact claim, show the saved evidence, start the next legal Experiment episode, or open the artifact that RCP just persisted. The agent can do that operational work from a familiar conversation while the researcher watches the same page and retains permission over what goes into the research graph. The demo Ask the browser agent to find and open the project. It tells you the question, the hypotheses, what evidence exists, and what's blocked. Point it at a specific claim in the graph, or have it pull up a figure. From the same conversation it can read back a saved thread, send a Discuss or Work turn, check whether an Experiment is ready, start the next episode, wait, and open the result. Stop only appears while an episode is live. The hosted project is a small reproducible continual-learning study. This used to mean juggling repo layout, subprocesses, schedulers, scratch directories, result ingestion, and several UI screens. Now the agent asks RCP for one research-level operation and gets a bounded, structured answer. Admission, provider routing, persistence, episode lifecycle, and artifact publication still belong to RCP. Why WebMCP fits, and how we built it Without WebMCP, a browser agent reads rendered pages over and over, guesses at opaque IDs, replays clicks, and has to infer whether an action is even legal. That burns context and invites stale decisions. The React app now registers eleven imperative Site Tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Two are top-level: discover a project, open it. The other nine are project-scoped and cover orientation, node and artifact inspection, conversation turns, and the bounded Experiment lifecycle. WebMCP is a second door into operations RCP already had, not a parallel API or a second state machine. Tools reuse the app's own navigation, conversation, Run, Stop, and artifact-viewer owners. Reads return compact bounded backend projections. Mutations are state-dependent and revalidate their target when the call executes, so Start vanishes once an episode is live, Stop takes its place, and both disappear when it finishes. The boundary is asymmetric on purpose. Approving proposals, choosing Decisions, changing graph truth, credentials, raw patches, project administration, and server administration stay human. The product gets better without the agent quietly gaining authority. Our challenge-only HTTPS gateway gives each browser identity its own persistent copy of the project, pins every provider profile to a deterministic RCP Demo provider, blocks management and filesystem-facing routes, and survives refreshes and restarts. A clean browser gets a clean project. We verified the ordinary provider path separately with Codex; the hosted deployment stays deterministic so every judge reproduces the same result. What we added during the challenge RCP predates August 25, 2026. Only the WebMCP extension is submitted for evaluation. The pre-webmcp tag in the public repo marks the audited baseline, and the challenge commits are dated September 1, 2026. The challenge work adds imperative top-level registration, eleven bounded tool schemas and results, state-dependent discovery with execution-time revalidation, shared ownership of navigation, Send, Start, Stop, and the artifact viewer, the deterministic synthetic study and provider, browser-isolated public HTTPS hosting with resource and route limits, and journey evaluations in the target browser. The research graph, authority queue, provider execution, Experiment loop, watchers, artifact storage, and the ordinary UI were already there and aren't claimed. The exact comparison is at https://github.com/Zhi0467/rcp-webmcp-demo/compare/pre-webmcp...main . After judging we want to take the same approach to collaborative team spaces and remote RCP servers, keeping these authority boundaries intact. title: WebMCP on saasmail
pitch: The first email server with WebMCP support (built for this challenge) that is self-hostable on Cloudflare
about_excerpt: The first email server with WebMCP support (built for this challenge) that is self-hostable on Cloudflare Like Comment Story Updates saasmail Inbox View saasmail WebMCP Agent View saasmail is a self-hosted inbox for SaaS teams on Cloudflare Workers. As far as we know, it's the first open-source email server with WebMCP support. An in-browser agent works the inbox through the same interface you do: the per-customer timeline, the compose drawer, the enroll modal. It stays in front of you the whole time. Why our use case is a strong fit for WebMCP TL;DR: We can't see fully autonomous inboxes getting any love. Inbox work is repetitive yet must be personalized: you triage the overnight mail, pull a customer's history, draft a reply, enroll a contact. It's exactly the work you'd only want to hand off to a real human, since the mail runs from support tickets to investor interest. Every email-plus-agent tool we found is headless. The agent talks to an MCP server off to the side, work happens out of sight, and you're asked to trust the result. WebMCP closes that gap by pointing the agent at the product itself: the inbox we already built, one timeline per customer, driven through the same controls a person uses. How it creates a better user experience TL;DR: agents working with WebMCP can perform actions faster because they don't parse the DOM, and done right (we think we have), WebMCP allows the user to be in the loop the whole time. The agent acts as you, in your tab, through the interface you already know. Two things follow. It's faster and more reliable, because it calls typed actions instead of parsing the DOM. And it's visible, because writes surface before they happen. Automation feels like supervising: review it, correct it, or take over at any point - it's just interacting with the UI anyway! What people and agents can do together that was hard or impossible before TL;DR: a very clean human-in-the-loop experience versus a regular MCP server. We're not reinventing a human-in-the-loop UI - we're just hijacking the original. MCP enabled agents to interact with web applications through an API - but a human doesn't do that. They interact with buttons and interfaces. So previously, when you build a MCP integration, you had to build an monitoring interface on top of it anyway. WebMCP allows you to skip that, which is really cool. I like to compare saasmail with Cloudflare's own agentic-inbox, the closest project that does cool stuff with agents directly within the app - though we find that releasing that control to the person's own AI harness increases adoption, rather than being stuck with a particular model/vendor. How we implemented WebMCP TL;DR: each tool mimics what a human would do when interacting with an email client. We started by mapping our interactions with saasmail. Then we started to build each tool with the intention that the agent will find useful. That was the hard part. The easy part was implementing the WebMCP layer. Since there wasn't any auth that we had to wire in (it just used the user's existing session), the implementation was much easier than an MCP server! Another challenge was to come up with the right mock data for demo purposes, which I did a few iterations on. Same self-hosted $5/month Workers app, with WebMCP layered on top. You can self host this as well! title: Televerse
pitch: a teleportation channel for codex agents on its own computer
about_excerpt:
a teleportation channel for codex agents on its own computer

 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Millions of hours are spent every month watching your AI agent debug a side problem while your main task sits frozen. The checkout flow is half-built, but the payment API is returning 500, and now your agent is stuck investigating instead of shipping. 

 We wanted to build something that doesn't make you choose between progress and debugging. What if your agent could teleport a copy of itself into a separate desktop, fix the bug over there, and hand you the result while the original agent keeps building? 

 So we built Televerse. 

 What it does 

 Televerse is a WebMCP-powered web app. Your coding agent (Codex, ChatGPT, any browser-based agent) discovers seven tools on the page. When a side problem comes up, the agent calls teleport_agent with a task description. Televerse captures context from the current session, spawns a fresh Daytona sandbox with a browser and terminal, and a second agent investigates independently. When it finishes, it returns a summary, root cause, evidence, files inspected, commands and tests run, and an optional patch. The primary agent reviews and decides whether to apply. Your main task never stops. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js 16 custom server with Socket.io for real-time streaming. The WebMCP draft API ( document.modelContext.registerTool ) registers seven tools on every page load. Each teleport creates a separate session with its own Daytona sandbox, Socket.io room, and whiteboard, the primary session is never touched. Context is captured as a compact packet (prompt, recent todos, whiteboard, errors, constraints) and seeded into the teleported agent's system prompt. The frontend has a teleport modal, a live detail page with activity log and evidence panel, and a dev harness at /dev/mcp for testing tools without a browser agent. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The WebMCP API is a draft, only in Chrome 149+ behind a flag. We built a dual registry: real document.modelContext when available, a dev fallback on window for testing. The Daytona swap was mechanical but tedious, every sandbox tool call had to be rewritten to Daytona's unified API. The hard part was designing the TeleportContext: enough context to be useful, but compact enough that the teleported agent doesn't waste tokens. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The WebMCP surface works. Open the site in Chrome with the flag enabled, and any browser-based agent discovers teleport_agent immediately, no config, no API keys, no MCP server setup. The teleport lifecycle is fully observable: every state transition is logged, cancellable, and debuggable from the /teleport/[id] page. Zero LLM keys needed for the WebMCP path, just DAYTONA_API_KEY for sandbox provisioning. The teleport store has 15 passing tests covering creation, lifecycle, result storage, cancellation, and ownership. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes the agent-web contract. Instead of the agent scraping the DOM and guessing what to click, the site declares high-level tools with explicit schemas. The agent delegates, the site executes. The hardest design problem was the handoff, not how the sandbox boots, but how the teleported agent's result gets back to the primary agent in a structured, reviewable format. 

 What's next for Televerse 

 Adding DB persistence so teleports survive server restarts. Multi-session picker for the teleport modal. Optional autonomous computer-use agent that drives the desktop and collects evidence by actually clicking around. Git-aware teleport context that captures the current branch, diff, and recent commits. Daytona screen recordings for replaying the teleported agent's activity.

title: Tartarian.ai — WebMCP MMO Prototype
pitch: A persistent 3D MMO where ChatGPT operates the live human player session through native WebMCP Site Tools—observing, reading inventory, moving, targeting, and interacting with the world.
about_excerpt: A persistent 3D MMO where ChatGPT operates the live human player session through native WebMCP Site Tools—observing, reading inventory, moving, targeting, and interacting with the world. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Its the Interwebs all over again!! Inspiration OpenClaw was a game changer for my AI experience. It gave feet and hands to a virtual automaton. Then came the first social networks for AI, and it seemed obvious to me that a persistent simulation world would be next. My 25+ years of alpha and beta testing popular games gave me a lot of hands-on experience with game UI, UX, systems, and player behavior. That experience eventually came together in Tartarian.ai. Structured web tools for agents feel like the next step. Humans and AI can coexist in the same digital spaces, and I want to help make that possible. Adding WebMCP support to Tartarian is part of that direction: giving agents structured ways to understand and act inside the same live world as human operators. What it does The live Tartarian browser client exposes six native WebMCP Site Tools: tartarian_observe_world tartarian_read_inventory tartarian_move tartarian_select_target tartarian_activate_target tartarian_activate_command Through these tools, ChatGPT can observe the surrounding world, inspect the operator's real inventory, move the character, select world objects, interact with resources and structures, and activate prepared Command Bar actions. The human remains in control of the same visible character and interface. There is no separate "AI world." Human and agent share one operator session and one persistent simulation state. Why WebMCP I run a QA bot that uses classic operator mouse and clicks at my Day job, with Chrome MCP dev tools, the mouse and entry actions are poor, WebMCP is the next evolution over the mighty Pixal How we built it Tartarian existed before the challenge with its 3D browser client, persistent simulation, movement, inventory, resources, targeting, world interaction, combat, authentication, and autonomous-agent MCP system. During the WebMCP Challenge we added a new native WebMCP browser layer using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each Site Tool is deliberately a thin adapter to an existing Tartarian production authority. For example: ChatGPT ↓ tartarian_activate_target ↓ WebMCP bridge ↓ existing interaction runtime ↓ authoritative simulation WebMCP does not create a second movement, inventory, combat, or resource system. Lovely layering instead of nasty forking! ## Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering the tools. It was defining the semantics clearly enough for an agent to choose the correct one. Small differences that are obvious to a human — selecting an object, clicking it, activating it, using a Command Bar action — had to be translated into clear Site Tool behavior so the agent would not confuse one action for another. The other major challenge was time. I only learned about the WebMCP Challenge two days before the deadline while using ChatGPT Work. That forced me to prioritize a working, understandable prototype over polish. I had to make a lot of tradeoffs and leave several ideas unfinished simply because there was not enough time. Given more time, there are many parts I would improve, but the goal became very simple: make the WebMCP integration real, make it work inside the live Tartarian world, and ship it. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of Indentfing another Front door for the roaming automaton , and the chance to participate in this contest ## What we learned WebMCP becomes especially interesting when a website represents a persistent, stateful environment rather than a collection of forms and buttons. During the demo, ChatGPT encounters a depleted Wood node, recognizes the real world state, finds another node, navigates to it, and successfully harvests through Tartarian's normal resource authority. That was the behavior we wanted: the agent observes what is actually true and adapts rather than pretending an action succeeded. ## What's next for Tartarian.ai — WebMCP MMO Prototype The current prototype intentionally exposes only a small WebMCP surface. I plan to keep adding Site Tools and push WebMCP much further as the ecosystem around it grows. The goal is to be ready when more agents and humans begin entering shared digital worlds together. Tartarian will keep expanding the ways agents can observe, navigate, interact, trade, build, and cooperate inside the same persistent simulation as human operators. **The agent does not get a second world.
